News.title: Brit tourist rushed to hospital after being bitten by toxic pufferfish as vicious critters wreak havoc off Greek island
News.content:
SEA MENACE Brit tourist rushed to hospital after being bitten by toxic pufferfish as vicious critters wreak havoc off Greek island







Next

A BRIT tourist has been rushed to hospital after being bitten by a toxic pufferfish amid mounting alarm over the vicious critters in Greece.

The woman suffered the nasty bite while in the water at Kalamaki in Zante before seeking urgent treatment at a private clinic.



She reportedly told medics she had been bitten by what she thought was a monkfish, and was given first aid for her wound.

Port authority sources said the frightening incident will now be investigated.



It comes as razor-toothed silver-cheeked pufferfish spread through the Mediterranean.

There have been reports of the invasive predators attacking swimmers and savaging fishing nets.

Officially known as Lagocephalus sceleratus, the toxic species is normally found in the tropical waters of the Indian and Pacific oceans.

But the menacing fish has muscled its way into the Mediterranean after migrating through the Suez Canal and has been spreading “aggressively” since it was first spotted there in 2003.

The pufferfish packs a vicious bite powerful enough to inflict serious injuries – while its flesh and organs contain the deadly neurotoxin tetrodotoxin.

The potent poison can cause heart and lung failure if the fish is eaten.



In June, an elderly Greek woman was reportedly bitten by a silver-cheeked pufferfish after one suddenly lunged at her.

Scientists have also sounded the alarm after the species was discovered as far north as Medulin Bay off Croatia, warning the invasion poses a “direct threat to tourism, especially in areas frequented by swimmers”.

Study co-author Dr Neven Iveša said: “This invasive species is known for its aggressive behaviour.



“With reported cases of bites causing significant injuries.

“Alarmingly, recent evidence from the southern and eastern Mediterranean shows that these bites can result in severe injuries, such as partial amputation of fingers.”

Researchers caught a 52cm male weighing just over a kilo around 65ft below the surface in May last year.

It marked only the fourth recorded catch in the Adriatic and the most northerly discovery yet — fuelling fears the species is pushing deeper into popular European waters.

Scientists warn the toxic invader poses a growing menace to marine life, fisheries and “public safety” as it increasingly turns up in catches along Mediterranean coastlines.



The voracious predators are also hammering fishermen by devouring fish, crustaceans and squid and tearing through valuable nets.

The destruction is estimated to cost each fishing boat around £8,000 a year in damage and lost income.

Dr Iveša, of Croatia’s Juraj Dobrila University, said: “The presence of Lagocephalus sceleratus in the northern Adriatic is a clear warning sign of the species’ expanding range and potential ecological and economic consequences.

“Proactive monitoring and management strategies are important to mitigating its impact on local marine biodiversity, fisheries, and public safety.”

The first sighting of the fish in the Adriatic came on the northern side of Croatia’s Jakljan Island in October 2012.



Several more have since been recorded, with scientists now warning its brutal bite could also spell trouble for holidaymakers.

Dr Iveša said: “Although such cases are rare, they highlight the potential danger this species poses to humans.

“These risks not only create safety concerns for swimmers, but also threaten the image and appeal of tourist detistinations.

“Potentially leading to economic losses in local tourism and related industries.”

Scientists are now calling for the targeted removal of the species during its spawning period as they scramble to curb its march through the Mediterranean.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

They have also urged the public to be warned about the dangerous invader and encouraged to report sightings.

The research was published in Acta Ichthyologica et Piscatoria.

News.title: I was left for dead after random attack in home 25 years ago – no one has ever been arrested… I just want to know why
News.content:
UNANSWERED QUESTION I was left for dead after random attack in home 25 years ago – no one has ever been arrested… I just want to know why







Next

A WOMAN who was brutally attacked and left for dead 25 years ago continues to live with the agony of not knowing who did it.

Clare Carmichael was assaulted on September 28, 2001, at her new home in Leintwardine, Herefordshire – but cops have never made an arrest.

Upon entering the house at around 9.15am, Clare sensed that something wasn’t quite right, as items had been moved around.

Alarmed, she contacted relatives, before ending the call and looking further around the property when she was brutally assaulted.





Cops were called to the scene at around 9.45am when no one was able to get hold of her.

Officers found her unresponsive on the upstairs landing, having suffered a drawn-out attack that left her with severe head injuries she was not expected to survive.

Clare, who was 36 at the time of the attack, spent several months recovering in hospital, followed by a long rehabilitation period.

From limited vision and poor memory to difficulties forming sentences or linking words, her life was unalterably changed on that day.

But exactly 25 years on today since the savage attack, she still has no idea who was responsible.

Several suspects were identified during initial investigations, but no one was ever charged and the case remains unsolved.

Speaking about the impact on her life, Clare said: “I still live with the impact of the injuries I suffered on that day.

“I struggle to walk and can’t use my right arm; this affects most daily tasks I do.



“The attack took away much of my independence, I have not been able to drive again.”

Medical complications from the head injury continue to plague her, including seizures which have left her bedbound in hospital.

She is awaiting another operation to replace a plate in her head.

Clare added: “I struggle with speaking and finding the right words when I’m talking, this frustrates me as I really enjoy talking to people and being social.

“My life has not been what it should have been. I wanted to be involved in every aspect of my children’s upbringing, I loved being an active mum with my two boys, but I wasn’t physically able to do this afterwards.



“So much changed for me on that day, the life I wanted to live was taken away from me.

“I manage to stay positive, I always say that you can laugh or you can cry – I choose to laugh, that’s how I get by.”

As for the person responsible for the attack, Clare said: “If I was able to talk to the person who did this, I would just want ten minutes, to ask why?

“Why did you do this to me? I would simply like the answer to that one question.”

Today, she is appealing to anyone who might have information about the attacker to come forward.



A review into the historic investigation, known as Operation Krypton, is now underway, with West Mercia Police using forensic technology and revisiting witnesses in the hope of making a breakthrough.

Detective Sergeant Amy Kitosi-Isanga, from the review team, said: “Twenty-five years have now passed since the attack on Clare but our commitment to securing justice for her remains as strong as ever.

“We know that someone, somewhere, has information about what happened that morning.

“It may be something that seemed insignificant at the time, or information that a person has been reluctant to share.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Over the years circumstances change and loyalties change. We would urge anyone who knows anything about this incident to come forward and speak with us.



“Even the smallest detail could prove crucial.”

News.title: What is the polar vortex and how could it affect winter weather in the UK?
News.content:
Next

SUMMER is over in the UK, although we might get a final taste of warmer weather this week before autumn sets in fully.

But while some Brits could see highs of 26C in the coming days, reports are also warning of the effect that the “Polar Vortex” could have on weather conditions ahead of winter – here’s what it actually means.



What is a polar vortex?

Despite its ominous sounding name, the polar vortex is a completely natural weather system.

It’s a massive, spinning low-pressure system of icy air locked high in the stratosphere, roughly 10 to 30 miles above the Earth‘s surface at the North Pole.



When the vortex is strong and stable, it keeps the Arctic’s coldest air contained at the top of the world.

When that happens, Britain enjoys milder, wetter winter weather driven by gentle Atlantic breezes.



But if the vortex weakens or collapses, that Arctic air is no longer tightly contained and can move southward toward Europe and the UK, bringing much colder winter conditions.

Disrupted polar vortices have driven some of the UK’s most memorable winter freezes, including the 2018 “Beast from the East”.

The polar vortex can be disrupted by heat rising from lower within the atmosphere, which can trigger what meteorologists call Sudden Stratospheric Warming (SSW).

When this happens, temperatures in the Arctic atmosphere can jump by up to 50C in just a few days.



This sudden change in temperature disrupts the vortex.

What is El Nino?

El Nino is another natural climate pattern that you may have heard about over the past few weeks.

It is marked by unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the tropical regions of the Pacific Ocean.

Even though the Pacific is thousands of miles away, its sheer size means that ocean heat can reshape weather conditions on the other side of the globe.

The heat rising from tropical waters can alter high-altitude pressure patterns and reshape the jet stream.



These atmospheric changes can destabilise the polar vortex and increase the odds of a Sudden Stratospheric Warming event.

What does it all mean for British weather this winter?

It’s worth bearing in mind that while meteorological bodies have confirmed a particularly strong El Nino event, its existence does not guarantee a big UK freeze.

However, it makes disruption to the polar vortex much more likely, and forecasters are currently monitoring atmospheric conditions.

If the effects of a powerful El Nino do weaken the polar vortex, it could impact weather conditions in the UK.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Though autumn weather could initially be pleasantly warm, we would still see unsettled and windy conditions, with strong Atlantic weather systems likely bringing prolonged heavy rain.



But as atmospheric waves triggered by El Nino destabilise the polar vortex, the chance of freezing snaps, biting easterly winds, and heavy snowfall increases significantly as we head deeper into winter.

News.title: Cop who Tasered amputee, 92, three weeks before his death ‘made care home joke with lightning emoji hours after horror’
News.content:
Next

A COP who Tasered a 92-year-old amputee just weeks before his death shared a care home joke with a lightning emoji after the horror, a tribunal heard.

Bodycam footage showed Donald Burgess screaming out during the horror at Park Beck Residential Care Home in St Leonards-on-Sea, East Sussex.



PC Rachel Comotto and PC Stephen Smith had been called to the residence after the 92-year-old poked a worker in the stomach with a butter knife.

The pair were later found not guilty of assault occasioning actual bodily harm following a trial.



But they today appeared before a disciplinary panel to answer allegations they used “excessive force” against Donald.

They are both accused of “escalating the situation” and failing to treat the “vulnerable and confused” pensioner with compassion.



PC Comotto is also accused of placing “inappropriate comments’” on Facebook about the tragic incident.

If the allegations are proven at the disciplinary hearing then both officers could be sacked from the force.



Aaron Rathmell, lawyer for Sussex Police, said: “They acted hastily, harshly and lost control. It’s a case of a serious breach of force against an elderly man in his care home.”

Bodycam showed Donald clutching a specially adapted butter knife while sat in his wheelchair when Smith and Comotto entered his room.

PC Smith can be heard saying: ‘Put it down mate. Come on, Donald, don’t be silly.

“We can solve it without having to resort to this…Do as you’re told.”

The footage also showed Smith making his way towards the pensioner with his baton extended before striking him.



PC Comotto then deploys her 50,000-volt Taser as Donald screams out in pain before the officers took the knife from him.

After shooting him, PC Comotto asked Donald how he was feeling, leading him to reply: “I’m dying, I’m dying.”

The tribunal heard the cops massively “escalated the situation” and were confrontational and antagonistic towards him.



Mr Rathmell said that at no point in the use of three separate uses of force had the two officers tried to de-escalate the situation.

He also told the tribunal later the same day, PC Comotto interacted with a colleague after they posted a message on Facebook saying: “Happy birthday, the care home is getting closer and closer.”

The cop replied: “We all know what happens in care homes” before adding a lightning emoji.

Mr Rathmell said this was in reference to the taser she had used on Donald at the care home.

He said PC Comotto had “made light of the actions” and her response was “inappropriate and unprofessional”.



Donald suffered from multiple health conditions including diabetes and carotid artery disease.

He was taken to hospital following the incident and died 22 days later after contracting Covid.

The disciplinary hearing was told that it was not alleged that the actions of officer contributed to his death.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

After the incident Sussex Police voluntarily referred itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC).

The tribunal continues.

News.title: When will the warm weather arrive this week? Latest forecast for the UK as October arrives
News.content:
Next

BRITS holding on for the final days of summer can look forward to a surprisingly mild start to October.

While autumn has officially arrived, the Met Office is forecasting some lingering warmth and sunshine, with higher-than-normal temperatures across parts of the country.



Here is everything you need to know about when the warm weather will arrive this week, along with the Met Office’s latest long-range forecast for the rest of October.

When will the warm weather arrive this week?

According to the Met Office, Tuesday is set to be a key day for warm weather, particularly in eastern areas.



Although the morning is expected to start cloudy with early drizzle, conditions will change as warm air moves in.

But that isn’t quite the case everywhere, and the Met Office also forecasts a day “turning increasingly windy with gales in the northwest.”



By late Tuesday afternoon, heavy rain will arrive in the west before sweeping across the rest of the UK.

By Wednesday, an active weather front is expected to push eastward across the country.

The Met Office says that heavy rain will move across the UK on Wednesday, “bringing a fresher feel.”

The rest of the working week will see more familiar autumn weather settle in.



Expect breezy conditions accompanied by a mixture of sunny spells and scattered showers on Thursday and Friday, feeling noticeably cooler than earlier in the week.

What is the long-range forecast for October?

Looking further ahead into October, there’s promising news for anyone hoping for settled weather and above-average temperatures.

Between Friday, October 2 and Sunday, October 11, high pressure is set to build following brief initial spells of rain.

This will lead to a “drier than average period overall, with lighter winds than average” across much of the nation.

For those hoping for mild autumn days, forecasters say that “temperatures are likely to remain warmer than average” throughout early October, even with occasional unsettled periods.



And the mild trend looks set to continue into the second half of the month.

Looking ahead from Monday, October 12 to Monday, October 26, high pressure may give way to more changeable, wet, and windy conditions.

But the overall temperature trend remains mild, with the Met Office predicting that “temperatures are likely to be above average for the period as a whole.”

News.title: How Iranian terror cells are plotting coordinated attacks across Britain as regime ‘recruits criminals for just £1,000’
News.content:
Next

IRANIAN terror cells are plotting coordinated attacks across the UK – as the regime recruits rent-a-thugs for just £1,000, a security expert has warned.

Fears are mounting Britain’s emergency services will be overwhelmed if Tehran unleashes a simultaneous assault on multiple targets.



It comes after a heroic farmer foiled an alleged terror plot near RAF Fairford on Sunday – with cops arresting five suspects and seizing three vans filled with explosives.

The men, all Brit nationals from London in their 20s, have since been bailed following the ordeal at the base used by the US to launch bomber strikes on the regime.



If the Fairford attack proves to be state-sponsored it would be one of the biggest by a foreign nation on British soil since WW2.

Iran has denied involvement in the suspected bomb plot, with Tehran’s embassy in London slamming “unfounded and malicious speculation” on Monday.



The latest suspected bomb scheme is hardly surprising for two main reasons, security expert Will Geddes said.

Firstly, the UK has already faced “threats by various terrorist groups” funded by Iran.



Britain is also being prepared for a looming terror attack.

Geddes told The Sun: “We’re being prepared for potential simultaneous terrorist attacks by various different cells, all occurring within close proximity of each other in terms of time.

“This would bring a huge load onto the emergency services and their ability to react and respond to these various incidents… however unsophisticated they might be.”



Tehran has already targeted countries across Europe including the UK that it accuses of boosting US military actions.

The regime has been linked to a string of plots in recent months – including the stabbing of two Jewish people in London, an explosion at the US embassy in Oslo, and the shutdown of a British power plant.

Geddes added Iran has a well-documented history of using proxies and third parties to carry out attacks – sometimes paying them measly sums for seismic plots.



He said individuals “from low-level criminality environs” are usually paid “basic low level fees” of just £1,000 to prepare Iran-backed schemes.

These recruits are “susceptible to recruitment, but also highly motivated by a financial return”.

Geddes said: “They are not following a particular agenda, political or religious for that matter, but are simply motivated by financial reward.”

He also warned some terror cells would have infiltrated the UK through underground channels like illegal immigration.

“Iran has created and is developing sleeper cells in the United Kingdom, as well as in other countries that they are opposed to,” he said.



“The issue here, which really is concerning for the security services, is that they have in excess of 10,000 primary subjects of interest and many tens of thousands additional that are deemed a risk in some shape or form.

“This influx of individuals illegally into the country is only adding to the already over resourced or under-resourced, workload that the security services have to deal with.”

This weekend’s foiled attack may just be the first of many more to come, Geddes added.

The analyst said: “RAF Fairford is not an isolated incident or necessarily a closed incident.

“So we’re in a situation here where the threat will continue to prevail.”



It comes as counter-terrorism police chief, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, confirmed all five suspects have now been released on bail after extensive questioning.

A probe into the suspected terror plot – led by counter-terror cops – is ongoing.

A significant emergency presence remains at the scene, where explosives were reportedly found.

Counter-terrorism police were understood to be investigating if the potential plot could be linked to Iran, but the Iranian embassy has now rejected any speculation as “unfounded”.

In a statement on social media, it said: “The Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.”



“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives.”

News.title: Tourist, 27, plunges 100ft to her death down waterfall after losing balance on boulder in front of horrified friend
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

HOLIDAY TRAGEDY Tourist, 27, plunges 100ft to her death down waterfall after losing balance on boulder in front of horrified friend







Next

A UK-based tourist has died after slipping on a boulder and plunging down a waterfall in a horror holiday accident.

Valentina Stragliotto, 27, plummeted nearly 100ft in front of her friend while the pair were travelling through the town of Ella in Sri Lanka.



Emergency services raced to the scene and rushed Valentina to hospital.

But the woman, who had been living in Brighton, had suffered catastrophic injuries and was pronounced dead upon admission.



The tragedy unfolded at the secluded Kithal Ella waterfall on Thursday.

An investigation has been launched into the woman’s sudden death.

Valentina was from Italy – but had moved to Brighton several years ago and worked there as an online advertising specialist alongside running confidence coaching with her company Aligned & Free.

In a now-heartbreaking post, the young woman had previously described her love of the outdoors.

She wrote: “My place is in nature.

“I love hiking and climbing and I especially love waterfalls.”



Alongside her advertising work, she also worked as a group travel coordinator for WeRoad.

Her company profile also said she had visited 33 countries and spoke French, Italian, English and Spanish.

Emotional tributes have been made to the nature-loving traveller.



Former classmate Rafael Marchese said news of her death had left him “speechless” and filled with “great sorrow”.

A colleague at WeRoad said the team was “shocked” by the tragedy.

The mayor of her home town of Bassano del Grappa offered his condolences to her family.

He said the death of a young person was a “deep wound” for the whole community.

Valentina’s parents, Fabio Stragliotto and Barbara Zarpellon, have said they are unable to speak publicly during this “difficult” time.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The Kithal Ella region is beloved among tourists for its luscious greenery and cascading waterfalls but the safety measures at this site have come under fresh scrutiny, according to Sri Lankan news outlet Lanka Newspapers.

Several stakeholders are calling for clearer warning signs and designated safe viewing areas for tourists.

News.title: Horrifying moment scientists cling to window ledges as inferno rips through building after Russian drone strike
News.content:
Next

THIS is the horrifying moment a team of scientists are left desperately clinging to window ledges after a Russian drone strike.

At least one woman was killed in Vladimir Putin‘s latest barbaric attack which caused flames to engulf a historic research building in Kyiv.



Emergency services rushed to Ukraine‘s National Academy of Sciences following the deadly strike believed to have been caused by a jet-powered drone.

In the shocking footage, thick plumes of black smoke can be seen billowing from the 100-year-old building’s windows in central Kyiv.



Helpless bystanders are seen teetering on the brink of window ledges from what appears to be the third storey.

Stunned bystanders and firefighters rush to get the civilians to safety – with emergency services seen swarming the perimeter.

Kyiv has been under intense sustained strikes for a week, despite Russia facing setbacks on the actual frontline.

More than 250 of his fighters surrendered amid Operation Vivaldi as Ukraine retook swathes of land.



Volodymyr Zelensky said: “A rescue operation is currently underway, with firefighters battling the blaze and searching for people who may have been inside the building.”

Describing the widespread attacks through the country, the Ukrainian leader also said: “Today, in Kyiv, a pharmaceutical company and petrol stations were attacked.

“In Dnipro, a business center was targeted, and in other cities and regions, civilian facilities, businesses, and communication infrastructure were also hit.



“Sadly, there are casualties. My condolences to the families and loved ones of those who have died.

“There will be a response to this from Russia.”

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed one woman had died in the science building strike while three were wounded.

It appeared the fire services arrived in time to rescue scientists from the blazing structure.

The building attacked in Kyiv was close to the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence service, which Putin hit just weeks ago.



Ukrainian cities have been facing near constant air-raid sirens and explosions every day as Moscow ramps up its blitzes.

Cultural sites, government buildings and schools have all been targeted.

Russia has also been deploying newer jet-powered drones in recent months which are harder to intercept than older variants which use propellers.

The latest attack in Kyiv is believed to have been carried out by a Geran-5 Russian jet-powered one-way attack drone.

Meanwhile, a global shortage of missile interceptor systems due to the Iran war has also made it harder for Ukraine to prevent Putin’s air assaults.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

At least three people were killed and 12 were wounded after an office building in central Dnipro was struck on Monday.

And in Kharkiv, 38 people including 10 children were injured after another Russian attack.

News.title: What we know about RAF Fairford counter-terror probe
News.content:
Five men who were arrested on suspicion of explosive and terrorism offences after a major incident was declared at an RAF airbase in the west of England are due to be released on police bail.

Three vans were spotted near RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday morning and the police were called, before a huge police operation in Gloucestershire saw the area put under cordon.

Head of Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said on Monday that officers were exploring "multiple lines of inquiry", including whether proxies or individuals knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state were involved.

The five men are all UK nationals in their 20s from London.

Here is a summary of what we know so far.

News.title: UK tries to stop Trump's diesel export ban
News.content:
The UK is in talks with US authorities over a potential stoppage of diesel exports and has started preparing for a ban, Chancellor John Healey has told BBC News.

Diesel prices in the UK reached a new high on Monday due to supply pressures springing from the US-Israel conflict with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.

Fuel prices are rising globally and US President Donald Trump has threatened to ban diesel exports, stating at the weekend: "We're thinking about it very seriously."

Healey, who admitted that UK diesel prices are "extreme", said the government was in discussions with the US, adding: "We're also making the provision that we may need to and we have our own stocks in the UK."

Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, Healey said: "We work very closely with the Americans.

"In the end, we're also working with the Americans where we can try and put in place what will solve this, or at least significantly ease it, which would be a diplomatic settlement [and] an end to the fighting with Iran."

The UK depends on the US for around a third of its diesel imports and a ban would send prices even higher.

US sources suggest that Trump is considering a ban to attempt to bring down prices for domestic consumers ahead of the critical midterm elections.

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

In the UK, the average price for a litre of diesel reached 199.18p, according to the RAC motoring organisation, surpassing a previous high of 191.5p in June 2022 after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Petrol prices are also still rising, with a litre currently costing 174.13p.

Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil across the region, causing the price of fuels made from oil to surge.

The RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".

Healey said he was "very aware" of these cost of living pressures as he prepared what he called a "breathing space" Budget on 28 October.

A freeze on fuel duty, first implemented by the Conservative government in 2022, is due to expire at the end of the year. Duty is scheduled to increase by 3p in January and a further 2p in March.

Healey said: "Fundamentally, what we need is a settlement in the Middle East. We need an easing of the pressure of costs on business, the costs on households and on ordinary families that we see at the pumps in the most extreme level today for diesel."

News.title: Mahmood to reopen scheme to resettle refugees in the UK
News.content:
Shabana Mahmood has announced the reopening of a scheme to resettle refugees in the UK, as she hopes that offering "safe and legal" routes will deter small boat crossings.

The home secretary said the UK wants to "live up to our international obligations" by helping those who are fleeing war and persecution, but the process must be "capped and controlled".

The Home Office said the UK Resettlement Scheme (UKRS) will reopen immediately and expects that around 25% of arrivals will be Afghan women and girls and Palestinians.

Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp said Mahmood was making a "desperate attempt to appease" people within Labour who have been critical of her asylum reforms.

Hundreds of people are expected to arrive under the UKRS, which stopped taking new applicants in December 2024, and three new sponsorship routes.

The latter will involve communities, universities and companies hosting refugees from next year.

The Home Office expects arrivals to increase to the "low thousands" as levels of illegal migration fall.

A cap will be set for each year although details of the number have yet to be provided.

People arriving in Britain under the safe and legal routes will be be put on a five-year path to permanent settlement.

Mahmood told the Labour Party conference on Monday that "fairness" is behind her approach, limits are needed and communities must be "ready and able to welcome those who come here".

She also said: "That is what we can do, this is who we can be, as we restore control to our borders, bear down on small boat crossings and unlock the inherent generosity of this country."

More than 18,500 people have crossed the Channel in small boats this year compared to more than 32,000 than the same period in 2025.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the UK is "not obligated to take in more migrants", adding if his party was in power then those arriving under Labour's schemes would "not be able to stay".

He said: "If Labour are so sure the public wants their open borders policies, they'd call a general election to get a mandate."

In expressing his criticism, Farage also referenced a report in The Sunday Times, external about a former bodyguard to the leader of Hamas securing asylum and citizenship in the UK before "plotting" an attack against Jewish people in Europe.

The newspaper reported the man moved to the UK more than a decade ago and now faces extradition to Germany.

Jon Featonby, chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, welcomed the government's new proposals but said it came after a "drastic reduction in safe routes over the last year".

He said: "Safe and legal routes are essential to undermining people smugglers' business model, but they only work if they operate at scale.

"The government has to show ambition and commitment, and that means thousands of places, not hundreds.

"Alongside any new schemes, the government must also reopen refugee family reunion without delay."

News.title: Best thing we can offer young people is a job, not benefits, says chancellor
News.content:
The chancellor has warned against allowing Britain's benefits bill to balloon while not offering young people opportunities.

John Healey told Labour's annual conference in Liverpool that cutting welfare spending was "more than an economic must - it's a moral duty".

"The best thing we can offer a young person is not a benefit payment - it's a first job with training and a wage," he said.

He announced the expansion of a Local Apprenticeships Service for mayors in England, which he said would deliver thousands more apprenticeships for young people.

Healey's speech comes as he faces pressure to cut public spending or raise taxes ahead of next month's Budget to bring down government borrowing costs.

In an attempt to reassure the markets, he said all promises the government made would be "built on the rock of fiscal discipline" with him and Prime Minister Andy Burnham "united on meeting the fiscal rules".

Fiscal rules are the government's self-imposed constraints to manage decisions on spending and tax.

The Budget would "give families and businesses a bit of breathing space", the chancellor said.

And he admitted that "the money New Labour had in the '90s is simply not there now".

Healey blamed the Conservative Party's time in government for leaving Britain spending more on debt than on the Home Office, Ministry of Defence and Ministry of Justice combined.

Tory shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said in response to the speech that "Labour MPs will never support cutting the out-of-control welfare bill" and "with Labour, it's always more taxes if you work and more benefits if you don't".

Healey praised young people as "digital natives, whip-smart, questioning, ambitious, brave" who could move from "generation jeopardy to generation hope".

But he pointed to the million young people not in education, employment or training - known as Neets - which he said created a necessity to make benefits a bridge into work, rather than a "trap".

"It is not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill, and a system which offers an income but doesn't offer a future," he said.

Asked how quickly the bill might come down, when he appeared on the BBC's Newscast later on Tuesday, Healey said he "won't set a timeline" for the UK's benefits bill coming down by the time of the next election, adding that reducing the number of Neets cannot be done "overnight".

News.title: Slipknot fans hit back after Marilyn Manson announced as support act for UK show
News.content:
Heavy metal band Slipknot have announced a new world tour, with Marilyn Manson due to appear as a support act.

The eight-piece group, known for performing in masks, will be joined by the US rock musician during their shows at London's Wembley Stadium and multiple dates of the South American leg of the tour.

Some fans have reacted angrily to the news and said they will not attend the shows over past sexual abuse accusations against the 57-year-old.

Manson, real name Brian Warner, has always strongly denied any allegations against him.

Thousands of fans replied to an Instagram post featuring the line-up for the London gigs, which also includes metalcore band Hatebreed.

While some posts expressed excitement at the support acts, many were critical of Manson's presence on the bill, describing it as "disappointing".

Others, who described themselves as long-time Slipknot fans, said they would not buy tickets for the show in protest at his appearance.

One wrote: "Would've loved to see this but there's literally nothing you could do to get my cash in Manson's pockets."

Another added the announcement was "such a disappointment" and they would not be attending.

However, others disagreed, with one pointing out the two acts have a "huge fanbase overlap" and describing Manson as a "perfect support act".

News.title: Police block Protestant Orange Order from controversial parade route
News.content:
The protesters on the Garvaghy Road were joined by members of Sinn FÃ©in and the Social Democratic Labour Party (SDLP) throughout the day on Sunday.

Sinn FÃ©in First Minister Michelle O'Neill joined the protest, prompting the Democratic Unionist Party to accuse her of acting unlawfully.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant urged both sides to "double down on compromise".

He said "nobody should be attending an unlawful protest", but he added it was not his job "to decide whether somebody has or hasn't broken the law".

The two most senior members of Portadown Orange Order met Sir Chris at Hillsborough Castle on Monday. They described the hour-long talks as "constructive".

Asked if they still intended to walk down the Garvaghy Road, district master Nigel Dawson said "the law needs to be applied".

Democratic Unionist Party MP Carla Lockhart, who has been with the Orange Order members in Drumcree, called on police to ensure the parade can go ahead. She said "mob rule" cannot win.

BreandÃ¡n Mac Cionnaith, from the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, also met the secretary of state.

He said the Orange Order should use their outward route to Drumcree Church as their return route, rather than the Garvaghy Road.

Mac Cionnaith said he was agreeable to some form of mediation but did not trust the Orange Order.

Following a meeting with Sir Chris, Sinn FÃ©in President Mary Lou McDonald said her party "remain concerned" for the community, that even though the march did not go ahead, they need to know they can "breathe easy again" and "that they don't have the threat of a march being forced through their neighbourhood".

Meanwhile, Sir Chris said he was still "exploring every option".

He said talks on Monday had been "positive so far" and that there were many people acting "in good faith for a good outcome".

"Through the mist maybe I can see what that might look like," he added.

News.title: Women protest in the streets of Delhi after string of sexual assaults
News.content:
Hundreds of women have come together in Delhi to protest against the alleged gang-rape of a 17-year-old near Delhi university's campus.

This is one of multiple protests that have been taking place in the capital over the past week, after a string of sexual assaults and rape cases have made headlines.

BBC correspondent Azadeh Moshiri has been speaking to women at one of the protests who have told her they simply haven't felt safe for years.

News.title: Three dead, including child, in Channel crossing attempt
News.content:
A 10-year-old child and two 30-year-old women have died after a small boat that was attempting to cross the English Channel got into difficulty off the northern coast of France, local authorities have said.

Officials responded to a distress call from the boat, which was carrying 105 people, after it departed from the BlÃ©riot Plage in Sangatte on Monday morning.

Three passengers were treated on board but were later confirmed dead by an emergency medical team flown out by helicopter, the French Maritime Prefecture of the Channel and the North Sea said.

Pas-de-Calais prefecture said its initial findings suggested the deaths were caused by trampling but an investigation has been launched to determine the exact cause.

Of the 102 other people on board, nine were treated by emergency services upon their arrival in the port of Calais, the prefecture said.

FranÃ§ois-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, blamed the incident on smuggling networks, which he said expose vulnerable people, including children, to the deadly risks of crossings.

The prefecture described the boat as a taxi-boat, which requires migrants to wade out onto the water to board.

Three other people died after similar taxi-boat departures last week, French authorities said.

Monday's deaths take the total number of migrants who have died so far this year to 20, according to Pas-de-Calais prefecture. For the same period last year, it said the number was 21.

Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous journey from France to the UK every year. In doing so, they cross one of the most dangerous and busiest shipping lanes in the world.

More people attempt the route in the summer months when the weather is warmer and when seas are calmer.

The UK recorded the highest number of migrant arrivals so far this year on Wednesday - with a total of 781 arriving in 10 small boats, according to Home Office figures.

Two boats also reached UK shores last week without being intercepted by UK authorities, at Folkestone and Samphire Hoe in Kent.

In July last year, France and the UK agreed on a "one in, one out" returns deal, which was designed as a deterrent to stop boats from crossing the Channel.

The deal allows the UK to return some small boat arrivals while agreeing to take in the same number of people from France who are believed to have a legitimate claim to come to Britain.

In August the UK government said it was making progress in tackling small boats, with the percentage who had made the journey in 2026 much lower than for the same period in 2025 but added it needed to "push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade".

So far, 2026 has seen 18,609 people successfully make the Channel crossing, which is 42% lower than the same period in 2025 when 32,188 had crossed in small boats.

News.title: UK diesel price hits all-time high, the RAC says
News.content:
The RAC data is based on the average price of diesel at a range of supermarkets, motorway service stations and independent retailers.

The Chancellor said on Monday that the the "place" and "time" for the government to deal with questions around rising petrol and diesel prices and fuel duty is next month's Budget.

John Healey told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm acutely concerned and conscious about how hard it is for families. I see that at the pumps myself.

"We can't remove the cost of living pressures, we can't remove the prices that people are having to pay, but where we can we will act and we will give people just a bit of breathing space, and the same goes for the cost to business."

Simon Williams, the RAC's head of policy, said record diesel prices "spell pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans".

"Undoubtedly these increased costs will be passed on to consumers," he said. Williams said prices at the pumps will not come down until there is a "sustained lower oil price - over several weeks, not days".

The price of Brent crude, a benchmark for global oil used to make petrol, diesel and other fuel products, rose over the weekend and is now hovering at around $108 per barrel. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.

Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.

Russia, which is also a major producer, has also implemented an export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply.

Diesel is harder to refine than gasoline and, because it is used by the haulage industry and in agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The UK is heavily reliant on imports. Although the four refineries in the UK make more than enough petrol to meet demand, they do not make enough diesel for the country's needs.

News.title: Thousands of illegal ghost plates on cars revealed by new cameras
News.content:
Thousands of illegal registration plates on cars and other vehicles have been detected by a new camera system currently being tested on motorways in south-east England, BBC Panorama can reveal.

These plates have been adapted to avoid their details being identified by automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) systems, which are used to enforce speed limits and low emission zones as well as to track criminals.

Illegal plates are putting the public at risk and are far too easy to get hold of, according to one former government advisor.

We have spoken to families who say their lives have been devastated by road deaths where illegal plates were involved.

Filming undercover, we also discovered how easy and cheap it is to buy plates without any background checks.

The minister responsible for vehicle registration across the UK has told us a national plan has now been instigated to understand how widespread the problem of illegal number plates is, and what can be done about it.

The UK has one of the largest networks of ANPR cameras in the world, with 14,000 sites capturing 100 million number plates each day. Many experts believe this system is failing to keep up with tactics used by some drivers determined to avoid recognition.

News.title: Lithium-ion battery caused fire that killed mum and 3 children
News.content:
A house fire that killed a mother and her three children was caused by a lithium-ion battery.

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, eight, and Prudence, seven, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle, Merseyside, in the early hours of 22 September.

Following an investigation with Merseyside Police, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service (MFRS) said the fire was caused by an electrical event linked to a lithium-ion battery, which are used in e-bikes and e-scooters.

Kev Johnson, of MFRS, said: "This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire."

Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property, at 03:45 BST.

MFRS said four people "showing no signs of life" had been found in an upstairs bedroom.

A man was taken to hospital suffering from burns.

News.title: Angela Scanlon takes over Sara Cox's drivetime slot on Radio 2
News.content:
Angela Scanlon is to take over BBC Radio 2's drivetime show after Sara Cox moved to the breakfast slot.

The Irish personality said it was "properly exciting" to be hosting the station's 16:00-19:00 show every weekday from November.

She said: "Millions of people, all having completely different days, piling into the same conversation for a few hours - what a strange and lovely thing!"

Scanlon, who hosted a Sunday early morning programme on the station from 2018 to 2021, was among a number of people who filled in after Cox vacated the drivetime slot in May, including Joel Dommett, Jason Manford, Ellie Taylor, Alex Jones and Gary Davies.

Scanlon is also known for The One Show, This Morning, Your Home Made Perfect, The Apprentice: Unfinished Business, and for taking part in Strictly Come Dancing in 2023.

News.title: Bulger killer's parole hearing to be held in private
News.content:
Child killer Jon Venables will have his latest parole bid heard in private despite a plea from his victim's mother for it to be public, the Parole Board has decided.

Venables tortured and murdered two-year-old James Bulger in 1993.

The 44-year-old will have his case heard by parole chiefs at an oral hearing more than two years after his last appeal.

James's mother Denise Fergus had demanded that the hearing be held in public to help combat "misinformation" about the case which had a "retraumatising impact" on her.

Parole Board hearings are usually held in private but they can be made public "in the interests of justice".

Various media organisations also applied for a public hearing.

In reaching its decision, the Parole Board said a public hearing would make it "very difficult for Jon Venables to give evidence" because he could be "being listened to by people who are seeking to get information so that they can kill him".

In 2023, the Parole Board rejected the bid and found he still posed a danger to children and could go on to offend again.

News.title: Faslane dry docks and research ship to be built in UK, says chancellor
News.content:
Orders for three floating dry docks, worth Â£6bn, to maintain the Royal Navy's nuclear-powered submarine fleet at Faslane will go to a UK-based shipbuilder, the chancellor has confirmed.

John Healey told the Labour conference the facilities were vital to national security and would support domestic shipbuilding as part of a "new age of industrialisation".

A UK-only bidding competition will decide who builds the floating docks but Navantia UK, which owns sites in Fife and Belfast, is seen as a frontrunner.

Healey has also pledged Â£115m for construction in the UK of a new marine research vessel to replace Cefas Endeavour, built by the Ferguson shipyard on the Clyde more than 20 years ago.

He told delegates in Liverpool: "I want to confirm today that we, this government will commit to Â£6bn of contracts for our British shipyards.

"They'll build the new docks for the submarines that will defend us all for decades to come, built in Britain by British workers because of the decisions of this Labour government."

News.title: British chess prodigy, 11, becomes youngest woman grandmaster
News.content:
A British child chess prodigy has become the youngest player in history to earn the woman grandmaster (WGM) title.

Bodhana Sivanandan, 11, from north-west London, secured her third and final WGM norm - a certified title-level performance - while representing England at the 46th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, the International Chess Federation (FIDE) confirmed.

Speaking to FIDE, Sivanandan said she was happy about the achievement but wanted to "keep making history".

It is the latest milestone in a remarkable rise for the schoolgirl, who has already become Britain's youngest women's chess champion and the youngest person to represent England internationally in any sport.

Sivanandan, from Harrow, played all 11 rounds on England's top board - a position assigned to the team's top player - and finished the tournament with eight points.

She had already passed the 2300 rating threshold required for the WGM title before securing her third and final norm.

She told Fide in an interview on Sunday about making history: "I'm happy to do it, but I want to keep going and keep making history as well, instead of just stopping here."

Kateryna Lagno, who has represented both Russia and Ukraine, previously held the age record for the WGM title, having achieved it aged 12. Hou Yifan, from China, also achieved the title at 12 and remains the youngest woman to have earned the higher, open grandmaster (GM) title, which she achieved aged 14.

Woman grandmaster is the highest woman only title a female player can attain and the rank is held for life.

Sivanandan's success in Samarkand also earned her a second International Master (IM) norm, taking her another step towards the higher title.

Players normally need three qualifying norms and a rating of at least 2400 to become an international master. Sivanandan now has two IM norms.

The international master title, open to both sexes, ranks higher than Sivanandan's current accolades - the woman grandmaster and woman international master titles.

Speaking to Fide about her love of the game, she added: "I like travelling and also because I do full-time school as well, it links to loads of school subjects, so it's really useful there as well."

News.title: Carer at home investigated by BBC struck off for threatening elderly man
News.content:
The panel ruled Sani told Christie's father: "We will call the police and they will take you to court" and, referring to a male cleaner, "do you think that man is going to hit you?" or words to that effect.

She also pulled his duvet off without any warning, causing him to become distressed and agitated.

Delivering the panel's judgment, the chairman said: "We agree with your solicitor's submissions that you were let down by your employer, and there is little doubt that there was institutional failure.

"None of the failures you have highlighted absolve you from your personal responsibility as a registered social care worker.

"It is clear throughout the video clips that you did not show any kindness or compassion to the resident. At one point you and your colleague can be seen laughing in response to something the resident says or does.

"It does not appear to us to be laughing with the resident, but it appears more disrespectful in nature. We find that the resident suffered harm and you did not respect his dignity."

Burke added that the panel felt Sani's treatment of the man was "not something that could be remediated with training" as it reflected her attitude.

It also noted she failed to use any de-escalation techniques.

In closing submissions, Sani's legal representative said her client wished to apologise to the family.

Christie, who moved her father into a new home shortly after the incident, said: "I think it was the right decision.

"Whilst the panel did comment on institutional failures, this hearing is about her own personal accountability. And I think it sends the message that personal accountability matters.

"In a care setting, people living with dementia, like my father, should be treated with respect, dignity, and patience and courtesy. They should be treated as human beings and that's all I was asking for."

Some members of President Donald Trump’s “Front Row Joes” loyalists have turned during his second term, with one denouncing him as a “fraud and a liar.”

The “Joes” are a group of devoted MAGA supporters who follow Trump around the country, sleeping outside venues ahead of campaign rallies and speeches to get the best seat. With the midterm elections around the corner, their opinion could ring alarm bells for Republicans.

Two prominent members, Trisha Hope and Rick Frazier, have split from the group after becoming disillusioned with Trump over his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein scandal and the war in Iran, they told Politico. Hope, a self-declared “J6 activist” who joined the Joes in 2018, said that she lost faith in the president after he vented his frustrations about Epstein at a Cabinet meeting in July 2025.

“Are you still talking about Jeffrey Epstein?” Trump fumed at a reporter. “This guy’s been talked about for years.”

Hope, from Texas, described that moment as “a dagger in my heart” to Politico. “It was like a light switch went on and a veil lifted, and I saw him for who he was, and I have not been able to unsee it since,” she added.

open image in gallery Some members of President Donald Trump’s ‘Front Row Joes’ loyalists have turned during his second term, with one denouncing him as a ‘fraud and a liar.’ The group follow Trump around the country ( AFP/Getty )

open image in gallery Two prominent members, Trisha Hope and Rick Frazier (pictured in 2023), have split from the group after becoming disillusioned with Trump over his handling of the Jeffrey Epstein scandal and the war in Iran ( Getty )

Trump’s war with Iran, now in its eighth month, cemented Hope’s view of the president. “He’s said the war is over 600 different times,” she said. “He tells us they don't have a military, they don’t have a navy. They’re still blowing up things. It’s just all lies.”

Hope is so fed up with the president that she said she would support an impeachment. “If we do lose the midterms and he is impeached again, I will be walking the halls of Congress in support of that impeachment,” she said.

While Frazier, a founding member of the Joes, shares Hope’s frustrations, he acknowledged the pair are just two people and said that 95 percent of the group are “unwavering.”

Still, he pointed to the same issues as Hope for departing.

“Epstein crimes and feeding the industrial military complex…those are big nos for me,” Frazier, who has attended more than 100 Trump rallies, told Politico. “He promoted himself as a no-war president. That didn’t work out.”

Frazier, who lives in Ohio, said he is so frustrated he may not even vote in November.

Trump praised the devotion of the group at a July rally in Georgia as he promoted his “Trump Accounts” investment program.

open image in gallery Frazier acknowledged that he and Hope are just two people, and said 95 percent of the Joes remain ‘unwavering’ to Trump ( Getty Images )

“The Front Row Joes, I love these people,” he said. “I love these people. I think there are about 280… I don’t know what the hell they do, I think they make a lot of money, too.”

“I’m hearing they’re very rich. They follow us. It’s a rock concert right? You have a good time, right? Thank you. They’ve been with me right from the beginning,” he said.

Hope hit out at Trump at the time over his assertion that the group was “rich.”

“This shows me how absolutely clueless he is on what these folks have sacrificed in order to support him,” she said.

“They DO NOT MAKE MONEY!!” Hope continued. “In fact it costs them a GREAT deal of money and time to attend. They drive sometimes all night to get in line, they spend money on flights when driving isn’t an option.”

Other former Trump loyalists have soured on the president during his second term over the Epstein case and Iran, including ex-congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene and right-wing pundit Tucker Carlson.

They are not alone. Trump is approaching the midterm elections with a historic 50 percent of Americans strongly disapproving of his job performance — shattering the rejection record he set before the 2018 midterms, according to CNN.

The White House dismissed unfavorable polling in a previous statement. “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” a spokesman said.

Chancellor John Healey has said he is “concerned” as diesel prices in the UK hit a record high.

The average price of a litre of diesel stood at 199.18p on Monday, according to figures compiled by the RAC.

This is 56.8p more expensive than at the start of the US-Iran war on February 28 this year, when a litre averaged 142.38p.

Diesel prices in the UK have hit a new high, passing the previous record set in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The average price of a litre of diesel stood at 199.18p on Monday, according to figures compiled by the RAC.

It also passes the previous record of 199.09p, reached in June 2022 in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine earlier that year.

Mr Healey told ITV News: “It’s something I’m concerned about and people have seen the diesel and petrol prices rising over recent months.

“They’ve seen us put in place a Fuel Finder so people can find out the cheapest price on the forecourts around them.

“They’ve seen us put in place a freeze on any rise in diesel (duty) until the end of the year.”

Asked whether he will consider extending the current 5p cut in fuel duty beyond the end of this year, the Chancellor said he will announce that decision in the Budget on October 28.

He said: “I’m conscious of the pressure this is putting on people, on businesses as well as people at the pumps, and this is a government that will do what we can to give people a bit of breathing space…

“But those are decisions that I will make in the round at the Budget when I announce it in a month today.”

The cost of diesel has risen steadily in recent weeks due to the impact on global supplies from the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and from renewed hostilities in the Middle East.

Russian exports of diesel have dropped sharply after many of the country’s oil refineries were targeted by Ukraine, with a key facility near Moscow damaged earlier this month as part of a huge drone operation.

open image in gallery

This has led to extra demand for fuel from other diesel-exporting countries, causing wholesale prices to rise.

Meanwhile, the ongoing war between the US and Iran is continuing to disrupt the global trade in refined oil and other petroleum materials, with Iran’s effective blockade of the Strait of Hormuz limiting the production and supply of fuel needed by consumers.

Now, US President Donald Trump is threatening a diesel export ban to tackle rising prices in the US.

Asked about about Mr Trump’s potential export ban, Mr Healey said: “It’s a concern. But we’re talking, we always talk very closely with the US, especially on trade matters.

“We’re also talking, of course, to the US about what will help deal with this problem at its roots, which is solving the Middle Eastern conflict.

“A peace plan that will mean an end to the fighting, an opening of the Strait of Hormuz and Britain’s a country that is ready to lead a multinational mission, a military mission to help secure the Strait if we can get a peace plan, and that will do more than anything else of course to help bring down prices, relieve the cost of living and the cost of business pressures.”

The RAC data is based on the average price of diesel at a range of supermarkets, motorway service stations and independent retailers.

The cost of unleaded petrol has also been climbing in recent weeks and currently stands at an average of 174.13p per litre, up by 41.3p since the start of the US-Iran war.

RAC head of policy Simon Williams said: “The average price of a litre of diesel has now reached the highest level in UK history, in what will be a financial blow to households and businesses that use their vehicles regularly.

open image in gallery Record diesel prices ‘could be disastrous for the economy and for diesel drivers’, the AA said (Aaron Chown/PA) ( PA Wire )

“The cost of filling up an average family car is now almost £110, £31 more than it was at the start of the US-Iran conflict.

“This spells pain not only at the pumps for drivers, but for everyone who buys goods or services that rely on diesel lorries and vans; undoubtedly these increased costs will be passed on to consumers.

“Only a sustained lower oil price – over several weeks, not days – will lead to cheaper prices at the pumps.”

A total of 15.1 million diesel-fuelled vehicles were licensed to be on UK roads at the end of June this year, down from 15.7 million 12 months earlier, according to the latest figures from the Department for Transport.

There were 9.8 million diesel cars, down year on year from 10.4 million.

Some 20.4 million petrol vehicles were licensed to be on roads this June, including 18.8 million cars.

Edmund King, president of the AA, said: “Record diesel prices could be disastrous for the economy and for diesel drivers.

“Diesel helps run the business backbone of Britain. Most delivery trucks use diesel and most goods transported on the roads to our ports or shops are fuelled by diesel.

“When we hit high diesel prices, most hauliers pass on their extra costs to their customers and hence the hikes hit the price of goods on our shelves, which in turn fuels inflation.”

Michael Wynn Jones, the husband of celebrity chef Delia Smith, has died at the age of 85.

Mr Wynn Jones was also the honorary life president of Norwich City Football Club.

He was a joint majority shareholder of the club, alongside his wife, until 2024 when American billionaire Mark Attanasio took over.

Norwich announced Mr Wynn Jones’ death on its website on Monday afternoon.

It said that he had died peacefully at home that morning.

open image in gallery Michael Wynn Jones and Delia Smith lift the EFL Championship trophy in 2019 ( Getty )

“He will be greatly missed,” the statement said.

“His family are grateful for the wonderful care provided by the community nursing team at St Elizabeth Hospice in Ipswich.

“Our deepest condolences are with Delia and Tom, and with all of Michael’s family, friends and loved ones.

“At the family’s request, we ask that their privacy be respected at this difficult time.”

Mr Wynn Jones’s parents were a Church of England vicar and a teacher.

He studied at the University of Oxford and married Ms Smith in 1971 in Stowmarket, Suffolk.

He was the deputy editor of the Daily Mirror's midweek supplement Mirror Magazine and The Spectator, and established New Crane Publishing, which produced some of his wife's books.

The couple, who were based in Stowmarket, were deeply involved with Norwich and oversaw a number of promotions to the Premier League.

“Such sad news, he stayed out of the limelight but all at [the club] owe him so much,” former Norwich forward Darren Huckerby said on X.

A popular story about a lesbian bar in Massachusetts has gone so viral that Hollywood studios are now considering potential adaptations for the article, according to an industry report.

On September 22, the Boston Globe published the piece in question, titled “A Western Mass. lesbian bar required KN-95 masks. When it changed the rules, all hell broke loose.” The article, written by Annalisa Quinn, quickly became a hot topic on social media feeds and sparked online discussions and think pieces on all corners of the internet — and the buzzy conversation has apparently made its way over to film and TV executives.

According to a new report from The Hollywood Reporter, talent agency UTA “has been fielding inquiries about potential adaptations for the article — both in the scripted space and the documentary sphere.”

UTA, which represents the Globe, confirmed the report to The Independent.

A spokesperson for the newspaper told The Independent: “This story has certainly resonated with a wide range of audiences nationally and internationally. It is now one of the most-read stories we’ve published, and has already garnered many thousands of subscriptions.”

open image in gallery The Boston Globe is fielding inquiries regarding a potential adaptation of its recent viral article ( Lane Turner/Globe Staff )

The article follows a lesbian establishment, Last Ditch Bar, in Greenfield, Massachusetts, that faced chaos after lifting its mask mandate.

Bartenders announced in an Instagram post issued to the “immunocompromised disabled divas” in August that patrons no longer had to wear KN95 masks on Saturday nights.

The decision was met with backlash and accused of being “complicit in a mass disabling event.”

Quinn’s article was praised online for its relaying of the dramatic saga, which was complete with zinger one-liner quotes from scorned customers as well as sympathetic details about the bar owner who is in a mountain of debt because of the crisis.

open image in gallery 2015 movie ‘Spotlight’ was based on the Boston Globe’s investigative reporting ( Kerry Hayes )

It quickly became one of the most read stories in the newspaper’s history, with a leaked staffer memo reporting that more than a thousand new subscribers flocked to the Globe in less than a day after the story was published.

The viral article’s success is notable considering the stark contrast in subject matter of other monumental articles in the Globe’s history that have been adapted.

In the early 2000s, the newspaper published a Pulitzer Prize-winning series of bombshell articles that exposed the systemic cover-up of abuse within the Catholic Church. The journalism inspired the 2015 Academy Award-winning film Spotlight.

Years later, the paper’s investigative reporting on the crimes and death of former New England Patriots star Aaron Hernandez also led to the podcast Gladiator: Aaron Hernandez. The podcast eventually led to scripted FX series American Sports Story: Aaron Hernandez, which was executive produced by Ryan Murphy.

A New Jersey man was sentenced on Monday to nearly six years in prison for taking homemade explosive devices to a Washington, D.C., church that was preparing for an annual Mass celebrating the start of the Supreme Court’s term.

Louis Geri declined to address the court before U.S. District Judge Randolph Moss sentenced him to five years and 10 months in prison followed by three years of supervised release.

Moss said he balanced the danger that Geri poses to the public with the defendant's history of “very serious mental health issues” and his need for adequate treatment.

“This was an extremely serious offense,” the judge said. “It may have been carried out in a bizarre manner, but the threat of violence was a serious one.”

Geri was arrested on Oct. 5, 2025, outside the Cathedral of St. Matthew the Apostle, where police officers were clearing the area before the annual Red Mass. Police said they found in Geri’s possession paperwork that expressed “significant animosity” toward the Roman Catholic Church, Jewish people and the Supreme Court. Some justices usually attend the celebration, but none went to last year’s ceremony.

On steps outside the church, Geri had set up a tent containing more than 100 homemade explosives along with a nine-page “list of written demands,” according to a court filing. Geri told police that he had explosive devices and said “several of your people are gonna die from one of these” if his demands weren’t met, the filing says.

Geri's written demands included requests for money, for an “expatriation flight” to Japan and for the Supreme Court to remove Arizona from the United States.

“The defendant’s intent was clear: If his list of demands was not met, innocent people would die and prominent, historic landmarks, such as the Washington Monument, the Supreme Court, and the White House, would be destroyed,” prosecutors wrote.

Geri's attorney said the New Jersey native, who had traveled to Washington from Arkansas, was diagnosed with bipolar disorder more than two decades ago and had stopped taking his medication in the months leading up to his arrest outside the church.

“His conduct was the product of a treatable medical condition spiraling out of control, not malice or an actual intent to harm,” defense attorney Elizabeth Mullin wrote.

Geri pleaded guilty in March to two felony counts: illegal possession of a destructive device and extortion by wrongful use of force, violence or fear.

Geri and prosecutors agreed that a prison term ranging from five years and 10 months to seven years and three months would be appropriate. Moss wasn't bound by that recommendation, but Geri could have withdrawn his guilty plea if the judge had imposed a longer sentence.

Chancellor John Healey has brought back plans for welfare reform as he vowed not to allow Britain’s benefits bill spiral out of control.

Speaking at his first Labour conference speech as chancellor, he told members it is not progressive “to allow a bigger and bigger benefits” bill.

He was later even clearer in an interview with ITN.

He told ITN: “We have to bring the benefits bill down. I made the case that as a moral case, not just an economic case, that we can't have a bigger and bigger benefits bill. We can't have a system that offers payments and no help.

“And the best thing, especially for young people who at the moment are too often locked out of any future, the best thing we can offer is not a benefits payment, but a first job with a wage and with a future.”

His speech was cheered by Labour members who had previously been sceptical about the Starmer government’s attempts to curtail welfare with £5bn of cuts.

After laying out his credentials as a Labour politicians from his roots in the miners strike in the 1980s through to Tony Blair’s New Labour government and to the Treasury with Andy Burnham, Mr Healey made it clear he shared the values of the audience in the conference centre in Liverpool.

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey has hinted at welfare reform as he vowed not to allow Britain’s benefits bill spiral out of control ( PA )

He told them: “Conference, it is not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill, and a system which offers an income but doesn’t offer a future,” he said.

“So once again, as a Labour government, it falls to us to act. And this is more than just an economic must. This is a moral duty.

“I refuse to write off a million young people like the Tories have done.”

He added that this was a “moral duty” for the government as he went on to announce a £100m boost to the local apprenticeship services to get Britain’s Neets into employment.

“Our social security system must always be there for those who can never work,” he said. “But for everyone else, benefits should be a bridge to work, to wider participation, to a better life, not a trap that people can’t escape.”

Treasury sources said the speech was Mr Healey’s attempt to “make a moral case for welfare reform in a way that bringing the party with them”.

Sir Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves faced a massive backbench rebellion when they sought to table their own welfare reforms in June 2025.

But Treasury sources pointed to the “really positive response from the hall” on Monday, which they said “perhaps hasn't happened previously” under previous chancellors.

They said it was “a sign of how this this road that the party is on” in its efforts to get “welfare reform done in a sustainable way”.

The chancellor announced in his speech that mayors will be handed £100 million to fund a new scheme aimed at getting young people into apprenticeships.

Mr Healey said the new “Local Apprenticeship Service” would see teams acting like “football scouts” to link young people with firms, including those who had never been offered an apprenticeship.

open image in gallery ( PA )

It came as a series of ministers privately admitted that the yneeded to revisit attempts to cut the welfare bill which derailed Sir Keir Starmer’s government after a backbench revolt last year.

But they hoped that “better presentation” from Mr Healey and the prime minister would allow them to succeed where Sir Keir and former chancellor Rachel Reeves failed.

“We need to do it,” one minister said but added: “We need to tell a different story.”

Mr Healey told the party conference in Liverpool: “The best thing we can offer a young person isn’t a benefit payment, it’s a first job with training and a wage.

“Our determination to help, matched by their determination to hope.”

Mr Healey described the service as “a down payment” on the work of former Cabinet minister Alan Milburn to tackle the almost one million young people not in employment, education or training (Neet).

The new service was the first announcement in a speech setting out Mr Healey’s economic vision for the country, pledging to bring about a “new age of industrialisation” for Britain.

In his speech, the Chancellor announced that Rolls-Royce would invest £300 million in factories in Derby, Bristol, Glasgow and Rotherham, describing the investment as a “new confidence in Britain lit by this Government, driven forward by business”.

And he stressed that his first Budget next month would maintain his party’s commitment to fiscal discipline, saying it would also give the public “breathing space” and drive “good growth and jobs in more places”.

But he warned that the UK faced more straitened times than when he had served as a junior Treasury minister under Gordon Brown’s chancellorship, blaming the Conservatives for the country’s debt burden.

News.title: UK borrowing costs hit highest level since 2007
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2007 after Middle East tensions pushed oil prices above $108.

Yields on 10-year gilts, which determine the price the treasury pays to borrow money, rose above 5.43pc on Monday, before edging back to 5.42pc.

These are levels not seen in almost two decades, underlining the challenge facing John Healey as he prepares for next month’s Budget.

The Chancellor is coming under pressure to slash spending or raise taxes to bring Britain’s borrowing costs under control, against a backdrop of growing debt and rising inflation.

The surge in 10-year gilt yields pushes them above the 19-year high of 5.41pc recorded earlier this month, threatening to put a dent in Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom – a self-imposed guardrail to guide public spending.

Economists said high costs reflect the scale of Britain’s near-£3tn national debt and the rise in inflation facing the country.

“The uncomfortable truth for the PM and his Chancellor, John Healey ... is that the wide spread of gilt yields over peers is fair, in our view, given the UK’s dire fiscal position and the inflationary pressures stemming from high energy prices,” said Elliott Jordan-Doak, at Pantheon Macroeconomics.

“Gilt yields will fall if energy prices drop, but investors will continue to be driven by the economics and the Government’s willingness to take tough fiscal decisions, both of which point to yields staying high.”

UK borrowing costs are growing amid a wider bond market sell-off after Donald Trump rejected a peace deal with Iran over the weekend, pushing oil prices higher.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 3pc to just over $108 a barrel on Monday, adding to global inflation pressures. Bond traders reacted by demanding higher yields from governments to lend them money.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds rose to above 5.24pc, the highest level since 2007.
