News.title: Taylor Swift becomes most-awarded artist in MTV history
News.content:
Taylor Swift broke records at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards (VMAs) on Sunday, becoming the most-awarded artist in VMA history.

The pop star, 36, was previously tied with Beyoncé for the title, with 30 VMAs each. However, Swift took home three awards at the ceremony, bringing her career total to an unmatched 33.

The Fate of Ophelia, ⁠Swift’s first single from her record-breaking The Life of a Showgirl album, claimed the top trophy – Video of the Year – and she dedicated the honour to the late country music legend Dolly Parton.

During her speech, Swift praised Parton as “the ultimate showgirl” who told stories that were “so vivid and so rich”.

“I think that we were all very lucky to share this planet with Dolly Parton for a time,” she said.

Parton, an award-winning country singer, died in August at the age of 80.

Swift also received the inaugural Artist Director Honors, a new award meant to recognise artists “whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling”.

The 36-year-old has written and directed 18 videos of her roughly 60 videos during her career. The ‌most recent, for ‌her new single Patient Zero, debuted during ⁠the ceremony.

News.title: Five reasons why Australia’s win over Boks was an all-time classic
News.content:
If the Wallabies play like this in their own backyard at their own World Cup next year, boy we are in for a treat. After years in the doldrums, this five-try victory over South Africa was the latest reminder of their transformation under the stewardship of Les Kiss.

Their gritty performance in Perth – the city where Australia will open rugby’s showpiece in 12 months’ time – was caveated by the fact they were facing a second-string Boks side. But there can be no denying they are on an upward trajectory, even if their discipline dramatically deserted them late on.

In a helter-skelter denouement, Australia played the majority of the final 10 minutes of the match with 11 men on the pitch as South Africa threatened to mount a late comeback. Tom Wright’s eye-catching intercept try looked to have secured a match-winning moment, but it was scratched off after Hunter Paisami joined Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan and Joseph Sua’ali’i in the bin.

Ox Nche’s 80th-minute score made it a four-point game with time left for the restart, but Australia had enough fight to secure a dramatic victory largely built on execution and patience.

Five tries by the hour mark, including a Len Ikitau first-half double, ultimately gave South Africa a mountain to climb. The Wallabies’ field coverage and industriousness in defence was far superior to that of the four-time world champions, while Max Jorgensen and Sua’ali’i were pillars of excellence out wide.

After clinching a 3-1 win over New Zealand in their historic “Greatest Rivalry” series, Rassie Erasmus had the luxury of resting several of his A-listers for this one-off Test in Western Australia. The changes ultimately had an adverse effect, with the visitors faulty at the set-piece and lacking their usual snarl and bite. They found themselves playing catch-up in a chaotic game that Australia, despite their discipline creaking in the dying moments, deserved to win.

Here, Telegraph Sport explores five reasons why this was one of the craziest Test matches in recent memory.

Wallabies outmuscle Boks over 60 emphatic minutes

The Wallabies front up impressively to earn a seven-point lead at the break after a quickfire Len Ikitau double cancels out tries from Johan Grobbelaar and Edwill van der Merwe, before Ben Donaldson finishes a sublime attacking set from the hosts.

News.title: England show ODI depth in thrashing of Sri Lanka
News.content:
England’s international summer comes to an end at the Oval with a series decider against Sri Lanka. After England won the first game in Durham, Sri Lanka bounced back to take a 16-run win at Headingley on Thursday to set up this winner-takes-all match today. Sri Lanka put up a much better fight in the second one-day international than they have throughout the rest of their white-ball tour. The tourists posted 321 for six, with their captain Kusal Mendis leading the way with 121 off 100 balls, his seventh ODI century.

England’s reply got off to the best possible start, with both openers Tom Banton and Ben Duckett hitting fifties. It appeared to be going well for England, with Jos Buttler and Will Jacks also registering half centuries, but Buttler’s hamstring injury in addition to the regular loss of wickets meant Sri Lanka were able to claim victory to take us to a series decider in London today.

“I am so happy winning and getting the hundred,” Mendis said. “The overall performance was very good. We started really well and the middle order batted really well. Nothing special, basic cricket and I was very happy with 320, we wanted more than 300 on this pitch. [Dunith] Wellalage bowled really well, the whole team, after the powerplay. The guys gave 100 per cent. Today [Thursday] is finished and now we have to focus on the next game and do the basics right.”

When Buttler retired hurt in the 38th over of England’s run chase, the hosts were 254 for four and were in a great position to chase the total down and claim a series victory. From the 37th over onwards, England were only able to score one four and one six.

“It was an outstanding game,” England captain Harry Brook said. “You can look back and dwell on some many different areas but that is not what this team does, we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the Oval. We put up a really good fight with the ball. To restrict them to 320 and have the chance to chase that down was a hell of an effort.

“The lads got the chase off to a flyer. You could not really ask for much more. We probably stalled in that middle period and lost a few too many wickets, but the fight we showed was great. We have got a great opportunity now to try and win this series, and a great opportunity for 12 months’ time. In pressure situations, like the one that awaits us at the Oval, it will be great to see where we are as a team.”

Buttler has been ruled out of this match due to a hamstring injury and has been replaced in the squad by Dan Lawrence, who had been playing for Surrey in the final round of the County Championship.

Play from the Oval will get under way at 10.30am.

News.title: Saracens storm Leicester to launch new Venter era in style
News.content:
Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this mouthwatering Gallagher Prem meeting as Leicester Tigers host Saracens at Welford Road.

Last season, Leicester reached the play-off semi-finals in Geoff Parling’s first full season at the club, before losing to arch-rivals Northampton Saints, who went on to win their third title in the competition.

In a new era for Leicester as they plot a route back to the very top, Aaron Wainwright and Mako Vunipola make their Prem debuts.

Leicester head coach Geoff Parling is brimming with excitement ahead of this tasty match and has talked about his side’s preparation for the new season.

“Firstly we are looking to evolve our game, we’re not looking to rip it up and completely restart,” he said. This team is built on being competitive and winning, we’ve got to be in the mix every year. For me it’s all about being consistently near the top and then getting in those big games and having the ability to perform in them.”

“I’m well aware that there’s lots of elements from the season and different circumstances but the main thing is that the league is designed to have a top four that go into the play-offs so the top four is the aim.”

Saracens finished one place below Leicester in the previous campaign and missed out on the play-offs after a 32-12 final round loss to Exeter Chiefs.

Boss Joe Shaw has handed debuts to Tomos Williams and Alfie Barbeary, and he’s raring to go ahead of this fixture.

“We’ve had a great pre-season, but we’re itching to get stuck into the league campaign now,” he said. “We have a really competitive squad who are driving standards and good habits across the pitch. We are confident in the squad we have put together and are excited to see what they can achieve this campaign.”

Kick-off is at 15:00.

News.title: England throw it away with defending unworthy of a top nation
News.content:
Tuchel does not plan to address the issue with his players ahead of the remaining Nations League games against Czech Republic and Croatia.

Asked if the City verdict had been a cause of discussion ahead of the Spain game, Tuchel replied: “Not for me, but I can imagine maybe for the Man City players. I won’t comment on it as it’s an ongoing case.

“I didn’t make it a topic. It was not a topic for me. I’m just thinking about Spain and the team and meetings. The players have more time than me. So I can imagine they talk about it. It’s good they do. I don’t think it was a distraction for them.”

Kane added: “There was a discussion, but when we’re with England, we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week.”

Tuchel also refused to point the finger of blame at Guéhi, O’Reilly or Kane, who missed a penalty, for England’s defeat despite admitting his team got off to the worst possible start by conceding a goal after two minutes.

“We will focus on the positives, but also highlight the stuff we can do better,” Tuchel said. “Not even speaking about individual mistakes because this is normal. It just happens. It should not happen, and for sure not in this amount. But there is no sense in showing the individual mistakes or telling them ‘please don’t make mistakes’. That is normal, but we can do things better. We can defend the third goal better. But we will focus on the positives. There is a lot to take away from the game.

“We wanted to be the team desperately to beat them [Spain] and we think we had them. We still think we had them at half-time. That was the way the team showed up after half-time. So we will focus on that, but the reality is we lost and the reality is we need to prove it again.”

News.title: Red Roses triumph over New Zealand in chaotic late scenes – how it unfolded
News.content:
Just when it looked like the Red Roses’ lustre was beginning to fade, up stepped Zoe Harrison.

In one of the most dramatic finishes to an England match in recent memory, the fly-half gobbled up Amy Du Plessis’s pass to glide over the whitewash and secure a pulsating win over New Zealand.

Ever the epitome of calmness, Harrison was undeterred by the fact she had just missed what would have been a match-winning penalty from 42 metres out with the score locked at 19-19.

But after their arm-wrestle with Canada last weekend in Exeter, which finished 26-26, there was simply no way the Red Roses were going to settle for a draw for a second week running.

A year to the day since they were crowned world champions in their own back yard, England’s status as the most dominant side in the women’s game was all but confirmed by this never-say-die victory over the Black Ferns.

News.title: Russell holds his nerve to see off Verstappen and win Azerbaijan GP
News.content:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend went the way many believed the 2026 season would play out. George Russell strolled to victory from pole, though with a little late jeopardy, whilst Kimi Antonelli’s crash in qualifying meant he had to fight his way through the field to finish fifth. That, after all, was the order of things last season.

Yet the past few days in Baku are an inversion of the season’s storyline. It is Antonelli who has been the faster driver, heading for a maiden world title at the second time of asking. Russell has been the troubled one. This was only the Briton’s third victory of the season and his first since Austria in late June. Antonelli has racked up eight wins and, before this weekend in Baku, a well-deserved 81-point lead over Russell.

Russell’s dominant and impressive run from pole to the chequered flag on Saturday is both a reminder of what he is capable of and also what might have been, had he been able to find this type of form earlier and more often. The reality, though, is that he needs to replicate this for the rest of the season to even be in with a sniff, barring a catastrophic meltdown from Antonelli. Still, Russell looked elated to have ended his barren run.

The finish was a little more tense than Russell deserved, having established a healthy lead in the first half of the race. Two late safety cars eradicated his advantage and helped put Max Verstappen’s Red Bull on his gearbox. In the end, he triumphed by just under 0.2sec and, as Antonelli finished fifth – with some help from two safety-car inducing crashes – he made up 15 points on his Mercedes team-mate. Isack Hadjar completed the podium for Red Bull after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.

Sports.title: Leicestershire's points deduction for poor pitch reduced
Sports.content:
Leicestershire’s 27-point deduction for breaching pitch regulations in August's win over Glamorgan has been reduced to 19.

The Foxes were relegated from Division One of the County Championship last week following an innings defeat by champions Warwickshire.

Leicestershire's groundsman Callum Lewin had argued filming of an unscheduled Bollywood film - believed to be for a biopic of former India captain Sourav Ganguly - had taken place at the ground four days before the Glamorgan fixture between August 20-23, preventing the pitch from being covered for eight hours in bright sunshine and heatwave temperatures.

The Cricket Discipline Panel (CDP) upheld the charge against Leicestershire for a breach of the ECB's Pitch Regulations.

It imposed an immediate eight-point deduction from the County Championship plus the 19 points Leicestershire earned from winning the match by 42 runs.

A further eight-point deduction was also suspended until the end of the 2027 season and a £5,000 fine.

Leicestershire confirmed last Thursday that they would appeal against the original sanction.

Following the CDP holding a further hearing last Wednesday, the sanction has been amended with Leicestershire having eight points reinstated.

Leicestershire chief executive Emma White said in a statement: "The (CDP) Panel made clear that the latest hearing and Amended Decision, which relates to the sanction alone, were not appeal proceedings.

"Our position on the charge is therefore unchanged. We continue to believe it should not have been upheld, and that we ought not to have suffered the points deduction we have. We therefore still intend to appeal, focusing upon the process and resultant evidential position upon which the Panel was caused to decide the case.

"Our recently instructed counsel, Craig Harris, and Oliver Laurence of Periculum Sport shall continue to act for the Club throughout the appeal process.

"As we are now engaged in that process, it would not be appropriate for the club to comment further at this stage. I would again ask all supporters to do the same, and to treat everyone involved, including players and staff from other counties, and those administering this process, with courtesy and respect, both at the ground and online."

The amended decision adjusts Leicestershire's points tally in Division One to 119, 17 behind third-from-bottom Essex.

A wholly successful appeal would lift Leicestershire out of the relegation zone and above Essex.

Sports.title: Man City charges: The big questions answered
Sports.content:
Sky Sports News chief reporter Kaveh Solhekol is back to answer the big questions surrounding the Premier League's long-running dispute in their 115 charges against Manchester City.

Reports last Friday said an independent tribunal has reached decisions in the case between the league and the club, and Sky Sports News understands the process is moving to the appeal stage.

Here's the latest on developments since, which have included chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak penning an open letter to the club's fans over the weekend and the news that the Premier League's case over the alleged breaches could still have years to run...

Why has the Premier League not commented?

Because it's a private and confidential process.

I've heard people criticise the Premier League for not issuing a statement, but their hands are tied behind their back.

They have to respect the process, which says that everything has to be private and confidential.

That's the reason why Premier League CEO Richard Masters has given nothing away when he has been asked about this subject. He's always said there isn't much he can say, he just has to let the process play out.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Former Manchester City midfielder Rodri says nobody can take away Manchester City players' success

When can we expect to hear an official judgement?

What we got on Friday was a leak. It's been widely reported that Man City have lost the majority of the 115 charges they faced, but there has been no official confirmation that this is the case.

The two parties involved, the Premier League and Man City, both have to agree for any judgement to be released.

There is no definitive answer about when the judgment will be released - we just have to be patient.

How serious is Friday's leak to the process?

I think the issue of the leak could be serious if City felt they were forced to take this all the way, for instance, to the High Court. They could argue that this process has not been fair and impartial because of what happened on Friday.

Man City have argued something like this before, in their case against UEFA they brought up the fact there had been leaks to the media.

Many well-respected sports lawyers are refusing to comment on this case at the moment because they have not seen the judgement.

The judgement will probably be hundreds of pages long, it will take a while to digest, and only then will we all be in a position where we can comment on it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player According to reports, an independent tribunal has reached decisions in Manchester City's 115 charges case

Could other clubs sue if the Premier League's charges are proven?

We're into the realm of hypotheticals but if the charges are proven, I'm sure clubs will be contacted by lawyers who want to represent them and help them seek compensation.

We've seen in the past clubs sue other clubs for compensation so it is something that could happen but you have to remember that the Premier League is made up of 20 clubs.

Going forward, those 20 members have to think about the Premier League as a whole as well, so we have to wait and see how much appetite there is to take legal action against Manchester City if that possibility arises in the future.

Man City previously took UEFA to the Court of Arbitration for Sport to appeal. Why couldn't that happen here?

The Premier League regulations don't include the possibility of being able to go to the Court of Arbitration for Sport. The rules are very clear. There is an independent tribunal. After the judgement of the independent tribunal, both sides can go to an appeal board.

The appeal would be heard by a new three-person panel. After that you effectively reach the end of the road because you can't go to CAS.

Having said that, if you have some serious issues with the way the process was conducted, then you do have the option, for instance, of going to the High Court and arguing it was unfair.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Why has Italy head coach and former Manchester City manager Roberto Mancini distanced himself from the club's charges from the Premier League?

What did former City boss Roberto Mancini talk about on Sunday?

This is all to do with an allegation published by German outlet Der Spiegel in 2018. They said they had documents which they claimed showed that when Roberto Mancini was the Man City manager, he had two contracts.

These emails apparently alleged that Mancini was being paid £1.45m net to be the manager of Man City, while at the same time he also had a contract which was worth £1.75m a year to coach four days a year in Abu Dhabi at a club called Al Jazira.

Man City have always said these emails have been taken out of context and are part of a wider effort to discredit the club.

Sports.title: Does the Presidents Cup need changing to stop Team USA’s dominance?
Sports.content:
The United States maintained their Presidents Cup winning streak over the International Team, with the latest victory reigniting debate about whether change is needed in the biennial contest.

Brandt Snedeker's side produced the largest final-day comeback in Presidents Cup history at Medinah, winning 9.5 of the 12 points on offer in the Sunday singles to close out a record-extending 11th consecutive victory.

A 17-13 winning margin doesn't tell the full picture from a closer-than-expected contest, including a foursomes session sweep for the Internationals on Friday and them leading going into the final day for just the fourth time ever.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the second day of the Presidents Cup, where the International Team swept Team USA 5-0 in the Friday foursomes

The harsh reality, however, is that the International Team fell short again after threatening a shock victory, extending their wait for a first win over the United States since 1998.

Geoff Ogilvy's side were more than a match for the Americans over the first three days but were outclassed on Sunday, meaning Team USA have now won 14 of 16 Presidents Cups ever played.

"It was sort of on a knife's edge all day," Ogilvy said. "Some of those one downs that we had out there, if they'd flipped to one up, the numbers look really good and who knows what momentum can give."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Brandt Snedeker spoke to the media after winning the Presidents Cup with Team USA and said he was proud of their singles comeback

Could schedule changes boost the Internationals?

The Presidents Cup is a four-day event with 30 total matches, which is a day longer and two matches more than the format used for both the Ryder Cup and Solheim Cup.

The disparity in strength of teams in the Presidents Cup is greater than in the two involving Europe, so could a tighter schedule of fewer matches be of benefit?

Playing foursomes and fourballs on both Friday and Saturday means fewer matches but more opportunities to bench weaker members of a team, plus puts less pressure on the marquee names to play in every session.

"They need to start the President's Cup on Friday and reduce the number of points," Golf Channel's Brandel Chamblee insisted. "Reduce it to 24. If they're playing for 28 in the Ryder Cup, why in the heck are they playing for 30 in the Presidents Cup when there's a bigger separation between the talent?

"If it were just 24 points, you would only need 12 and a half to get to a victory. The first three Presidents Cups were started on a Friday and if you go back and combine the points from 1994, 1996 and 1998, they [Team USA and Internationals] were dead even after those three.

"There's no point in it going four days, drawing it out. The longer you go out, the more the better players and the better team are going to come to the fore. That was evidenced very poignantly."

Should LIV Golf players be allowed to play?

The Presidents Cup being a PGA Tour-owned event immediately makes LIV Golf League players ineligible, which has had a bigger impact on the International Team's depth than it has on the United States.

The early years of the Presidents Cup saw the Internationals have former world No 1s Greg Norman, Nick Price, Ernie Els and Vijay Singh at their disposal, but their strength had already weakened before the emergence of LIV Golf.

Chilean Joaquin Niemann and 2022 Open champion Cameron Smith are two of the players no longer able to feature, with Lucas Herbert - who impressed this season - and International Team stalwart Louis Oosthuizen among the others who can't be involved.

"Give the Internationals autonomy to choose who they want," Chamblee added. "You're telling me they wouldn't have chosen some LIV players to be on this team?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Guardian journalist Ewan Murray discusses what will happen next for LIV Golf and their players, as well as the impact it has had on the sport

"The PGA of America runs the Ryder Cup on the US side and the DP World Tour has their own set of rules, so it allows them to choose a Jon Rahm or - in the case of the US team - a Bryson DeChambeau.

"It certainly mattered to the European Ryder Cup team at Marco Simone [2023]. It would have mattered for this Presidents' Cup team, which has been gutted by six of the players that made 2019 so competitive going off to LIV Golf."

How about adding LPGA Tour stars to the team?

The idea of a mixed Presidents Cup has previously been suggested to make the contest more balanced, given five of the world's top six in the women's game - as of September 29 - would be eligible to represent an International side based on the current criteria.

"Maybe they [the PGA Tour] go into a partnership with the LPGA Tour to create something like that," former Ryder Cup captain Paul McGinley recently told Sky Sports. "Whether they do it for the Presidents Cup is doubtful, because they've already said no to that situation evolving.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Following Luke Donald's comments suggesting a possible mixed team event in the future, former Ryder Cup captain Paul McGinley discussed how - or if - the idea could work

"They may open up a new pathway for it, you never know, but it does make a lot of sense to do that because then you would get two really good, balanced teams. If you add half of the ladies internationally combined with the men, you would have a pretty formidable team that would be very strong against the might of America."

Any addition of female participation would offer its own challenges on the course in terms of tee positions and the formats used, along with schedule agreements and tour partnerships off it, but it's something Min Woo Lee would be open to see happening in the future.

"It would be nice to have her [Minjee Lee, his sister] on the team and me on the team - think it would be very fun," Lee said ahead of this year's event. "It would make it interesting, for sure. Even just the best ball, like mixed best ball, mixed foursome would be unbelievable."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Sunday singles at the Solheim Cup, where Team Europe closed out a 15-13 win over Team USA

Should the Presidents Cup go global more often?

The PGA Tour already offers an American-heavy schedule of events, so why not take their marquee team event elsewhere and show off their star players to a global audience?

Some 18 different nationalities have represented the Internationals at a Presidents Cup, including seven at Medinah, yet only four countries - outside the United States - have ever hosted the biennial contest.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nico Echavarria silenced the American crowd with a sensational chip-in birdie at the 16th during the Sunday singles, then shushed the home fans in celebration

South Africa, a nation with huge golfing history and one that produced huge crowds for a LIV Golf event earlier this year, hasn't held the Presidents Cup since the historic 15-15 tie in 2003.

Australia, Canada and South Korea are the only other previous other host nations, with the Middle East, India, Japan and New Zealand all potential golfing markets for the Presidents Cup to explore.

Always playing the Presidents Cup outside of the United States would take the PGA Tour to new areas and could inspire a new generation of international stars. Plus, more away matches could also help Team USA's bid to end a dismal Ryder Cup record on the road.

Could Europe help the International Team?

Europe have used a variety of different match play events to give players experience of playing in a team environment, but could one involving the Internationals be of benefit to both?

The now-defunct Seve Trophy and the current Hero Cup have been events where Great Britain and Ireland have faced Continental Europe, while the EurAsia Cup was a team competition previously played between Europe and Asia.

All three have given potential Ryder Cup players the chance to impress, with Ramsus Hojgaard featuring in the Hero Cup last January before making his Team Europe debut at Bethpage Black later that season.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the key moments from the final day of the 2025 Ryder Cup, where Team Europe held on for victory

While those team competitions haven't typically included all of Europe's marquee talent, a new competition would give the Internationals a bonus week together to experiment with different partnerships and prepare to face the United States.

The biggest challenge for his idea would be where it fits in the schedule, given the Presidents Cup and Ryder Cup take place in alternate years. Would an early-season slot - like the Hero Cup uses - work ahead of the PGA Tour campaign?

Image: Team USA celebrate extending their winning record at the Presidents Cup

How about a different team tournament?

Should the golfing calendar get in the way of Europe providing the Internationals with another team tournament, could they create their own biennial event for the non-Presidents Cup years?

Asia vs the rest of the world, outside of Europe and United States? A Northern Hemisphere vs Southern Hemisphere team contest? A nation vs nation competition to bring together possible future pairings? There's plenty of fun to possibly be had.

We already have the Hanwha LifePlus International Crown on the LPGA Tour, a team tournament that sees different nations go head-to-head across multiple formats, but a similar event is currently lacking from the men's schedule.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the final day of the 2025 Hanwha LifePlus International Crown, where Australia lifted the trophy

One could slot into the post-season during Ryder Cup years, which is not administered by the PGA Tour, giving them another team event to sell globally and be another way to allow the International players practice of competing in team golf.

The Ryder Cup and Solheim Cup have both continued to grow in stature within the sporting calendar. Another Presidents Cup defeat for the Internationals means the contest may need to evolve and make changes to improve its own status.

What's next?

The United States will be back in action next September when they take on Team Europe in the Ryder Cup, held at Adare Manor in Ireland from September 17-19. Sports.title: Giants trade for McCarthy after Dart injury
Sports.content:
The New York Giants are trading for Minnesota Vikings quarterback J.J. McCarthy after losing Jaxson Dart for the rest of the 2026 NFL season.

Dart suffered a year-ending knee injury early in New York's Week Two defeat to the Los Angeles Rams as they begin a new chapter in their first season under head coach John Harbaugh.

Veteran Jameis Winston replaced Dart under center and started on Sunday as the Giants beat the Tennessee Titans to improve to 2-1 on the year.

NFL Network reported that the Giants are trading a 2027 fifth-round pick to the Vikings in exchange for McCarthy, who was the 10th overall pick in the 2024 Draft.

For more than one reason McCarthy has failed to establish himself as Minnesota's starter since being drafted out of Michigan, where he played under Jim Harbaugh, brother of Giants head coach John.

He suffered a year-ending injury in preseason of his rookie campaign, paving the way for Sam Darnold to launch his career revival by spearheading Kevin O'Connell's side to an unlikely playoff berth.

Darnold departed the following offseason to sign with the Seattle Seahawks, opening the door for McCarthy to get his Vikings career up and running upon his return to full health.

McCarthy marked his NFL debut by helping the Vikings overturn an 11-point fourth-quarter deficit to beat the Chicago Bears in Week One of the 2025 season. He threw two interceptions against the Atlanta Falcons the following week, during which he suffered an ankle injury that would rule him out of the next five weeks.

Sports.title: Israel captain stokes feud by saying ‘our country is 10 times better than Ireland’
Sports.content:
Manor Solomon claimed Israel was “10 times better” than Ireland as fallout intensified from their Nations League match and stated bluntly: “They hate us and we don’t like them.”

Players in the Republic of Ireland side stared at the ground during Israel’s anthem and their staff faced away from the pitch. Ireland’s players also chose not to shake hands or exchange pennants with their opponents in protest at Israeli military actions in Gaza which have killed tens of thousands of people.

Solomon, who plays for West Ham, told Israel’s Sport 5 channel: “If I say what I think about them I’ll probably be banned for a few games, so I don’t want to say what I think about them. Obviously they hate us and we don’t like them.”

View image in fullscreen Republic of Ireland captain Dara O'Shea (left) turns away from Israel captain Manor Solomon before kick-off. Photograph: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP/Getty Images

Ireland won the game 3-0 in Debrecen, Hungary, on Sunday and the return next Sunday will also be played on neutral territory, in Serbia. “I’m already looking forward to the next game against them,” Solomon, Israel’s captain, said.

Pressed on Ireland’s behaviour during Israel’s anthem, he said: “They don’t interest me. We have a country 10 times better than theirs, stronger than theirs. We have an amazing country with amazing people.

“We’re proud to wear the national team’s uniform and to be Israelis; proud of our country and our soldiers. And they can pull all the stunts they want and do whatever they want. We are Israelis, we love our country – and that’s how it will always be.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | Manchester City come out swinging haymakers after charges galore
Sports.content:
A STAIN ON THE PREMIER LEAGUE?

Football Daily wasn’t alone in spending the weekend wondering if we might have a legal case against Manchester City, while pondering what fiscal value we’d put on the mild disappointment of seeing our team lose the 2014 Fizzy (nee Credit Card) Cup final to a team since found guilty of cheating. Elsewhere, Tony Pulis has made it clear he wants the FA Cup his Stoke City sophisticates didn’t win in 2011. Romelu Lukaku used a Nations League match to accuse Gianluigi Donnarumma of owing him two Premier League titles and the Michael Sheen/Brian Clough “chuck all your medals in the biggest effing dustbin you can find” gif has been doing seriously big numbers on Social Media Disgrace.

While the Premier League has yet to confirm Friday’s leaked news that City have been found guilty of the vast majority of more than 100 charges, it’s already clear the ramifications will be far-reaching and potentially endless. Enormous fines, relegation, multiple giant asterisks, staggered points deductions and demotion to the North West Counties League have all been mooted as possible punishments. If the most pessimistic harbingers of doom are to be believed, the club will do well to end this episode in their history without having their entire Etihad Campus uprooted and catapulted straight into the sun.

Considering we’ve all seen them protest their innocence throughout the entire investigation into their financial shenanigans, all but the most delusional City conspiracy theorists could be forgiven for presuming the club might now prostrate itself obsequiously before the beaks and beg them for some modicum of mercy. Sadly, that is not and has never been how they roll under their nation state owners and on Saturday they came out swinging haymakers. “The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began,” huffed the club chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, in a letter to fans conveying the impression that if the laws of physics ever rule against his club, Isaac Newton will be hearing from their army of lawyers.

Of course while Martin Tyler and Sergio Agüero mournfully contemplate the fact that the goal they made more famous than any other scored in Premier League history may ultimately be consigned to the big dustbin of Didn’t Happen, it remains to be seen what effect the guilty verdicts will have on the current City team. While they lead the Premier League, costly mistakes made by Nico O’Reilly and Marc Guéhi in England’s defeat at the hands of Spain suggest the potential for apocalyptic sanctions being imposed on their club may prove quite the distraction. “I don’t think automatic relegation will be applied,” said the football finance expert Kieran Maguire, a man currently getting more radio airplay than Taylor Swift. “We’re at the end of September and if we do that at the end of September, what’s Manchester City going to do until next August?” Appeal any judgments against them, is Football Daily’s best guess. And ideally in a process that can’t be hurried.

LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE

Join Michael Butler from 7.45pm BST for hot clockwatch action in the Nations League with Belgium 2-3 France, Northern Ireland 0-2 Hungary and more.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“It’s probably been the toughest day of my coaching career. But it’s not about me. It’s about the players and they’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them. They represented themselves on the pitch with dignity but also with the power of proud Irishmen. They’ve shown today how much playing for Ireland means to them and hopefully they will have the support of the Irish people.” – Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, after his side’s 3-0 victory against Israel in the Nations League. Before Sunday’s controversial Nations League fixture, the Irish players looked down at the grass with their heads bowed and hands behind their backs during the Israeli national anthem, and the Irish captain, Dara O’Shea, shook hands with the referee and his assistants but there was no attempt to shake the hand of the Israel captain, Manor Solomon.

Sports.title: Defensive flux gives Tuchel headache but Alexander-Arnold could be remedy | Jacob Steinberg
Sports.content:
England ended 2025 protected by a shield of deceptive strength. They went through qualifying for the World Cup without conceding a goal and secured a shutout during a routine friendly win against Wales. However, clean sheets have been harder to come by this year. England have kept four in 13 games in 2026, meaning it may not be long before Thomas Tuchel rethinks his suggestion that the way to deal with his side’s lack of control is to embrace chaos.

There is, of course, an irony to telling Tuchel to sort out his defence. Isn’t this what we wanted? England were limp and passive when they lost their World Cup semi-final against Argentina. At least the mindset was positive when Tuchel’s side opened their Nations League campaign with a sprightly but flawed 3-2 defeat against Spain last Saturday.

England played on the front foot and led after a thrilling surge. They had Spain on the ropes but it was unsustainable. Another lead was squandered against elite opposition, and although a lack of ambition was not to blame this time Tuchel still came away with tactical issues to solve before facing Czechia in Prague on Tuesday evening.

This is England’s second of four games during this break and they need a win to give themselves a proper shot of reaching the quarter-finals in March. Croatia await in Rijeka on Saturday and are likely to be tougher than a Czechia side who failed to make it out of a weak group at the World Cup.

England could do with a confidence-boosting clean sheet. They were worryingly fragile against Spain, who created an expected goals of 3.08 from open play, and could have been 4-0 down by the time Anthony Gordon cancelled out Lamine Yamal’s early goal.

Neutralising Albania, Andorra, Latvia and Serbia during World Cup qualifying told us nothing. England have since been breached by Uruguay, Japan, Croatia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Mexico, Norway, Argentina, France and Spain. They were not tested when they kept clean sheets in World Cup warm-ups against against New Zealand and Costa Rica. They were fortunate not to concede during group games against Ghana and Panama.

There are individual and collective issues. Two of Spain’s goals were errors, with Marc Guéhi and Nico O’Reilly punished. Jordan Pickford had some ropey moments in goal during the World Cup and Ezri Konsa has lacked consistency as Guéhi’s partner in the middle.

Tuchel wants an aggressive line. He has favoured a mobile pairing of Konsa and Guéhi in central defence in seven of the past 13 games. Alternatives such as Jarrad Branthwaite, Trevoh Chalobah and Levi Colwill are untested. A viable replacement for John Stones is yet to emerge. Stones starting forces England to move deeper but one of their better defensive displays at the World Cup came when the 32-year-old nullified Erling Haaland during the win against Norway.

However there is a misconception that England are experts at backs-to-the-wall defending. They were heroic when down to 10 during their last-16 win against Mexico, but they conceded a lot of chances from crosses when the numbers were even at the Azteca. The pressure eventually tells. Argentina saw England fall back, repeatedly hit them from the wide areas and grabbed the winner when Lionel Messi crossed for Lautaro Martínez to head home. Gareth Southgate’s England conceded from crosses and set pieces in crunch knockout games against Croatia, Italy and Spain.

View image in fullscreen Ezri Konsa is a mobile centre-back but he made a glaring error against Spain. Photograph: MI News/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Harry Maguire, a powerful aerial presence, played in two of those games. Tuchel has discarded him and is looking for a more progressive way than absorbing punches. Yet England’s lack of control leaves them susceptible in a variety of ways. Uruguay won an equalising penalty with a deep cross. Japan ran through midfield to score on the counterattack. Mexico profited from set pieces. Croatia and the DRC caused problems with switches of play. Spain cut through the middle for their winner on Saturday. It was easy to focus on the defenders being pulled out of position. It is worth remembering that England are not the same when Declan Rice is unavailable in midfield.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

England do not function without Rice’s interceptions, positional discipline and ability to fill holes. There was a moment against Spain when Konsa goofed the interception after leaving his position to challenge for an Unai Simón clearance, forcing James Trafford to save after Ferran Torres darted through a big gap in England’s defence. The risks were extreme. England tried to go man-for-man but the centre-backs were missing and Jarell Quansah was 10 yards deeper than O’Reilly, the other full-back.

This can partly be put down to inexperience. O’Reilly and Quansah, more comfortable at centre-back, are young. Individual attributes also play a part. Southgate had the cheat code otherwise known as peak Kyle Walker, whose recovery pace at right-back gave England freedom to push up. Reece James is Tuchel’s first choice but does not have Walker’s durability. James is out of this camp after yet another injury and often plays as a midfielder for Chelsea, who feel their captain lacks the physical capacity to function as a modern full-back.

It is not ideal that Tuchel has had to chop and change so much. Southgate knew his best defence – Walker, John Stones, Maguire and Luke Shaw – but Tuchel has struggled to find a settled back four.

The Newcastle full-back Tino Livramento withdrew last week. Stones, Djed Spence and Dan Burn are also unavailable. There is a lot of flux. O’Reilly and Konsa followed individual programmes before England flew to Prague on Monday. Lewis Hall, who has four caps, could replace O’Reilly at left-back. Trent Alexander-Arnold could make his first international appearance since a brief runout against Andorra in June 2025.

Tuchel has looked at eight right-backs since last giving Alexander-Arnold a chance. He did not take the Real Madrid right-back to the World Cup and does not trust his defensive acumen. The counter-argument is that England are not exactly solid without Alexander-Arnold; what do they have to lose by trying to tap into his creative threat?

Sports.title: Europe’s top-flight clubs to get share of £185m from Club World Cup
Sports.content:
Europe’s top-flight clubs will share half of the $250m (£185m) solidarity pot from the Club World Cup last year, ending a saga that had caused widespread frustration among those who did not participate in the tournament.

Fifa and European Football Clubs (EFC) are close to an agreement that would bring a 50-50 split between sides in Europe and the rest of the world. The fund, set aside to ensure the competition contributes to football’s wider ecosystem, will be distributed once the deal has been ratified.

EFC had sought a share of just over 60% , but compromised after Fifa insisted on a more equal global distribution. A portion of the $125m will be given to all top-division European clubs not involved in the Club World Cup, with amounts varying depending on the number of seasons a side competed at that level between 2021 and 2024.

An amount will also go to clubs with the best performance in Uefa club competitions during that period, again provided they did not play in the tournament in the US in 2025. It raises the likelihood of clubs receiving wildly varying payments. Liverpool, the Champions League runners-up in 2022, would be among those to benefit at the higher end of the scale.

EFC will stage its general assembly in Copenhagen on Tuesday and the agreement is likely to be confirmed after approval by the Fifa council, which is scheduled to meet in Zurich on 15 October.

Clubs from smaller leagues had grown particularly exasperated at the drawn-out timeline for receiving funds that, in many cases, can present a welcome lifeline. The Club World Cup winners, Chelsea, have long since benefited from their £84m payout out of the £740m set aside as prize money.

EFC threatened Fifa it would not cooperate with future Club World Cups if Gianni Infantino did not withdraw his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme. In the same letter, EFC said the lack of a solution on Club World Cup solidarity payments was “of serious disappointment to EFC and our member clubs”.

A joint venture between EFC and Fifa, intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions, remains on the table, but is unlikely to be signed in the near future given the turbulence surrounding world football’s leadership.

Infantino addressed the EFC general assembly in Rome last year, but a repeat performance is not likely this time given the prospect of a direct encounter with adversaries such as the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino spent Monday attempting to boost his standing in Europe by travelling to Riga for the opening of new offices at the Latvian Football Association. The Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, is expected to be among the delegates in Copenhagen.

Sports.title: The Nations League is a welcome example of soccer done well
Sports.content:
England’s first game after the 2022 World Cup was a 2-1 win away over Italy. Their first game after the 2018 World Cup was a 2-1 defeat to Spain. Their first game after the 2014 World Cup was a 1-0 friendly win over Norway – and that was not the Norway of Erling Haaland, Martin Ødegaard and Antonio Nusa but of Joshua King, Håvard Nordtveit and Tarik Elyounoussi. The first game after the 2010 World Cup was a 2-1 friendly win over Hungary.

The Italy and Spain games perhaps had their appeal, but the sense of anticlimax was palpable. It’s inevitable, of course: how can a side or its supporters pick themselves to go again after the unparalleled drama of a World Cup? Major tournaments, whether a team does well or badly, are sport played with maximum emotion; there cannot be anything except a comedown, whether after glorious victory, thrilling defeat or ignominious exit.

Which is why the Nations League is such a boon. It is not a meaningless friendly, instantly forgotten amid the squadrons of paper airplanes swooping down from the bored masses at Wembley. It is not the start of a qualifying process for another, distant tournament. It matters as much as a team decides it does. A manager who wants to experiment can do so, safe in the knowledge that nobody will become too distraught about results.

But equally there is a purpose to winning, a prize at the end – even if it did sound a little desperate when Roberto Martínez defended his record as Portugal manager by pointing to his Nations League success in 2025. And as a quick test of just how relevant the Nations League is, ask yourself how many of its former winners you can name. In that sense, it occupies a similar role to the Carabao Cup, a competition that is not nothing but is not obviously something either. In the international calendar, it operates as a palate-cleanser.

Admittedly in part because of the breaking news in the Manchester City case, Saturday’s game between England and Spain arrived almost unnoticed. The Premier League paused. There was some mild relitigation of England’s World Cup exit to Argentina. And then suddenly there was the game: England against the world champions at Wembley, which soon became a contest that took on a life of its own.

In one sense, the outcome was much the same as it was for England against Argentina in Atlanta. England led the reigning world champions by a single goal with 55 minutes played, and then collapsed to concede twice. But in other ways, this was a significant improvement. Two of Spain’s three goals were the result of individual errors (both, oddly, by City players, which perhaps raises the question of how much the previous day’s revelations were playing on their minds). Harry Kane slipped while taking a penalty that would have made it 3-1 and slammed it against the bar. Although Spain missed chances and their margin of victory could have been greater, on another day England might easily have won by a couple of goals. And against a team as good as Spain, maybe that’s the best that can realistically be hoped for. England, perhaps no side, can hope to squeeze them out completely, but to make it a game either side could have won, even if Spain shaded it, is an achievement in itself.

Would English soccer suddenly have been redeemed had Kane converted and England won 3-1? Of course not: the frustrations of the Argentina defeat would still linger. But equally this was an opportunity for England to move on, for Thomas Tuchel to begin the process of learning from the mistakes of the semi-final. Perhaps England will achieve positive results against Croatia and Czechia and qualify for the quarter-finals next March; perhaps not. Far more important is that they continue the process of preparation for the Euros in 2028. But equally, it’s far easier to do that within a structure of at least semi-competitive matches that are simultaneously less important and more challenging than qualifiers.

That, admittedly, is the perspective of a nation like England, for whom qualification for major tournaments can be taken almost as read. But the Nations League has also helped smaller nations. Everybody benefits from playing opponents at roughly their same level. Nobody wants the likes of Andorra and Liechtenstein shut out of international competition, but equally defending desperately to avoid a hammering against even moderate opposition suits nobody. If smaller teams play each other, though, there is a chance of a proper game, with attacking and defending. And, thanks to the way Euros qualification is structured, there is a potential route to the Euros through playoffs, short-cutting for a gifted generation a process that might previously have taken a decade or more of gradual improvements to the coefficient.
