The Nations League was treated with a degree of skepticism when it was introduced in 2018, and not all of the adjustments to the format seem to have been entirely beneficial. But fundamentally it has worked, and serves as a welcome reminder that, sometimes, this sport’s administrators get things right.

Sports.title: Arsène Wenger and Arsenal: 30 years on from appointment that changed English football
Sports.content:
As feedback goes, even a character as relentlessly optimistic as David Dein might have considered the reaction to his bold managerial appointment suboptimal. Thirty years ago, Arsenal were in a state of chaotic flux, having sacked Bruce Rioch, with the interims Stewart Houston and Pat Rice in charge. There had been talk of Johan Cruyff arriving and Dein wanted to fill the information vacuum. Summoning the team, he reassured them a new manager would soon be appointed and that he was a world-class addition.

“His name is Arsène Wenger,” Dein, the club’s vice-chair, beamed. A brief pause ensued before a player’s voice called out: “Who the fuck is he?” His exclamation echoed conventional wisdom. “Arsene Who?” famously read The London Evening Standard’s billboards prior to Wenger being confirmed as manager on 30 September 1996.

Ultimately Dein’s decision was arguably the most seismic managerial appointment in modern English football history, not only providing proof that a foreign manager could succeed in this country but also ushering in an irreversible era of multiculturalism, giving birth to the globalised Premier League we know today. Wenger described the Arsenal dressing room he inherited as “culturally English” and set about making his first signings, the characteristically unknown Frenchmen in Patrick Vieira and Rémi Garde; when he departed the job in 2018, every Premier League dressing room was a veritable United Nations.

He was the trailblazer, preceding Gérard Houllier and Rafael Benítez at Liverpool and, ironically given their mutual animosity, José Mourinho at Chelsea, all beneficiaries of his success. On the flip side, there would never have been Tottenham’s ill-advised experiments with Christian Gross and Jacques Santini were it not for Wenger.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal’s squad for the 1996-97 season. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

Undoubtedly he was the right man at the right time: Chelsea were already embracing the continental drift, having appointed Ruud Gullit, and Wenger’s arrival chimed with contemporary geopolitics. Tony Blair was about to become prime minister and a wave of European Union migration was coming; Polish plumbers and French footballers alike. Equally, Sky TV’s money was making England the best-paid country for footballers.

The first non-British or non-Irish manager in the top flight had been Dr Jozef Venglos, appointed by Aston Villa in 1990, ticking all the boxes of English football’s old prejudices: foreign, academic, whimsical, tactical. Gratifyingly for sceptics, he was an utter failure. Wenger seemed to fit the Venglos mould. Nicknamed Le Professeur (because he wore glasses and spoke five languages), his captain, Tony Adams, thought him a “geography teacher”, while Ian Wright noted his clumsiness and dubbed him Clouseau, taking delight in pranking him about a bomb scare. “There is bum?” replied a bemused Wenger, oblivious to the hilarity among Wright’s teammates.

View image in fullscreen Arsène Wenger’s arrival brought many changes for the Arsenal squad. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

“Arsène Wenger’s been in Japan, he doesn’t know anything about the English game,” said Sir Alex Ferguson, laying the foundations for a decade-long feud that would become, in Ferguson’s words, “toxic”. Yet even the bastions of the English game acknowledge the magnitude of Wenger’s contribution. “Wenger changed the whole course of [English] football,” says Neil Warnock, not a natural soulmate. “He made people who’d been in the game a long time [realise] that you had to change with the times because of all the nutrition coming, the fitness guys who were coming, and that if you didn’t move with the times, you got trodden on.”

Wenger’s aesthetic playing style was encapsulated upon securing his first Premier League title in 1998, with a pastiche of Total Football that culminated in Steve Bould drifting out of the back four to chip a pass on to the advancing Tony Adams, who finished perfectly in a 4-0 win over Everton. “Would you believe it?!” said a stunned Martin Tyler in commentary, reflecting the views of the nation. “That sums it all up.” Derided as a donkey, Adams had become a thoroughbred.

View image in fullscreen Arsène Wenger with Tony Adams after Arsenal had turned on the style against Everton to clinch the title. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Action Images

Wenger’s genius was in maintaining an English core to his early side, grafting on Vieira, Emmanuel Petit, Marc Overmars and allowing Dennis Bergkamp to flourish. “There were rumours that he was advised to get rid of the back four,” said Nigel Winterburn, part of that legendary quartet. “But I think he made his own decisions when he saw the players playing and training, and saw the desire they had.” Later Thierry Henry, Robert Pires and Freddie Ljungberg would arrive to reach the even greater heights of the Invincibles.

Dr Yann Rougier joined as a sports scientist and Ferguson, in charge of a dominant Manchester United team, was instinctively suspicious of the new methods challenging his success. When the England manager Glenn Hoddle, a Wenger protege at Monaco, used Rougier at the 1998 World Cup and United players came back singing the praises of his nutritional approach, Ferguson was infuriated, demanding FA investigations. Yet most of the interventions nowadays would be regarded as standard, such as using creatine to supplement diets.

Chocolate was famously banned at Arsenal but Winterburn revealed the manager’s strictures were not always adhered to. “We’d wait for Arsène to walk [away], then most of the players would pile into the little kiosk and buy chocolate and eat Mars bars under the table.” What became known as the “Evian broccoli” diet was introduced just as Adams had announced himself an alcoholic, lager being the habitual post-match refreshment of British football. Adams attributed his late-career transformation to Wenger’s nutrition and his teetotalism. Eschewing alcohol is unremarkable among elite England players now.

View image in fullscreen A 2-1 win over Leicester at Highbury in May 2004 saw them finish the season with a record of P38 W26 D12 L0, which led them to acquire the nickname ‘The Invincibles’. Photograph: Sean Dempsey/PA

Hoddle had also been transformed by Wenger’s holistic approach to exercise. “We were in the dark ages [in England] by comparison,” he said. “I had never had a massage or done a warm-down at Tottenham. I became more supple and I was soon fitter than ever.” Wenger employed a French osteopath, Philippe Boixel, and used the English psychologist David Elliott. Arsenal were the first club to sign up with ProZone, using stats to analyse performance. There aren’t many innovations in modern English football not pioneered by him and, in that respect, his influence is greater than even Ferguson’s, even if his success never measured up to the Scot’s achievements. By the end, Wenger’s French revolution had become common practice; he was a victim of his own success, his competitive edge dulled.

Only when the prizefighters had laid down their gloves was Ferguson able to articulate his appreciation. “Arsène is, without doubt, one of the greatest Premier League managers and I am proud to have been a rival, a colleague and a friend to such a great man,” he said when Wenger left Arsenal. Wenger might raise a quizzical Gallic eyebrow at the “friend” description. But 30 years on, few dispute the scale of Wenger’s transformation of the English game.

Sports.title: WSL talking points: Chelsea punish Arsenal and Putellas finds her rhythm
Sports.content:
1 Same old Arsenal problems

How to solve the problem of an inability to take your chances? That is the question that will haunt the Arsenal head coach, Renée Slegers, over the coming days. In their 1-0 defeat by Chelsea, Arsenal applied more than enough pressure to make a difference, but in registering two of their 18 shots on target, a fundamental lack of ruthlessness remains. They dominated the opening stages at Stamford Bridge, but, as has often been the case this season, they were made to pay for their wastefulness. None of their nine first-half attempts troubled the goalkeeper, Hannah Hampton. Chelsea, however, had five of eight on target and scored just before half-time through Alyssa Thompson. “I wanted to keep it away from the players because they can score goals and they can finish and they will get the rewards for their work,” Slegers said. Solutions need to be found quickly. Sophie Downey

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Arsenal

View image in fullscreen Arsenal’s lack of ruthlessness was on display in their loss to Chelsea. Photograph: Naomi Baker/WSL Football/Getty Images

2 Putellas finds her rhythm

There was almost a sigh of relief from Alexia Putellas as she watched the ball fly past the Brighton goalkeeper, Chiamaka Nnadozie, before turning to the crowd in celebration. The weight of expectation has been heavy for the Spaniard, who arrived at London City Lionesses in July, and it has taken her time to settle. The 2-0 win against Brighton featured her best performance as she began to dictate play from central areas. Putellas created the most chances and her goal gave Eder Maestre’s side something to build on as they continue to show progress. Brighton continued to look bright in phases, but struggled to create anything of note. A core problem is their lack of versatility in attack. They still lack a proper striker, which has been the case for almost a year, and is hampering them. SD

3 Liverpool rave about Ramos

Liverpool appear to have pulled off a masterstroke by signing Natalia Ramos from Tenerife in August. The Spanish midfielder entertained the Anfield crowd on Sunday with a performance full of creativity and energy, as well as deadly set-piece deliveries, including an assist for the opener in their 2-0 win. After eight years with Tenerife, she has quickly become a fans’ favourite at Liverpool. “She brings such personality,” said the head coach, Gareth Tayor. “I can imagine people enjoy watching Natalia play because she’s very humble and very open to learning, even at 27 years old. She’s been a ray of sunshine coming into this group because she’s very caring, very honest and very open – she’s just a brilliant teammate.” Tom Garry

Match report: Liverpool 2-0 Everton

View image in fullscreen Natalia Ramos provided the assist for Liverpool’s opener much to the delight of the Anfield faithful. Photograph: Becky Oliver/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

4 Pelova sets the tone

Victoria Pelova is beginning to look like the player Tottenham hoped they had signed. The midfielder followed two goals against Crystal Palace a week earlier with another double in the 4-0 win over Aston Villa. Her influence stretched beyond goals, with her movement and pressing helping Spurs maintain their dominance. They had 15 shots in the first half without scoring, but found their cutting edge after the break. “She sets the tone for the team,” the Spurs head coach, Martin Ho, said, praising Pelova’s “attitude and mentality” under pressure. Her confidence appears to be returning and Ho believes the freedom provided by those around her is allowing the best of Pelova to emerge. Mitul Samji

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

5 Midweek tonic pays off for United

IManchester United enjoyed themselves during a 10-1 victory over Sheffield United last Wednesday in the new Subway Players Cup, recording their first victory since March. That seemed to help them play with far greater self-assurance on Sunday than in their previous league fixtures. For some teams, midweek games and fixture congestion can be a burden, but it seems to have come at the perfect time after a tricky start and they appeared to be enjoying playing together as they beat West Ham 2-1 in a tight game. West Ham have lost seven times in a row in the league at United. For Eva Olid, it was a first league win in England. TG

View image in fullscreen Andrea Medina scored the winner in Manchester United’s win against West Ham. Photograph: Poppy Townson/Manchester United/Getty Images

6 Charlton show signs of improvement

Saturday brought Charlton’s fourth straight defeat of the WSL season, but they may have emerged from their encounter with Manchester City with renewed belief. In losing 1-0 to the champions, they proved they have more grit than might have been thought. The head coach, Karen Hills, had called for them to be brave and return to the defensive fundamentals that brought them promotion. They had only 25% possession, but their diligence defensively, structure out of possession and willingness to leave everything on the field was clear. “I’m so proud of them,” the head coach said. “I thought the players bought into what I was asking them to do and they delivered it and executed it to the best they can.” SD

7 Hurtré makes mark despite Blues’ struggles

Océane Hurtré jumped to joint-top of the WSL Golden Boot race with a fantastic double for Birmingham against Crystal Palace. The 22-year-old struck inside the opening minute with a curled effort, using the outside of her left boot and hit the target again from a tight angle after 33 minutes. It moved her to four goals, level with Pelova and Manchester City’s Khadija Shaw , despite Birmingham not having won a match. They twice let their lead slip before coming back to score a late equaliser in Sunday’s 3-3 home draw. Hurtré said: “It’s not easy, but we want to win. Crystal Palace scored for 3-2 and we came back so it’s a positive.” Emillia Hawkins

Sports.title: Chelsea turn up heat on Arsenal as Alyssa Thompson strike settles WSL derby
Sports.content:
Arsenal’s title chances were dealt a significant blow after a narrow defeat at the hands of Chelsea. Alyssa Thompson’s first-half finish was the difference on a competitive afternoon at Stamford Bridge but one that ultimately left Renée Slegers with more questions than answers about how to save their season.

“Worried? No,” Slegers said. “Confidence is something that fluctuates. They know who they are and they know what they can bring. What’s important is that there’s always phases in the season and there’s different things you need to work on or focus on.

“It’s important that we keep any pressure and any complexity away from the players because we believe in them. It’s just really important that we keep that simplicity and clear minds for the players.”

There is no game quite as eagerly anticipated in the Women’s Super League as the meeting between Chelsea and Arsenal. While other derbies and duels are in their early development, the London derby is the one year after year that brings the pressure, the drama and, of course, the eyeballs. While both sides clearly respect each other off the pitch, there is a distinct sense that once they cross the white line there is true competitive animosity there, one that lifts the levels of everyone in the vicinity.

This edition was no different with expectation and apprehension buzzing around Stamford Bridge before kick-off and no shortage of new narratives. This was the first time Katie McCabe, 11 years a Gunner, would face her old team having moved in the summer. Would she help Chelsea to inflict more pain on Arsenal’s stuttering start, or could Slegers’s side put a pin in the pressure balloon and breathe new life into their search for a first title in eight years?

Both teams came into this encounter having not yet hit form. Arsenal have created opportunities but have looked predictable in their buildup and lacked a finishing touch. In contrast, Chelsea have looked energetic and full of ideas but, excluding their win against Manchester United, have also struggled with ruthlessness in front of goal.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea’s Katie McCabe took on her former Arsenal teammates for the first time since her summer move. Photograph: Harriet Lander/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Sonia Bompastor was handed a significant boost before kick-off with the news that both Keira Walsh and Lauren James were available to start. Lexi Potter was given the nod alongside Walsh in midfield, a sign of how much trust the head coach has in the 20-year-old, while Melvine Malard was fit enough to begin up front.

Slegers, meanwhile, rang the changes from Arsenal’s hard-fought victory against HB Køge during the week. Two who remained were Kyra Cooney-Cross and the goalkeeper Anneke Borbe, who kept out Misa Rodríguez.

The visitors came out full of energy and looking to make an early statement. They dominated early on with 44.2% of the action happening in Chelsea’s defensive third in the first quarter and Arsenal looking to reap the rewards of their high press.

Their biggest threat early on came from Lisa Baum. The 19-year-old has been one of the more positive aspects of their season to date and was given space down the right by Chelsea.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

For all of their control, however, it was much of the same old story for Slegers’s side, haunted by their inability to take their chances. Of the eight shots they created, they failed to register one on target and hit the woodwork twice through Kim Little and Mariona Caldentey.

With every rattle of a post that reverberated around Stamford Bridge, Arsenal’s early confidence dwindled and Bompastor’s side started to find more joy. In direct contrast to their opponents, the Blues took their chance when it came when Malard pounced on Steph Catley as she played out from the back. Borbe made a good save to deny Walsh initially but the rebound fell perfectly for Thompson to hammer home.

It was the ideal time to score and Chelsea went in ahead at the break with the momentum of the game having shifted significantly. They went on to create big opportunities of their own with Malard dragging a shot narrowly wide on two occasions.

While Arsenal were able to create opportunities, the hosts looked comfortable in the circumstances and defended resolutely to see out the game and take home a valuable three points.

Sports.title: Why Premier League's Man City verdict is treacherous for Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the threat it poses to the British economy and how the Abu Dhabi investment in Manchester is not all it seems
Sports.content:
Manchester City’s celebrity friends were weighing in to defend the club on Monday.

The former Sun editor David Yelland, who co-hosts a podcast about doing good PR, alleged a confidentiality breach had cost the club ‘hundreds of millions’ in reputational damage. Liam Gallagher posted a foul-mouthed message about the ‘red cartel’.

But there are reasons why the emergence of half the story, with proper detail still awaited, helps City, who have been found guilty of all substantive charges of the 115 brought by the Premier League.

In the current hiatus, Abu Dhabi, whose club have denied all charges and may appeal, will be applying pressure on the UK Government and Prime Minister Andy Burnham about the risk to the Gulf state’s trade and investment with the UK, should public humiliation ensue.

Abu Dhabi warned the UK in 2023 that a negative outcome to the 115 charges could damage relations with the UK. Beyond myriad obvious threats – the UAE is behind attempts to save struggling carmaker McLaren and expressing interest in spending a fortune on British defence technology – it has also been involved in the rejuvenation of a part of east Manchester, which helped burnish Burnham’s credentials in his nine years as the city region’s mayor.

That apparent Abu Dhabi dependency in Manchester has brought rich praise for the Gulf state from Burnham in the past. ‘They are more than building a football club. They have been huge partners for the city and they have improved a lot of lives here,’ he said in 2023.

‘They are more than building a football club. They have been huge partners for the city and have improved a lot of lives here,’ Prime Minister Andy Burnham said of Abu Dhabi in 2023

Khaldoon Al Mubarak (right), the City chairman, is also chief executive of Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan's mega-corporation Mubadala

Burnham, who spoke by phone with Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in July, will certainly know the powerful individuals the Premier League are up against.

Khaldoon Al Mubarak, Manchester City chairman and chief executive of Bin Zayed’s mega-corporation Mubadala, which has assets of £290billion invested in businesses around the globe. Simon Pearce, who made his name at the public relations firm Burson-Marsteller before joining Team Abu Dhabi to advise on business possessions like City as well as matters of domestic and foreign policy.

On the face of things, Burnham and Manchester owe Abu Dhabi for the transformation of inner-city areas like Ancoats and New Islington. But within the city itself, there is an alternative view.

Many say those areas of Manchester were already changing, under a masterplan drawn up in the early 2000s by Manchester-based developer Urban Splash and architect Will Alsop, before the Abu Dhabis bought City in 2008. The local vision was for re-development which would include social housing so locals would not be priced out.

The financial crash of 2008-10 saw the newly-arrived Abu Dhabi United Group – City’s owners – forming a partnership called ‘Manchester Life’ with Manchester City Council and taking over all the redevelopment.

The story of what happened next is told in substantial detail by the writer and broadcaster Adrian Goldberg in his book Where’s the Money Gone? The Battle for the Soul of English Football.

Goldberg details how the requirement for social housing was quietly dropped, making this an immensely lucrative, upmarket development for the Abu Dhabis. Taxpayer money had already done the ‘heavy lifting’ by preparing the polluted land for development. Mansour has now built around 1,500 homes in the area and takes rent.

Who earns what has been shrouded in secrecy for years. But after a Freedom of Information request, the independent Manchester investigative news site The Mill revealed the council had granted Mansour first right of refusal – carte blanche – on all development sites in a huge area of land in Manchester.

Weavers Quay and the Ancoats regeneration area of Manchester, which has been funded in large part by Abu Dhabi

Manchester City celebrate winning the Premier League title - a competition they have dominated over the last decade

Another Freedom of Information request, by the BBC, uncovered how Manchester city council received no rental income from Mansour’s Manchester Life until 2023/24, when it was paid £2.9million by them.

Mansour’s companies had, by then, earned more than £39m from Manchester Life over a period of five years.

Private developers, backed by independent academic analysis, are furious that land provided to Abu Dhabi by the council was not offered on the open market via a transparent tendering process.

The council, which had been forced to cut £443m from its budget after 2010, was desperate for cash at that time. Goldberg cites an academic whose research shows the land was sold too cheaply by local politicians who were ‘wary of challenging’ the Abu Dhabis ‘in case it dampened Emirati enthusiasm for the football club’.

This alternative narrative demonstrates that City's owners' arrival on Manchester’s property scene is not the story of altruism and beneficence that the club have always pressed home.

The same can be said of the Al Nahyan dynasty’s UK investments in British children’s homes and special needs schools, detailed by the Daily Mail’s award-winning foreign correspondent Ian Birrell last year.

Through Witherslack, a company owned by Mubadala, Abu Dhabi raked in £208m of revenue in 2024 by running 38 children’s homes, at a time when demand for special needs education had left English councils struggling to find places in state schools.

One Witherslack school, Birrell showed, was charging up to £116,611 per pupil aged between five and 19 – almost double the fees for Eton – despite a witheringly negative Ofsted report.

An aeriel view of the regenerated Ancoats and Islington Cotton Fields neighbourhood in Manchester

Manager Pep Guardiola won four Premier League titles in a row and six in total during his time at Manchester City

That is the state of play at what might be called the micro level. But the bigger picture looks different. The UK is struggling to find the money to develop in ways that are required. A report on the state of the nation’s infrastructure recently found that £258bn of public investment is needed. And in 2021, Britain struck a £10bn UAE commitment to invest.

During David Cameron’s leadership of a Conservative government in 2015, Britain’s perceived failure to take a hard stance on a pro-Islam political group led the UAE to threaten a block on billion-pound arms deals.

‘The difficult conversations we’ve been having will become far more difficult,’ Al Mubarak warned the UK Government. It was a minor spat, compared with this one. The discussions with people he once lavished praise on look treacherous for Burnham.

Sports.title: Andy Murray calls out pushy parents and reveals tennis mum asked him if her son, 6, should see a sports psychologist over 'mental' problem
Sports.content:
Sir Andy Murray has questioned pushy tennis parents after recently being asked by a mum whether her six-year-old son should see a sports psychologist.

The three-time major winner was asked on Andy Roddick's Served podcast about whether he was a 'good sports dad'.

Murray, a father of four, declared that he is a 'good sports dad' and is 'definitely not' a parent who shouts while watching his children play.

The two-time Wimbledon champion, who retired in 2024, however revealed he has come across some 'interesting parenting' when watching.

Murray cited the example of a tennis mum, who believed her six-year-old son had a 'mental' problem that had prevented him from winning matches.

'I have seen some interesting parenting at some of the sports,' Murray said.

Sir Andy Murray has questioned pushy tennis parents after recently being asked by a mum whether her six-year-old son should see a sports psychologist

Murray revealed to Andy Roddick that he had seen 'interesting parenting' while watching his own children play sport

'My son went to his first tennis competition a few weeks ago. He has been playing for like three months.

'I had one of the parents come to me and they were like, "What do you think is wrong with my son? He keeps losing matches, he gets to match point and he just can't get over the line".

'The kid is six.

'These matches are first to 10 points so they are done in about three or four minutes. The kids have no idea what's going on.

'I was like, "I don't know, I have never seen your child hit a ball", and she was like, "I think it's definitely mental".

'She said, "Did you ever use a sports psychologist?" And I went, "I did, but not when I was six".'

Murray's comments reflect similar concerns raised by his own mum Judy earlier this year.

Judy, who pushed back at her own portrayal as a pushy parent during Andy and Jamie Murray's careers, revealed she had learned not to put pressure on her sons after seeing how scared their peers were about disappointing their parents.

Judy Murray said earlier this year that she learned not to put pressure on her sons after seeing how scared their peers were about disappointing their parents

She described how youngsters playing alongside her sons would often approach her after games to discuss their trepidation after losses.

Murray said the children would be upset, knowing their parents would be ‘angry’ at them or distant if they didn’t win.

‘I learned a lot about how not to parent by observing many parents in junior tennis, how they behaved with their kids,' she said on the Tennis Insider Club podcast.

‘The kids would come to me and they're upset and they've lost, and they don't want to get in the car with their father on the way home because [they say] “He's going to be really angry with me. He is not going to talk to me all the way home”.

‘You learn this from the kids.

'They're telling you and it's making them anxious and then you realise why they play with fear and caution and they don't want to risk anything because they're scared to lose because of the way that the parents behave.’

Sports.title: Man City's legacy will be 'GONE' if they lose appeal against Premier League - and Liverpool could be handed two titles as a result, argues Graeme Souness
Sports.content:
Graeme Souness believes Manchester City's recent legacy will be forever ruined if their guilt in their battle with the Premier League is confirmed.

The Liverpool legend says City should be stripped of their titles – and hand them over to the Reds in the years they beat them to top spot.

City have been found guilty of 114 of their 115 rule-break charges, according to sources, with the club accused of widespread financial cheating over an era of sustained success.

The process will move to an appeal stage, but any eventual punishment could include a fine, points deduction, relegation, or even the stripping of trophies.

Souness told Track Radio: 'The legacy is gone. If it goes the wrong way for them they'll be consigned to history that they were cheats and whatever they did, whatever they won in that period, should not count.

'There’s an argument for Liverpool to have a couple of Premier Leagues given to them.

Graeme Souness says Man City will lose their legacy if their war with the Premier League fails

'For them [City] to be stripped of whatever they’ve won in that period of time, for them... money's not an issue.

'So whatever fine is just like a scratch in the surface. Relegation [as an option]... I don't know.

'But I come back to it. I think this is going to open a can of worms, which I think may go well beyond the realms of football.'

City have publicly maintained their innocence throughout the process, with chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak saying last week: 'Our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began.'

Man City were charged in February 2023 by the Premier League with a hearing concluding in December 2024.

Their statement that February insisted that they were 'surprised' by the charges.

The Premier League accused Man City of multiple breaches of financial rules and of failing to co-operate with a subsequent investigation. The alleged rule breaking was claimed to have taken place over a 14-year period, with the most serious across an eight-year spell.

A three-man panel was tasked with considering the evidence, with the initial expectation a verdict would have been reached on the case within months. It has since taken three-and-a-half years.

The verdict could lead to a variety of punishments including huge points deductions, financial penalties, and even relegation

The charges stretch from the years 2009 to 2023, encompassing much of the Pep Guardiola era, though the most serious end at 2018

The original 115 charges were extended to a total of 130 after an administration issue in what is the most expensive and wide-ranging case in English football history.

City remained steadfast in maintaining their innocence over more than 115 alleged breaches across eight years, some including the start of the Pep Guardiola era.

The club were accused of failing to report accurate financial information for nine seasons stretching from 2009-10 to 2017-18, as well as failing to provide full details of former manager Roberto Mancini’s pay between 2009-10 and 2012-13.

They were also alleged to have failed to provide full details of money paid to players between 2010-11 and 2015-16 and failing to co-operate with the probe from 2018 to 2023.

Between the years mentioned, Manchester City won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League, four FA Cups and seven EFL Cups.

In 2022, Guardiola said he would quit the club if he felt the club's hierarchy had ever lied to him. The next year, he said he would not walk out on his deal, even if he was relegated to League One.

Guardiola always insisted he was 'fully convinced' that the club is innocent and said in May: 'I trust them, I trust them. Because I spoke with them and I trust how they behave and how they did.'

City vehemently denied any breaches of financial rules but the investigation started in December 2018 after German website Der Spiegel published documents from a Football Leaks cache which had originated from Portuguese hacker Rui Pinto.

The club have maintained that they are innocent throughout the process and are expected to appeal

It alleged that City had overstated sponsorship income with money paid from the club's owners instead of sponsors linked to Abu Dhabi.

Roberto Mancini's wages were said to have doubled via a secret contract with an Abu Dhabi club when he was at Man City, while they were also alleged to have broken rules over approaching young players.

The Mail on Sunday has led the way on reporting the story. In July 2021, they reported on emails that appeared to suggest that Man City had millions funnelled into the club by Abu Dhabi to help inflate their income.

Back in February 2020, the club were banned from the Champions League and fined £25million after they were found to have seriously misled European footballing governing body UEFA and broken financial fair play rules.

This was then lifted by the Court of Arbitration for Sport which also reduced the club's fine to £9m.

City spent £440million over the summer, equalling the British transfer record by signing Enzo Fernandez for £125million.

Staff at the City Football Academy learned of the news via Daily Mail Sport and other media reports. There was no official email, with some initially left fearing for their jobs and asking senior managers for an explanation.

'It felt like the club was completely blindsided,' one employee, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told this newspaper.

Sports.title: REVEALED: Why Christian Horner could land dream Ferrari role, how Bernie Ecclestone is pushing his cause, Geri's view on an Italy move and the Prancing Horse chief who's under pressure - VOICE OF THE PADDOCK
Sports.content:
REVEALED: Why Christian Horner could land dream Ferrari role, how Bernie Ecclestone is pushing his cause, Geri's view on an Italy move and the Prancing Horse chief who's under pressure - VOICE OF THE PADDOCK

If Ferrari want to live up to their reputation and create a new chapter in their storied history, they should sign Christian Horner immediately.

They have not won a world championship since 2008, nearly 20 years ago, in which intervening years Horner accrued 14 titles at Red Bull, taking in the drivers’ and constructors’ garlands.

I can reveal that Bernie Ecclestone, best man at Horner’s wedding to Geri Halliwell 11 years ago, has lobbied for this outcome. And persistently so.

I understand that Piero Ferrari, second and only living son of the Scuderia’s founding father Enzo, is in support of the proposition Ecclestone is promulgating, and Piero remains a big player at the team, as vice-chairman and eminence grise.

He can see the benefits of the union, but it requires a leap of faith from chairman John Elkann – one over which he havers – to go outside mainland Europe to employ his team principal.

Horner gets on well with Elkann, very well. Indeed, Elkann supported Horner when he lost his job at Red Bull last year.

Frenchman Jean Todt was given the Ferrari team principal role to great success with Michael Schumacher in the late Nineties and the early years of this century, delivering five drivers’ titles, but, among the Maranello hierarchy, ‘an Englishman?’

Bernie Ecclestone was Christian Horner's best man in 2015 and is lobbying for him to get a new role at Ferrari

Upon that thought alone hinges whether Horner will ever take up the position at Ferrari.

Make no mistake, Horner is open to the idea of running the team, as he revealed in an interview in The Times last week.

‘At this stage in my life, there’s only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership,’ he said. ‘Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula One. It’s the dream. And arguably it’s the sleeping giant of Formula One.’

I understand that Geri would be open to the move to the Maranello area, living in Italy and splitting her time between their estate in Oxfordshire and house in Highgate, London, to support her husband.

For Ferrari, it would make eminent sense. They are struggling under the current clownish leadership of Fred Vasseur, whose health issues also cloud the issue.

He missed a day in Monaco this year with heart problems exacerbated by the stress of the job.

Vasseur’s CV also indicates he is ill-prepared for the task.

This Frenchman can count himself fortunate indeed ever to have been handed the chance to lead the Scuderia. For, based on his track record in Formula One, he hardly warranted such promotion. He entered the top tier of motor racing in 2016 as team principal of Renault. They finished ninth out of 10 in the constructors’ championship.

He moved to Sauber, later to be rebranded Alfa Romeo, the following year. He joined midway through the season and they finished 10th. Next year, eighth. Then eighth, ninth and sixth. He did not take them to one victory in that span, nor into the top half of the table.

This year Ferrari are doing OK, but with no chance of winning either title, despite lying second in the constructors’ standings behind Mercedes. There are grumblings at Maranello behind the cryptic scenes about his future.

Horner and wife Geri are open to the move to Ferrari's Maranello base

Vasseur, so successful as a boss in junior formulas, is widely seen as a man at sea where he is. And everyone at Maranello knows it. He has not bothered to learn more than a few words of Italian, either, which is not conducive to working there. There is an arrogance or a laziness in his failure to do so.

For Horner to work at Ferrari, he needs a free hand, to be able to hire and fire.

As Ecclestone explained: ‘He should say to them give me five years and I do it my way, totally, entire freedom, and if it works, I stay; if it doesn’t, you get rid of me.’

Bernie's got his gun back!

On the subject of Bernie Ecclestone, he was recently stopped by police after flying from Switzerland to Portugal – the two countries where he predominantly lives with his Brazilian wife Fabiana – for carrying a shotgun into the country.

I can reveal that the situation has been resolved amicably through talks with the authorities in Portugal.

Fabiana, 49, explained to police in Lisbon that the gun was being transported for clay-pigeon shooting and that, despite the lack of documentation Bernie carried (no ‘blue book’), all was above board.

The Ecclestones are happily reunited with the gun, and all is well.

‘It’s all been sorted and there is no problem; there never was any problem at all, really,’ Ecclestone, 95, told me.

Ecclestone and his wife Fabiana have their shotgun back after he was stopped upon entering Portugal

Time to give it up, Fernando...

Another abominable weekend just gone for Aston Martin in Azerbaijan. Both cars retired. How much longer should Fernando Alonso race on, one wonders? He is a great driver in my estimation. Yes, a two-time world champion, and a great one at that, but he has not won a race for 13 years.

The Spaniard is 45 and in a team going nowhere fast. Is it not time to stop to preserve his own dignity?

Sports.title: Pep Guardiola's Man City glory has been built on the club's cheating, lies and institutional filth, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI - now he must publicly shame his old bosses to salvage his reputation
Sports.content:
The first time Pep Guardiola’s legacy was threatened by serious accusations of cheating, it took eight years and some vials of unstable urine to clear his name.

We’re going back a fair while for the retelling of this tale. In fact, we’re rewinding all the way to the autumn of 2001, when Guardiola was aged 30 and had rocked up at Brescia in Serie A near the end of his garlanded days as a player.

Many will know the broader brushstrokes of the storm that came next but possibly not the extraordinary details. In other words, there might exist a faint memory of his two positive drug tests for small amounts of the banned steroid nandrolone but not his journey to exoneration.

Now that was a proper legal saga. At different stages, Guardiola was given a four-month sporting ban and a seven-month suspended prison sentence, but he maintained his innocence all the same. He challenged the findings, lost an appeal that had been based on a contamination defence, and after several years pivoted to something else entirely.

To review some excellent reporting from the investigative journalist Edmund Willison, the genesis of a new strategy came from a former Olympic polo player, Manel Estiarte, one of Guardiola’s closest friends and later a hugely-valued confidante on his backroom staff at Manchester City. His thesis? Unstable urine.

You see, Estiarte had evidently become aware of research conducted around 2005 that showed rare cases of low-level positives for nandrolone, brought on by chemical reactions when urine is stored in vials. Guardiola’s team started exploring the route and the courts agreed it was a valid line of concern. That led into a decisive phase, when it was then discovered that the samples couldn’t be retested for instability because there were no samples left to examine.

Pep Guardiola was exonerated from a doping charge after a lengthy eight-year battle

Guardiola staunchly maintained City's innocence and said he would walk if he had been lied to

First, the criminal conviction was wiped out in 2007 and then, in May 2009, 12 months after he was named manager of Barcelona, the sporting sanction was scrubbed from history, too. After eight years, Guardiola was completely cleared on all charges and the course of modern football would go on to change forever.

Looking back from today’s vantage point, that was a remarkable episode for a couple of reasons – one is the nature of the events that spread across the thick end of a decade and the other is how few people ever discuss it. In different sports, the court of public opinion can be unforgiving, even when the final reckoning is innocence, but in football the walls tend to be coated in Teflon. People move on fast.

Why is this relevant now? Because the theory faces its greatest test - there is no suggestion that Guardiola knew what his bosses were up to at Manchester City but his many achievements will be skewed through the prism of their wrongdoing nonetheless.

Manchester City won’t get any benefit of the doubt from neutrals in the public – for all their ongoing protestations of innocence, the image of that club is in ruins. Smashed. Destroyed.

Pending their inevitable appeals, everything they won in their years of Abu Dhabi ownership belongs under the weight of the heaviest asterisk ever imposed in British sport. If those appeals fail and it becomes indisputable that City doped their finances on a grotesque scale, relegation should be the starting point of any conversation about what comes next.

But Guardiola’s legacy is of sharper concern in my mind. What will this mean to one of the greatest thinkers that sport has ever known? In short, it is impossible to separate the beauty of what he delivered from the cheating, lies and institutional filth that appears to have enabled it.

The eras now live as links in a sordid chain of questions – without cooking the books, would City have got Roberto Mancini? Without Mancini, do we get that Aguerooooo moment in 2012? Without Aguerooooo, do we see Manuel Pellegrini and three more trophies? Without Pellegrini, does Guardiola step in? Without Guardiola, do City sign Erling Haaland? Without Haaland is there a treble?

I loved watching Guardiola’s City. It was sporting excellence. It was art mixed with science mixed the head-scratching madness of the man who designed it; the disciple of Cruyff and his truest heir.

Was Guardiola the greatest coach we have known in the Premier League era? By the time he left, I was starting to lean that way, but football is a results game. And results need to be trusted. But we cannot trust those results and that means everything Guardiola achieved at City, all 20 of his trophies, is tainted by an unwitting association with cheats.

He has been robbed by them, but so have we. So have City’s rivals, who will now assemble lawyers of their own and kickstart the chaos of compensation claims.

My view is that the most fitting outcome, once the appeals are done, is that City’s entire list of prizes from the commencement of the Abu Dhabi regime until now is expunged from the record. They should be scratched out like Ben Johnson and Lance Arsmstrong, because doping the accounts in modern football is no less beneficial than doping your blood if you’re a sprinter or cyclist.

He left last summer but he should publicly shame his former bosses if he wishes to salvage his reputation

The only difference I would put forward is that the titles should not be reallocated – leave them blank to signify this situation for what it is. One of no winners. We all lose, Guardiola and his beautiful mind included.

We should remember at this juncture that he defended his club to the hilt. And of course he did. But he also said if they were ever found guilty, he would walk. His resignation overtook that possibility.

But he still has the power and populist capital to punish them. He can’t walk away from what he has already left, but he can confront the executives responsible. He can shame those friends of his who lied to his face and left his reputation among the debris of their deception.

If he is half as righteous as he had us believe, he would do just that, because the mud of this scandal will coat him as much as Manchester City. It won’t be forgotten.

I’m unsure if I’d sacrifice a pot of unstable urine in the club’s word at present. But Guardiola can still do some good with his.

Sports.title: The ugly stories around Man City's 'warfare' over the 115 charges: The army of lawyers, the brick through the window, the tracker on a car, tension, paranoia and journalists targeted for reporting the truth, as revealed by IAN HERBERT
Sports.content:
There’s no suggestion that the tracking device found under a UEFA investigator’s car, at the height of a forensic investigation into Manchester City’s finances, had anything to do with the club under suspicion.

But it was an emblem of the tension and paranoia at the heart of an extraordinary, unremitting 15-year war which has concluded with the Premier League finding the club guilty on all but one of 115 charges.

The device was found when the independent forensic accountant, recruited by UEFA to assist investigators poring over hacked emails which suggested City were involved in Gulf state-sponsored strategies to cheat football financial rules, had his car taken in for service. The matter was not pursued. ‘But everyone was on edge,’ says one source familiar with the inquiry. ‘It felt like warfare.’

UEFA were not the only ones who have felt besieged and threatened by City, who have brought immense legal and financial muscle to counter suggestions that they cheated football’s financial rules.

The Premier League have always known that their case is strong but have been unable to provide so much as a deep background briefing on the case’s progress, knowing that City could publicly accuse them of manipulation.

A section of the club’s fanbase has repeatedly insulted and attacked journalists who suggested there were grounds for conviction. One reporter who questioned City had a brick put through a window of his property. Those who posed questions and were sceptical about City’s conduct are vindicated today.

Man City chiefs Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Ferran Soriano are two of the most powerful men at the club - and the guilty verdict handed down today will be a bitter pill to swallow for them

City faced early difficulties in their bid to upset the establishment, having to deal with the agents of players like Yaya Toure (centre) treating them with contempt

The club did not exude such aggression in the early days of Abu Dhabi ownership in 2008 when, under the leadership of former chief executive Garry Cook and his team, they were likeable and approachable.

The club boldly took on football agents like Kia Joorabchian who wanted a high level of involvement in their transfer business and responded very badly to Cook’s insistence that he – and not outsiders - would be driving transfer negotiations from now on.

The Abu Dhabi state’s strategic communications executive, Simon Pearce, who was sent in to help the new ‘City project’, was charm personified, in November 2009, as he mingled with journalists on the touchline of a floodlit football pitch created in the garden of Abu Dhabi’s seven-star Emirates Palace hotel.

City’s sponsorship deal with Abu Dhabi state-run mobile telephone company Etisalat – hugely contentious and central to allegations of cheating, as things would turn out – had just been announced. This was commercial ‘low hanging fruit,’ Pearce said, beaming, at the start of City’s mid-season winter tour of the state.

City were patronised and mocked by those who considered them upstarts but with excellent executives like Cook, Brian Marwood, Jon Stemp and Mark Allan around, they brushed off the insults.

The club’s recruitment team ignored the bare-faced contempt of agent Dimitri Seluk, who represented Yaya Toure. 'Manchester City?' Seluk scoffed after one City executive arrived at his hotel room in Rome, in 2009, trying to negotiate the player’s move from Barcelona. 'Why should he sign for you?' Toure proved a steal at £24million.

But in the face of the seemingly unlimited spending capacity of the Abu Dhabis and Russian billionaires like Chelsea's Roman Abramovich, Michel Platini’s UEFA announced plans for new cost-control regulations which would prevent owners from piling cash in. The Premier League began formulating their own controls.

City and the Abu Dhabis were indignant – feeling they were being constrained by a self-serving establishment at precisely the time they were trying to bring something modern and progressive to football.

City did not exude as much aggression in the early days of Abu Dhabi ownership in 2008 under the leadership of former chief executive Garry Cook (centre) and his team

But it was after Cook was replaced by Spaniard Ferran Soriano in 2009 that the club became a more combative and joyless place and the club lost many friends in football. In 2014, UEFA found City guilty of breaching Financial Fair Play rules – imposing a small fine and transfer market restrictions. The club were not chastened in the slightest.

City continued to seek ways of navigating a course around the financial rules imposed on them. Amid the subsequent legal challenge which led to the Premier League’s 115 charges, City’s lawyer, Simon Cliff, insisted this battle against British football be called 'Project Longbow' in tribute to the weapon the English used to beat the French at Crecy and Agincourt.

City were being accused of disguising state income as sponsorship deals to flood the club’s transfer kitty with cash. One email, from Pearce to a ‘Mohamed’, said that the ‘annual obligation’ for Abu Dhabi sponsor Aabar was £3million a year and that ‘the remaining £12m requirement will come from alternative sources provided by His Highness’.

Another from Pearce to the chief executive of state-run Etihad Airlines detailed a £99m sponsorship commitment from the company – ‘of which you will provide £8m’. These emails were sent without the remotest awareness that a Portuguese computer hacker, Rui Pinto, would discover them and make them public in November 2018 on a platform called ‘Football Leaks’.

When The Independent revealed how they had ‘sold’ the image rights of players to a company called ‘Fordham’ for £24.5m – despite still taking earnings for those rights – the club demanded the report’s removal and an apology that the title must tweet. An unprecedented level of 'contrition'.

A 1,500-word defence of the story was sent to the club by return and nothing more was heard. Football Leaks later confirmed that story. ‘Fordham’ was an Abu Dhabi entity.

The Gulf state and Sheikh Mansour had bought the club as a vehicle to enhance its reputation across the globe

Trophies followed in abudance - but are City's titles in the 2010s and beyond now tainted?

Soriano ensured that others within the club adopted a harsher and far more confrontational tone. A string of Spaniards followed him into senior management roles at City, creating a Spanish clique.

City’s British executives joked that you needed to be an FOF (‘Friend of Ferran’) or else be considered valuable by the Abu Dhabis, if you wanted to keep your job. There were moves from Soriano to shift club lawyer Cliff out indefinitely to Melbourne City FC, one of the new sister clubs in the growing ‘City Football Group’ Soriano was creating. Cliff resisted and his value to the Abu Dhabi owners kept him in position.

Cliff took the heat as one of the most aggressive exponents of ‘Project Longbow’ – especially when an email from the Football Leaks cache, which had been sent by him, suggested pleasure being taken in the death of one of the seven members of UEFA’s ‘investigatory chamber’ which was investigating City. 'One down, six to go,' Cliff joked to colleagues.

It was the low-profile Soriano who drove City’s aggression – seemingly impervious to how widely unpopular it would make the club among many within British football. Cliff, an urbane and popular individual among City’s longer-standing executives, was tasked with doing the work.

One source describes Cliff as the legal equivalent of a GP within the club, referring aspects of City’s growing and multi-faceted legal battle with the football authorities to specialists in many fields of the law.

City’s Manchester-based team viewed the football authorities as a cartel, intent on nobbling City, a nimble, excellent competitor who had reimagined player acquisition and built the best training complex in the world to help recruit stars. But the Abu Dhabis’ fury had a more geopolitical motivation.

The Gulf state had bought the club as a vehicle to enhance its reputation across the globe. It was the indignity of being found guilty of fraudulent accounting, a very bad look, which maddened them, and most particularly the power behind owner Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al Nahyan’s throne – club chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.

Al Mubarak has been the individual with whom some of the top-level City players have communicated over the years, going over the head of Soriano with WhatsApp messages detailing their personal gripes.

Al Mubarak has never changed his mobile number, making him accessible, though he has avoided direct intervention in squabbles, reluctant to get into the weeds of a club which represents no more than ten per cent of his role as overseer and distributor of the Gulf state’s immense petro-chemical wealth. He delegates completely to Soriano.

Al Mubarak (pictured with Pep Guardiola) has been the individual with whom some of the top-level City players have communicated over the years

Where the financial investigations are concerned, though, it’s been a different story. When UEFA first began pursuing City in 2014, Al Mubarak told club executives that he 'would rather spend £30m on the best 50 lawyers in the world and sue them (UEFA) for the next 10 years than agree to a financial penalty'. He’s seen it as his mission to fight this.

Insiders describe Al Mubarak as a deeply patriotic Emirati, whose loyalty to the Gulf state is borne of background. His father served as the UAE’s ambassador to Paris, where he was assassinated in 1984, at the age of 36, as he left his apartment building a few hundred yards from the Eiffel Tower. The lone gunman was never caught. For Al Mubarak, fighting UEFA and the Premier League has been a matter of national pride.

It was he who led the fight for City in 2018, four years after the UEFA conviction, when the publication of the hacked emails led the same governing body to open a new investigation.

This time, the club refused to supply documents, make witnesses available and even went to court to challenge UEFA’s right to charge them.

‘The request for the most basic piece of information from City became a form of warfare,’ says the source familiar with that inquiry, which spanned six months. ‘They were operating with virtually unlimited wealth. There was no limit to the number of lawyers they can engage.’

UEFA concluded that City had disguised £204m in cash injections from Abu Dhabi state funds, by pretending that the cash came from sponsors, and in 2020 banned them from European competition for two seasons.

City were so confident of appealing the decision that they didn’t even bother contesting the ban. The Court of Arbitration in Sport upheld the club’s appeal. Some of the alleged malpractice had taken place too far into the past and UEFA could not provide enough information to build on the leaked emails.

When the Premier League’s own investigation saw 115 more charges levelled against them in February 2023, City ratcheted up the warfare. More than 50 charges related to sponsorship deals. Others related to alleged disguised, off-the-books salary payments to football staff like manager Roberto Mancini and Toure, made to persuade them to sign.

Some of City's charges related to sponsorship deals. Others related to alleged disguised, off-the-books salary payments to football staff like manager Roberto Mancini

It took the Premier League nearly five years to complete the investigation which led them to charge the club. City’s refusal to cooperate over that time led the league to take them to court to force them to give evidence.

That would have remained a secret had Daily Mail Sport’s publishers, Associated Newspapers, not gone to court to seek the right to report it. Associated’s barrister, Jude Bunting KC, won that argument, after going up against Lord Pannick KC, who would lead City's defence team in ‘the 115’ case.

Sir Stephen Males, one of the High Court judges that heard the Associated case, drew attention to City’s refusal to cooperate. 'It is surprising, and a matter of legitimate public concern, that so little progress has been made after two-and-a-half years – during which, it may be noted, the club has twice been crowned as Premier League champions,' he said.

Before the six-week ‘115’ case even opened, City sought to damage the Premier League’s credibility by mounting a separate legal challenge against the system of rules governing sponsorship deals. They sent seven lawyers from the Freshfields Bruckhaus Deringer firm in to fight that case.

When the panel hearing that earlier case found that the Premier League’s system was fundamentally sound, with several rules in need of correction, City nonetheless claimed victory and accused the league of communicating a dubious interpretation.

Cliff was sent on the attack. He declared in an email to all 19 other clubs that City would take further legal action and that they, not the Premier League, would help interpret the verdict for them if they needed help. Other clubs found this deeply patronising.

The details of the earlier case revealed the extraordinary financial complexity of the Abu Dhabi sponsorship deals that ‘the 115’ panel would have to grapple with.

City had submitted a 600-page document to get their Etihad Airways sponsorship deal approved. Premier League staff worked weekends and into the early hours to get through the detail before rejecting City’s arithmetic. The league were clearly facing a legal and intellectual onslaught from a hugely oppressive and immensely argumentative club.

Despite City executives' confidence, for now it is the Premier League and Richard Masters who have won the legal war

A few days after ‘the 115’ hearing had finished, a senior figure at the Premier League indicated to Daily Mail Sport that City had swamped the proceedings with mountains of evidence on the sponsorship deals. ‘You will see this when the verdict comes,’ said that figure.

But one former City executive, who would have seen the controversial sponsorship transactions at first hand before leaving the club, had felt sure that the Premier League would be unable to prove a ‘deliberate’ attempt to deceive and would only find City guilty of a refusal to cooperate – enabling the club to avoid a points deduction. It now looks as if that optimism was misplaced.

There has been a hope among some in football that the verdict in this case can finally bring nearly a decade of warfare between the Premier League and Manchester City to a close.

‘It’s a shadow on the wall at every board meeting. The constant sense of war is damaging and suffocating,’ says one Premier League club board member.

Now, we must wait to see if Al Mubarak and Soriano green light a legal challenge and line-by-line rebuttals of the findings. The battle is over, but the war which has been such a stain on British football’s reputation for fair play may well go on.

Sports.title: Furious Martin Odegaard aims X-rated slur at Bernardo Silva with ex-Man City star lucky to escape red for VERY late tackle on Arsenal captain
Sports.content:
Martin Odegaard had a two-word slur for Bernardo Silva after his rival's nasty kick on international duty – and it started with 'f' and ended with 'you'. The Arsenal and Norway star was left fuming by Silva, who kicked him in the ankle long after the ball was gone and sent him tumbling. Silva was booked, but was arguably lucky to escape without a red, and so Odegaard took it on himself to discipline the Portugal and Real Madrid man by bellowing 'f*** you'. 'He completely lost his head,' Odegaard told reporters. 'He just kicked me down long after I had played the ball. I didn't understand what he was doing.' Odegaard had to sit on the grass for a while to recover from his injury and appeared shaken after the match. Bernardo Silva was lucky to escape a red card for this late kick on Martin Odegaard Odegaard was hurt and fuming with his rival and later said he had a knock on his ankle The Arsenal and Norway star shouted 'f*** you' to Silva, who has joined Real Madrid 'I took a knock to my ankle. It probably won't feel great tonight, but I'm hoping it clears up over the next few days,' the 27-year-old added. Silva was confronted over his behaviour by journalists in the mixed zone but kept on walking before turning to simply say: 'That's football, my friend'. It's safe to say that his adversaries did not find his kick within the acceptable bounds of football behaviour. Fresh in everybody's minds is how Odegaard suffered seven separate injuries last season, causing him to miss 30 games for club and country. Norway defender Leo Ostigard said: 'It's very late. When you see it afterwards on video, it's very ugly. It could well be red. 'It’s a terrible tackle. It’s just appallingly bad. That’s the sort of thing we don’t want to see for our captain. When it comes that long after the play, it looks quite deliberate. 'He was unlucky with a lot of injuries last year, and there’s nothing he can do about that. 'They’re going after him because he’s run rings around most of them in midfield. They’re obviously frustrated, but you can’t do things like that.' Meanwhile, Norway manager Stale Solbakken added: 'He got a real bump on his ankle. It would be wise to get off the field to get ice and compression on.' Unfortunately for Norway, there was no good karma as Portugal won 2-1 away in their Nations League match. With Cristiano Ronaldo left to simmer on the bench, Joao Felix and Goncalo Ramos scored either side of an Erling Haaland equaliser to go top of their League A group. But Norway will have the chance to have the last laugh, at least for now, when they travel to Norway on Sunday.

Sports.title: Norway could become first nation to scrap VAR - with clubs working to axe controversial technology after three years following fan protests
Sports.content:
Norway could become first nation to scrap VAR - with clubs working to axe controversial technology after three years following fan protests

Norway could become the first nation to scrap VAR, with clubs working to remove it from the top flight following a series of fan protests.

Several clubs in the Eliteserien, Norway’s equivalent of the Premier League, would like to see the technology gone having used it since 2023.

While Sweden’s Allsvenskan rejected its introduction in 2024, no country has yet introduced it and then voted to remove it.

‘Lillestrom Sports Club has a clear annual meeting resolution that the club will actively work to phase out VAR, and the board and the club of course support this,’ said Lillestrom chairman Raymond Gabrielsen.

‘This means, among other things, that we have a dialogue with other top clubs and are working on concrete initiatives that could lead to a liquidation.

‘We are against the very idea behind VAR. However, we believe that the quality of the current solution neither corresponds to what was communicated at the time of its introduction, nor to the expectations that have been created that the system would improve over time.

Fans at Norwegian club Valerenga protest with a 'No to VAR' banner last year

'We therefore believe that the matter should be ripe for a new assessment, where the clubs that use the system should be heard,’ he told Norwegian broadcaster TV2.

Norwegian clubs proposed abandoning VAR last year but the idea was rejected by a clear majority.

Even though there is no such movement in the Premier League, VAR continues to create controversy virtually every weekend.

In 2024, Wolves – who were then a top flight club – wanted VAR axed but they were outvoted 19-1 by the other members of the Premier League.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."
