World.title: Trump aims to leave a physical legacy in D.C., bulldozing norms along the way
World.content:
Trump aims to leave a physical legacy in D.C., bulldozing norms along the way

AFP via Getty Images/Collage by Emily Bogle/NPR

President Trump has spent much of his second term trying to make his physical mark on Washington, D.C., earning — or perhaps awarding himself — the moniker of "builder-in-chief."

"The best thing I do in life is build," he told reporters in May.

Trump tore down the East Wing of the White House to build an even bigger ballroom (and military complex underneath). He built a helipad on the South Lawn after separately paving over the Rose Garden. He had the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool repaved in "American flag blue," a project that was supposed to take two weeks but is still unfinished many months later, after a botched installation and several unfounded arrests.

Sponsor Message

He's had new statues installed and existing ones restored, including two equestrian statues glaringly gilded over the summer. He wants to build a sculpture garden of "national heroes" in West Potomac Park and overhaul the locally beloved East Potomac Golf Links, changing it from a municipal resource into a championship-level venue.

The list goes on. Trump seeks to add his name to the Kennedy Center building, or else have it demolished altogether. He's trying to fast-track a controversial 250-foot arch near Arlington National Cemetery, most recently rebranding it as a military complex — despite originally telling reporters it was intended to honor "me."

"I have heard the president say: 'I am president because I am rich. I am rich because I am a developer. I am a developer because I have exquisite taste,'" said Greg Werkheiser, whose law firm, Cultural Heritage Partners, is involved in several lawsuits against Trump's projects. "It would appear that much of his self-worth is tied to this mythology of Trump as a builder."

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in a statement that "President Trump can walk and chew gum at the same time," saying he is delivering on campaign policy promises while also "ensuring the People's House and our Nation's Capital will be properly glorified and remain in excellent condition for generations to come."

Sponsor Message

"Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, no other president has done more to beautify our Nation's interior than President Trump," he added.

toggle caption Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

Trump's second-term projects have prompted lawsuits, protests and tens of thousands of public comments overwhelmingly in opposition. While some of these undertakings are pegged to the country's 250th anniversary, critics have long accused the president of rushing to memorialize himself out of fear that no one else will. And Trump confirmed as much in a New York Magazine piece published earlier this month.

"Nobody will do it once I'm gone," said the 80-year-old, second-term president. "When I leave here, nobody will."

Trump and those in his orbit maintain he is uniquely qualified to put his stamp on D.C. because of his decades-long career as a New York City real estate developer. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told Fox News last year that "in large part, he was reelected ... because he is good at building things."

But people who worked with him at the time point out that his early-career building projects and strategies were fraught too, boosted by financial workarounds and plagued by lawsuits. And, more broadly, historians and legal experts worry that Trump is setting a dangerous precedent by treating D.C. as his personal construction playground.

"The worse his approval ratings, the economy and the war get, the more time he spends in the sandbox playing with America's historic sites as if they were his personal toys," Werkheiser said.

Barbara Res, who served as head of construction for the Trump Organization in the 1980s, says Trump's efforts to cut corners with ambitious projects are not new, but take on a painful significance in a moment when he is "ripping through" the nation's capital.

"There was no regard for the law back then. But he wasn't the king of the world; he wasn't the president," Res said. "Now he has no regard for law … and he gets away with it."

Sponsor Message

A history of disregard for historic preservation

toggle caption Marty Lederhandler/AP

Res, who left the Trump Organization in 1998, stressed that there is a big difference between a builder and a developer.

Trump was the latter, overseeing big-picture decisions like hiring architects, engineers and contractors. Even so, she said he often made demands about details that usually made the job harder, such as telling crews to reuse old HVAC equipment in new ductwork as a cost-cutting measure.

"His father was a builder in Brooklyn … and Donald seems to think that gives him credibility as a builder, 'cause he walked around with his father," she said. "Maybe he does now, but when we were doing the work, he didn't really know much about construction."

Res is an outspoken Trump critic: in 2020, she published the book Tower of Lies: What My 18 Years of Working with Donald Trump Reveals About Him. She concedes that "he did do good things" for real estate, but that was before he was president.

"The White House and the capital are not to his credit, so I don't think that would be part of his legacy," she said. "Probably his most important building is Trump Tower."

Trump Tower was Trump's second major independent project, and his first built-from-scratch skyscraper. And it was marred by a historic preservation scandal before it even opened.

In 1979, Trump — then a budding developer in his early 30s — bought the flagship building of the Bonwit Teller luxury department on Manhattan's Fifth Avenue, with plans to tear it down and build Trump Tower in its place.

Penelope Hunter-Stiebel was a curator at the Metropolitan Museum of Art at the time. When she heard of Trump's plan to demolish the 1929 building, she jumped into action to save the historic artwork on its facade: two classical-style 15-feet-high limestone sculptures of nudes dancing with scarves, and a massive art deco decorative metal grille.

toggle caption AP/AP

Hunter-Stiebel believed the sharp contrast of two different architectural styles — added to the same building in the span of a single year — would make for a great addition to the Met's collection. And she thought Trump could benefit, too.

Sponsor Message

"We had been chasing wrecking balls as buildings of architectural ornament that were significant were destroyed around New York," she said. "I thought in this case, looking up Trump, it was a chance of changing the direction."

Hunter-Stiebel approached the Trump Organization with an offer: "Young Donald," as he was called, could not only get some positive PR for salvaging the artwork, but he could likely also get a tax deduction.

She said Robert Miller, who owned the gallery across the street, had agreed to appraise the works and valued them at around $200,000. He told The New York Times in 1980: "The reliefs are as important as the sculptures on the Rockefeller building. They'll never be made again."

Hunter-Stiebel says she reached an agreement with the Trump Organization. But shortly after scaffolding and demolition crews arrived in the spring of 1980, she noticed the metal grille had vanished (its whereabouts remain a mystery). Then came a panicked call from Miller, who spotted jackhammers across the street.

"[I] got in a taxi, and got in a classic New York City traffic jam, nothing moving down Fifth Avenue," she recalled. "So I got out and I ran 10 blocks, which I remember because I was nine months pregnant."

They decided that Miller — a less recognizable player in the drama — would approach the foreman, with cash he frantically collected from his employees, to try to save the sculptures.

Hunter-Stiebel says the foreman told Miller, who died in 2011: "The young Donald has said specifically that there's this crazy woman at a museum up the avenue who wants them, and I have to be sure they're absolutely destroyed."

They watched in horror as the jackhammers went to work. As of 2016, at least one piece of the sculptures lived on the Miami balcony of former Trump Organization executive Louise Sunshine, who did not respond to NPR's interview request.

Sponsor Message

There was immediate fallout from the incident. The New York Times ran a front-page story in which Trump Organization executive "John Baron" (now a well-known Trump alias) said removing them carefully would have cost more than three times their appraisers' estimated value and delayed demolition by over a week. (Almost two decades later, in 1998, Trump paid $1.375 million to settle a class-action lawsuit involving the use of undocumented Polish laborers during that demolition.)

Res said Trump told her a different version of the story: He offered the sculptures to the Met, but was turned down. Because they were not "landmarked," she said, "I don't see anything wrong with that except lying about it."

But to Hunter-Stiebel, the incident represents "Trump's first experience of the negative delights of power."

"I'm afraid we have seen the same behavioral pattern in large scale, and a strange delight in doing things that can only be destructive … including [to] the person making those decisions," she added.

Acting not as a builder, but as an owner

toggle caption Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images

There's a world in which Trump's career experience as a developer could benefit D.C., said historian Tim Naftali, a professor at Columbia University's School of International Public Affairs.

"But the president hasn't acted just as a builder," he said. "He's acted as an owner, and that's the difference. The president of the United States does not own the United States. The president of the United States doesn't even own the White House."

Naftali said previous presidents have all approached their White House role as custodians. That doesn't mean they didn't make changes: There's a long history of presidents renovating the White House. But other than Truman, who paid for the second-story balcony with his government-funded "household account," they all went to Congress for authorization and funding.

Trump has not done that for his building projects, even though his party controls both houses of Congress. Experts say that creates a dangerous precedent for future occupants of the White House.

"The building projects are simply a symptom of President Trump's theory of government, which is that he alone is the federal government of the United States," Naftali said.

Beyond the White House, Naftali said D.C.'s most iconic monuments — honoring George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Thomas Jefferson and more — were built through "presidential inspiration mixed with congressional action." Presidents angled for monuments honoring their predecessors, not themselves.

Sponsor Message

Naftali thinks of four-term president Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who made clear in his lifetime that the only memorial he wanted for himself was a small block of granite with his name on it.

"Yes, he pushed for a memorial, but it was the Jefferson Memorial," Naftali added. "Not the 'Jefferson Memorial brought to you by Franklin Delano Roosevelt.' It was the Jefferson Memorial, built [and] financed by Congress."

Charles Birnbaum, the CEO and founding president of The Cultural Landscape Foundation — which sued the administration over the reflecting pool — says Trump has made clear that "the sort of social norms and decorum that existed historically is no longer being applied."

He noted, for example, that Trump has appointed non-expert allies to the federal arts panels tasked with reviewing D.C. construction. At the same time, the administration is also moving to roll back legal protections for historic places across the country.

"All of these proposals that we're seeing, what they have in common is they're not preserving and protecting. They are destroying, diminishing, altering," said Birnbaum. "And that is where Washington is a case study right now of what this administration wants to export to the rest of the nation."

When most recent presidents think about their legacy, Naftali said, they think about the work itself and, to some degree, the one building they expect will eventually bear their name: their presidential library, usually built outside of D.C. in a location of personal significance. Trump has said his — a planned skyscraper in Miami — will most likely be a hotel.

When it comes to shaping his own legacy, Trump has bucked presidential norms in many ways. Beyond his controversial construction projects, he's the first sitting president to have an airport named after him, and the first in a century to have his face on currency.

Sponsor Message

And while these acts may seem relatively trivial at a time of broader economic and international turmoil, Naftali said, they should ring alarm bells to anyone who cares about the separation of powers. He suspects Trump may be eager to jam his projects through before the midterms, when the makeup of Congress may shift.

Trump told New York Magazine that the embattled White House ballroom will be made of "nuclear concrete," saying it would physically be hard for Democrats to one day tear it down. The reporter of that story, Ben Terris, told NPR that Trump is "trying to cement his legacy, literally, and … make something that nobody can take away from him."

But to Naftali and others, the greater risk is in what might be lost along the way.

"We Americans will pressure Congress in one way or another to do something with whatever is left of the building program once the president leaves office," Naftali said. "The bigger issue is, do we want our separation of powers of doctrine to survive through our 300th birthday?"

World.title: 5 British suspects arrested, explosives found near U.S.-run air base. Iran denies role
World.content:
5 British suspects arrested, explosives found near U.S.-run air base. Iran denies role

toggle caption Alastair Grant/AP

FAIRFORD, England — Police were holding five men on Monday and examining suspected explosives found near a U.S.-operated air force base in England, as counterterror detectives investigated whether the arrests foiled an attempted attack linked to Iran.

The men were detained early Sunday after three vans were spotted near RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.

Investigators have not concluded whether the incident is a state-backed attack. They are investigating a possible link to Iran, Russia or non-state-backed militant groups. RAF Fairford has also been the focus of protests by anti-war campaigners.

Iran denied involvement. It's London embassy said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" about the incident.

toggle caption Alastair Grant/AP

The five suspects, who have not been named, were initially held over suspected explosives offenses, and later also arrested on suspicion of preparing an act of terrorism. Police said the men are all British nationals from London and in their 20s. They can be held in custody for up to 14 days before they must be charged or released.

Sponsor Message

Residents were evacuated from 85 homes in the village of Whelford near the base on Sunday and army bomb-disposal experts used a robot to examine three white vans. The villagers had not been able to go home as of Monday morning, and the vans had not yet been moved.

Arrests came after reports of suspicious vehicles

President Donald Trump said the suspects had been detained following cooperation between the U.S. and Britain, and had been "under view" for some time. Police, however, said the arrests were triggered by a late-night call about "suspicious vehicles" near the base.

British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting declined to give details of the operation, but said "it was a proud moment" that Trump had recognized "the work that our police and intelligence services do every day."

"As and when we can, we will report back to the public about these individuals and about the nature of the threat," Streeting told Times Radio.

The arrests come at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British intelligence services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on British soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states, including Iran, increased 50% in the six months to December 2025.

Sponsor Message

Iran has been linked to a series of attacks in Europe

Britain did not join the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran that began Feb. 28 and initially denied Trump's request to use bases in the U.K. to strike Iran. But then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed in March to let the U.S. use bases in Britain for what he called "defensive" operations against Iran's missiles and their launch sites following Iranian attacks on U.K. interests and Britain's allies in the Gulf.

American B-1 and B-52 bombers have taken off from Fairford, 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, for operations during the Iran conflict.

Iran has said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

British security officials say proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson and sabotage attempts in the U.K. and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community. They have previously warned that Tehran could expand its targets in the U.K. if conflicts in the Middle East continue.

British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Monday that the incident is a "reminder of the threats our country faces."

Miliband met Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi at the United Nations in New York last week and told him that "Britain will not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on U.K. soil," according to a U.K. readout of the conversation.

U.S. Air Force says personnel remain vigilant

The U.S. Air Force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford "remain vigilant," but "for operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures."

The U.S. Embassy in London has warned Americans in Britain to be cautious and mindful of their personal security.

Trump said authorities had the suspects "under view for a long time and we got them."

Sponsor Message

"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday.

World.title: What to know about the $810 million in spending canceled by President Trump
World.content:
What to know about the $810 million in spending canceled by President Trump

toggle caption Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images North America

Each year, Congress passes laws which allocate money to the federal government's various programs and agencies. Trump, for the second year in a row, is refusing to send some of that money to the places that Congress says it has to go , setting off a fresh battle with lawmakers over who controls federal spending.

Of the $810 million being withheld, $567 million comes from programs that "provided services to refugees, asylees, and other non-citizens," according to a memo from the White House.

The move, called a pocket rescission, is illegal, according to the Government Accountability Office , an independent, non-partisan watchdog agency charged with providing federal agencies fact-based information.

Sponsor Message

Article 1 of the Constitution gives Congress t he power to levy taxes and decide how federal funds are spent — known as power of the purse. If the president disagrees, he or she can send a request to Congress to cancel the fund, but that is supposed to happen with 45 days notice in order to let Congress agree or disagree.

A pocket rescission happens when the president decides to cancel funds without ample time for Congress to weigh in or reallocate the money. With the end of the fiscal year less than a week away, the announcement means the funds will go unspent and Congress can't respond.

"This is the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to undermine Congress's Constitutional power of the purse," Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations committee, wrote in a statement posted to X. "OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding."

The canceled funds are fueling anger from Democrats who say OMB director Russell Vought is violating the separation of powers and undermining Congressional authority.

"This is theft from the American people, plain and simple," wrote Washington Sen. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee on X. "Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because Vought is saying their votes don't count."

Sponsor Message

"Donald Trump knows he can't get these cuts through Congress, so he is illegally making them through the back door," Rep. Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget committee, said in a statement. "Trump's actions are a blatant attack on Congress's constitutional power of the purse."

The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

The administration also says it withheld $15 million to a Justice Department team tasked with "preventing and resolving racial and ethnic tensions, incidents, and civil disorders, and in restoring racial stability and harmony," $70 million to "programs provide grants and fellowships to support institutions bringing foreign students and faculty to the United States to study or teach language," and tens of millions to various research and non-profit grant programs that target climate change or racial and gender minority work.

World.title: This tiny N.S. community was frustrated with big-box grocers. So they opened their own store
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

High prices. Long travel times. Poor-quality produce. Food insecurity.

There were so many reasons that some people in the tiny, rural community of Bear River, N.S., in the Annapolis Valley were growing frustrated with their grocery options at large, mainstream grocers.

“The prices are, you know, inhumane,” said Bear River resident Drew Tozer. “You're getting produce that has been rotting on the trucks for 48 hours … It's like half-spoiled because Nova Scotia is at the end of the food supply chain.”

Another resident, Amy Rubin said, “You see your bill, like, oh, is that how much money I'm really giving this giant grocery store that doesn't seem to be holding our best interests in mind?”

Over the past few years, there has been a backlash against some big-box grocery stores due to rising prices, questions about labelling, weighing practices, price discrimination, anti-competitive conduct and security at some of the country's biggest chains.

In Bear River, some residents decided to take matters into their own hands.

After holding meetings, writing a business plan and grant proposal, connecting with local suppliers and wielding paintbrushes to spruce up a storefront, a new community-run grocery store opened its doors in July.

Bear River is a community of about 1,000 people that straddles the boundaries of Annapolis and Digby counties. The co-op is in a historic building on stilts above the river. (Dave Laughlin/CBC)

So far, Fiddlehead Market Co-op has 130 members — not too shabby, considering Bear River is home to only about 1,000 people.

The co-op offers fresh fruits and vegetables, meat, dairy products, dried goods, pantry staples, bulk products and cleaning supplies as well as a few takeout options.

Anyone can shop at the co-op, but people can also choose to buy a $100 share to become a member, which allows them to vote on how the co-op is run and decide what to do with any surplus profits. People can also volunteer instead of buying a share to become a member.

Drew Tozer is the chair of the board of directors of Fiddlehead Market Co-op. (Frances Willick/CBC)

Rather than being an impediment to the co-op's long-term success, Tozer feels Bear River's small size will be a boon because people feel connected to it and responsible for it.

“The response has been just totally overwhelming,” said Tozer, who is the chair of the co-op’s board. “People have a really strong sense of pride and ownership over the endeavour. It's not just a place where they're getting groceries. People come in here and it makes them really emotional.”

Bear River does have a few other grocery options besides the co-op, including a convenience store that also sells hot meals, a gas station and a seasonal, biweekly farmers' market.

Tozer said the co-op worked with the local businesses to ensure they were filling the gaps in food availability rather than competing with existing enterprises.

WATCH | Residents band together to open community-owned grocery store: Why this small community opened its own grocery store | Duration closed caption 2:05 Some residents in Bear River, N.S., opened Fiddlehead Market Co-op, bringing affordable prices, fresh produce and local convenience to the area. The CBC's Frances Willick reports.

The closest large grocery stores are a 15-minute drive to Digby or a 25-minute drive to Annapolis Royal — a barrier in a community without public transportation and for those who don’t have access to a vehicle.

Fiddlehead sources its items from local suppliers as much as possible, Tozer said, allowing food to stay fresher longer and money to stay closer to home rather than being funnelled to corporate offices in other provinces or countries.

Sourcing local also helps keep the price of some items lower than big-box grocers, even leading to reverse sticker shock for some shoppers.

“There are lots of things that are much, much cheaper — to the point that sometimes I do a double take,” said Rubin, who recently bought a head of lettuce for $1.75.

Rubin said the co-op is helping Bear River create a reliable food supply during tumultuous times.

“We're living in times when things are pretty uncertain in terms of tariffs and in terms of trade," she said. "To be already building a sustainable source of things that we need is very comforting and it feels really good ethically.”

Amy Rubin is a Fiddlehead Market Co-op member and volunteer. (Frances Willick/CBC)

Members say shopping at the co-op helps them meet new people and feel connected with the community.

"My favourite thing is just seeing the people that you know and that you can just check in on and have good talks and build that resilient community," said Aly Coy.

Fiddlehead is also concerned about minimizing food waste, so some items that are no longer fit to sell are donated to farmers as animal feed. Food that has imperfections is cooked and sold as grab-and-go meals in the store, and some items are donated to the community kitchen or left in the community cupboard.

A menu shows some food options at Fiddlehead Market Co-op. (Frances Willick/CBC)

Tozer said since the co-op formed, she's heard from someone on the South Shore who's interested in opening one, too. She encourages other communities to give it a try.

"I feel like we spent a long time trying to fight the grocery system, trying to fight pricing," she said.

"You don't need to fix the grocery store systems.… You can just create your own. And having the power as a community to govern your own grocery store and choose your prices and choose the suppliers and having that control over your food system is so inspiring and powerful."

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Trump's tariffs are unpopular in Maine. A Republican senator may pay the price
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If U.S. President Donald Trump's tariffs could bring manufacturing back to places it has fled, the town of Millinocket, Maine, ought to be a likely candidate.

Millinocket was for decades a thriving paper mill town, until Great Northern Paper ceased operations in 2008. Its fenced-off property sits abandoned, and although there's a growing outdoor recreation sector in the town of 4,100, its economy has struggled ever since.

Then came a plan, backed in part by Norwegian investors, for a $300 million US aquaculture venture repurposing the giant lagoons on the old mill site, to be called Great Northern Salmon.

"It was a marriage made in heaven," said Gail Fanjoy, the president of the local chamber of commerce. "Out of the gate, they were going to employ 50 people. That's a home run."

The project was about 80 per cent toward completion when the company announced last month it was pausing indefinitely, resting blame squarely on the uncertainty caused by the Trump administration's tariffs. Much of its salmon farming equipment was to be imported from Canada.

"That was a huge, huge, huge blow," Fanjoy told CBC News. "The Norwegian investors just said, 'We're done, we just can't deal with this.'"

One of the abandoned buildings on the former site of Great Northern Paper in Millinocket, Maine. A new $300 million US aquaculture venture repurposing the lagoons on the site, to be called Great Northern Salmon, was put on hold last month over what its backers described as the volatility caused by the Trump administration's tariffs. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Fanjoy, a lifelong resident of Millinocket, says nothing will make her believe Trump's claim that his trade policy will revive manufacturing in places like this.

"It's a fallacy," she said. "Paper companies all up and down the Penobscot River and the state of Maine closed, went bankrupt, and a tariff is not going to bring them back."

Cross-border trade matters to Maine

Maine does $6 billion US in annual two-way commerce with Canada — a significant amount in a state that's less populous than Manitoba.

The trade war is playing out amid a tight race for U.S. Senate in Maine, an election that will help determine which party controls Congress for the second half of Trump's term.

Maine's incumbent Sen. Susan Collins is something of a political phenomenon. The Republican has held her seat for the past 30 years in a place that hasn't voted statewide for a GOP presidential candidate since 1988.

If the Democrats are to win a majority in the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms, Maine is a seat they'll almost certainly need to flip.

Tim Woodcock is a lawyer in Bangor, Maine, who has known Collins since the late 1970s and is supporting her re-election campaign. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

One big question in the race is if Maine voters will punish Collins as a proxy for their antipathy to Trump, whether over the trade war or other issues.

Tim Woodcock, a Bangor lawyer and a staunch backer of Collins, says many businesses have been adversely affected by tariffs, including those on Canadian products.

"These two economies are deeply intertwined," Woodcock told CBC News. "Anybody who is either trying to conduct a business in Maine or is dependent on a business in Maine would be very concerned about all the uncertainty that these tariffs have imposed."

'Canada's our friend'

CBC News spoke with Collins on the weekend as she walked in a parade in Carmel, a town of about 2,900.

Asked how concerned she is that Trump's tariffs will hurt her re-election chances, the 72-year-old senator parried the question.

"I'm much more concerned about the impact on the people of Maine in general. Many of our products, whether it's blueberries or potatoes or timber or lobster, are harvested here but processed in Canada," Collins said.

"Canada's our friend, our neighbour, our biggest trading partner," she added. "I urge the administration to get back to the table and both sides should engage in negotiations."

In 2020, Collins was the only Republican Senate candidate in the country to win in a state that voted for Joe Biden. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Among the townspeople lining the parade route was Chris Morang, who shook hands with Collins.

"I love her. She's always voted for helping the people in Maine. She's kept a lot of the hospitals going. She helped the lobster industry a lot," Morang told CBC News.

Although Collins has opposed Trump's trade war, Morang sides with the president.

"I think Canada has taken advantage of the United States a lot," he said. "They had unfair tariffs on us for many, many years, especially on lobster and lumber. I think at this point we're just getting what we deserve."

Collins has often tried to distance herself from Trump and his tariffs.

She was one of only seven Republican senators who voted to convict Trump in his impeachment trial for his role in the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the U.S. Capitol. Last week, she supported a resolution calling for an end to the war with Iran.

Carmel resident Chris Morang sides with Trump on tariffs, saying he believes that Canada has taken advantage of the U.S. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Collins claimed victory this month when the White House lifted tariffs on two imports that Maine relies on from Canada: cement and road salt.

Her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, says tariffs are crushing Maine and he's dismissive of Collins' approach.

'Concerned letters' to Trump

"Everything costs more for people, and you can tell it's a big deal because Susan Collins was writing concerned letters to Donald Trump," Jackson told CBC News.

"She got us rock salt back, but we can't eat that."

Both Collins and Jackson grew up in northern Maine, each within a half hour's drive of the Canadian border. But that's where the similarities end.

Collins comes from a prosperous family who owned a lumber yard, and now has a net worth as high as $9.6 million US, according to a Democratic Party analysis of her Congressional financial disclosures.

Troy Jackson, the Democratic Party candidate for U.S. Senate in Maine, greets a supporter following a town hall event in Bethel, Maine. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Jackson was a logger and union activist who jumped into local politics after participating in a border blockade protesting companies bringing lower-paid Canadian loggers into Maine in the late 1990s. If he wins, he'll become the only sitting U.S. senator without a four-year college degree.

During a weekend town hall in the small coastal city of Belfast, Jackson wore a ball cap while talking proudly of his roots in northern Maine and his two decades in local politics.

Jackson replaced Graham Platner

"I speak funny, I know that. I didn't go to the right schools and all that. But what I think people have come to understand is that I am 100 per cent dug in on getting shit done," Jackson said to whoops and cheers from the audience.

Jackson only became the Democrat candidate in July after the original nominee Graham Platner stepped down when a former partner accused him of sexual assault.

John Luft, who came to the town hall from the nearby coastal town of Lincolnville, says Jackson is different from the typical political candidate.

"He actually speaks to what Mainers need right now. He actually gets it," Luft said.

The audience at Jackson's town hall in Belfast, Maine, cheered when he told them, 'I am 100 per cent dug in on getting shit done.' (Mike Crawley/CBC)

Luft calls the trade war with Canada atrocious.

"I see no reason for this at all," he said. "Canada and United States have been friends forever and that's the way it should be."

Canadian companies have major investments in Maine, notably New Brunswick's Irving family empire with interests in logging, forest products and petroleum.

Despite what polling suggests is widespread opposition to Trump's tariffs among Maine voters, it's only one of the issues at play in the election contest between Jackson and Collins.

Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine Farmington, says while both candidates have staked out positions against the trade war, Collins can pitch Mainers on her influence in Washington as a veteran senator and her record of defying Trump.

"In some ways, how this (trade war) has played out may favour her more than Jackson," Melcher told CBC News.

At the same time, Collins is seeking a sixth term from an electorate that Melcher describes as weary of the status quo.

"Certainly Troy Jackson is different, more blue collar, has a different approach to things," he said. "The perception of the economy and the national Republicans, I think, isn't helpful to [Collins] either."

Woodcock, the lawyer in Bangor, remains optimistic about Collins' re-election chances given what he calls the long tradition of independent judgment shown by Maine voters.

"They have tended to support, I'd say, the candidates who are willing to reach across the aisle, who are prepared to put the merits of an issue ahead of party," said Woodcock.

In her last election in 2020, Collins defied the anti-Trump wave. Despite polls that suggested she was poised to lose, she defeated her Democrat challenger by nine percentage points. She was the only Republican Senate candidate in the country to win in a state that voted for Joe Biden.

World.title: 'Thrown under the bus': Former defence chief's memoir lays bare his battles with the Trudeau government
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's former top military commander considered resigning "several times" during his tenure in battles with the former Trudeau government over the sexual misconduct scandal, and the lack of commitment towards defence spending.

Retired general Wayne Eyre's new memoir, Into the Breach: A Soldier's Journey, also peels back the curtain on the internal debate that took place over how to end the convoy occupation of downtown Ottawa in early 2022.

The prologue to the book, titled The Accidental CDS, is a tongue-in-cheek reference to his unusual, unexpected rise to the position of chief of the defence staff.

Eyre was promoted from being army commander to the top job after now-retired admiral Art MacDonald stepped aside in February 2021 because of allegations of inappropriate behaviour. Those allegations never resulted in charges and MacDonald didn't return to the defence chief's job.

Eyre was left to navigate the wider sexual misconduct scandal and a flurry of allegations which engulfed several high-ranking military leaders — an experience he described as "soul crushing."

He candidly writes about how, in the first few months, he often questioned whether he was up to the task.

Eyre's memoir recounts a highly charged incident in June 2021 where he said he felt thrown "under the bus" by former deputy prime minister Chrystia Freeland.

At the time, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and Freeland both publicly questioned Eyre's decision to allow the now-former commander of the navy, Vice-Admiral Craig Baines, to remain in his post after he took part in a golf game with former chief of the defence staff Jonathan Vance, who had been under military police investigation following allegations of inappropriate behaviour.

In Eyre's view, Freeland's criticism amounted to forcing the prime minister to choose between his deputy and his senior military adviser.

"If there's no trust between the nation's senior military leader and the nation's senior elected leader, one of them has to go, and it's not going to be the elected leader," Eyre said in an interview with CBC News.

Support from Trudeau kept him from resigning

The incident culminated, Eyre said, when he was on the phone with the prime minister to discuss the decision to retain Baines. He was just about to resign when Trudeau stopped him by saying he still had confidence in him.

After his initial criticism, the prime minister made a further statement of support for his defence chief — remarks Eyre had not seen when the phone call was placed. The crisis was defused, but the tension remained.

WATCH | Eyre thought about resigning 'several times' during tenure: Former military commander Eyre says he thought about resigning 'several times' | Duration closed caption 4:01 Retired general Wayne Eyre speaks to CBC senior reporter Murray Brewster about a description in his memoir of a moment when he considered resigning as chief of defence staff after being thrown 'under the bus' by the former deputy prime minister, Chrystia Freeland.

Eyre served another three years after the incident.

Resignation crossed his mind "several times" as internal battles unfolded over defence funding and the deteriorating state of readiness in the military.

Ultimately, he decided to stay because quitting would have precipitated a further crisis in an already wounded institution.

"You've got to be very careful as a military leader about resigning. You can fall on your sword, but generally it hurts and you can only do it once," he said.

"Resigning is an inherently political act, which could further fray political-military relations, [and] would cause a momentary blip in the media cycle. But at the same time, [it would] cause significant turmoil in the institution."

Throughout his tenure there was a series of rolling crises including the various waves of the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022. Canada received advanced warning from Washington on Feb. 11 that Russian President Vladimir Putin had decided to proceed with the invasion.

At the time, the Trudeau government faced public criticism about its reluctance to approve lethal aid for the embattled Eastern European country. It was a struggle, Eyre acknowledged.

"What we experienced at that time was a collision of ideology with reality," he told CBC.

"The ideology being, we are Canada, we don't supply weapons to a conflict zone. The reality was, OK, this is coming, Ukraine is a friend, this [is] one way we can help."

'Lethargy to approve a new defence policy'

Eyre's book is littered with further examples related to Canada's mission to train Ukraine troops and the transfer of M-777 artillery, underlining his frustration with the government's seeming "inability to make decisions at the speed of war."

He did note there were times when Canada later outstripped its allies in the swift delivery of war supplies and equipment, such as Leopard tanks.

The overall sense of frustration came into sharp focus during Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's September 2023 visit to Canada, which included a series of speeches in Toronto.

"Both the PM and Deputy PM Freeland gave bellicose, impassioned speeches about being strong and supporting Ukraine," Eyre wrote, noting the contradiction between the political rhetoric and the fiscal reality that faced the Canadian military at the time.

"I, like the handful of CAF senior leaders present, had a hard time reconciling these otherwise great speeches with both the billion-dollar budget cut that they had just inflicted on us and their lethargy to approve a new defence policy."

The deeper the war in Ukraine became, the more concerned Eyre became about the state of Canada's readiness.

WATCH | Eyre urges Canada to support Ukraine's defence: ‘Urgency is required,’ says outgoing chief of defence staff Gen. Wayne Eyre on Russia-Ukraine war | Duration 2:48 In his final words as Canada’s chief of defence staff, Gen. Wayne Eyre said ‘evil walks this earth' and urged Canada to continue to support Ukraine's defence.

He described how, in June 2022, during the run-up to the unveiling of Canada's new policy commitment to NORAD — the binational aerospace command — no one seemed to know where $38 billion in funding was going to come from, or where it would be allocated.

"Most galling was the 'smoke and mirrors' funding approach, with billions already allocated for other military equipment taken away and reallocated, with most investments only coming years into the future," Eyre wrote.

"With confusion persisting several days later, I drew some government ire when I frankly told a journalist that the source of funds 'wasn’t clear to me.'"

Military 'compartmentalized' Ottawa convoy involvement

The memoir also sheds light on a passing reference that appeared in the public hearings related to the invocation of the Emergencies Act to end the convoy protest.

Former deputy defence minister Bill Matthews testified that the military prepared operational plans as a precaution, but they were dismissed due to significant concerns that deploying troops would escalate tensions and mirror the 1990 Oka Crisis.

Throughout the convoy protest crisis, Eyre was firmly opposed to the notion that the military had any sort of role whatsoever. He attempted to correct the public perception by saying there's a difference between planning and scenario spinning.

"We looked at various scenarios, and it wasn't planning because a plan entails assigning troops to task and warning at all levels and the like," Eyre told CBC News.

"No, it was more thinking about various scenarios, and what questions would we have to ask, what measures would have to be taken. But given the sensitivity at the time, it was very compartmentalized."

Most of the discussion, he said, revolved around the use of military tow-trucks to remove protest vehicles.

In his memoir, Eyre wrote: "At the time one of my staff commented, 'If you accomplish nothing else as CDS, keeping the CAF out of this mess is a singular achievement.'"

Canada 'on the right path,' Eyre says

During his final months as defence chief and in his departure speech, Eyre warned about how dangerous the world had become and how Canada needed to prepare.

Prime Minister Mark Carney's government reversed many Trudeau-era policies and has begun substantially investing in defence — taking the country to the NATO standard of two per cent of the gross domestic product.

Several European political leaders, as well as security and intelligence agencies have warned that the West is likely to face a major conflict with Russia and possibly even China by the end of the decade.

Asked by CBC whether he thought the country was ready for what may be coming in the next few years, Eyre said no.

"But we're on the right path, and we are getting there."

World.title: Crows are being given naloxone after suspected drug overdoses in Prince George, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An animal welfare group has been administering nasal naloxone to crows that are suspected to have eaten toxic drugs left accessible outside in downtown Prince George, B.C.

The Good Caws Crow Rescue Society (GCCRS) has posted multiple videos showing their volunteers giving nasal naloxone to crows that are otherwise unresponsive.

The videos then show the crows alert and able to fly again.

Naloxone is a medication commonly used to reverse or reduce the impact of an opioid overdose in people, and Dayna Slater of GCCRS says the crows they are helping are centred in an area of town where illicit drug use is known to occur.

"It's disheartening, it's scary," she told CBC Radio West host Sarah Penton. "It's a whole bunch of factors coming together to make, like, the perfect storm."

Slayter said they've had one or two suspected drug overdoses a year in the past, but said they've recorded more than a dozen among crows this year alone, an alarming rise.

"Their wings are spread out, their eyes are closed, their heartbeat slows right down. They're unresponsive but alive," is how she described the symptoms, adding some have a brown liquid foam coming out of their beaks.

Slayter says she believes the crows are getting toxic drugs through garbage left outside. (Andrew Kurjata/CBC)

While some of the birds have died, she said most were able to be released after recovering within 24 hours.

Dr. Kaitlyn Liukaitis of the Birchwood Veterinary Clinic has helped treat some of the crows, and said their symptoms are consistent with a toxic drug overdose.

She also said she isn't surprised using naloxone helps reverse the symptoms, as it has become a common tool used in veterinary care to treat a variety of animals.

"It's always frustrating that, as a human population, we're so damaging to the environment," she said.

Increase in drug toxicity

Cities across British Columbia have seen a rise in toxicity in the illicit drug supply, leading to multiple public warnings.

In Prince George, overdose calls have tripled at times — leading to a constant wail of sirens downtown, which is where the crows are being found.

Outreach groups say, as there is a growing political backlash to harm reduction measures like supervised consumption sites, it is becoming more difficult for people living with addiction to access prescribed alternatives to street drugs.

They advocate for safe, indoor spaces for people to access and use drugs — in part, so they aren't left outdoors.

Naloxone is used to reverse the symptoms of an opioid overdose. (Andrew Kurjata/CBC)

Slayter said she is working with harm reduction groups, who have been key to identifying crows experiencing suspected overdoses, and who have also helped supply expired naloxone kits for her volunteers to use.

She said she doesn't think anyone is intentionally harming the birds but, rather, the overdoses are a symptom of larger problems.

"They live side-by-side with us. They're in our garbage, they're in our yards. They're a direct mirror of the environment that we are living in."

She said she suspects the crows are accessing the drugs as they are mixed in with garbage that is openly available downtown.

She said her suggestion for a solution is more covered garbage cans that would prevent crows from accessing disposed materials.

"A crow doesn't know the difference between a sandwich bag and a bag that had something in it. And it takes something the size of like a grain of sand to affect a bird," she said.

World.title: Hockey Night in Canada to return in PWHL partnership, CBC/Radio-Canada announces
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

CBC’s Hockey Night in Canada is returning for a 90th season this fall after all.

But instead of six-plus months of NHL action, the longest-running sports program in the world will air eight prime time Professional Women’s Hockey League games on Saturday nights, the CBC announced Monday morning.

Beginning Dec. 5, with the defending Walter Cup champion Montreal Victoire hosting Hamilton’s expansion team, HNIC will provide comprehensive coverage, including pre- and post-game panel analysis and accompanying digital content on CBCSports.ca and social media.

On June 16, the CBC announced it would no longer broadcast NHL games after it and national rights-holder Rogers Sportsnet were unable to come to agreement on a new sublicensing deal.

Canada’s national public broadcaster retained the Hockey Night in Canada trademark should it wish to incorporate the brand into future coverage.

WATCH | 'Exciting' for girls to see women's players on HNIC, PWHL's Brianne Jenner says: Brianne Jenner on the return of Hockey Night in Canada featuring the PWHL | Duration closed caption 5:56 The PWHL Hamilton forward shares her favourite Hockey Night in Canada memories and her reaction to women's hockey being featured on the historic CBC program.

'New chapter'

“Our partnership with the PWHL opens a new chapter in sports history,” Chris Wilson, CBC’s executive director of Sports and Olympics, said. “We are proud to announce the return of the iconic Hockey Night in Canada brand, building on this beloved Canadian tradition with the PWHL’s growing fanbase and providing audiences across the country with free access to world-class hockey.”

The PWHL will launch its fourth season December 5, with a full schedule to be released on October 2. The league now boasts 12 teams after adding expansion teams in Detroit, Las Vegas, San Jose, and Hamilton for the upcoming season.

Keeping with tradition, each HNIC game will feature a Canadian-based team.

Amy Scheer, PWHL executive vice-president of business operations, said the partnership with CBC has been instrumental in the accessibility and growth of the league.

“Hockey Night in Canada is a fixture in Canadian sports culture, and its Saturday night schedule has ritually captivated hockey fans for nearly a century,” she said. “The opportunity to be part of this iconic brand represents another groundbreaking step for the PWHL to connect with our fans and forge new traditions together.”

CBC Sports Primetime premieres Oct. 3

Beyond airing eight Saturday games, CBC/Radio-Canada has acquired exclusive audio broadcast rights for all Victoire games in Canada during the 2026-27 season.

CBC Sports Primetime, a new weekly Saturday show hosted by Andi Petrillo, will premiere Oct. 3. Radio-Canada’s new weekly Sunday show, Rendez-vous Podium, follows with an Oct. 18 debut, hosted by Jacinthe Taillon.

Primetime, airing on CBC and streaming on CBC Gem, will launch with the Canada Super60 cricket league. It will feature major sporting events, professional women’s sports and unmatched coverage of Canada’s high performance as they compete at home and around the world, in Olympic and Paralympic sport.

The October broadcast schedule will include the Grand Slam of Curling and ISU Figure Skating Grand Prix.

“We’re delivering on our commitment to equal coverage of women’s sports across our platforms and look forward to elevating the athletes and stories at the heart of the game,” Wilson said.

Radio-Canada’s Rendez-vous Podium will combine athletic performances with human stories and be available on ICI Tele, the French-language general television network, on Sunday afternoons along with the ICI TOU. TV French streaming service.

The series will combine live events and stories about people making a difference at the elite and amateur levels, allowing the viewer to catch up with athletes and follow their journey to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

World.title: SpaceX sends giant Starship into orbit for the first time but ends the flight early
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. SpaceX launched its enormous Starship into orbit for the first time Monday and successfully delivered the most advanced Starlink satellites yet, but decided to cut short the flight, splashing down in the Pacific Ocean after just over three hours. The company had been aiming for a 10-hour flight, spanning six full laps around Earth, to prove its readiness for NASA's Artemis moon program. The spacecraft almost didn't make it to orbit after one of its engines shut down too soon shortly after liftoff. But with everything else working well and the bad engine no longer needed, flight controllers decided after several tense minutes to proceed as planned. "Starship is orbital," SpaceX mission control announced to cheers. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX on reaching orbit and "managing every step in a safe, responsible and especially inspirational way." Most advanced Starlinks put into orbit Founder Elon Musk's showpiece rocket — the biggest and most powerful ever built — carried 26 of the latest and most advanced Starlink satellites to join the 11,000 older models already providing internet service. They popped out of the spacecraft one by one, drawing more cheers from the SpaceX crowds looking on from the launch site at Starbase, Texas. The decision to end the flight early came soon afterward. No reason was provided. It was Starship's 14th full-scale launch from Texas's southern tip in three years. The earlier test flights ventured no farther than the Indian Ocean halfway around the world. Liftoff of Starship! pic.twitter.com/40D8bXSkr2 —SpaceX This time, SpaceX was intent on circling the globe from an altitude of 275 kilometres — not just once but six times over almost 10 hours, ending with a Pacific Ocean splashdown near Chile. While Starship achieved the proper orbit zipping along at 28,000 km/h, flight controllers opted to play it safe and bring it back several hours sooner, after just a couple laps. The first-stage booster was never meant to return to the Starbase launch site either, instead dropping into the Gulf of Mexico within minutes of the morning liftoff. SpaceX wants to ensure that everything works before flying Starship back to Starbase and catching the spacecraft. If it breaks apart over land and rains debris onto people, "our popularity would diminish very rapidly," Musk said at a business summit earlier this month. "That's why we're being extremely cautious here." In 2025, Starship exploded shortly after liftoff, causing flights to be diverted over the Caribbean. WATCH | Video shows fiery, falling debris after SpaceX rocket breaks up in Jan. 2025: Video shows fiery, falling debris after SpaceX rocket breaks up | Duration 0:27 Social media video recorded in Turks and Caicos shows debris streaking across the sky after the new Starship rocket broke up during a test flight. Depending on the findings from Monday's orbital debut, the next Starship could return to the launch pad with giant mechanical arms grabbing the hovering spacecraft. If the catch works — Musk gives it even or slightly better odds — then SpaceX will refly the spacecraft by year's end or early next year. The 124-metre rocket was designed from the start to be fully reusable — a key to lowering launch costs. SpaceX managed to salvage the last Starship from the Indian Ocean in July. Engineers modified the newly launched Starship's heat shield based on hands-on inspections from the recovered spacecraft, which is being tugged back to Starbase. SpaceX wants Starship to be certified for orbital flight SpaceX is pressing hard to certify Starship for orbital flight, a vital step toward moon and Mars travel. NASA's Artemis III mission is coming up as soon as next summer, a triple-launch docking exercise in orbit around Earth between an Orion capsule full of astronauts and competing lunar landers. Jeff Bezos's Blue Moon will blast off first, then Orion — which will close in for a linkup — then Musk's Starship for a docking with Orion once Blue Moon is unleashed. The following mission — Artemis IV, slated for no sooner than 2028 — would have astronauts landing on the moon in either Blue Moon or Starship, whichever is ready first. Subsequent moonshots will alternate between the two billionaires' landers. Musk originally developed Starship for Mars, intending to launch scores of them with the red planet's first settlers. For now, he plans to focus on the moon and use Starship to haul satellites into orbit by the truckload, phasing out the company's frailer Falcon 9 rocket within several years. A second Starship launch site is nearing completion at Florida's Kennedy Space Center and a third is planned for Louisiana.

World.title: British police release 5 London-based men after arrests near airbase used by U.S.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Police have arrested five men near the RAF Fairford airbase not far from the village of Whelford, England. Authorities suspect the men of preparing a terrorist plot possibly linked to the war in Iran, as the airbase is used by the U.S. to launch strikes.

British police said on Monday ‌they had released on bail five ​men who were ​arrested on suspicion of terrorism and explosives ​offences near ⁠a British airbase ⁠used ‌by the U.S., although they remain under investigation.

Officers arrested the men in the early hours of Sunday after a tipoff that three large white vans were heading to the military airfield in west England.

Officials earlier said the five men were all British nationals from various London boroughs, between the ages of 23 and 25. At the Labour Party's conference in Liverpool on Monday some time later, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood described them as British citizens.

"We are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state," Laurence Taylor, head of the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said in a prepared statement he read to reporters.

"However, I ask that at this time, CTP are given the space to work carefully and clearly.”

The main gate of RAF Fairford is pictured on Sunday. (David Bown/Getty Images)

The Iranian Embassy in London said in a statement that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" surrounding the arrests.

U.K. Prime ⁠Minister Andy Burnham was set to chair an ​emergency ⁠response meeting on Monday due to the incident.

A local farmer, who has not been named, said she ⁠had alerted police after seeing a ⁠group of "hooded and masked men" running into the fields.

"I believe that my ‌999 call foiled whatever plans they had," the farmer told BBC Radio, referring to the British equivalent to 911.

Defence Minister Wes Streeting told the BBC that the farmer had only a "partial picture" and said he would not speculate about motives of a live investigation.

U.S. President Donald Trump said the suspects had been looking to do "big damage" and had been under investigation by British and American authorities. But it's unknown whether the suspects ​were under the level of surveillance that Trump suggested.

Nearby residents can soon return

In Fairford, police have imposed a 400-metre cordon around the base and evacuated residents from 85 homes.

A bomb disposal robot could be seen on Sunday operating around the three white vans, while security was stepped up around the base. Armed police stood guard at the main entrance while large machinery was used to block other access points.

Mahmood said "the scene is now safe," and that the affected residents who had to leave their homes in the nearby village of Whelford will soon be able to return.

Security was stepped up at other ⁠U.S. bases in Britain.

Police officers guard a road leading to RAF Fairford on Monday. (Alastair Grant/The Associated Press)

Responding to the Fairford arrests, the U.S. Embassy issued a security alert, saying U.S. citizens should "exercise caution" and be "mindful of ⁠personal security."

U.S.-associated facilities, gatherings and organizations may be at heightened risk," the statement said.

In April, Britain had raised its national terrorism threat level to "severe" from "substantial" after a series of antisemitic incidents in north London, indicating a terrorist attack within the ‌six months is considered highly likely.

In May, Britain sanctioned 12 individuals and entities linked to Iran, accusing them of involvement in hostile activity, including plotting attacks and providing financial services to groups seeking to destabilize the U.K. and other countries.

The British government had given authorization to the U.S. ⁠to use bombers based at Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards had warned Britain in July not to ​allow U.S. bombers to fly from ⁠Fairford, saying any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.

"We know that Iran and their proxies wish to do us harm. We know that ⁠they hate our democracy, and we know that we regularly have to thwart Iranian attempts to threaten either our interests or indeed our allies," Streeting told BBC.

Iran ​has repeatedly denied involvement in attacks or plots in the United Kingdom and elsewhere.

World.title: Myanmar military airstrike hits market, killing at least 33 people in Rakhine state
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An airstrike carried out by Myanmar's military near a market in territory controlled by a powerful rebel group killed at least 33 people and wounded 36 others on Monday, the group and a rescue official said.

The attack in western Rakhine state was the latest in a series of deadly airstrikes against pro-democracy resistance forces and ethnic armed groups across the country.

Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on Feb. 1, 2021, triggering widespread opposition. After security forces suppressed peaceful protests with lethal force, many opponents of military rule took up arms, plunging large parts of the country into conflict.

The attack on Monday occurred in Kyauktaw township, about 340 kilometres west of Mandalay, the country's second-largest city, according to the Arakan Army, a powerful ethnic armed group based in Rakhine which controls Kyauktaw. It said a fighter jet dropped two bombs near a local market around noon, killing 33 people, including vendors, shoppers and pedestrians.

People walk through smoke and smouldering debris following a military airstrike on the market and adjacent bridge in Kyauktaw, on Monday. (AFP/Getty Images)

Wai Hun Aung, a senior rescue official in Rakhine, confirmed the casualties to The Associated Press, citing rescue workers at the scene. He said the market was the region's main wholesale centre, drawing traders and shoppers from across the state.

"This is one of the most severe airstrikes in Rakhine," he said.

Photos and videos posted on social media showed buildings on fire, damaged vehicles and parts of a nearby bridge destroyed.

The military did not immediately comment on the attack. It has previously said it strikes only legitimate military targets and has accused resistance groups of terrorism.

The Arakan Army is the well-trained and well-armed military wing of a movement seeking autonomy for Rakhine's ethnic minority from Myanmar's central government. It launched an offensive in Rakhine in November 2023 and has since captured a strategically important regional military headquarters and 14 of the state's 17 townships.

The military has imposed severe restrictions on trade routes since fighting intensified in Rakhine, worsening food shortages.

In December, a military airstrike on a hospital in Rakhine's Mrauk-U township killed at least 34 people and wounded 80 others.

Rakhine has also seen clashes between the military and insurgents which, beginning in 2017, has led to hundreds of thousands of Rohingya flee to Bangladesh and elsewhere. Myanmar, formerly known as Burma, does not recognize the Rohingya as one of the country’s 135 lawful ethnic minorities, as countries like Bangladesh and Malaysia seek to repatriate some of the refugees.

World.title: What was B.C.’s David Eby thinking by calling the maddest Canadian election ever? Full Comment podcast
World.content:
Article content

If you’ve got a majority government with two years left and an unpopular record to defend, calling a snap election might not seem like a great idea. But it did to B.C. Premier David Eby. Brian Lilley is joined by B.C. politics columnists Vaughn Palmer (Vancouver Sun) and Les Leyne (Victoria Times-Colonist) to try to find method in Eby’s seeming madness. They consider his scheme to pounce on his rivals’ disarray, with the Conservatives at war over a divisive leader. But they seem to be quickly reconstituting themselves under a new, more popular captain, even as some star NDP candidates step aside. It’s all unfolding amid municipal elections already underway, creating confusion for voters, and leaving British Columbians baffled as to why it’s happening at all. (Recorded Sept. 25, 2026.)

World.title: At first, case stumped doctors who determined Ontario woman had fatal case of rat bite fever
World.content:
For days and days on end, doctors didn’t know exactly what kind of organism they were up against.

The infection spreading through the 48-year-old Ontario woman was so aggressive, large parts of her heart were destroyed. But all the usual blood work, all the cultures for typical bacterial infections came back negative. Doctors couldn’t fully understand what was feeding the infection.

Until her sister wondered, could it be the rats?

The woman’s death last year, published in a new case report, is being described as the first reported fatal case of rat bite fever that defeated even the most advanced “Hail Mary” form of out-of-body heart and lung bypass.

The case “was a bit of a conundrum,” said cardiologist and intensivist Dr. Craig Ainsworth, chief of critical care at Hamilton Health Sciences, and co-author of the report in JACC, the Journal of the American College of Cardiology.

“Normally, when we have people with that degree of heart and heart valve infection, we usually get something in the blood work,” he said, typically one of the aggressive bugs “that do this sort of thing.”

In this case, everything was negative until weeks later, when valve tissue taken during the woman’s emergency heart surgery was sent for specialized DNA testing, which ultimately identified streptobacillus moniliformis, a bacterium found in the oral, nasal and respiratory tract secretions of rats.

The bug can be transmitted to people via broken skin, bites or scratches, but also from close contact, without a bite or scratch, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control. It can also be spread through exposure to contaminated food or water.

Diagnosis can be challenging: the organism is “fastidious, difficult to grow and has limited diagnostic tests available for early detection,” Ainsworth and colleagues wrote in the Sept. 12 edition of JACC Case Reports.

The woman ultimately died, despite being treated with the proper antibiotics. “We just guessed and happened to guess properly,” Ainsworth said, however, the infection was too far gone by the time she was transferred to his ICU.

“It wasn’t obvious to us for days and days what we were actually treating.”

Rat bite fever is a rare infection with an estimated mortality rate of up to 13 per cent if left untreated. The disease often starts with vague symptoms such as fever, rash and generally just feeling unwell, which can delay people seeking medical attention.

The woman was a bit of a “homebody” who kept to herself, Ainsworth said. She had some medical problems, including asthma and inflammatory bowel disease, and was a smoker. “She wasn’t a perfectly healthy 48-year-old, but she was totally functional and ambulatory.”

After six to eight weeks of fatigue, lower back pain, facial flushing and peripheral numbness, the woman went to her local hospital’s emergency department, about 100 kilometres outside Hamilton.

She described worsening diarrhea and fainting spells — spells owing to, in retrospect, “the infection eating into the electrical system of her heart,” Ainsworth said.

Doctors suspected sepsis and started antibiotics, but while in emergency the woman suffered a cardiac arrest. The upper chambers of her heart were no longer communicating with the lower chambers, causing a dangerously slow heart rate.

A temporary pacemaker was inserted. Three days later, a special echocardiogram that involves guiding a thin tube down the throat to examine the heart from inside the esophagus revealed extensive infection of various parts of the heart and valves.

She was referred to a second hospital for urgent, complicated and prolonged heart surgery.

Because of low oxygen levels, doctors couldn’t take the woman off the machine used to take over the function of her heart and lungs during surgery. She was placed on ECMO, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, an advanced form of life support.

Her heart muscle continued to deteriorate, and the woman was transferred to Hamilton General Hospital, “still without a specific diagnosis or a bug,” Ainsworth said.

“By the time we received the call, she was at best a Hail Mary; she was very unwell,” he said. But because she was 48 and otherwise fairly healthy, they tried every measure they could.

“She just didn’t get any better,” Ainsworth said.

At one point her sister, from whom she was semi-estranged, remarked to Ainsworth, “You know, I just wonder if it’s related to the rats she has in her house.”

“As a non-infectious disease doctor, I didn’t put two and two together,” he said. “I thought it was like a guinea pig or a hamster, just a little more unusual.

“But when we ultimately got this bug back from the DNA testing, it became clear that almost certainly this was related to her pet rats.”

After several weeks in hospital, the woman succumbed to the infection. Life support was withdrawn “given the unfortunate futility of what we were doing and her worsening, despite all the heroic interventions,” Ainsworth said.

It’s not clear if the rats were purchased or had infested her home. The sister said the rats seemed more like pets. “I don’t think they were just innocent bystanders,” Ainsworth said.

The bacterium S. moniliformis is ubiquitous in all rodents, said infectious disease specialist Dr. Omar Mourad, a co-author of the case report. “It lives in their mouth, in their oral flora. Any rodent — though certainly rats are the famous ones — will have it.

“It’s not harmful to the rats, similar to how we have a number of bacteria in our mouth and on our skin,” he said. But it can cause trouble when it gets into humans.

Despite its name, more often than not rat bite fever is transmitted merely by handling rats, Mourad said.

“Some people like to kiss the rat on the mouth, which I would not recommend,” he said. Or they don’t wash their hands properly after handling the rodents and get the bacteria into their mouth.

“Once it gets in, occasionally it will make its way into the bloodstream and cause more trouble,” Mourad said.

Classic symptoms of infection — rash, joint pain, vomiting and other GI symptoms — typically start three to 10 days after exposure.

Most people who get infected get better on their own after feeling flu-like for a couple of days.

“But you have to get it before it does anything like this,” Mourad said.

Left untreated, severe cases can cause not only endocarditis, as it did in the 48-year-old woman, but also meningitis — infection of the brain and spinal cord.

Although uncommon in Canada, rat bite fever is increasing because of “changing patterns of urban living (more dense urban housing) and pet-keeping practices,” other researchers have warned.

As of 2106, the-then-largest single episode in Canada found 11 cases of reported rat bite fever on Vancouver Island between 2010 and 2016. Seven cases required hospitalization, but there were no deaths “or significant morbidity.”

From the intensive care physician’s perspective, “It comes back to, if something is weird and a bit of a unicorn (exceptionally rare) case, I think it behooves us to dig deeper and start asking questions of loved ones and family members,” Ainsworth said.

“Just by having a conversation with the sister and asking about habits and unusual things, the rats came out, which was helpful information.”

It was the second case of a pet rat infection Mourad saw last year. The other involved a different bacteria called leptospirosis, spread through the urine of infected rats.

The man, who got infected from handling his pet rats, spent a few weeks in hospital “until we figured it out,” Mourad said.

“Fortunately, it ended much better, and the patient did very well,” he said

“As far as I know, he did give away the rats.”
