World.title: The Monobloc chair: The plastic throne that rules Mexico
World.content:
I grew up on a chair.

Not literally. That would have been weird.

Instead, I come from an Italian family where chairs were everywhere. Sitting was merely one of their many functions.

On a good day, you sat in them and observed the family theatrics. On a bad day, they became climbing rigs for reaching my cousin’s secret stash of Nutella. They made glorious goalposts too and, when the mood was ripe, even served as Hulk Hogan-style wrestling weapons.

So perhaps it was inevitable that, when we arrived in Mexico, my attention was drawn to chairs.

Not just any chairs. Plastic ones, branded and unbranded. Stacked outside shops, scattered around taco stands and lined up for parties.

I soon realized something important: The Mexican plastic throne is bona fide everyday infrastructure.

This, of course, raised questions. Where do they come from? Who makes them and, most crucially, who tests them? Is there a government-appointed Chair Inspector whose career involves dropping heavy tíos onto spindly legs and taking notes? “Load tolerance: not bad. Man: slightly sweaty. Chair: 100% unbreakable.”

Is there a Ministry of Seating with a maximum permissible wobble? And who decides the colors?

I began to suspect a secret council: 12 people in a windowless room, surrounded by polypropylene, debating whether next year’s official hue should be turquoise or something more adventurous. Perhaps they never sit, preferring to stand and nod, secretly longing for a bar stool.

The superhero of street seating

There could even be a Mexican chair superhero, but not the sort who fights crime; Mexico has enough people for that. His superpower is knowing exactly how many chairs the perfect quinceañera requires.

He arrives at the venue, surveys the courtyard, then whispers, “148 … 84 green, 36 red and 28 fuchsia.”

Nobody asks how he knows; they just start stacking.

His other powers remain classified, although rumors suggest he can identify a broken chair from 900 yards away and appear instantly whenever somebody says, “We’re going to need more chairs, dude.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Dastaangoi (@dastaangoi)

I might be digressing.

To understand how a single injection-molded object achieved near-mythological status, I did what any self-respecting journalist would do when confronted with patio furniture: watched an unhealthy amount of completely irrelevant TikTok videos, nearly polished off a whole jar of spreadable Dulce De La Rosa Marzipan and, with the deadline looming, contacted Mexico’s academics.

First, I spent an afternoon at a taquería near my house.

One taquero used a single chair as a stepladder, cash stand and footrest in under four minutes. It didn’t flinch. It simply creaked around its torn backrest, as if puffing out its plastic chest, and muttered: “Is that all you got, hermano?”

Fascinating.

Defining community through cheap plastic

Dr. Armando Cisneros, a sociologist at UAM-Azcapotzalco, took the question considerably more seriously than I did.

“Objects don’t just serve communities,” he told me. “They define them. The chair’s petroleum-born virtues — dirt-cheap and stubbornly durable — don’t just suit street life; they help shape it.”

Cisneros elegantly calls it a “culture of rest,” a nationwide understanding that wherever commerce or conversation happens, a place to sit will follow.

If Cisneros explained the chair’s DNA, Dr. Mario Ortiz Murillo, a sociologist at UNAM, deftly mapped its territory.

“It serves rich and poor alike, because everyone gets tired,” Ortiz Murillo told me.

But in Mexico, he explained, it does more than hold weight. It holds space.

“Tied to a lamppost, it claims a curb. Stacked in a pickup, it’s a pop-up taquería.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by 𝙋𝙖𝙡𝙖𝙘𝙚 𝘾𝙡𝙪𝙗 (@gio_palace)

“The plastic chair,” Ortiz Murillo said, “is how Mexicans move through and confidently claim the city.”

And claim it they do.

I asked Rosa, who runs my neighborhood grocery, why she keeps three by the door.

“Honestly, I never really thought about it,” she said. “Locals like sitting and sipping sodas … that’s how they relax, or in the case of my husband, spend an inordinate amount of time gabbling nonsense with local gringos about football.”

I felt chuffed.

Built to outlive your phone

That contrast — Rosa’s practical indifference versus the chair’s actual ubiquity — led me to the broader point.

We live in an age of flat-pack furniture and Allen wrenches. Luckily, the Mexican plastic throne rises above all that. It arrives fully formed and morally uncomplicated. Best of all, it’s ready to be abused. Leave it in the July sun until it fades to the color of old teeth? No problem. Stack it. Drop it. Drag it. It will probably outlive your phone and possibly your career. Take that, AI.

I grew up thinking chairs were supposed to earn their keep, but in Mexico, they run the place.

So next time you’re handed a slightly warped, suspiciously wobbly plastic throne, don’t test the legs.

Just sit.

Listen to the comal sizzle. Listen to the overlapping conversations. Mexico doesn’t need Roche Bobois or Poltrona Frau to hold its people together. It has cheap polypropylene, and against all economic and gravitational odds, it works.

Besides, if a 250-pound tío can balance on it like an Olympic gymnast, so can you.

Just skip the Hulk Hogan routine. The chair will survive, but your dignity might not.

Paolo Ferrari is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: How Oaxaca’s La Ventanilla turned tourism into conservation
World.content:
Standing on La Ventanilla beach is a breathtaking experience. In the distance, a rock formation shaped like a window frames 15 kilometers of pristine beach — one of the last protected areas on the Oaxaca coast. This area remains largely untouched thanks to the Zapotec community, which began transforming it into an oasis for local wildlife, particularly turtles and crocodiles, 30 years ago.

By the late 1990s, the crocodile and turtle populations in La Ventanilla, located in the municipality of Santa María Tonameca, were on the verge of extinction. Their skins were highly valued in trade, and turtle meat and eggs were part of a local culinary tradition, often prized for their supposed aphrodisiac properties.

National laws protecting crocodiles were enacted in the late 1970s, followed by turtle protection in the early 1990s. By 1998, Mexican authorities in La Ventanilla had imposed stricter penalties for poaching and strengthened the reserve’s overall protection. “It was then that the community, led by individuals like Agustín Reyes and Vicente García and guided by NGOs, began a revolutionary shift in both mentality and economics,” said Eulalio Cortés, a member of the cooperative.

This community effort led to the creation of the Ecotourism Cooperative La Ventanilla. Today, it is a global model for conservation, successfully balancing ecotourism with the protection and well-being of local flora and fauna.

The importance of La Ventanilla for conservation

La Ventanilla is renowned for its beauty, but it also hosts a unique ecological phenomenon. During the rainy season, saltwater from the sea and freshwater from the lagoon converge. This mixing supports rich biodiversity and creates an ideal breeding environment. This period is also optimal for crocodile mating, and these predators play a crucial role in the mangrove and lagoon ecosystems by controlling the populations of other species. Simultaneously, the healthy mangrove forests act as a natural barrier against hurricanes and are vital for carbon sequestration in the fight against climate change.

Furthermore, turtle nesting is essential to maintaining this ecological balance. La Ventanilla thrives thanks to the efforts of 30 families dedicated to protecting this equilibrium. The project is registered as a Wildlife Conservation Management Unit and operates under a management plan approved by the Department of the Environment and Natural Resources, known by its Spanish acronym Semarnat.

Conservation activities include protecting the lagoon and mangroves, managing crocodile populations on a small island, and conducting nightly monitoring for biometric research. These efforts provide valuable opportunities for university students and researchers, while responsible tourism supports the project’s sustainability.

Today, the cooperative protects at least 300 American crocodiles, along with species such as deer, iguanas and various birds, using a self-sustaining model. This is funded through silent, nonmotorized boat tours of the mangroves and visits to the small island where the animals are cared for.

Science, tourism and livelihoods

The cooperative organizes two activities for tourists that double as vital conservation efforts. During the turtle nesting season, members monitor the beach nightly to collect eggs, transferring them to a protected shelter to shield them from predators and poachers. A small group of tourists is welcome to assist in this process.

Additionally, around 6 p.m., cooperative members release thousands of hatchlings into the sea. Tourists can also participate in this experience, directly contributing to conservation. According to Rocío García, a member of the project, between 25,000 and 30,000 turtles are released here annually.

The island tour allows visitors to see crocodiles up close, with the fees from these tours used to feed the animals. Today, the community relies on tourism not only for its livelihood, but as a means to protect the lagoon, the mangroves and the thousands of creatures that call this area home.

Their work is increasingly vital, demonstrating that local communities are essential to mangrove conservation at a time when, according to the National Commission for the Knowledge and Use of Biodiversity (Conabio), Mexico has lost more than 27,000 hectares of mangrove forest in the last five years alone.

Ana Paula de la Torre is a Mexican journalist and collaborator for various outlets, including Milenio, Animal Político, Vice, Newsweek en Español, Televisa and Mexico News Daily.

HAITI · ELECTIONS

Key Facts — The country Haiti, which shares the island of Hispaniola with the Dominican Republic. It has had no elected president since Jovenel Moïse was assassinated in July 2021.

— Why it matters The vote is meant to be Haiti’s first national election in a decade and to end years of transitional rule by unelected leaders.

— What happened Nine men had registered online to run for president by the morning of 23 September, Le Nouvelliste reported. The electoral council’s own count two days earlier was seven.

— Who is involved Candidates include former interim prime minister Claude Joseph, former interim president Jocelerme Privert and Wilner Joseph, who launched his campaign on Sunday 27 September.

— What it means for you A 13 December first round is still the official date. Any slip would extend transitional rule, which business groups say must end to restore confidence and economic activity.

— Still open The final electoral rules, the length of the next presidential term, and which candidates the electoral council will approve.

The field for the Haiti presidential election is taking shape, with nine men registered by the morning of 23 September. The Port-au-Prince daily Le Nouvelliste obtained the list from the online platform of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP), which runs Haitian elections.

The first round is set for 13 December. It would be the country’s first national vote in a decade, but its rules are still not final.

Who has signed up

Le Nouvelliste named them as Claude Joseph, Ricardo Jean-Pierre, Gary Beaudo, Wilson Jeudy and Wilner Joseph. The others are Jocelerme Privert, Maxo Joseph, Munir Joseph Moura and Gandy Dorfeuille.

Claude Joseph founded the Engagés pour le Développement party and served as interim prime minister, the news site Juno7 reported. Privert was interim president before Moïse took office in February 2017.

On Sunday 27 September, the Viktwa platform launched Wilner Joseph’s campaign at a rally in Pétion-Ville, Juno7 reported. Viktwa says it groups 52 parties and political structures.

What the electoral council says

The CEP’s own statement of 21 September counted seven presidential candidacies, 162 for the Senate and 419 for the lower house. Both Juno7 and The Haitian Times reported those figures.

The council has extended online candidate registration to 9 October. It also reported 628,755 registered voters, just over 10 percent of the potential electorate.

The Haitian Times reported that nearly 20 municipalities could not receive candidate filings at their usual offices because armed gangs are present. On Thursday 24 September, Peterson Pierre-Louis took over as CEP president from Jacques Desrosiers, Juno7 reported.

Pressure for a credible vote

Four business associations said on 22 September that Haiti needs “a realistic and definitive timetable”. They said the private sector refuses to let elections become “a mere formality”, Le Nouvelliste reported.

Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé spoke at a United Nations meeting on 24 September. “The next Government of Haiti must go through the ballot box,” he said.

What Is Not Yet Known

Le Nouvelliste, in an editorial, said candidates are still waiting for a third version of the electoral decree. It argued they cannot know if the next term lasts four, five or six years, as a new constitution is drafted.

The CEP has not yet ruled on which candidacies are valid, and Le Nouvelliste called its list provisional. Candidates must still file documents in person before a final list is published.

It is also unclear how diaspora voting will work. Nor is it known whether registration will reach enough voters before the Haiti presidential election on 13 December.

World.title: Canada Denies Its Diplomats Spied for the US in Cuba in Havana Syndrome Era

CUBA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — The country Cuba, the one-party Caribbean state where Canada kept an embassy and close ties throughout the decades when Washington had cut relations.

— Why it matters Havana Syndrome, the unexplained illness that struck US and Canadian diplomats in Havana from 2016, is still unresolved. Ten Canadian diplomats and their families are suing their own government.

— What happened On Saturday 26 September The Globe and Mail, citing two unnamed sources, reported that Canadian diplomats worked with US intelligence in Cuba between 2016 and 2018.

— Who is involved Global Affairs Canada, the foreign ministry, disputes the report. Its Global Security Reporting Program, the unit named by the sources, is “not an intelligence collection program,” it said.

— What it means for you Nothing changes for visitors to Cuba. The report does reopen questions about why diplomats fell ill and how Ottawa treated them.

— Still open Who or what caused the illnesses, whether Parliament’s security committee will investigate, and how Havana will respond.

Canada has denied a report that its diplomats in Cuba worked with American spies as the Havana Syndrome illnesses emerged. The Globe and Mail, a Toronto daily, published the claims on Saturday.

What the sources told The Globe

According to The Globe, one source said a Canadian diplomat gathered human intelligence in Cuba between 2016 and 2018. The diplomat occasionally passed information directly to American spies in Havana, the source said.

A second source said the United States shipped satellite equipment to Cuba in diplomatic sea containers in late 2016. Under the Vienna Convention, the treaty governing diplomats, Cuban officials could not open them.

That source said the equipment was installed on the roof of the Canadian embassy and at some diplomats’ homes. The paper did not name either source.

Ottawa’s denial

In a statement on Friday, Global Affairs Canada disputed that its diplomats shared intelligence with US spies. It said staff in its Global Security Reporting Program work “overtly, legally and in compliance with the Vienna Convention.”

The Globe noted a 2023 finding by a federal watchdog, the National Security and Intelligence Review Agency. It said the program operated in a “distinctly grey zone”.

Why the case is still alive

Ten Canadian diplomats and their families sued Ottawa in 2019. They allege they were denied leading-edge care and their brain injuries were played down.

The Justice Department confirmed it has used a rare national-security law to keep new details of the case secret.

On Monday, The Globe reported that former Canadian intelligence and security officials want Parliament’s security committee to investigate. A Global Affairs report in February 2024 found the illnesses “were not the result of any malicious act of a foreign power.”

Cuba has always denied any official involvement, OnCubaNews noted. An earlier Rio Times report covered cases detected among US embassy staff in Colombia.

What Is Not Yet Known

No government has confirmed the spying claims, which rest on two anonymous sources. The cause of the illnesses also remains unproven; some investigations have pointed to Russia, which no official finding has confirmed.

It is not yet known whether Parliament’s security committee will open an inquiry, or whether Cuba’s government will respond. For background on the island, see Cuba Explained 2026: The Economy, the Exodus, the System and What to Watch.

World.title: Study: 337 Reporters and Activists Killed in Mexico Under López Obrador
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

MEXICO · PRESS FREEDOM

Key Facts — The country Mexico, where Andrés Manuel López Obrador was president from December 2018 to September 2024. His ally Claudia Sheinbaum now governs.

— Why it matters Journalists in Mexico have long faced some of the world’s highest murder rates. The new study argues the violence under López Obrador was not random.

— What happened On Thursday 24 September, the Human Rights Center at the University of California, Berkeley published a platform counting 337 journalists and rights defenders killed during his term.

— The numbers 78 journalists and 259 human rights defenders, according to the study. It puts impunity for crimes against both groups at 93 to 99 percent.

— What it means for you No court case exists. The researchers say they dropped a planned submission to the International Criminal Court because of US sanctions on it.

— Still open Whether any prosecutor, in Mexico or abroad, takes up the material, and how López Obrador and the government respond.

A university study says 337 journalists and human rights defenders were killed in Mexico while Andrés Manuel López Obrador was president. Its authors argue that attacks on journalists in Mexico formed a pattern that could be examined as crimes against humanity.

The Human Rights Center at the University of California, Berkeley published the findings on Thursday 24 September, El Universal and Expansión reported. These are the researchers’ conclusions, not the findings of any court.

What the study claims

Of the 337 dead, 78 were journalists and 259 were rights defenders, according to both El Universal and Aristegui Noticias. El Universal noted that Article 19, which tracks attacks on journalists in Mexico, had counted 46 or 47 killed.

The study says a secret military intelligence centre used Pegasus spyware and other tools without court orders, El Universal and Expansión reported. López Obrador repeatedly said his government did not spy on journalists.

It also accuses him of using his daily televised press conferences, known as the mañaneras, to single out named reporters as enemies. The researchers say they analysed more than 1,400 of them with the help of AI software.

The international court route

The material was first prepared for the International Criminal Court in The Hague, which tries crimes against humanity. Mexico accepted the court’s jurisdiction by ratifying its founding treaty in 2005, Aristegui Noticias noted.

Lindsay Freeman, a senior director at the centre, told Aristegui that US sanctions on the court made working with it a “legal risk”. The team published everything online instead.

“It really looks like a concerted campaign against the people trying to hold power to account,” Freeman told Aristegui. That is her assessment; no prosecutor has opened a case.

A reporter under threat the same week

On the day the study appeared, investigative reporter Anabel Hernández presented her new book, “Narcocracia”, in Mexico City. It accuses officials of ties to drug cartels.

She said she had received death threats, Aristegui reported. She held President Claudia Sheinbaum and the ruling Morena party responsible for her safety.

She said the federal protection scheme for journalists had stepped up her security, Aristegui reported. Alianza de Medios MX, a news site, reported that she had been admitted to the scheme.

What Is Not Yet Known

None of the outlets that covered the study carried a response from López Obrador or from the Sheinbaum government. It is not known whether Mexican prosecutors will review the cases.

It is also unclear whether anyone will bring the material to the International Criminal Court, and whether the court would act. Hernández’s allegations remain untested in court.

World.title: Six Dead in Guatemala as Officials Deny a Raid on a US-Wanted Trafficker
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

GUATEMALA · ORGANISED CRIME

Key Facts — The country Guatemala, in Central America, lies on a main route for cocaine moving from South America through Mexico to the United States.

— Why it matters Local media linked the violence to a reported attempt to catch Haroldo Lorenzana, for whom Washington offers up to US$5 million.

— What happened Gunfire in Huíté, Zacapa, on Sunday 27 September left six dead, according to the Public Ministry. The Interior Ministry confirmed five.

— Who is involved Defence calls it a clash between two trafficking groups; police say they took no part. La Hora’s unnamed sources describe a capture blocked by residents.

— What it means for you The east of Guatemala remains contested trafficking ground. Anyone travelling there should follow local reports before setting out.

— Still open Which force, if any, went into the town, whether anyone was detained, and what the government will say officially.

Six people died in gunfire in Huíté, a small town in Guatemala’s eastern Zacapa department, on Sunday 27 September, the Public Ministry said. Local outlets linked the violence to a reported attempt to capture Haroldo Lorenzana, a man the United States wants on drug charges.

The newspaper La Hora reported, citing sources it could not name, that residents stopped the arrest. Guatemala’s defence and interior ministries both denied running any operation inside the town.

What the authorities confirm

The Public Ministry, Guatemala’s prosecution service, said it processed three crime scenes, Prensa Libre reported. Three women were shot in a car at the town entrance, two men died in the El Campo district and a third man in the village of La Oscurana.

Interior Minister Marco Antonio Villeda, whose ministry runs the National Civil Police, confirmed five deaths to the broadcaster Emisoras Unidas. “It is an incident on which I need more information,” he said, as quoted by La Hora and Prensa Libre.

Villeda said the police had neither taken part in nor been called to any operation in Huíté. He added that the case would go before President Bernardo Arévalo’s cabinet on Monday.

Two competing accounts

Defence Ministry sources told Prensa Libre the shooting was a clash between two criminal groups allegedly dedicated to drug trafficking. They said armed men in military-style gear, seen in videos shared online, were not soldiers.

The ministry told the news site República that troops stayed on the outskirts to protect civilians. According to Prensa Libre, the ministry said residents blocked the streets and kept soldiers from reaching the scene.

La Hora’s sources gave a different picture: an attempt to capture Lorenzana that failed because of local opposition. They said one member of the family had even been caught, but people stopped him being held.

Who Haroldo Lorenzana is

US authorities accuse him of drug trafficking and of links to Mexican groups including the Sinaloa cartel, La Hora and República reported. Washington offers up to US$5 million for information leading to his arrest or conviction.

He is a grandson of Waldemar Lorenzana Lima, the clan’s founder, who was extradited to the United States in 2014 and died there in 2021. The violence came days after five US attorneys met Guatemala’s Arévalo to widen anti-crime cooperation.

What Is Not Yet Known

It is not confirmed which force, if any, entered Huíté, or whether US agencies helped. República reported that no official answer had been given by Monday morning.

Nor is it confirmed that Lorenzana was in the town, or that anyone was detained. The toll also differs: six according to prosecutors, five according to the Interior Ministry.

Publinews reported that officials were expected to give a position after the cabinet meeting. For background on the country, see Guatemala Explained 2026.

MEXICO · ORGANISED CRIME

Key Facts — The country Mexico, where criminal groups trade in illegal fuel as well as drugs.

— Why it matters The government says such raids aim to cut off cartel funding from the illicit fuel market, a priority under President Claudia Sheinbaum.

— What happened On Sunday 27 September officials announced the arrest of Jesús Manuel “N”, alias “El Bebo”, after 19 raids in three northern states. Two other people were detained.

— The numbers About 500,000 litres of fuel, 84 tractor units, 107 tanker trailers, two aircraft and 13 properties were seized, according to the Defence Ministry.

— What it means for you Little directly. For businesses in Tamaulipas, Nuevo León and Chihuahua, it signals continued federal pressure on illegal fuel networks.

Nineteen raids in three states

According to El Universal and El Financiero, army special forces, the National Guard and the Attorney General’s Office carried out 19 searches. They took place in Chihuahua, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas, the states along much of the US border.

El Financiero reported, citing the Defence Ministry, that the arrests came on 24 and 25 September after military intelligence work. Two other people were detained alongside him.

The ministry listed 13 properties, two aircraft, 50 vehicles, 84 tractor units and 107 tanker trailers among the seizures. It also listed four storage tanks, 11 fuel pumps and 49 rubbish lorries.

About 500,000 litres of fuel were taken, El Universal and Animal Político reported, along with methamphetamine, ammunition and cash.

The US ambassador to Mexico, Ronald Johnson, praised the arrest on social media on 27 September, El Universal and Excélsior reported. He said such operations target the wider networks that sustain the cartels.

What he is accused of

He had an arrest warrant from a federal judge for organised crime, in the form of handling illicit funds. El Universal reported that investigators tie him to smuggling foreign fuel to dodge taxes.

Mexicans call this huachicol fiscal. Unlike pipeline theft, it relies on false import papers to avoid customs duty and fuel tax.

Infobae and MVS Noticias reported that he answered directly to César Morfín, alias “El Primito”. Officials identify Morfín as the head of Los Metros.

Infobae, citing US drug agency assessments, described the Gulf Cartel as split into rival factions. Los Metros is one of its two main factions, fighting rivals for routes in Tamaulipas.

The case follows the jailing of a former navy officer over fuel smuggling, reported in Mexico: Fuel Smuggling Case Puts Ex-Rear Admiral Behind Bars. It also follows a pact covered in Mexico Unites Treasury, Financial Intelligence and Pemex Against Fuel Theft.

What Is Not Yet Known

The exact date and place of the arrest are unclear. The Defence Ministry, via El Financiero, gave 24 and 25 September; sdpnoticias said 27 September. XEVA reported that he was held in Chihuahua.

No court has yet ruled on the charges. He is presumed innocent, and no statement from his defence has been reported.

Officials have not named the other two detainees, nor said what share of the seized fuel was smuggled.

World.title: Colombia Kills Rebel Accused of Financing a Presidential Hopeful’s Murder
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

COLOMBIA · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Colombia, about 53 million people, signed a peace deal with the FARC guerrillas in 2016. Several splinter groups never disarmed or later took up arms again.

— The background Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay, 39, a right-wing presidential hopeful, was shot at a campaign event in Bogotá on 7 June 2025 and died on 11 August. Prosecutors say the Segunda Marquetalia, a FARC splinter group, ordered the attack.

— Why now President Abelardo de la Espriella, in office since August, has put military offensives against armed groups at the centre of his government.

— What happened On Sunday 27 September 2026, an Army, police and air force operation in rural Tello, in the southern department of Huila, killed alias “Robinson Gutiérrez”. Three other group members were captured.

— Who is who Intelligence files cited by Colombian newspapers name him as Miguel Orlando Guzmán González, political and finance chief of one of the group’s regional units. The armed forces commander says he was accused of helping finance the senator’s murder.

— What it means for you The operation took place in the countryside of Huila, far from Bogotá, Medellín and the Caribbean coast. For investors, it is another sign the new government favours military pressure over talks with armed groups.

— Update, 28 September Army and armed forces communiqués confirm his death and list rifles, grenades and a grenade launcher seized. The three people captured remain unnamed.

— Still open No evidence for the financing allegation has been published, and no court has ruled on his role.

Colombian security forces have killed a guerrilla commander accused of helping to pay for the murder of a presidential hopeful. The Army has confirmed the death, which President Abelardo de la Espriella first announced as preliminary on Sunday 27 September.

The dead man, known as alias “Robinson Gutiérrez”, belonged to the Segunda Marquetalia, a splinter of the old FARC guerrilla army. Prosecutors say that group ordered the 2025 shooting of Senator Miguel Uribe Turbay in Bogotá.

What changed on 28 September

The Army and the armed forces general command confirmed on Sunday evening that alias Robinson Gutiérrez died in the operation. Their communiqués describe him as the unit’s political and financial chief, with about 35 years in armed groups.

Troops seized three rifles, two handguns, 13 grenades, 22 magazines, a grenade launcher and computer equipment, the Army says. It also accuses him of extortion, burning a vehicle and three kidnappings in Caquetá.

The Army calls him a financier of the senator’s murder. It has published no evidence, and no court has ruled on that claim.

What happened in Huila

The operation took place in the rural area of El Cadillo, in the municipality of Tello. Tello lies in Huila, a department in Colombia’s south-centre that borders the jungle region of Caquetá.

Troops from the Army’s Deployment Force Against Transnational Threats led the action, supported by the air force and the National Police. Three other members of the group were captured; their names have not been released.

De la Espriella announced it on X, saying the operation had taken place “a few minutes” earlier. “This criminal is implicated in the murder of Miguel Uribe Turbay,” he wrote. “I will not stop demanding that the whole truth about that crime be established.”

He added that the result was preliminary and that he would say more once verification was complete. The Army confirmed the death that evening.

Who Robinson Gutiérrez was

Intelligence files cited by the newspaper El Tiempo name him as Miguel Orlando Guzmán González. He was political and financial chief of the Teófilo Forero Castro unit, which operates in Huila and neighbouring Caquetá.

According to the same files, he had run the unit’s finances since 2024. The government accuses him of directing extortion and threats against farmers, recruiting minors and attacking civilians and security forces.

He faced an arrest warrant for criminal conspiracy aimed at murder and extortion. Some outlets called him a right-hand man of the group’s leader, but officials described him as a regional commander.

What officials allege about the senator’s murder

The claim is narrower than the headlines suggest. Nobody accuses him of pulling the trigger or giving the order.

General Erik Rodríguez Aparicio, the armed forces commander, said he was accused of “alleged participation in the financing” of the assassination. El Tiempo reported that his role lay in “the financing logistics”.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara went further, calling him “part of the criminal scheme that murdered Miguel Uribe”. No official has published the evidence behind either statement.

In March 2026 the Attorney General’s Office, which runs prosecutions, ordered seven group members arrested over the murder. His name was not on that list.

The group and the murder case

The Segunda Marquetalia was founded in 2019 by Luciano Marín Arango, alias Iván Márquez. He had been the FARC’s chief negotiator in the peace talks that ended in 2016, then returned to arms.

Uribe Turbay was a senator for the right-wing Centro Democrático party and grandson of former president Julio César Turbay. His mother, the journalist Diana Turbay, was killed in 1991 after being kidnapped by Pablo Escobar’s Medellín cartel.

A 15-year-old fired the shots at a rally in the Modelia district of Bogotá. He was sentenced to seven years in a youth detention centre.

Nine people have been arrested and four convicted, according to AFP. In March 2026 prosecutors said the order came from the group’s leadership, passed down through a commander known as “El Zarco Aldinever”.

Those March warrants also named Márquez himself. Investigators say the attack was planned in Venezuelan border areas, where the group’s leaders, Márquez included, have long taken refuge.

What comes next

The Army has now confirmed the death, but the three detainees are still unnamed. Whether they will be questioned about the murder is unknown.

The killing is part of a wider offensive. A week earlier, police killed a senior Caribbean armed-group commander near Santa Marta. The president has also said he signed 85 extraditions in six weeks.

On Sunday the president also reported 19 arrests and 907 kilograms of drugs seized nationwide in 24 hours. Five Clan del Golfo members were detained in Pueblo Viejo and Medellín.

On Friday night, 25 September, two explosives were thrown from a motorcycle at a security checkpoint in rural Jamundí, south of Cali. One went off, nobody was hurt, and officials provisionally blame a FARC dissident faction.

“To the narco-terrorists who attack our police in Ábrego and throw explosives in Jamundí: we are pursuing them,” De la Espriella wrote. “They will not impose terror in Colombia.”

It does not close the Uribe Turbay case. A death in a military operation is not a court finding, and the men prosecutors say gave the order are still wanted.

Nor is it the end of the Segunda Marquetalia. The group still has a leader, fighters and extortion income in Huila and Caquetá.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Miguel Uribe Turbay?

He was a 39-year-old Colombian senator for the right-wing Centro Democrático party who planned to run for president in 2026. He was shot at a rally in Bogotá on 7 June 2025 and died on 11 August 2025.

What is the Segunda Marquetalia?

It is an armed group founded in 2019 by former FARC commanders who rejected the 2016 peace deal, led by Iván Márquez. Colombian prosecutors say it ordered the attack on Uribe Turbay.

Was Robinson Gutiérrez the man who ordered the murder?

No. Officials say he allegedly helped finance it. Prosecutors say the order came from the group’s leadership, and no court has ruled on his role.

Is it safe to travel to Colombia?

The operation took place in rural Huila, away from the main tourist and business centres. Visitors should follow their government’s travel advice, which treats conflict areas in the countryside differently from the big cities.

World.title: Dominican Republic: Police Killed at Least 37 People in September
World.content:

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country The Dominican Republic, a Caribbean nation of about 11 million people that shares the island of Hispaniola with Haiti. It has no death penalty.

— Why it matters Deaths in what police call “exchanges of gunfire” have long been disputed by rights groups, who say many are executions.

— What happened Diario Libre counted at least 37 such deaths between 6 and 27 September, 23 of them between 18 and 25 September.

— Who is involved Police chief Ernesto Rodríguez García, in post since 17 August, told criminals on Sunday 27 September to surrender or stop offending.

— What it means for you The new chief’s first weeks are setting the tone of Dominican policing, and the state’s own ombudsman is already objecting.

— Still open Whether any of the September deaths will be independently investigated, and whether the government will respond.

Dominican police killings have surged this month. Diario Libre, a leading Santo Domingo daily, counted at least 37 people killed in September in incidents the National Police report as “exchanges of gunfire” with officers.

The count came a day after the new police chief warned criminals they had two paths: turn themselves in or stop offending. A leading rights group calls the deaths executions.

What the count shows

Diario Libre reported that 23 of the September deaths occurred between 18 and 25 September, the first on the sixth.

Santo Domingo province had the most deaths, with 11, followed by Santiago with six. The newspaper’s running tally since 5 January stands at 115, so September alone accounts for about a third of the year.

El Día, another national daily, reported eight such deaths in a single 24-hour stretch ending on Friday 25 September. Among them, police said, was a man they accused of shooting two officers.

The police chief’s warning

Major General Ernesto Rodríguez García took over the National Police in mid-August. He replaced Andrés Modesto Cruz Cruz, who was retired after six months in the job.

Addressing officers in the north-east on Sunday, he said offenders must choose to surrender or stop, “because otherwise we will come looking for you, no matter where you hide.” Both Diario Libre and Acento, a news site, reported the remarks.

He framed this as proportional use of force and promised to make offenders feel “the powerful arm of the state.” According to Diario Libre, police say those killed were wanted for crimes such as murder and robbery.

Ombudsman and rights groups object

The Ombudsman, Pablo Ulloa, a constitutional office that defends citizens against the state, said no one may be killed as a substitute for a court sentence. He noted the country has no death penalty.

Manuel María Mercedes, who heads the National Human Rights Commission, a non-governmental rights group, called the deaths a “massacre”, El Nuevo Diario reported. He said the group would take its complaint to international bodies.

The commission estimates about 4,500 such deaths between 2018 and 2025. That is its own figure, not an official record. Background: Dominican Republic Explained 2026 and Abinader Opens New Dominican Police Training Complex.

What Is Not Yet Known

How each of the September deaths happened. The accounts so far come from police statements, and El Día noted they still have to be tested by investigations.

Whether the government or prosecutors will open any independent review of the Dominican police killings.

The final September figure. Diario Libre’s count, last updated on Monday 28 September, runs only to 27 September.

Sources: Diario Libre, 28 September 2026; Diario Libre, 27 September 2026; Acento, 27 September 2026; El Nuevo Diario, 27 September 2026; El Día, 25 September 2026.

World.title: Peru Says Troops Drove Back a Colombian Armed Group on Its Amazon Border
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

PERU · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Peru, a nation of about 34 million, shares a remote jungle border with Colombia. Much of it follows the Putumayo river, where Colombian armed groups tied to drug trafficking operate.

— Why it matters Peru has put its Putumayo province under a state of emergency. A joint military and police command there aims to tighten territorial control.

— What happened On Sunday 27 September the Defence Ministry said forces clashed with the Comandos de la Frontera near San Belín de Yaricaya. It said three fighters fell into a river.

— Who is involved The Comandos de la Frontera, which the ministry calls FARC dissidents formed in 2017. On Peru’s side, a joint command for the area known as CUPUMA.

— What it means for you Nothing changes for visits to Lima, Cusco or Iquitos. Anyone travelling near the Putumayo border should check official travel advice first.

— Still open When the clash took place, whether the three men in the river died, and whether any soldiers or police were hurt.

Peru’s soldiers and police clashed with a Colombian armed group on the country’s Amazon border, the Defence Ministry said on Sunday. According to the ministry, the fighters fled and three of them fell into a river.

The ministry named the group as the Comandos de la Frontera, dissidents from the FARC, Colombia’s former Marxist guerrilla army. Colombia’s El Heraldo, carrying the EFE news agency’s report, and Peru’s La República both relayed the official account.

What the Defence Ministry reported

A joint unit of soldiers and police, the Comando Unificado PUMA, carried out an operation code-named “Zancudo” (mosquito), the ministry said. After intelligence work, the unit located the group near the village of San Belín de Yaricaya, in the Teniente Manuel Clavero district.

The clash “forced the criminals to flee”, the ministry said, and three of them fell into the Yaricaya river. It said security conditions and the depth and current of the river made a search for the bodies impossible.

On the Amazon border, troops then recovered an M16 rifle with magazines, two pistols, a grenade and ammunition, according to the ministry. It also listed Colombian-style army uniforms, medicines and tools.

Who the Comandos de la Frontera are

The ministry said the group emerged in 2017 and operates along the borders of Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. It linked the group to drug trafficking and illegal mining.

La República reported that it began as an alliance of FARC dissidents and La Constru, a gang rooted in former right-wing paramilitaries. According to the paper, it controls coca-growing zones and moves cocaine towards Ecuador and Brazil.

Colombia extradited its reputed leader, alias Araña, to the United States on 25 September. The Rio Times covered that in Colombia Sends Armed-Group Boss From Peace Talks to Face US Drug Charges.

A border under pressure

El Heraldo noted that the operation followed a Peru–Colombia border commission meeting, Combifron, held in Lima from 21 to 25 September. Peru’s Joint Command of the Armed Forces said the two militaries signed agreements there to deepen border security cooperation.

Putumayo province, in the Loreto region, has been under a state of emergency that puts the armed forces in charge of order. The Defence Ministry announced a 60-day extension in June. In late July the government extended the emergency in Loreto’s border areas for a further 60 days from August, El Peruano and La República reported.

What Is Not Yet Known

The ministry did not say when the clash took place. Its statement mentions no casualties among soldiers or police.

Whether the three men who fell into the river died is unconfirmed, since no bodies were recovered. No account from residents or from the group itself had emerged by Monday.

It is also unclear whether the emergency, last extended in July, will be renewed again. Any link to the Combifron agreements is unstated.

Sources: Peru Defence Ministry, 27 September 2026; El Heraldo / EFE; La República; La Lupa; Joint Command of the Armed Forces (Combifron); Defence Ministry, state of emergency, June 2026.
