World.title: Another puppy abuse video surfaces as Buddy’s alleged abuser remains at large
World.content:
Another puppy abuse video surfaces as Buddy’s alleged abuser remains at large

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Another disturbing video showing the alleged abuse of a dog has surfaced in Belize, prompting renewed calls from animal advocates for stronger action against animal cruelty.

The latest footage, which was sent to Breaking Belize News, appears to show a man abusing a puppy. Animal advocates who have seen the video are now appealing for members of the public to help identify the man so that the matter can be investigated and, if warranted, charges brought against him.

The video comes while Steven Barrow, the man police identified in connection with the widely condemned abuse of Buddy the dog in Cotton Tree Village, remains at large.

Police previously reported that Barrow allegedly attacked Buddy, also identified in the police report as “Big Boy,” on July 19, 2026. According to investigators, Barrow was reportedly under the influence of alcohol when he struck the dog with a gallon containing gasoline, causing gasoline to spill over the animal, before continuing to beat it with a stick.

Buddy was later rescued and placed with a foster family, where he began recovering from the abuse.

Police subsequently confirmed that Barrow had been identified but could not be located after moving from his Cotton Tree residence. Authorities said multiple attempts had been made to find him and that the case had been documented so that proceedings could continue once he is detained.

The emergence of another animal abuse video has renewed concern among animal advocates, who are calling for the man seen in the latest footage to be identified and for police to investigate the incident.

World.title: Three Belizean Food Companies selected for UK Export Support program
World.content:
Three Belizean Food Companies selected for UK Export Support program

By Zoila Palma: Three Belizean food and beverage companies have been selected for tailored export support under the UK Government-funded Making Trade Happen (MTH) programme, aimed at helping local businesses enter international markets and create new commercial opportunities.

The selected companies are Naledo Belize Ltd, Smithy’s Natural Blend and Julie’s Zucchini Salsa.

The programme provides export-ready Caribbean businesses with practical support, including product development, regulatory compliance guidance and marketing advice.

Following the preparation phase, the companies will have opportunities to participate in funded UK and international trade shows and business matchmaking activities designed to connect them with overseas buyers.

British High Commissioner to Belize Alistair White said he was pleased to see the three Belizean businesses selected, describing them as part of Belize’s “dynamic community of entrepreneurs” producing products with international potential. He said the initiative will help the companies strengthen their export readiness, connect with international buyers and explore new commercial opportunities.

UK Head of Caribbean Trade Policy and Regional Trade for Development Advisor Lorcan O’Brien said the programme is designed to help Caribbean businesses turn their ambitions into export success.

He noted that Belizean goods have tariff-free access to the UK under the Economic Partnership Agreement, while the programme will help businesses address challenges involving regulations, marketing and connections with buyers.

World.title: Guatemalan military plane that violated Belize’s sovereign airspace was donated to Guatemala by United States Government
World.content:
Guatemalan military plane that violated Belize’s sovereign airspace was donated to Guatemala by United States Government

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The Guatemalan military aircraft that Belize says entered its airspace and spent more than an hour operating near Lighthouse Reef was donated to Guatemala by the United States government and previously served in Afghanistan as part of a U.S.-funded special-operations aviation programme whose PC-12 aircraft were used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions.

Guatemalan Air Force FAG706, a Pilatus PC-12/47E, was transferred to Guatemala in 2024 for surveillance and light-transport duties, including security and border-control operations. Specialist defence reporting says the aircraft retained several pieces of equipment from its previous configuration, although the exact surveillance systems currently installed aboard it have not been publicly disclosed.

The aircraft’s history has become particularly significant as Belize and Guatemala now present completely contradictory accounts of what happened on the night of September 24.

Belize says its primary and secondary radar systems specifically identified FAG706 entering Belizean airspace at approximately 7:29 p.m., flying at around 4,000 feet, before repeatedly circling between Lighthouse Reef and an aviation waypoint known as KIRAP.

Guatemala says the overflight never happened.

Exercising its Right of Reply before the United Nations General Assembly on September 26, Guatemala “categorically” rejected Prime Minister John Briceño’s allegation that a Guatemalan Air Force aircraft had entered Belizean airspace.

“This overflight never occurred,” the Guatemalan delegation told the Assembly.

Guatemala went further, accusing Belize of going before the United Nations to “spread misinformation” and of using the dispute with Guatemala as an “instrument of domestic policy.” Guatemala also said it would request an investigation by the Organization of American States office in the Adjacency Zone and would make available its reports and “even the aircraft in question.”

The dispute therefore presents two irreconcilable accounts: Belize says it has radar evidence identifying the aircraft, its altitude, flight pattern, entry time and exit point, while Guatemala says the alleged overflight never occurred.

Belize says radar identified FAG706

According to Ministry of National Defence CEO Francis Usher, Belizean authorities reviewed data from the country’s primary and secondary radar systems following reports of a Guatemalan military aircraft operating near Belize.

Usher said the radar information specifically identified the aircraft as FAG706.

“We pulled the data from our primary and secondary radars that we have for the country, which are internationally recognized,” Usher explained.

According to Belize’s reconstruction, FAG706 entered Belizean airspace from the east at approximately 7:29 p.m. on September 24, flying at around 4,000 feet.

It then began circling near Lighthouse Reef and KIRAP.

“They circled in between the Lighthouse Reef and the aviation fix called KIRAP, and they began circling as if though they were looking for something,” Usher said.

At approximately 8:07 p.m., Belize says the aircraft disappeared from its secondary radar system, which Usher said indicated that its transponder had apparently been switched off.

But Belize says it continued tracking the physical aircraft through its primary radar, which does not depend on a transponder signal.

Usher said FAG706 remained inside Belizean airspace until approximately 8:40 p.m., when it departed to the south past the Sarstoon River.

That would place the aircraft inside Belizean airspace for approximately one hour and 10 minutes.

Guatemala says it never happened

Guatemala’s public position has become progressively stronger since reports of the incident first surfaced.

Its Ministry of National Defence initially issued a statement on September 25 saying that all activities and operations of the Guatemalan Army are conducted in strict accordance with national and international law.

The initial statement notably did not directly confirm or deny the alleged overflight and provided no operational explanation concerning FAG706. Guatemala’s state news agency reported that the statement did not provide details about the aircraft or the specific circumstances of the reported incident.

When Guatemalan newspaper La Hora subsequently asked the Defence Ministry directly whether the overflight had occurred, its communications office responded:

“We have no record of that alleged overflight.”

Guatemala then went significantly further at the United Nations following Briceño’s address.

It told the General Assembly that it “categorically” rejected Belize’s accusation and stated unequivocally that “this overflight never occurred.”

The Guatemalan representative said existing monitoring mechanisms through the OAS Adjacency Zone should be used to investigate the matter and said Guatemala would provide all its reports and even the aircraft itself.

Guatemala then accused Belize of using the international forum to “spread misinformation” and of using the territorial dispute as an “instrument of domestic policy.”

That language suggests Guatemala believes Belize is using what Guatemala considers a false allegation for internal political purposes, although Guatemala did not specifically accuse Belize of staging or fabricating radar evidence.

Not an ordinary transport aircraft

Regardless of the dispute over where it flew on September 24, FAG706 itself has a well-documented and specialized history.

The aircraft is a Pilatus PC-12/47E, construction number 1445, manufactured in 2013.

It was initially registered in Switzerland as HB-FQT, later became N445NX in the United States and eventually operated as YA1445 in Afghanistan.

Defence reporting says it formed part of a group of 18 PC-12 aircraft modified by Sierra Nevada Corporation under a US$218 million U.S. contract for the special-operations forces of the Afghan Air Force.

The Afghan Special Mission Wing’s PC-12 fleet was used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance — ISR — missions, supporting special operations and security activities.

Following the collapse of the Afghan government, the aircraft eventually returned to U.S. control before being transferred to Guatemala.

By early 2024 it had become Guatemalan Air Force 706.

United States donated FAG706 to Guatemala

Available defence reporting indicates that Guatemala did not purchase FAG706 as an ordinary commercial aircraft acquisition.

It was donated by the Government of the United States.

Infodefensa reported in May 2024 that Guatemala had incorporated the PC-12/47E donated by Washington for surveillance and light-transport missions.

The aircraft was expected to be employed for security and border-control missions in Guatemalan territory and airspace.

Pucará Defensa similarly reported that FAG706 had been donated by the U.S. government and would be used for surveillance, security and border-control work. The publication reported that the aircraft retained several pieces of its original equipment.

Exactly what that equipment includes remains unknown.

There is no publicly available inventory establishing which cameras, infrared sensors, communications equipment or other intelligence and surveillance systems are currently installed aboard FAG706.

What can be established is that the aircraft came from a fleet designed for special-operations ISR work and was subsequently donated to Guatemala specifically for surveillance and security-related missions.

U.S. arms shipment arrived three days earlier

The disputed flight came just three days after Guatemala received a major shipment of U.S. military weapons on September 21 — Belize’s Independence Day.

Unlike FAG706, the weapons were not donated. Guatemala purchased them through the U.S. Foreign Military Sales programme as part of a US$5.03 million acquisition that includes 2,699 M4A1 rifles, 59 M240 machine guns, 57 grenade launchers and 11,220 magazines. Guatemala’s state news agency said the September 21 shipment arrived aboard a U.S. Army aircraft, with the first M4 rifles destined for Guatemala’s new Jungle Operations Brigade in Petén.

There is no evidence establishing a connection between that weapons shipment and the disputed September 24 flight, but the timing places the controversy amid a broader expansion of military and security cooperation between Guatemala and the United States following the lifting of long-standing restrictions on U.S. arms sales to Guatemala.

Why Lighthouse Reef and KIRAP?

Belize’s description of the flight raises questions because it says FAG706 did not simply pass through its airspace.

According to Usher, the aircraft approached from the east, entered near Lighthouse Reef and repeatedly circled between Lighthouse Reef and KIRAP.

KIRAP itself is an established aviation navigation fix and is part of published aviation routes, meaning an aircraft travelling near KIRAP would not on that fact alone be conducting an unusual operation.

What Belize has highlighted is the repeated circling.

Usher himself described the aircraft as moving “as if though they were looking for something.”

KIRAP is also located near the southern end of Lighthouse Reef and roughly 10 nautical miles from Half Moon Caye.

There is presently no publicly available evidence establishing what, if anything, FAG706 may have been observing or searching for. Guatemala’s position is more fundamental: it says the overflight described by Belize did not occur at all.

The aircraft’s route before and after the alleged incursion

Public flight-tracking information also showed an aircraft using the FAG706 callsign around Guatemala City earlier in the evening before moving toward the Caribbean.

Belize says the aircraft subsequently approached its territory from the east rather than crossing directly from Guatemala over Belize’s western land border.

According to Belize’s radar information, the aircraft crossed into Belizean airspace near Lighthouse Reef, conducted the circling pattern and later departed south beyond the Sarstoon.

Public tracking information disappeared during part of the flight before showing the aircraft again in Guatemala and ultimately returning to the La Aurora area.

However, civilian tracking information alone cannot establish whether an aircraft crossed a national airspace boundary, which is why Belize has placed particular emphasis on its own primary and secondary radar records.

What happened between 8:07 and 8:40 p.m.?

One of the most important outstanding pieces of evidence concerns the approximately 33 minutes between 8:07 p.m. and 8:40 p.m.

According to Belize, FAG706 disappeared from secondary radar at 8:07 p.m. but continued to appear on primary radar.

“We were able to pick them up on the primary radar, and we continued following them,” Usher said.

Belize therefore says it possesses a radar record of the aircraft’s movements during a period when publicly available tracking data did not show its position.

Those records have become considerably more important now that Guatemala has categorically denied the flight occurred.

If released, Belize’s primary-radar data could show precisely where the aircraft travelled after 8:07 p.m., along with its direction and potentially other characteristics of its flight.

Guatemala, meanwhile, should also possess military operational records capable of establishing where FAG706 was at the same time.

Its UN representative has now said Guatemala will make those reports — and the aircraft itself — available to an OAS investigation.

Questions Belize’s Defence Ministry can answer

With Guatemala now publicly denying the incident, several questions for Ministry of National Defence CEO Francis Usher and Belizean authorities become increasingly important:

1. Will Belize release the complete primary and secondary radar tracks showing FAG706’s movements on September 24?

2. Will Belize release the coordinates showing precisely where the aircraft entered and exited Belizean airspace?

3. What does Belize’s primary radar show FAG706 doing between 8:07 p.m. and 8:40 p.m.?

4. Exactly where were the aircraft’s reported circles centred — KIRAP, Half Moon Caye, another part of Lighthouse Reef or open water?

5. What were FAG706’s altitude, speed and heading during the reported circling pattern?

6. Did Belize’s primary radar detect any other aircraft in the area at the same time?

7. Were Belize Coast Guard, BDF, Fisheries Department or other government operations underway around Lighthouse Reef or Half Moon Caye that evening?

8. Did FAG706 or Guatemalan authorities communicate with Belizean air traffic control, CENAMER or Belize’s defence authorities before or during the reported flight?

9. Has Belize requested Guatemala’s own flight logs or operational records for FAG706 between 7:29 p.m. and 8:40 p.m.?

10. Has Belize sought information from the United States regarding exactly what surveillance equipment was transferred with FAG706 when the aircraft was donated to Guatemala?

A dispute that should be technically verifiable

The controversy has now moved beyond questions about what a Guatemalan military aircraft may have been doing near Lighthouse Reef.

Guatemala says there was no overflight to explain.

Belize says it has technical radar evidence identifying:

FAG706 as the aircraft;

7:29 p.m. as the entry time;

approximately 4,000 feet as its altitude;

Lighthouse Reef and KIRAP as the area where it circled;

8:07 p.m. as the time it disappeared from secondary radar;

continued tracking by primary radar; and

approximately 8:40 p.m. as the time it exited south past the Sarstoon.

Guatemala, on the other hand, has now told the United Nations:

“This overflight never occurred.”

It has accused Belize of spreading misinformation and using the dispute for domestic political purposes, while saying it will cooperate with an OAS investigation.

At the centre of the dispute is an aircraft with an unusually specialized history: a U.S.-donated Pilatus PC-12 that previously served in Afghanistan as part of a special-operations aviation programme whose aircraft performed intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance missions, before being transferred to Guatemala for surveillance, security and border-control work.

The competing claims should therefore be capable of being tested against technical records from both countries.

The central question is now straightforward:

Where exactly was FAG706 between 7:29 p.m. and 8:40 p.m. on September 24?

World.title: International News: Pope Leo urges Europe to choose dialogue over military buildup
World.content:
International News: Pope Leo urges Europe to choose dialogue over military buildup

By Zoila Palma: Pope Leo XIV has urged European leaders to pursue dialogue and negotiation rather than relying on military buildups to address conflicts threatening the continent.

Speaking in Metz, France today, the pope warned against what he described as the “illusion that rearmament is the answer” and called for greater commitment to peaceful solutions.

Addressing religious and civil leaders at the Robert Schuman conference center, Pope Leo said war had returned to Europe and called for “patient dialogue” and courage in negotiations. He acknowledged that the pursuit of peace should not be confused with what he called “a naive form of pacifism,” but said leaders must actively work toward peace rather than simply preparing for future wars.

The pope also called for stronger multilateralism and respect for international law, describing them as an “antidote” to the desire for domination that he said lies behind conflicts.

He pointed to Europe’s experience over the past eight decades, saying the continent had demonstrated that different opinions and interests can be addressed through engagement rather than conflict.

Pope Leo also addressed migration, urging European leaders to view the arrival of migrants and refugees fleeing war, persecution and poverty as an opportunity for cultural integration rather than exclusion.

World.title: International Day for Universal access to information highlights importance of reliable Information in Digital Age
World.content:
International Day for Universal access to information highlights importance of reliable Information in Digital Age

By Zoila Palma:Today, September 28, 2026, marks the International Day for Universal Access to Information, with this year’s theme focusing on “Upholding Information Integrity in the Digital Age: The Role of Access to Information in Addressing Information Disorder.”

The observance highlights the importance of ensuring that people have access not only to information, but to timely and reliable information.

UNESCO says credible public information can strengthen trust, support informed decision-making and allow people to participate meaningfully in society.

In an increasingly digital environment filled with misinformation and disinformation, access to reliable official information, proactive disclosure, credible data, media and information literacy, and responsible use of digital technologies are seen as important tools for creating a healthier information environment.

Universal access to information means that everyone has the right to seek, receive and share information, a right closely connected to freedom of expression and freedom of the press. UNESCO declared September 28 as the International Day for Universal Access to Information in 2015, with the UN General Assembly adopting the observance in 2019.

World.title: Tropical Storm Hanna forms in Central Subtropical Atlantic
World.content:
Tropical Storm Hanna forms in Central Subtropical Atlantic

By Zoila Palma: The National Hurricane Center informed that Tropical Storm Hanna has formed in the central subtropical Atlantic.

At 11:00 a.m. AST (1500 UTC), Hanna was located near latitude 36.6° North and longitude 50.4° West, moving eastward at approximately 17 mph (28 km/h).

The system has maximum sustained winds of 45 mph (75 km/h), with higher gusts.

Forecasters expect Hanna to continue moving east to east-southeast over the next several days.

Little change in strength is expected during the next couple of days.

World.title: International News: CARICOM, Nordic Ministers strengthen cooperation on Climate, Security and Development
World.content:
International News: CARICOM, Nordic Ministers strengthen cooperation on Climate, Security and Development

By Zoila Palma: Foreign Ministers from the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) and several Nordic countries held discussions on climate resilience, sustainable development, food and energy security, regional and international security, and reform of the United Nations system.

The annual CARICOM-Nordic Ministerial Meeting was held on September 22, 2026, at the Permanent Mission of Norway to the United Nations in New York, on the margins of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly.

The meeting was co-chaired by Suriname’s Foreign Affairs Minister Melvin Bouva and Norway’s Minister of International Development Asmund Aukrust.

During the meeting, ministers welcomed the CARICOM-endorsed candidacy of Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett for Secretary-General of the United Nations. They highlighted the importance of leadership focused on strengthening multilateralism, building global consensus and upholding the principles of the UN Charter.

CARICOM and the Nordic countries also reaffirmed their longstanding partnership and shared commitment to multilateralism, sustainable development and international cooperation.

World.title: International News: El Niño could push up food prices, hit Caribbean Economies
World.content:
International News: El Niño could push up food prices, hit Caribbean Economies

By Zoila Palma: The prospect of an exceptionally strong El Niño event is raising fresh concerns across the Caribbean, with the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC) warning that the climate phenomenon could drive up food prices, strain electricity systems, increase poverty and cause significant economic losses across the region.

In a special report released September 23, ECLAC warned that an extreme El Niño could result in cumulative economic losses of at least 2% of regional Gross Domestic Product (GDP) over three years, with half of those losses occurring during the first year following the event.

The Commission also estimates that declining household incomes could push up to 4.8 million additional people into poverty by the end of the decade, compared with a scenario without El Niño.

The potential economic impact comes as global food prices are already rising. The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization reported that global food prices in August reached their highest level since 2022, as major crop-producing countries faced growing impacts from the climate event.

Experts have warned that shortages and production disruptions could further increase the cost of food, particularly for vulnerable populations.

Among the commodities facing potential supply pressures are rice, wheat, coffee, cocoa, chocolate and sugar.

Experts cited in the report estimate that global food prices could rise by the mid-teens percentage range, with some forecasts suggesting the effects could last up to two years.

World.title: Jamaica welcomes first cohort of Ghanaian healthcare workers
World.content:
Forty-three Ghanaian specialist nurses arrived in Jamaica.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica on Monday welcomed the first cohort of Ghanaian healthcare workers as part of ongoing efforts to strengthen the country’s healthcare workforce and support the delivery of quality healthcare services.

The majority of the 43 nurses will be assigned to the Western Regional Health Authority (WRHA), which manages health facilities in St James, Westmoreland, Trelawny and Hanover and the South East Regional Health Authority (SERHA), which oversees Kingston & St Andrew, St Thomas and St Catherine.

The nurses, who are specialists in various areas, including critical care, paediatrics, operating theatre, nurse/midwife, emergency, oncology and mental health/psychiatric, will also serve in the other two health regions and at the University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI).

Their arrival follows the signing of a Bilateral Health Cooperation agreement between the two countries earlier this year, which aims to place 400 healthcare workers in Jamaica.

“We warmly welcome the Ghanaian nurses and look forward to the valuable contribution they will make to our health system and the people we serve. This is not only in keeping with our Vision for Health 2030 plan but is fully aligned with the Ministry of Health & Wellness Jamaica’s Human Resource for Health (HRH) Stabilisation Strategy,” said Minister of Health & Wellness, Dr Christopher Tufton in a statement on Monday.

The ministry said the four-year agreement between Jamaica and Ghana has established a structured framework for the voluntary recruitment and temporary deployment of Ghanaian health professionals, particularly nurses and doctors, to support Jamaica’s healthcare system while promoting bilateral cooperation and ethical international recruitment practices.

It added that Jamaica and Ghana will further strengthen their partnership in health through additional technical cooperation in areas such as primary care reform, national health insurance and management of non-communicable diseases, among others.

World.title: Defence attorneys to withdraw services from courts islandwide Monday
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Following unsuccessful discussions with the Ministry of Justice, defence attorneys have been directed to withdraw legal services from all criminal courts islandwide on Monday as clashes over minimum mandatory sentences in the Firearms Prohibition Restriction and Regulation Act 2022 continue.

The action is expected to affect Parish Courts, Circuit Courts and Gun Courts.

Another day of industrial action, specifically targeting the Gun Courts, is scheduled on Tuesday.

A joint statement from the Jamaican Bar Association (Jambar) and Advocates Association of Jamaica (AAJ) indicated that members had voted overwhelmingly in favour of withdrawing legal services this week.

The vote followed a silent protest on Thursday in front of the Supreme Court in downtown Kingston by association members, where they lobbied for a review of the mandatory minimum sentences applied to certain gun crimes in the 2022 law.

READ: Lawyers protest mandatory minimum sentences under Firearms Act

Maintaining that the legal fraternity does not oppose stringent measures against violent gun crime, it emphasised that the legislation as currently constructed contains structural gaps and rigid mechanics that undermine the broader legal framework.

They described “significant shortcomings, gaps and statutory weaknesses” impacting the justice system, including what the attorneys describe as the erosion of judicial discretion, the dismantling of guilty plea incentives and the practical friction with statutory sentencing discount frameworks.

A meeting was held with Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Delroy Chuck on Thursday to address the issues, but the lawyers say those discussions concluded without any definitive legislative timeline to address their concerns.

READ: Chuck to meet with protesting lawyers over Firearms Act discontent

The associations, however, urged attorneys to manage urgent remand list matters, emergency bail applications involving juveniles or vulnerable persons, and time-sensitive constitutional applications in a manner that ensures no client’s fundamental rights are prejudiced during this period.

The associations say they are again calling for urgent and meaningful legislative amendments to ensure the justice system functions efficiently for all Jamaicans.

World.title: New boys Tru Juice beat Molynes to go top of JPL
World.content:
In this file photo, Tru Juice FC's Daniel Roberts attempts a shot as he is being closed down by Reno FC's Raheem Kerr in the semi-finals of last season's Jamaica Football Championship at Llandilo Sports Complex in Westmoreland. Tru Juice won the game on penalties after playing out a 0-0 regulation and extra time score. (Photo: Paul Reid)

KINGSTON, Jamaica – Promoted side Tru-Juice extended their strong start to the Jamaica Premier League on Sunday as they edged Molynes United 1-0 at Stadium East to take over the lead in the points table.

Tru-Juice are joined by Montego Bay United on seven points after the St James-based club ended Racing United’s perfect start, winning 1-0 in the first game of a double header at Drewsland.

Meanwhile, defending champions Portmore United made a winning start to their title defense, beating Humble Lion 4-1, while Mt Pleasant FA got their first win, beating Dunbeholden 2-0.

Cavalier FC outscored Arnett Gardens 3-2 while Waterhouse FC beat Treasure Beach FC 2-0 to win their second straight game.

At Stadium East, Daniel Roberts scored in the 62nd minute, his third goal of the season, to lead Tru Juice to their second win of the season. The newcomers have gone three games without conceding a goal.

Jourdain Fletcher scored his first goal of the season to give Montego Bay the win, firing a rebound past goalkeeper Aaron Ennis in the Racing goal in the 27th minute.

Waterhouse scored two quick goals in the first half as they continued their good start to the season. Colorado Murray in the 35th minute and Mario Simms in the 37th minute punished mistakes by the Treasure Beach defense but, despite creating a handful of scoring chances, were unable to add to their tally.

Cavalier FC held off Arnett Gardens 3-2 to win their first game at new home venue Turners Oval, after leading 2-0 after the first 20 minutes.

Jeovanni Laing scored a stunning goal from well outside the area, into the far left corner to give Cavalier the lead in the 14th minute and Luis Watson doubled the advantage in the 20th minute with a powerful shot from close range.

Arnett Gardens started the fight back when Giovanni Taylor, scored in the 26th minute before Jamone Shepherd pulled them level in the 70th minute, both scoring their third goals of the season.

Cavalier reasserted themselves, however, and took all three points when Adrian Reid converted a penalty in the 83rd minute.

It took Portmore just over 60 minutes to break down Humble Lion but, once they got the first goal, scored four in a 23-minute span with Tarick Ximines getting a double.

Ximines opened the scoring in the 64th minute with Stephen Young getting a second in less than a minute. Ximines then completed his brace in the 70th minute before Kemar Mullings managed to pull a goal back for Humble Lion, their first goal of the season. Tedj Bryan restored Portmore’s three goals lead, scoring in the 87th minute.

Mt Pleasant, who had failed to score in their first two games, both losses, scored two early goals, Trayvone Reid in the 17th minute and Nicholas Nelson in the 22nd minute, to hand Dunbeholden their third straight loss of the season.

Meanwhile, Tivoli Gardens and Chapelton Maroons played out a 1-1 draw at the Edward Seaga Complex with two veteran players getting on the scoresheet.

Leaunghn Williams gave Tivoli the lead in the 29th minute before Brian Brown equalised for Chapelton in the 40th minute.

Sunday’s Games-

Tivoli Gardens-1, Chapelton Maroons-1

Cavalier FC-3, Arnett Gardens-2

Portmore United-4, Humble Lion FC-1

Dunbeholden FC-0, Mt Pleasant FA-2

Molynes United-0, Tru-Juice FC-1

Racing United-0, Montego Bay United-1

Waterhouse FC vs Treasure Beach- 8:00pm

-Paul A Reid

World.title: Bad roads backlash
World.content:
Minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan addressing Jamaica Observer editors and reporters last Friday.

ARGUING that Members of Parliament (MPs) and the central Government are taking undeserved flack for state of roads which are the responsibility of the municipal authorities, minister with responsibility for works Robert Morgan has urged Jamaicans to put the pressure where it rightfully belongs.

“That’s why I came up with the Jamaica Road Register…to empower citizens to know which road belongs to which entity. The Members of Parliament are more visible a lot of the times, they sit in Parliament, and people feel that they have better access to them, so they pressure the MPs… But Jamaica has 27,000 kilometres of roads and most of the roads are owned by parish councils [municipal corporations],” Morgan told the Jamaica Observer during a sit-down last Friday.

He pointed out that, while the central Government is responsible for only 5,000 kilometres of roads, it has fixed several roads that are outside of its remit.

“The challenge we have is that a lot of the municipal corporations — whether it be a resource issue or whether it be a lack of interest — are not keeping up their end of the bargain. As a minister, and as a Member of Parliament, I have been elected to be accountable, so when somebody comes to me and criticises me about Hagley Park Road or Spanish Town Road, I have to take responsibility.

“But I find that I’m not getting that from the parish councils. For example, most of the roads that the Government has fixed in Kingston and St Andrew are not NWA [National Works Agency] roads, they are KSAMC [Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation] roads, and before this new Mayor [Andrew Swaby] came in, the Parochial Revenue Fund was about $700 million a year; it is now over $1 billion, and we have not seen a commensurate increase in the allocation for repairing roads,” Morgan charged.

According to Morgan, while it is agreed that neither the NWA nor the municipal corporations have all the resources needed to fix every road, the measurable outcomes of the resources that the corporations get are still not being manifested.

“It was only when I went public — I think it was a couple months ago — that the mayor [Swaby] decided to increase allocations to each councillor for road work. The mayor has been there for over two years. Why didn’t he increase the allocation?” questioned Morgan.

“We have so many instances where MPs come to me and say, ‘Minister, the people are complaining to me about the road,’ and when I go and look, it’s not NWA’s responsibility, it is local government. So you have to make a decision — Is local government going to step up and do their job? And when I say local government, I mean the municipalities, because if they are not willing to fix the roads, then give it to central Government,” Morgan stated.

Claiming that there have been occasions in which the NWA went to fix roads and the entity was written to and told by a mayor to, ‘Leave the road alone, it’s a parish council road,’ Morgan charged that there is a desire by municipal corporations to hold on to what they cannot manage, “and that doesn’t make any sense, because clearly you are demonstrating that a majority of the roads that people are upset about are not main roads”.

Morgan admitted that several major thoroughfares in the Corporate Area are in need of repair but argued that many, including South Avenue, Lindsay Crescent and Beechwood Avenue, are municipal corporation roads and are to be fixed by the KSAMC.

“Duke Street, where the grates that are falling apart and, damaging people’s tyres, those are not the responsibility of the National Works Agency, those are the responsibility of the municipal corporation and yes, there are some mayors, across the island who are trying their best, but I don’t believe, particularly the Kingston and Saint Andrew [Municipal Corporation] is trying its best.

“So my point is, hold me accountable for my responsibilities as an elected representative and as a member of the Cabinet who has been given the responsibility for roads, but also hold the other people who are also elected responsible. They campaigned and promised you manna from Heaven and all the wonderful things. They need to come and deliver, and it’s not just roads,” charged Morgan.

While encouraging Jamaicans to use the JamaicaRoadRegister.gov.jm portal to see which roads are the responsibility of their local authorities and which are not, Morgan expressed hope that the soon-to-be introduced One Road Authority will make municipal corporations more accountable.

“It is not the intention of the One Road Authority to disempower municipal corporations, it is to give them tools and give citizens tools to hold both central government and local government accountable.

“For example, the people who throw the things on the road off the trucks, the trucks that are driving without cover, the people who are letting go water on the road, destroying the road, the cement trucks, the people who are digging up the road to run pipes and don’t fix it back, the developers who have destroyed most of the roads in Kingston with the sewage pipes that were not installed properly, those are things that disrespect the taxpayers of Jamaica, and those are things by next year will come to an end, because not only will the One Road Authority be able to find people, but the One Road Authority will also be able to go to court, and sue,” Morgan explained.

“We are going to take on the people who are destroying our roads and hold them accountable, because a lot of the damage to our roads is not necessarily because the road wasn’t fixed good, but because of the usage patterns of people who have the overweight trucks; your truck is supposed to only carry 80 tonnes, but you have 120. Our roads were not made for 120 tonnes.

“So we are thinking of working with Minister [of Transport Daryl] Vaz. I know that he’s working on bringing back scales, and it’s not just scales that are put down one place, I know that he’s planning mobile scales… You go to St Thomas, Paul Bogle Highway and it’s sand and gravel thrown away all over the road, and nobody wants to take responsibility. So, if the cement industry, the haulage industry, and other industries that use the road do not wish to voluntarily regulate themselves, then the Government has no choice but to regulate them,” said Morgan.

He added: “So what is going to happen is that we are going to impose harsh penalties on these companies, and it is not going to be the $300,000 that is in the Road Traffic Act — that is not being enforced — it is going to be worse because the One Road Authority is going to have its own enforcement officers.

“So it’s not police that is going to come and hold you accountable. The One Road Authority will have its own army of enforcement officers working with the police and others to show these people that the disrespect that they have shown to our roads cannot continue,” declared Morgan.

World.title: Alleged wife killer hospitalised after attack by jail inmates
World.content:
MONTEGO BAY, St James — A St James man accused of killing his wife has been hospitalised following an alleged attack by fellow jail inmates. Thirty-one-year-old Dane Watson was on Wednesday remanded in absentia after he failed to appear in court because of his injuries.

He is charged with the murder of 35-year-old Melissa Samnath, who was a Jamaican American living in New York.

Watson was scheduled to appear before St James Parish Court Judge Natiesha Fairclough-Hylton, but the court was informed that he was unable to appear. He is now scheduled to appear on October 8 when the judge is expected to examine the evidence already before the court and determine whether the matter should proceed to the Circuit Court.

Investigators told the court that Samnath was taken to Cornwall Regional Hospital on April 29 with multiple injuries and was later pronounced dead. Police allege that Watson transported her to the hospital, and then left the facility.

Investigators further allege that Watson subsequently left St James and was later located in Gayle, St Mary. Police said Watson contacted relatives because he was concerned about his safety. His relatives then alerted the Gayle police, prompting coordination between law-enforcement personnel in the two parishes.

Watson was eventually taken into custody and handed over to investigators in St James, where he was subsequently charged with murder.

According to media reports, Samnath was killed during what was a birthday trip to Jamaica. There were also reports that she realised she was in danger and sent text message to relatives who have played an active role in drawing public attention to the case.

World.title: Calypso icon the Mighty Sparrow dies at 91
World.content:
The Mighty Sparrow

PORT OF SPAIN, Trinidad (CMC) — Legendary calypsonian Slinger Francisco, better known as the Mighty Sparrow, has died at the age of 91.

His family said the Grenadian-born, Trinidad-raised performer died peacefully in New York on Sunday following a brief illness, surrounded by loved ones.

“It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of Trinidad and Tobago’s Calypso icon, Slinger Francisco, known to the world as The Mighty Sparrow,” the family said in a statement.

Sparrow, widely regarded as one of the most influential figures in Caribbean music, enjoyed a career spanning more than seven decades and became internationally known for his distinctive voice, sharp wit, and social and political commentary.

Born in Grenada in 1935, Francisco moved to Trinidad as a young child and went on to become one of calypso’s most decorated performers, winning Trinidad and Tobago’s Calypso King or Monarch title eight times and the Carnival Road March competition on eight occasions.

His extensive catalogue explored politics, social issues, relationships, culture, and everyday Caribbean life, helping to take calypso to audiences well beyond Trinidad and Tobago.

Known by many as the Calypso King of the World, Sparrow was also regarded as a mentor and inspiration to successive generations of Caribbean performers.

His family said his importance extended beyond the stage.

“He was also a husband, father, grandfather, great-grandfather, life partner, and friend,” the statement said.

The family also said that in his final days Sparrow had embraced Christianity, giving his life to Jesus Christ and being baptised into the Seventh-day Adventist faith.

Sparrow’s death brings to a close one of the most celebrated careers in the history of calypso, with his music and performances helping to define the art form for generations.

Tributes are expected from across the Caribbean and the international music community as news of his passing spreads.

World.title: Protecting the environment or just another tax?
World.content:
BENNETT-COOPER...as we consider this legislation, we must keep our eyes firmly on the environmental mischief that it seeks to address

GOVERNMENT Senator Rose Marie Bennett-Cooper and her Opposition counterpart Allan Bernard disagreed strongly about the impact of the Environmental Protection Levy as the legislation was debated in the Upper House on Friday.

Bennett-Cooper argued that the levy, which becomes effective October 1, is much more than a tax as it will ensure measures are implemented to protect the environment. However, Bernard questioned how much has been actually done to protect the environment since the levy was first implemented in 2007.

“I believe that, in considering this Bill, we must distinguish between the instrument and its purpose. The levy is the instrument. But the greater purpose is environmental protection. And so, as we consider this legislation, we must keep our eyes firmly on the environmental mischief that it seeks to address. We must focus on our responsibility to protect the Jamaica that we have inherited, not only for ourselves, but for the generations that will come after us,” said Bennett-Cooper.

She argued that the effects of climate change, pollution, improper waste disposal, and the degradation of the country’s natural resources are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

“In fact, we do not have to look very far to understand the scale of our environmental problems,” declared Bennett-Cooper as she pointed out that since February 2022 when barrier interceptors were installed at the mouth of nine major gullies as part of the Kingston Harbour Clean-up Project, they have trapped more than 7.25 million kilogrammes of waste.

‘This is not an environmental problem we have to imagine. We can see it. We can measure it. We can physically pull it out of our gullies,” the Government senator argued.

She also highlighted that Ocean Cleanup, a non-profit organisation dedicated to developing and scaling solutions to rid the world’s oceans of plastic, estimates that waterways connected to Kingston Harbour could be responsible for approximately 947,000 kilogrammes of plastic entering the Caribbean Sea each year.

“The problem is not simply the waste. It is also the way our patterns of production, consumption, and disposal can impose costs on the environment that are ultimately borne by all of us,” said Bennett-Cooper as she underscored that Jamaica’s coastline is one of the country’s greatest natural assets.

“Our beaches attract visitors. Our seas support fisheries. Our coral reefs, mangroves and other marine ecosystems provide protection and support livelihoods. When these resources are degraded, the cost does not remain with the person who discarded the plastic,” she remarked.

Bernard began his presentation by noting that apart from the imposition of a levy, the Bill goes back 19 years to regularise its collection. In this context, he said Parliament is entitled to ask a very simple question: Where, in this Bill, is the environmental protection?

Bernard reeled off several other questions including: Where is the statutory architecture that connects the money collected to the environmental problem it is supposed to solve? Where are the environmental targets? Where are the measurable outcomes? Where is the dedicated financing mechanism? Where is the reporting requirement? Where is the obligation to tell Parliament and the Jamaican people, year after year, not simply how much environmental protection levy was collected, but what environmental protection Jamaica received for the money?

Continuing, Bernard said, “We can see them, we smell them, we drive through them, we wade through them when it rains”.

According to Bernard, increasingly, Jamaicans are asking whether they can even access some of the natural resources that constitute their environmental inheritance.

“So before we increase an Environmental Protection Levy, and before we retrospectively regularise 19 years of its collection, Parliament should ask what 19 years of this levy has actually meant for the state of Jamaica’s environment,” added Bernard.

According to the Memorandum of Objects and Reasons of the Bill, the intent is to address the “negative impact on the environment arising from the consumption, use and disposal of imported and locally manufactured goods.”

According to Bernard, while that is a perfectly legitimate objective the design of the legislation should allow us to follow a clear chain.

The Opposition senator said such a chain would note that economic activity creates environmental harm, that the State imposes an environmental levy which generates resources and incentives, and that those resources and incentives reduce environmental harm.

He said the chain would also see the State measuring the improvement and Parliament holding Government accountable for the results.

“That is the chain I expect to find in legislation imposing an environmental levy,” said Bernard.

“But when I read this Bill, I can clearly see the first half of the chain — I can see who pays, I can see how much they pay, I can see who collects it, I can see when returns must be filed, I can see provisions governing books and records, I can see tax credits”.

“What I cannot readily see is the second half of the chain. Where does the environmental protection happen?”

World.title: ‘The complete woman’
World.content:
Annaliesa Lindsay (right) greets a friend during the Mass of Resurrection for the life of her mother Hyacinth Lindsay at the Church of the Transfiguration in Meadowbrook, St Andrew, on Friday. Joseph wellington

FAMILY and loved ones who assembled for the Mass of Resurrection for Hyacinth Lindsay on Friday, paid their final respects to the legal luminary, nation builder, mother and friend, bestowing on her the title: “The complete woman.”

“Our dearest mother, our dearest Hyacinth, our dearest all-round supporter, friend, and cheerleader, you were the complete woman… She was the complete woman. You lived fully, you ran your race, you fought a very good fight, and it is now your time to rest,” said Annaliesa Lindsay, as she delivered her mother’s eulogy at the Church of the Transfiguration in Meadowbrook, St Andrew.

Annaliesa described her late mother as a woman of many passions, uniquely gifted, and deeply dedicated to every role she assumed.

Starting out a landmark legal career in Jamaican and Caribbean law, Hyacinth Lindsay was called to the Bar at Lincoln’s Inn, London, in 1971, and later enrolled as an attorney-at-law in 1973 in Jamaica where she began to work with the country’s Office of Parliamentary Counsel.

By 1989 she became Jamaica’s first female chief parliamentary counsel, serving until her retirement in 2006.

Her professional prowess as a legal expert was also felt across several regional conventions, serving as the Caribbean Community’s (Caricom) legal consultant and member of the Organisation of American States (OAS) Inter-American Juridical Committee. Hyacinth Lindsay was also a founding member of the Commonwealth Association Legislative Counsel.

Additionally, she was a part of the Caricom Inter-Governmental Task Force, which was established to undertake the revision of the Treaty of Chaguaramas. She was also a major contributor to the agreement establishing the Caribbean Court of Justice, serving on various committees, and drafting legislation pertaining to the regional body.

Lindsay also served as the Caribbean representative on the Commonwealth Association of Legislative Counsel for 12 years.

Her contributions to the legal fraternity saw significant transformation in legislation, drafting laws around constitutional reform, access to information, anti-corruption, banking and finance, companies, consumer protection, child protection, and criminal justice, among others.

Annaliesa noted that her mother’s rise through the legal profession was widely recognised and celebrated. This success was highlighted by two major milestones: Her appointment to the Inner Bar as King’s Counsel, formerly styled as Queen’s Counsel, and her conferral into the Order of Distinction, Commander Class (CD), Jamaica’s fifth-highest national honour.

But Hyacinth Lindsay at her most impactful, her daughter said, was when she was presenting as just herself, She said outside of her many professional accolades, her mother was a lover of travelling the world, seeing historical sites, photography, and quite memorably — German chocolate cake.

“Taking away from all of her professional life, her academic qualifications, and the things that she achieved in work, nothing in all of that can compare to the remarkable wife, mother, sister, daughter, friend, and human being that she was. Her achievements pale in comparison to the time spent, shared, and cherished with family and friends,” said Annaliesa.

She told the church that even during her mother’s battle with illness in her later years, she was still a warm and loving person, who lived a full and holistic life.

“For me, I can say, I hate God’s timing. But I trust in him, because I know that he knows what is best…Love you forever, you will always be in our hearts. Rest in eternal peace,” she concluded.

Tributes were also heard from Lindsay’s cousin Yvonne Coore-Johnson, her niece Dorrett Lindsay, and her nurses Tamecia Albert and Keriann Taylor.

Hyacinth Lindsay, who was born on February 10, 1941, died on August 30, 2026. She is also survived by her son, founding co-chairman of the Jamaica Observer Delroy Lindsay, and her other children.

World.title: Treasury minister says City experience ‘not a conflict’
World.content:
The City of London is lobbying hard against a windfall tax on the banks, as Labour seeks to balance the books.

Questioned on the departure from the U.K. of billionaire Chris Rokos — who pays £330 million a year in tax to the U.K. — Reynolds maintained that "we have to have rules."

"We want to create the very best conditions for growth, for entrepreneurship," she said. "But we have to have rules, and people who make a living here should pay taxes here."

The Treasury minister would not be drawn on the budget, which will be announced in October, but said that the government is "not powerless" in dealing with financial insecurity caused by international crises.

"We do face big global economic headwinds and a very difficult geopolitical situation with the ongoing war, particularly in the Middle East, but also in Ukraine," she said. "But we are not powerless to deal with those things, and we will do all that we can in the way that John [Healey] talked about earlier to further take further action to give families and businesses breathing space."

World.title: UK Labour shouldn’t work with nationalists who want to break up UK, says Welsh secretary
World.content:
Stephen Kinnock speaking at the POLITICO Pub at the Labour Party Conference in Liverpool, England on Sept. 28, 2026. | Baldo Sciacca for POLITICO

LIVERPOOL, England — Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said Monday that Labour would struggle to work with Welsh nationalists Plaid Cymru after the next general election if no party wins a decisive victory.

Speaking at the POLITICO Pub at Labour Party conference, Kinnock said he “cannot see any circumstances where you could cooperate in any meaningful way, really, with a party that wants to break up the United Kingdom.”

Kinnock, who joined the Cabinet in July, said he does believe people in the center-left nationalist force “want what I want, which is the best for Wales.”

World.title: Ukraine regains territory and captures POWs in frontline push
World.content:
The latest phase recaptured 51 square kilometers of territory, bringing the total recovered during Vivaldi to 176 square kilometers, according to the Third Army Corps.

The operation shows that Ukraine can reuse some Russian advances. It also has significance beyond the battlefield: Kyiv sees such counterattacks as evidence to its allies — and particularly the Trump administration — that Russia's grinding advances in Donetsk are not inevitable and that Russian leader Vladimir Putin cannot simply wait for Ukraine's defenses and Western resolve to collapse.

Vivaldi has seen the integrated use of drones, armor, artillery and infantry against Russian forces attempting a pincer attack to seize control of Lyman, a lynchpin of the "fortress belt" cities that have stymied Russian advances for years.

"Russian forces had advanced right up to the Siverskyi Donets River, and holding Lyman as the primary defensive hub for the northern Donetsk region would have become significantly harder had they advanced further," said Mykola Bielieskov, a research fellow at Ukraine’s State National Institute for Strategic Studies and senior analyst at Come Back Alive Initiatives Center NGO.

"Any further enemy advances would have disrupted logistics and supply lines to Lyman, complicating the city's defense," he added.

In the operation, Ukraine emphasized the use of unmanned technology to spare its troops — from air-dropping tiny ground robots behind Russian lines to turning Soviet-era BTR-60 armored vehicles into kamikaze robots by stuffing them full of explosives and driving them into Russian fortifications.

World.title: Britain needs tougher steel trade defenses, Cabinet minister says
World.content:
Asked whether he is satisfied with the current position on steel tariffs and quotas, and whether the government should reconsider its approach before the measures are reviewed next July, Kinnock said: “I am not at all happy with the position on quotas and tariffs. There is clear evidence that the British steel industry is being undercut.”

In July this year, under Keir Starmer’s administration, the U.K. implemented a new steel trade measure, replacing the expiring EU-era safeguard regime with a 51% reduction in overall tariff-free quota volumes compared to previous levels.

But Kinnock complained that some of the original measures were “diluted,” resulting in plants like Llanwern being undercut by imports of galvanized steel from places like Vietnam, Turkey, and South Korea.

“We absolutely have to do something about that,” he said. “That is one of my top priorities as the Secretary of State for Wales.”

Kinnock added that he is liaising closely with Sarwar on the issue, adding that an independent auditor is also assessing the damage caused by potential dumping.

“I'm confident that we will get a result from that, which will enable us to have a more robust trade defense regime,” he said.

World.title: French far right’s Bardella denies reports he made antisemitic comments
World.content:
The comments were allegedly made mostly in 2013, when Bardella was 17 and shortly after he had joined the National Rally, whose presidential candidate Marine Le Pen is the front-runner in next year’s election.

“At a time when the victory of our ideas has never been so close, a certain activist press is ready to orchestrate smear operations to destabilize the presidential campaign and attack my honor,” Bardella said.

During a visit to a construction industry event Monday, Le Pen called the Mediapart report “insanity.”

The National Rally’s predecessor, the National Front, was founded in part by Nazi collaborators. Le Pen’s father and predecessor as party chief, Jean-Marie Le Pen, was repeatedly convicted of hate speech for downplaying the Holocaust.

Marine Le Pen has spent years trying to rid her party of its most extreme elements and absolve it from accusations of antisemitism since taking over in 2011, going as far as expelling her father in 2015.

In 2023, Bardella sparked controversy by denying that Jean-Marie Le Pen was an antisemite, before correcting himself a few days later.

World.title: London’s Oxford Street will be pedestrianized from Oct. 26
World.content:
Pedestrians walk across Oxford Street in central London on Sept. 21, 2025. | Niklas Halle'n/AFP via Getty Images

The London mayor said a kilometer of the capital city’s road will be traffic free from next month.

LIVERPOOL, England — A kilometer of London’s iconic Oxford Street will be pedestrianised next month, the capital’s mayor said Monday.

Speaking at the POLITICO Pub at Labour Party conference, Sadiq Khan announced parts of the road will be traffic free from Oct. 26 and said he believed this could help revive the popular shopping destination after challenges affected by the rise of online shopping.

“We’ll then spend some time trying to turn it into a really lovely pedestrianized street, which will lead to more retail, more leisure, more visitors, more tourism,” Khan told POLITICO, condemning the street’s previous “managed decline” which included “tat shops” that “really shouldn’t be there.”

The mayor, who has run London since 2016, highlighted the “massive increase in interest with good quality retail” since the initial announcement.

Tory Deputy Leader of Westminster City Council Tim Barnes warned that businesses “still have a long list of unanswered questions about how it will work,” including issues around access, air pollution, street cleaning and public safety.

World.title: Wes Streeting: Britain and Europe must get out of ‘defensive crouch’
World.content:
British-American relations soured towards the end of Keir Starmer’s tenure as prime minister, after Britain refused to give the U.S. military support for its war with Iran, including the full use of British military bases for strikes on Iran. New Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government is now seeking to repair the alliance.

Part of the challenge from Donald Trump’s administration to Britain is to raise defense spending to record post-World War II levels. Britain doesn’t currently have a costed plan to reach its NATO commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2030.

Ahead of next month’s budget, he said that Chancellor John Healey doesn’t need persuading about the importance of raising defense spending as he previously resigned on this issue as a point of principle, Streeting said.

“I don’t want any complacency,” Streeting continued, adding: “We can’t just send in John Healey’s resignation letter as our submission to the spending review.”

However, he noted that he no longer gets asked how he is cutting waste and bureaucracy since leaving his position of Health Secretary for the Ministry of Defence, despite the fact that procurement challenges have “plagued the MoD.”

Fairford latest

Streeting also declined to elaborate on Donald Trump’s comments regarding the arrest of five Britons under suspicion of preparing a terrorist attack near RAF Fairford on Sunday, except to thank the farmer who reported suspicious activity to the police.
