World.title: COA flags ghost, incomplete school projects in Davao del Norte
World.content:
In Talaingod, Davao del Norte, state auditors flag a ghost school building at Kamingawan Elementary School, and undelivered project inclusions at Dulyan Integrated School

MANILA, Philippines – Around P83.26 million worth of school infrastructure projects in Davao del Norte were flagged by the Commission on Audit (COA) as ghost or non-existent, as well as “abandoned and materially incomplete” even though payments were nearly completed.

In its 2025 annual audit report on the Department of Education (DepEd), COA said the infrastructure work for Kamingawan Elementary School in Talaingod town was a “ghost/non-existent project.”

“No structure was found upon inspection but paid up to 98.8%,” state auditors noted in the report released last Wednesday, September 23.

The project was for the construction of a one-storey, two-classroom school building with a solar photovoltaic (PV) system, school furniture, and rainwater collector and water system.

A similar project for Dulyan Integrated School in Talaingod was also flagged by COA.

State auditors said that while the building and the rainwater system were constructed at Dulyan Integrated School, the “solar PV energy system as well as school furniture were not delivered,” but it was already “paid up to 98.80%.”

Both school projects were covered by a contract amounting to P36.36 million under the DepEd’s Last Mile Schools Program (LMSP), according to COA.

The commission also found another problematic LMSP project at Dugayan National High School in Kapalong town.

It had a P25.61-million contract for a two-storey, six-classroom school building with a toilet, rainwater collector, school furniture, solar PV energy system, and water system. It was already paid up to 98.90%.

“Upon inspection, building construction was found to be largely incomplete and abandoned. Only the structural frame had been constructed,” state auditors said.

COA also reported that distribution transformers, multiple panel boards, and outlets “remain uninstalled and undelivered” for New Casay Integrated School in Braulio E. Dujali town and Carmen National High School in Carmen town. Roofing works at Carmen National High School were also not performed.

The flagged school electrification projects were worth P10.43 million.

Moreover, state auditors found that four classrooms at Datu Balong National High School in San Isidro town were “unrepaired but claimed as implemented and paid up to 98.18% on July 18, 2025.” The contract was worth P7.54 million.

They also said that the construction of health facilities at Gov. Dujali Elementary School in San Isidro was “largely incomplete and abandoned.” It had a price tag of P3.32 million.

COA recommended the issuance of notices of termination of all contracts for the flagged projects, and to initiate blacklisting proceedings against the erring contractors.

State auditors told the Davao del Norte Schools Division Office (SDO) to conduct a fact-finding investigation to determine the accountability of concerned officials, initiate recovery proceedings for all paid progress billings, and file appropriate administrative, criminal, and civil charges against responsible officers and private individuals.

They also told the Davao del Norte SDO to immediately conduct joint validation of completely delivered items to correct accounting records.

Potential ghost students, DepEd employees?

State auditors also flagged deficiencies in monitoring the implementation of the DepEd’s Senior High School (SHS) Voucher Program.

In particular, guidelines for the complete monitoring and validation procedures for the SHS Voucher Program in the Ilocos Region were “not consistently followed,” which undermined the reliability of monitoring results during the audit period.

According to COA, the DepEd regional office took corrective steps from August 18 to 26.

“While the measures appear responsive to the identified deficiencies, their actual implementation and impact on ensuring compliance, detecting program violations, and validating the existence and eligibility of beneficiaries remain to be established,” state auditors said in a rejoinder.

They requested the DepEd office in the Ilocos Region to submit the comprehensive results of the 100% on-site monitoring activities, including detailed documentation of validation procedures, discrepancies, and corrective actions.

The regional office was also told to use a uniform monitoring and compliance report template to “ensure consistent verification of the existence, eligibility, and completeness of records of all SHS [Voucher Program] beneficiaries, and to enhance detection of program violations, including ghost students.”

Meanwhile, there were “inadequate payment controls” in six DepEd regional offices, which “[increased] the risk of overpayment, ghost employees, and erroneous salary payments.”

The deficiencies found were in the established payroll systems, as well as preparation, processing, and payment of salaries.

The DepEd regional offices identified in the audit observations were in the National Capital Region, Ilocos Region, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, and Davao Region. – Rappler.com

World.title: After Gabby sold to Ramon Ang, Piki Lopez is securing the family’s crown jewels
World.content:
Gabby Lopez' branch turned part of their inheritance into cash—and put some of it toward keeping ABS-CBN alive. Their cousin Piki Lopez is securing control over what remains below.

When Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III, the former chairman of ABS-CBN Corp. and the grandson of the man who built the family’s broadcast empire, sold his branch’s stake in the clan’s private holding company to diversified conglomerate San Miguel Corporation chairman Ramon S. Ang in August, the story seemed obvious: after months of cousins fighting one another in court and in the business pages, an outsider had finally bought his way into the house the Lopezes built.

The reality is that Ang bought into the family’s private penthouse, Lopez Inc., a vehicle that holds prestige and voting shares, but produces no electricity, sells no condominiums, and operates no infrastructure.

The actual wealth, the real revenue, and the plants that light a fifth of the country’s homes sit three levels below. On Friday, September 25, Federico “Piki” Lopez, Gabby’s first cousin and the chairman and chief executive of First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH) since 2010, emerged from the company’s long-delayed board election with his leadership firmly intact after months of legal and corporate deadlock. FPH is the listed company that holds much of what remains of the family’s operating empire: the power plants, industrial estates, property developments and other businesses.

Whatever truce was struck at the top, and whatever Ang believes he bought there, control of the corporate chain leading to the Lopez power business remains with Piki’s side.

The real prize

To understand why the 3rd generation cousins spent months in an acrimonious standoff, follow the cash.

Over the past two decades, the family surrendered Manila Electric Co. (Meralco) to Manuel V. Pangilinan’s group, weathered the loss of ABS-CBN’s broadcast franchise in 2020, and carried heavy debt at the holding levels. What remained standing, and thriving, was FPH. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)

FPH is not merely a paper holding firm. It is the group’s cash engine, and 3 businesses account for most of it.

Energy Development Corporation (EDC) is the jewel within the jewel. With nearly 1,300 megawatts of geothermal capacity, drawn from volcanic fields in Leyte, Negros, Bicol and Mindanao, EDC has something difficult and expensive to replicate: geothermal fields, power plants, drilling and reservoir expertise built over decades, producing renewable electricity around the clock. Since the Lopez group acquired EDC from the government in 2007, FPH president Giles Puno said more than P200 billion has been invested in the geothermal business.

First Gen Corporation is the group’s primary energy platform, built over the past 3 decades from the country’s first natural gas plants into a portfolio of geothermal, hydro, wind and solar. In 2025, First Gen sold 60% of its natural gas business to Enrique Razon’s Prime Infrastructure, freeing capital for its next phase of expansion, including roughly P62 billion into two enormous pumped-storage hydro projects in Rizal and Laguna. These are giant batteries in another form: they use electricity to pump water uphill when power is plentiful, then release it to generate electricity when the grid needs it. Roughly 92% of First Gen’s asset base is now in renewables.

Alongside them sit Rockwell Land, the developer of the Makati enclave and the malls and condominium towers that carry its name, and First Philippine Industrial Park (FPIP) in Batangas, which hosts 159 locators employing more than 73,000 people. Rockwell and FPIP add property, industrial land, and recurring income to a group dominated by power.

In 2025, FPH posted record consolidated net income of P31.7 billion on revenues of P84.7 billion, although that profit included a one-time gain from First Gen’s sale of control of its natural gas business. Recurring net income attributable to FPH shareholders was P15.1 billion.

For a family facing liquidity problems several corporate floors above, FPH was no longer just another asset. It had become the economic center of gravity.

This was why the cousins’ argument over control was also an argument over cash. Who controlled the companies would influence how much money stayed inside them for the next power plant, geothermal field or property development; how much could be sent upward as dividends; and how much, eventually, could reach other parts of the family empire, including a cash-starved ABS-CBN.

Control determined who got to make those choices.

One floor down

The September 25 stockholders meeting of First Philippine Holdings was a direct sequel to the September 14 showdown at Lopez Holdings Corporation, formerly Benpres Holdings Corporation.

To see how control flows through the group, consider its vertical architecture.

At the apex sits Lopez Inc., the private, unlisted vehicle owned by the branches of the Lopez family, where Gabby’s Crème Investment sold its 25.68% stake to Ramon Ang. One floor down is Lopez Holdings Corporation, a publicly listed firm 54.74% owned by Lopez Inc. Below that is First Philippine Holdings, 60.67% owned by Lopez Holdings. Below FPH, the structure branches into the operating businesses: First Gen and, beneath it, EDC; Rockwell Land; the industrial park; and the rest of the companies that actually run the plants and build the buildings.

Control flows downward through those levels, and so does the proxy that carries it. At the September 14 meeting of Lopez Holdings, Piki remained chairman and CEO, while his brother Jay Lopez took over as president and COO. Their sister Mercedes “Cedie” Lopez-Vargas took another board seat, strengthening the hold of the Oscar Lopez branch on the 7-member board. Piki had secured the intermediate layer of the corporate chain.

The question was whether the consolidation would carry into FPH. That meeting had been delayed for months amid the proxy dispute between Piki and the majority cousins at Lopez Inc., with the Securities and Exchange Commission eventually ordering the election to proceed subject to a preliminary injunction issued by the Mandaluyong Regional Trial Court.

When the votes were counted on September 25, Piki’s position at FPH had survived the cousins fight. Piki was re-elected chairman and chief executive, his brother Benjamin Lopez remained vice chairman, and Francis “Giles” Puno, a career executive and his long-time second-in-command, was reappointed president and COO. Piki also kept the chair of both the executive committee and the finance and investment committee, two committees central to executive decisions and the allocation of capital.

What happened in the boardroom

The composition of the new 15-member board of FPH showed the controlling shareholder’s reach.

Roberta “Berta” Feliciano, a veteran director and a cousin from Gabby’s side of the family, had resigned in August, her disclosure stating plainly that her departure followed Crème Investment’s sale of its Lopez Inc. shares to Ang.

Then came the meeting itself. Shareholders elected Lee Benjamin Z. Lerma, a corporate lawyer and partner at Romulo Mabanta Buenaventura Sayoc & De los Angeles, one of the country’s older law firms, to the board. Lerma was not a returning FPH director. He was one of 5 new names nominated to the board this year.

Minutes later, Lerma was gone.

At the organizational meeting that followed the stockholders vote, Lerma resigned. According to FPH’s disclosure, he tendered his resignation “as decided by and agreed with the company’s major stockholder.” Its controlling shareholder is Lopez Holdings, which owns 60.67% of FPH and whose proxy decides the outcome of any FPH election. The board filled the vacancy the same afternoon with Victor Emmanuel B. Santos Jr., an executive vice president of the company, whose name had not appeared among the candidates shareholders were asked to elect.

The cash choke point

The dispute did not start over green ideology. It started over cash.

After ABS-CBN’s free-television operations shut down, the media company faced mounting losses and urgent debts, and needed billions in additional capital. The holding companies above it, Lopez Inc. and Lopez Holdings, depended on dividends flowing up to meet their own obligations.

The money was being generated at FPH. Much less of it traveled all the way up the corporate pyramid. The company routed a steady P567 million a year in dividends up to Lopez Holdings, the same figure in each of the past 3 years. Lopez Holdings, after its own overhead and creditors, declared its regular 10-centavo-per-share dividend, distributing roughly P452 million. Because Lopez Holdings is publicly listed, that money goes proportionally to all its shareholders. Lopez Inc., with 54.74%, therefore received only about P247 million.

So, billions were being generated several corporate floors below. But only a fraction made the entire journey to the family’s private holding company.

But the billions inside FPH were not simply family money waiting to be withdrawn. FPH is a publicly listed company whose shareholders include the Social Security System, which owns 6.62% and invests retirement contributions of ordinary Filipinos, alongside thousands of other shareholders. Its directors owe duties to the corporation and its shareholders as a whole, not simply to the Lopez family several corporate floors above.

Gabby’s side found another way to raise cash. It converted part of its Lopez Inc. ownership into cash, then redirected part of the proceeds toward keeping ABS-CBN alive. (READ: [Rappler’s Best] The day Gabby Lopez said, ‘We’re done’)

Days after Crème Investment sold its 25.68% stake in Lopez, Inc. to Ramon Ang, ABS-CBN announced a P6-billion rescue package. P2.2 billion would come from Gabby and the other majority cousins through Crème, Mantes and Presta. Outside investor I&C Holdings committed P3.5 billion, while Lopez Inc. would put in another P300 million.

That left a fundamental tension running through this family saga: take more cash out of the operating companies now, or leave capital inside them to build the next generation of clean energy assets. First Gen was doing the latter. Its next generation of projects included about P160 billion in geothermal redevelopment over the next 5 years, and roughly P62 billion for the Wawa and Pakil pumped-storage hydro projects.

No shortcuts at First Gen

The distinction between owning shares and controlling a company became even clearer one floor below—at First Gen.

KKR, the American private equity firm that had held roughly a fifth of First Gen for years, sold its entire stake to Angsana Finance Limited, a Cayman-registered vehicle managed by Singapore-based Gateway Partners, for about P25.8 billion, or P36 a share. The sale raised an immediate question: had Angsana bought a path into the boardroom, including the seat left vacant by the resignation of First Gen director Manolo Michael de Guzman?

Asked by Rappler at the September 25 meeting, Puno answered it directly: “Because KKR acquired its 19.9% stake in First Gen directly from the secondary market, no shareholder agreement was established with FPH,” he said. “Consequently, Angsana did not obtain any special or contractual governance rights through its purchase of KKR’s holdings, maintaining only the standard statutory rights granted to minority shareholders under the Revised Corporation Code of the Philippines.”

In plain English: Angsana bought KKR’s shares, not a separate governance agreement with the Lopezes. Its 19.9% stake gives it substantial economic and voting rights, but Puno said it came with no special contractual governance rights inherited from KKR.

P25.8 billion bought Angsana almost one-fifth of First Gen. It did not automatically buy a seat in the boardroom.

What they inherited

The Lopez cousins’ war did not produce a neat reconciliation. It changed who owns what at the top of the Lopez pyramid, while clarifying who controls much of what lies underneath.

Gabby’s branch sold its 25.68% stake in Lopez Inc. to Ramon Ang, converting part of its inheritance into cash. Some of that liquidity went toward the P2.2 billion that Gabby and the other majority cousins committed to keeping ABS-CBN alive. Piki, meanwhile, remained at the helm of Lopez Holdings and FPH. Farther down, FPH continues to control First Gen, which controls EDC.

One side monetized part of its inheritance. The other kept control of the operating businesses below.

The legal fight is not entirely over: Piki’s contempt petition against 4 Lopez Holdings directors remains pending before a Mandaluyong court. But when he addressed FPH shareholders on Friday, Piki did not mention the family feud.

Instead, he talked about inheritance. “Each generation inherits the results of choices made before it,” he said. “Each generation’s choices determine what it leaves behind.”

The 3rd generation Lopez cousins has spent much of 2026 fighting over that inheritance: who could speak for the family companies, who could nominate their directors, how their shares would be voted, how much cash should move upward, and ultimately who would decide what happened to the businesses previous generations had built.

Gabby’s branch turned part of that inheritance into cash—and put some of it toward keeping ABS-CBN alive. Piki Lopez is securing control over what remains below. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: Carlo Paalam saves PH’s boxing campaign in Asian Games, earns sure medal
World.content:
CELEBRATION. Boxer Carlo Paalam in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Carlo Paalam edges his Chinese foe as he advances to the semifinals of the men's 55kg division, preserving the Philippines' medal streak in Asian Games boxing

MANILA, Philippines – Carlo Paalam prevented what would have been a dubious first for Philippine boxing in the Asian Games.

Paalam assured himself of a medal after earning his place in the semifinals of the men’s 55kg division with a 3-2 win over China’s Zhang Jiamao at the Nishio Gymnasium in Japan on Monday, September 28.

The Olympic silver medalist won by scores of 29-28, 29-28, 29-28, 28-29, 27-30 as he preserved the Philippines’ medal streak in Asian Games boxing.

A loss by Paalam would have marked the first time the Philippines failed to win a boxing medal in the Asian Games since the sport made its debut in the 1954 edition as fellow Olympic silver medalist Nesthy Petecio earlier crashed out in the quarterfinals.

But Paalam rose to the occasion, earning the nod of three of the five judges in the opening round before delivering a more convincing second-round showing that practically sealed his victory.

Even as Zhang unanimously won the third round, he failed to erase the lead Paalam built.

With the victory, Paalam has matched his bronze finish in the 2018 edition in Jakarta, Indonesia, where he competed in the men’s 49kg category.

It does not get easier, though, for the pride of Cagayan de Oro City as he battles reigning world champion Makhmud Sabyrkhan of Kazakhstan in the semifinals on Wednesday, September 30.

Earlier on Monday, Petecio fell short of a breakthrough Asian Games medal as she suffered a 5-0 defeat at the hands of China’s Yang Chengyu in the women’s 60kg class.

Yang controlled the bout from start to finish, earning 30-26 scores from all five judges.

Other Filipino boxers have also bowed out of contention, with Junmilardo Ogayre (men’s 60kg) losing in the quarterfinals, Riza Pasuit (women’s 54kg) and Norlan Petecio (men’s 70kg) exiting the round of 16, and Aira Villegas (women’s 51kg) getting the boot in the round of 32.

Eumir Marcial, a silver medalist in the 2023 edition, was supposed to see action in this Asian Games but sat out after a mutual decision with the Association of Boxing Alliances in the Philippines. – Rappler.com

World.title: Mary Jane Veloso’s journey home is a story of grit
World.content:
Mary Jane Veloso did not lose hope that she would someday be free and reunited with her family, and that homecoming has finally become reality

Throughout Saturday, September 26, Mary Jane Veloso rubbed liniment oil on the temples of her head. It temporarily soothed the headache she had been feeling since Friday, September 25.

It seemed her weakened body held her back from moving freely all day. But her will was stronger. Maybe because she already endured 16 long years of imprisonment that being sick for another day could not stop her from doing engagements and traveling for hours.

After all, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. already granted the 41-year-old former overseas Filipino worker (OFW) an absolute pardon from her drug trafficking conviction handed down by an Indonesian court in 2010.

All Mary Jane needed to do was to reach her doorstep in Nueva Ecija, so she could announce to the world that she was home at last.

NEW MORNING. Cesar and Celia Veloso hold onto their daughter Mary Jane as they leave a hotel in Manila on September 26, 2026, after spending the night following the former overseas Filipino worker’s release from the Correctional Institution for Women. Photo by Rappler

Faith and courage

Mary Jane did not go home immediately after leaving the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City early Saturday.

She and her family spent the night in Manila, as she wanted to attend Mass first and hold a press conference before going back to her home province. It was her way of giving back to supporters and all other Filipinos who followed her case.

Overwhelmed by her reunion with her family, Mary Jane could not sleep.

During the ride to Siena College Chapel in Quezon City, sleepless Mary Jane took time to appreciate the world outside of prison in broad daylight, specifically the roads, as well as the trees and plants, her 46-year-old sister Maritess Laurente told Rappler.

The medicine they gave to Mary Jane did little to ease her motion sickness. Nuns gave her warm water and crackers. Afterwards, she wore her rosary then rested her head on the shoulders of her father, 70-year-old Cesar, as they waited for the Mass to start.

Play Video

The former OFW was fueled by her faith. Recalling the moments before her scheduled execution in Indonesia in April 2015, she told journalists: “Sabi ko kay God, ‘Patunayan mo sa buong mundo na wala akong kasalanan. Iligtas mo po ako.’” (I asked God, “Prove to the world that I’m innocent. Please save me.”)

She was granted a last-minute reprieve in Indonesia. Over a decade later, she was pardoned in the Philippines.

“Natutunan ko po talaga sa laban ko na ‘to na huwag tayong bibitaw. Huwag tayong mawalan ng pag-asa kasi ibibigay ni God ‘yan sa tamang panahon. At ito po ‘yong panahon na iniintay ko, dumating na po: Kasama ko ang aking pamilya.”

(What I learned from my fight for freedom is we should not let go. We should not lose hope because God will grant our desires at the right time. And the moment that I’ve been waiting for has arrived: I’m with my family.)

THANKSGIVING MASS. Mary Jane Veloso, accompanied by her family and support groups, attends a thanksgiving Mass at Siena College Chapel in Quezon City on September 26, 2026. Photo by Jire Carreon/Rappler

Clinging to family

The Veloso family also could not sleep after the release of Mary Jane, the youngest of five children of Cesar and Celia. Her siblings thought what was happening was a dream.

Christopher Veloso, 48, was working on their farm when he heard that his sister had been pardoned. With their eagerness to be reunited with her, they forgot to bring clothes for Mary Jane. It was supporters from rights group Migrante International who lent Mary Jane a pink top, which she wore during Saturday’s press conference.

When they settled at a hotel in Manila in the early hours of Saturday, they ordered pizza. Even with their separate hotel rooms, 14 members of the Veloso family crowded in one room to share the midnight snack and be with Mary Jane.

They wanted to make up for lost time with Mary Jane, the most affectionate Veloso, after her 16-year ordeal behind bars.

Darling Cando, 44, who was described as the sibling closest to Mary Jane, massaged her sister’s aching head.

Mary Jane clung to her mother when she faced the media after Saturday’s Mass. Celia, 66, would touch and fix her youngest daughter’s hair from time to time.

MOTHER’S LOVE. Mary Jane Veloso and her mother Celia join a press conference at Siena College in Quezon City on September 26, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

“Sa nakita ko sa kapatid ko, kahit gano’n ang nangyari sa kanya, talagang nilakasan niya ang loob niya,” Christopher told Rappler.

“Kung tatanungin ako kung ‘yong ginawa niya, nakulong siya nang matagal, kung kakayanin ko, baka ‘di ko kaya eh. Kaya bilib ako sa kanya. Salamat po at ginabayan siya ng Panginoon.”

(From what I’ve seen from my sister, she really remained strong even if she was imprisoned for a long time. If I were in her shoes, I think I wouldn’t be able to handle that. That’s why I’m proud of her. Thank you, Lord, for guiding her.)

With Mary Jane’s freedom, her siblings said they will strive to keep their promises, such as attending Mass every week and helping her start a business.

Play Video

And for Mary Jane, she can now fulfill her desire to take care of her aging parents and her own sons, Mark Daniel Candelaria, 23, and Mark Darren Candelaria, 17.

Daniel and Darren were only seven years old and one year old, respectively, when their mother left the Philippines to be a domestic worker in April 2010. She was supposed to take a job in Malaysia, but was asked by her recruiters to go to Indonesia instead with a new suitcase. In Indonesia, airport authorities found heroin hidden inside the lining of Mary Jane’s bag. She was arrested for drug trafficking and later placed on death row.

Maintaining her innocence, Mary Jane would spend the next 16 years fighting for her freedom. Her life was spared in 2015 due to the last-minute reprieve, and in December 2024, she again stepped on home soil as Indonesia agreed to transfer her to Philippine custody.

Now, Mary Jane will finally be with her sons on their birthdays — with Darren turning 18 on October 25 and Daniel turning 24 on November 28. Her sons, now young men, cried during Saturday’s press conference when their mother spoke, when she recited poetry, and when she sang “Maghintay Ka Lamang.”

Daniel and Darren also delivered heartfelt messages to the mother they grew up without, yet love so dearly. “Tandaan ‘nyo po palagi na proud na proud po ako na kayo po ‘yung naging nanay ko,” Daniel said. (Always remember that I’m so proud you’re my mother.)

Play Video

Nothing like home

After more than two hours of travel, Mary Jane arrived in General Mamerto Natividad, Nueva Ecija, at 5:43 pm on Saturday. Relatives and some neighbors greeted Mary Jane, who was still carsick but clearly thrilled to be home.

HOMECOMING. Mary Jane Veloso waves to supporters upon her arrival in General Mamerto Natividad, Nueva Ecija, on September 26, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

Carefully, she walked towards their house, where banners and balloons were put up to mark her homecoming. This was her first time to see their house in General Mamerto Natividad, as their family is originally from Talavera, another town in Nueva Ecija.

She was given warm water to drink before she changed into a more comfortable black shirt.

For her first meal back home, Mary Jane requested pinakbet — a Filipino vegetable dish — and grilled fish. The General Mamerto Natividad government also gave a chocolate cake.

Play Video

“Puro repolyo naman. Mahal po kasi ang gulay, pasensiya na (It’s full of cabbage. Vegetables now are expensive, please bear with us),” Christopher said of the pinakbet, which was prepared by his wife, Nerisa. Chuckles were heard around the table as the Veloso family gathered to eat.

As the night wore on, neighbors started a karaoke fest. Mary Jane inched closer to her relatives and friends, chatting about her imprisonment.

‘KUMUSTAHAN.’ Mary Jane Veloso spends the night chatting with family and friends back home in Nueva Ecija on September 26, 2026. Photo by Angie de Silva/Rappler

Color returned to Mary Jane’s face. “Nakakain na eh (I’ve already eaten, that’s why),” she told Rappler.

But perhaps it was because she was home at last. – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala opens quest for Asian Games gold, Olympic berth with dominant win
World.content:
FOREHAND. Tennis player Alex Eala in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.

Filipina tennis star Alex Eala needs just a little less than an hour to dispatch Thailand’s Patcharin Cheapchandej and advance to the quarterfinals of the women's singles event in the 2026 Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala means business as she opened her bid for a gold medal and an Olympic berth in the Asian Games.

The Filipina tennis star made quick work of Thailand’s Patcharin Cheapchandej, scoring a dominant 6-1, 6-0 win in the round of 16 of the women’s singles event at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center in Nagoya, Japan, on Monday, September 28.

Play Video

Shrugging off a rain delay that forced organizers to move the match indoors, Eala needed just 55 minutes to see off Cheapchandej, who is ranked outside the world top 500.

The highest-ranked player in the Asian Games at world No. 18, Eala received the top seed and earned a first-round bye.

Eala will face Chinese Taipei’s Joanna Garland in the quarterfinals, where a win would guarantee the Filipina another Asian Games medal after she clinched a bronze in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China.

Coming off a surprise exit from the Singapore Open, Eala looks to redeem herself as she seeks to end the Philippines’ decades-long drought for a tennis gold medal in the quadrennial showpiece.

The last time the country won an Asian Games gold in the sport came in 1962, when Johnny Jose ruled the men’s singles division.

Eala entered the competition as the title favorite, with world No. 1 Elena Rybakina of Kazakhstan, No. 17 Naomi Osaka of Japan, and defending champion Zheng Qinwen of China skipping the Asian Games to compete in the China Open.

A golden finish will also propel Eala to a maiden Olympic appearance as the men’s and women’s singles champions directly qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Games. – Rappler.com

World.title: From Deals to Delivery: What is at Stake in President Tokayev’s Germany Visit
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev will visit Germany from Sept. 29-Oct. 1, with meetings in Berlin and Munich coming at a time when Kazakh-German relations have grown significantly in both political and economic terms, but are also entering a more demanding stage.

Germany is one of Kazakhstan’s key European partners for investment, technology and industrial cooperation. For Berlin, Kazakhstan has become increasingly important as a source of energy and critical raw materials and as part of efforts to diversify supply chains. The question now is whether those complementary interests can translate into deeper industrial ties, particularly in processing, manufacturing and technology.

Munich is more than a stop on Tokayev’s German visit

The Munich part of the visit deserves particular attention because Bavaria is significant in Kazakhstan’s economic engagement with Germany. Bilateral trade between Kazakhstan and Bavaria reached 3.4 billion euros in 2025, putting Bavaria first among Germany’s federal states by trade with Kazakhstan, according to Kazakhstan’s Prime Minister’s Office. The two sides have expanded cooperation in industry, agriculture, technology and raw materials, with German companies including Horsch, Linde Gas and Rhenus already operating in Kazakhstan.

The significance of Bavaria is not only the size of its trade with Kazakhstan. It also lies in the structure of its economy, with strong positions in manufacturing, engineering and technology. For Kazakhstan, closer ties with such a region fit its broader effort to attract German companies into local production rather than rely mainly on imports of finished equipment.

That makes Munich a useful lens through which to view the wider relationship. It offers a closer look at whether the strategic agenda discussed between governments in Berlin will translate into decisions by companies.

Kazakhstan seeks to change its role in the relationship

The push for a more advanced economic relationship has been building since Tokayev’s visit to Berlin in September 2023. At the time, Kazakhstan and Germany were discussing critical raw materials, green energy, transport and logistics and greater German investment in non-resource sectors. Tokayev proposed a consortium for joint raw-materials projects and invited German companies to help develop production in Kazakhstan. Bilateral trade rose 25% to $2.8 billion in 2022, while German businesses invested almost $6 billion in Kazakhstan, nearly 90% of it outside the resource sector.

A year later, when German Chancellor Olaf Scholz made his first visit to Kazakhstan in 14 years, the agenda had expanded to energy, green transformation, mining, transport and logistics, agriculture and climate cooperation. A business forum in Astana produced 36 documents worth $6.3 billion covering mechanical engineering, innovation, logistics, petrochemicals, information technology and industrial automation.

The relationship continued to grow in 2025. Bilateral trade reached $4.4 billion, up 9.5% from the previous year. German investment rose 28.5% to $700 million, bringing cumulative German investment since 2005 to about $7.8 billion. More than 1,100 companies with German capital operate in Kazakhstan.

But Kazakhstan’s ambition is increasingly about changing the structure of the relationship, not only expanding its volume. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said in June that Kazakhstan wants to transform traditional trade and investment ties into deeper industrial and technological cooperation through production localization, technology transfer and training. The government pointed to CLAAS and Horsch as examples of phased localization that could be extended to other sectors.

Valeriy Sitenko, senior expert at the Institute of Foreign Policy Studies under Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, puts that shift in broader terms. He highlights that Kazakhstan’s role should evolve from transit to production.

“If previously the emphasis was mainly on transport connectivity and Kazakhstan’s transit function, today there is a transition toward deeper integration: the inclusion of Kazakhstan and Central Asia in global value chains. In the new model, Kazakhstan acts not only as a transit space, but as a production and technology hub,” Sitenko told The Astana Times.

That would change the logic of cooperation. Instead of simply connecting Kazakh resources with European markets, Kazakhstan would seek to retain more of the value created from those resources through processing and manufacturing.

Sitenko identifies machinery, chemicals, electrical engineering, critical minerals processing, IT and renewable energy as potential areas. He also points to Germany’s dual vocational education system, where companies are directly involved in training workers and aligning skills with production needs. The latter is particularly relevant to Kazakhstan’s industrial ambitions. German expertise could shape not only what is produced, but also the skills base built around new production.

Germany’s strategic interest is growing, but business is moving carefully

Germany has its own reasons to deepen the relationship. The German Federal Foreign Office describes Kazakhstan as Germany’s largest trading partner in Central Asia and an important supplier of energy and raw materials, noting that shifting global trade and energy flows have increased the region’s strategic importance.

Energy remains part of that relationship. By Scholz’s September 2024 visit, Kazakhstan was already supplying crude oil to Germany’s Schwedt refinery, and the bilateral agenda included energy, critical raw materials, mining and technological cooperation.

The economic relationship has also become more concrete this year. A Kazakhstan Investment Day in Frankfurt in February brought together around 200 representatives of German companies, financial institutions and industry associations. KfW IPEX-Bank and Solidcore Resources also signed a $100 million term sheet linked to the Ertis hydrometallurgical plant.

Yet strategic interest does not automatically mean that German companies will make large, long-term investments. Stephan Meister, a German expert on Central Asia, points to a basic commercial consideration that is less visible in government-level discussions: the size of Kazakhstan’s domestic market.

“It’s a difficult question, since Kazakhstan is in terms of population a small market, so there is a question about how much it makes sense to invest in bigger industrial production and for which markets,” he said to The Astana Times.

He also questions whether Kazakhstan’s investment environment has changed enough to encourage more German capital.

“German business is more cautious before they invest, and in terms of rule of law, transparency and business climate, not much has changed in the last years in Kazakhstan which has improved the investment conditions,” Meister said.

For Kazakhstan, that raises a practical question about the markets new production would serve. If large projects are not aimed primarily at domestic demand, they need to be competitive in wider regional and international supply chains. Market access, predictable business conditions and financing therefore matter alongside the availability of raw materials.

The constraints are not only on Kazakhstan’s side

Meister also points to a factor that complicates the usual discussion of why German investment may be slow: Germany itself is going through a difficult economic period. German companies, he argues, are becoming more cautious about where they commit capital, making the search for new markets more difficult even when the strategic case is strong.

This creates a gap between Germany’s growing political interest in Central Asia and the risk appetite of its private sector. Germany may see Kazakhstan as useful for diversifying energy and raw-material supply chains while companies continue to ask whether individual projects are commercially compelling enough to justify the risks. Meister sees another issue on the German side: political engagement.

“My impression is the main limitation on the German side is the lack of a political vision for relations with Central Asian countries, more investment on the leadership level into the countries of the region, including Kazakhstan, and a lack of understanding about the importance of the region,” he said.

According to him, German companies are slower and more risk-averse than some competitors and often lack sufficient political support when entering Central Asian markets. That leaves both sides with something to prove. Kazakhstan needs to make the country more attractive for long-term industrial investment and demonstrate that production can serve markets beyond Kazakhstan. Germany, meanwhile, faces the question of whether its growing strategic interest in Central Asia is strong enough to translate into more active support for German companies entering the region.

What the visit could clarify

The two governments already have a broad network of mechanisms for cooperation, from the Central Asia-Germany format launched in Berlin in 2023 to bilateral platforms bringing together ministries, businesses and financial institutions. Sitenko notes that the institutional tools for a strategic partnership are already in place and need to be used more effectively. Meister, however, points to Germany’s lack of a clear political vision and its companies’ cautious approach as factors that could slow new investment.

The difference between these two views is useful in understanding what will be at stake during the visit. Kazakhstan is looking to use German technology and capital to retain more value from its own resources and move further into production and processing. German companies, for their part, need projects with sufficient scale, predictable conditions and access to wider markets.

The Munich leg is therefore particularly relevant. Bavaria’s growing trade and business ties with Kazakhstan offer one of the clearest examples of where the broader relationship could go, especially in manufacturing, technology and industrial cooperation.

Sitenko also points to the less visible side of economic ties: education, skills and movement between the two countries. He notes that scaling German-style dual education and easing visa procedures could strengthen business, professional and academic links alongside larger industrial projects.

What emerges from the visit may therefore be more important than the number of new agreements announced. The stronger signal would be whether the existing framework produces projects that create more value in Kazakhstan and give German companies a stronger commercial reason to deepen their presence.

World.title: Kazakhstan Returns to Asian Games Show Jumping After 20-Year Absence
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s national equestrian team is completing final preparations in Tokyo ahead of its return to show jumping at the Asian Games after a 20-year absence, with four riders set to compete in the team and individual events at Aichi-Nagoya 2026.

The Kazakhstan team includes Oleg Sokolenko, Raisa Sokolenko, Nurila Turisbekova and Ksenia Batalova. The competitions will be held at the JRA Equestrian Park in Tokyo.

Speaking ahead of the draw, Kazakhstan national team head coach and Master of Sport Azamat Khassenov said the riders were following their training program and gradually approaching competition, Kazakhstan’s Equestrian Federation reported on Sept. 28.

“After a 20-year break, Kazakhstan is represented at this level again, so this is a significant event for us. We want to represent the country and achieve a good result,” he said.

Khassenov said the team had adapted well to local conditions, with close attention paid to the condition of both the riders and horses. The upcoming draw will influence the team’s tactics, notably the order of performances and the opponents they will face.

Kazakhstan will compete in both the team and individual show jumping events. The team competition is scheduled for Oct. 1 and will feature two rounds followed by the medal ceremony. The individual competition will take place on Oct. 3 and 4. Obstacles will range from 145 to 155 centimeters in height, depending on the round.

World.title: Kazakh President Honors Rybakina for Historic Tennis Achievements
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met with Elena Rybakina on Sept. 28 to congratulate her on winning the US Open and becoming the first Kazakh tennis player to reach the top of the WTA rankings.

He also awarded her the Barys Order, third degree, for outstanding sporting achievements and her contribution to the development and promotion of tennis in Kazakhstan.

During the meeting, Tokayev highlighted the historic significance of Rybakina’s achievements and her influence on the younger generation.

“After your victories, our children are taking an interest in tennis, enrolling in sections in large numbers and wanting to become champions themselves. You set a positive example for our children, and this is very important. Our children should engage in sports, as it is crucial for their future,” he said.

He noted that Rybakina’s three Grand Slam victories would become part of tennis history and said he was confident she would continue to achieve major results.

Tokayev also praised Rybakina’s conduct on and off the court, describing her as a person of “exceptionally high personal culture.”

Rybakina thanked President Tokayev for his personal support and attention to the development of tennis in Kazakhstan. She said she was proud to represent Kazakhstan on the international stage and would continue striving for high results.

Rybakina’s latest achievement caps a landmark 2026 season. She won the Australian Open and US Open, reached the finals of Indian Wells and Toronto, and became the first player representing Kazakhstan to top the WTA singles rankings. She is the 30th woman in WTA history to reach world No. 1.

World.title: Kazakhstan Women’s Chess Team Wins Silver at World Chess Olympiad
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s women’s chess team won silver at the 46th World Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, finishing the 11-round tournament undefeated with 18 points. China won gold, while India took bronze.

Undefeated run

Held from Sept. 16 to 27, the Olympiad brought together nearly 400 teams. Kazakhstan finished second among 189 women’s teams, recording seven wins and four draws.

The team faced Poland in the final, and the match ended in a draw. The silver medal marks Kazakhstan’s second consecutive runner-up finish, following the team’s result at the 2024 Olympiad in Hungary.

The Kazakhstan lineup comprised Bibisara Assaubayeva, Alua Nurman, Meruyert Kamalidenova, Yelnaz Kaliakhmet and Zarina Nurgaliyeva. For 16-year-olds Kaliakhmet and Nurgaliyeva, the tournament marked their Olympic debuts, reported Kazinform.

Kazakhstan has competed in the women’s section of the Chess Olympiad since 1992. This year, the team recorded its first undefeated campaign. Assaubayeva also extended her unbeaten run across three consecutive Olympiads.

Men’s team finishes with 15 points

Kazakhstan’s men’s team drew 2-2 with Vietnam in the final round. It finished the tournament with 15 points from six wins, three draws and two losses.

Uzbekistan won the men’s competition, followed by India in second place and Germany in third. Germany secured its first Olympic medal since 2000, when it won silver.

Timur Turlov elected FIDE President

Kazakhstan Chess Federation President Timur Turlov was elected president of the International Chess Federation (FIDE) on Sept. 26 during the organization’s General Assembly in Samarkand, held alongside the Olympiad.

Turlov received 110 of 196 votes.

He has headed the Kazakhstan Chess Federation since 2023. During his tenure, Kazakhstan hosted the World Chess Championship match and the FIDE World Team Rapid and Blitz Championships.

World.title: Kazakhstan Jet Fuel Production on Track to Exceed Annual Target
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan expects to produce 825,000 tons of jet fuel this year, exceeding its annual target of 750,000 tons and increasing output by 13% from 2025.

The country produced 591,000 tons of jet fuel in January-August. Production is expected to reach 825,000 tons by the end of the year, compared with 726,000 tons in 2025, the Energy Ministry reported.

The ministry is continuing work to increase domestic jet fuel production and ensure stable supplies to the domestic market. Domestic production fully covers the needs of Kazakhstan’s civil aviation sector, security agencies, civil protection services and the state material reserve.

Kazakhstan’s passenger aviation sector is estimated to demand 680,000 tons annually.

Jet fuel production is expected to increase further in the coming years, with output targeted to reach 1.5 million tons by 2031.

World.title: Tokayev Orders Radical Military Reform
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called for a radical reform of Kazakhstan’s Armed Forces, saying the safety and lives of service officers must be an unconditional priority for commanders at all levels, following the deaths of 14 military personnel during exercises in the Mangystau Region.

Speaking at a meeting with the leadership of the Ministry of Defense on Sept. 27, Tokayev said the Caspian Sea tragedy exposed systemic shortcomings in the military and underscored the need for fundamental changes in how the Armed Forces are managed, trained and equipped. He also introduced newly appointed Defense Minister Aidos Myrzakhmetov to the ministry’s leadership, Akorda reported.

The meeting began with a minute of silence for the 14 service officers who lost their lives during the exercises on Sept. 24. Tokayev said he had sent messages of condolence to the families of all those who died and assured them that they would receive the necessary assistance.

“It is time for a radical military reform. This is an urgent task,” Tokayev said.

President orders investigation into military exercise

Tokayev gave a critical assessment of the circumstances surrounding the deaths and said the investigation must go beyond establishing what happened during the exercise.

He instructed officials to examine how the exercise was designed, whether its objectives matched modern security threats, and how the General Staff coordinated its preparation and conduct.

President Tokayev questioned why the Commander-in-Chief of the Naval Forces had not attended the exercise and raised concerns about the military’s crisis-response plans and command procedures.

According to Tokayev, service officers participating in the exercise were not provided with necessary equipment, including marine life jackets.

He instructed the Government commission investigating the incident to assess the actions of all officials responsible for planning and conducting the exercise, supplying personnel and ensuring compliance with safety requirements.

Tokayev stressed that military ranks and positions could not exempt anyone from responsibility.

Comprehensive review of Defense Ministry underway

The Ministry of Defense has also launched a comprehensive review. The inspection covers the organization of military service, supplies, and the Armed Forces’ material and financial provision.

The commission, headed by Deputy Chair of the Security Council Aida Balayeva, has been tasked with identifying violations and determining which officials should be held accountable. The President placed the issue under his personal control.

Ten-day deadline set for military reform plan

Tokayev said the shortcomings revealed by the tragedy demonstrated the need for a comprehensive transformation of the defense establishment.

“The goal of the reform is to create an army of a new type,” he said, adding that Kazakhstan’s military command system should be rebuilt in line with international best practices.

President Tokayev criticized what he described as outdated approaches and called for the Armed Forces to pursue digital transformation, with technology replacing human involvement wherever possible. He said the military needed practical solutions rather than standardized approaches, ceremonial exercises and formal reports.

The Security Council Secretariat, together with the Ministry of Defense, was instructed to submit a Military Reform Plan within 10 days. The plan is expected to be considered at a Security Council meeting in the second half of October. Tokayev also ordered the reform to be presented as a clear, concrete, phased plan rather than a broad concept or roadmap.

Priorities for the new Defense Minister

President Tokayev identified several immediate priorities for Myrzakhmetov. First, improve the efficiency of military spending.

“All funds allocated must produce the maximum possible result for ensuring the country’s defense capability,” Tokayev said, stressing that misuse of funds and embezzlement would not be tolerated.

The second priority is to reform the Armed Forces to meet modern threats. Tokayev also called for transparent criteria for selecting and evaluating military personnel. He said appointments to command positions should be based on experience and competence, not personal loyalty.

The third priority is to strengthen ideological and educational work in the Armed Forces, with an emphasis on constitutional values, military history and the achievements of Kazakh and world culture.

Service officers’ safety placed at center of reform

Tokayev said the army should provide professional training, knowledge and a sense of patriotism, while the safety and lives of service officers must remain an unconditional priority.

“Service in the army should not instill fear and horror,” he said, stressing that the Armed Forces should develop young people into disciplined and patriotic citizens.

He also called for greater attention to service officers who perform strongly and receive recognition from their commanders, saying their service should be reflected objectively in public information.

President Tokayev separately emphasized the need to strengthen social support for service officers and their families. He highlighted the same priority during his Sept. 27 meeting with Myrzakhmetov, when he also instructed the new minister to improve professional training, military infrastructure, weapons and equipment, and the use of modern technologies and digital solutions.

Vice President Erlan Karin also held a meeting to coordinate the work of state bodies and public organizations involved in implementing decisions taken after the incident and conducting public information efforts.

World.title: Kazakhstan Appoints Myrzakhmetov as Defense Minister
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has appointed Aidos Myrzakhmetov as the Minister of Defense on Sept. 27.

Myrzakhmetov was relieved of his previous position as part of his appointment as Defense Minister, Akorda reported.

He graduated from the Military Academy of the Armed Forces of Kazakhstan in 2002. Since January 2024, he has served as Commander of the Special Operations Forces of the Armed Forces of Kazakhstan. Prior to that, he headed a department of the State Security Service. In May, President Tokayev awarded Myrzakhmetov the military rank of Major General.

Dauren Kossanov was relieved of his position as Defense Minister by presidential decree.

The appointment comes days after the deaths of 14 service members during naval exercises in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24. The General Prosecutor’s Office is conducting a pre-trial investigation into the deaths of service members during the exercises.

On Sept. 26, by presidential order, a commission has been established to conduct a comprehensive review of the state of affairs at the Defense Ministry.

World.title: From Tiny Corals to Caspian Seals: Exhibition in Astana Traces Nature’s Connections
World.content:
ASTANA – From coral reefs and the microscopic organisms that sustain them to marine mammals inhabiting the Caspian Sea, every species is part of a larger natural system. A photo exhibition that explores this interconnected world opened in Astana on Sept. 23, bringing together stories of biodiversity from Kazakhstan and around the world.

An exhibition, titled “Invisible World: A City Underwater” will run through Nov. 1.

One biodiversity story comes from a small laboratory in London, where marine biologist Jamie Craggs, a co-founder of Coral Spawning International, managed to recreate the natural conditions required for coral spawning. The work has opened new possibilities for producing young corals in controlled conditions while maintaining greater genetic diversity.

The project later expanded to the Seychelles, where Nature Seychelles established another laboratory as part of the Assisted Recovery of Coral (ARC) Programme. Unlike traditional coral gardening methods, the project uses sexual reproduction to produce genetically diverse corals. Early results recorded the settlement and growth of around 65,000 young corals.

As Maral Rakhimzhanova, corporate communications manager at Canon’s representative office in Kazakhstan, explained, the importance of coral reefs extends far beyond their colourful appearance.

“Corals are very colorful, but in fact their color is given by algae that live in symbiosis with them. It is a relationship between two living organisms,” she said.

When water temperatures rise, corals can become stressed and expel the algae living within their tissues, causing coral bleaching. If the stress continues, the corals may eventually die. Reefs also provide food and shelter for a wide range of marine species, linking corals to the wider food chain.

Rakhimzhanova noted that these connections are relevant for a landlocked country such as Kazakhstan, as changes in one part of the natural world can have consequences far beyond it.

The same idea takes a different form in Kazakhstan’s waters, where the Caspian seal is among the species facing a changing environment. The animal, which is found only in the Caspian Sea, is included in Kazakhstan’s Red Book and has been the subject of long-term research by scientist Assel Baimukanova.

“Field research shows that these animals have their own character and social interactions that we are still learning to understand. The Caspian Sea is their home, and protecting the Caspian seal has become my main goal. These animals are affected by a range of factors, including shipping, fishing, environmental pollution and climate change. As the sea changes, seals are also forced to adapt and change their usual resting sites,” Baimukanova explained.

“The health of the Caspian seal is closely connected to the health of the Caspian Sea itself. By observing how the animals are doing, we can learn a great deal about the condition of the ecosystem they depend on. Exhibitions like this help bring scientific research closer to the public, make science more accessible and encourage more people to take an interest in these issues,” Baimukanova told The Astana Times.

Her photographs are featured alongside works by Mirgaliy Baimukanov, a director of the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology, Dmitry Malakhov, a researcher at the Institute of Zoology of Kazakhstan, wildlife photographer Vladislav Yakushkin and birdwatcher Gennady Dyakin. Illustrations of rare fish by designers Vladimir Timokhanov and Timofei Bannikov add another perspective to the collection.

The story extends beyond photography through virtual reality technology, allowing visitors to virtually explore coral reefs and experience the underwater environment.

World.title: ‘Which neighbouring country would you visit?’ Tbilisi street poll – VIDEO
World.content:
Travel poll in Georgia

We asked people on the streets of Tbilisi which of Georgia’s neighbouring countries they would like to visit and why.

We also asked whether they had previously travelled to any countries in the region, why they chose those destinations and what impressions they came away with.

The answers vary widely. Turkey is mentioned most often, with respondents drawn by its picturesque coastline and the Bosphorus. Many also say they would be happy to visit Armenia or Azerbaijan, while some look further afield and name more distant countries in the region.

Russia is rarely mentioned in a positive context. Instead, it is named by almost every respondent when asked which neighbouring country they would not like to visit.

Through this survey, we sought to find out how well people in Georgia know the countries of the South Caucasus and their other neighbours, what interests them about these countries and what stereotypes they hold about them.

World.title: SOCAR, ExxonMobil sign deal to explore for oil and gas in Azerbaijan’s Middle Kura Basin
World.content:
Oil and gas investment in Azerbaijan

At the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku, SOCAR and ExxonMobil signed a production-sharing agreement for the exploration and development of unconventional hydrocarbon resources in the Middle Kura Basin. A final investment decision was also made on the full-field development of the Absheron gas field.

Speaking on 26 September about investment priorities for the coming decade, Ilham Aliyev said the oil and gas sector would retain a leading role.

What will ExxonMobil look for in the Middle Kura Basin?

The agreement provides for the exploration, development and production of unconventional hydrocarbon resources in the Middle Kura Basin. According to SOCAR, the companies will each hold a 50% stake in the project through their subsidiaries, with ExxonMobil acting as operator.

The project does not involve the development of an existing offshore field in the Caspian Sea, but rather the exploration of the oil and gas potential of an onshore basin. Bloomberg has linked the project to shale oil and gas production. It has also been reported that the project is awaiting parliamentary approval.

Aliyev said successful exploration “could lead to another oil and gas boom in Azerbaijan”.

Published information does not specify when commercial production could begin, targeted annual production levels, confirmed recoverable reserves or the project’s overall budget. The precise size and boundaries of the contract area have also not been disclosed.

For Azerbaijan, the significance of the agreement lies in bringing ExxonMobil’s technology and expertise in developing unconventional hydrocarbon resources into the search for new reserves. However, the basin’s resource potential and the commercial viability of development will have to be established before its possible economic impact can be assessed.

Absheron: annual gas production set to quadruple

SOCAR, TotalEnergies and XRG have taken a final investment decision on the full-field development of the Absheron gas and condensate field. According to TotalEnergies, which operates the project, the company holds a 35% stake. SOCAR also owns 35%, while XRG holds 30%.

Under the company’s plan, annual gas production will increase from 1.5bn to 6bn cubic metres, while daily condensate production will rise from 12,000 to 47,000 barrels. The new phase of development is expected to begin in 2029.

In his speech, Aliyev spoke of an additional 5bn cubic metres of gas within three to four years. However, the figures presented by the company imply an increase in annual production of 4.5bn cubic metres.

TotalEnergies says the gas produced will be supplied to the domestic market and Turkey.

GDP diversifying, but energy still dominates exports

Discussing the country’s future economic model, Aliyev said “oil and gas will retain a leading role in our economy”, adding that the revenues generated would be reinvested in the economy.

The president said the non-oil sector accounted for more than 70% of GDP, while, according to him, oil and gas still made up more than 90% of exports.

According to calculations by Marja based on State Customs Committee statistics, oil and gas products accounted for 71.22% of goods exports in January-August 2026.

Electricity, data centres and logistics

Aliyev linked the development of renewable energy to efforts to reduce domestic gas consumption and free up additional volumes for export. He also referred to the expansion of power transmission lines for electricity exports and projects to lay submarine cables across the Caspian and Black seas.

The president identified supplying electricity to data centres and artificial intelligence systems as a priority and said an Azerbaijan-Kazakhstan fibre-optic cable would become operational by the end of the year. Documents relating to the Oracle Alloy project were also exchanged at the forum. According to SOCAR, Caspian Mind AI will serve as the local operator.

In transport, the government aims to increase transit freight volumes from an expected 16m tonnes in 2026 to at least 25m tonnes by 2030. Discussing food and water security, Aliyev highlighted water shortages and the need to reduce dependence on food imports, while also calling for investment in agriculture.

What does the $10.8bn package actually represent?

According to the Economy Ministry, 23 documents covering projects worth a combined $10.8bn were signed at the forum. The ministry says these projects are planned for implementation.

However, the documents represent projects at different stages of development. A final investment decision has been taken on Absheron. The ExxonMobil agreement establishes the contractual framework for exploration and subsequent development. A framework agreement with Comstock provides for studying opportunities to liquefy US gas and sell it on international markets. A memorandum with Apollo concerns assessing potential investments, conducting due diligence and preparing final agreements.

Published information does not provide a full breakdown of the $10.8bn figure among individual projects, a financing timetable or details of how much has already been formalised as binding financial commitments. There is therefore no basis for treating the entire amount as a guaranteed inflow of foreign investment.

Aliyev described the government’s approach to investment policy as follows:

“All we have to do is create favourable conditions.”

The economic results of the forum will ultimately depend on the actual investment made in the announced projects, as well as growth in production and non-oil exports.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s president sees no serious effects of climate change, but UN report says otherwise
World.content:
Climate change in Azerbaijan

President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev says the country has yet to feel the serious effects of climate change. He bases this assessment on the snow cover he observes in the mountains during winter. However, the latest climate documents that Azerbaijan itself has submitted to the UN show that the country is already facing serious consequences of the climate crisis.

According to official data, the average temperature has risen by 1.1°C over the past 23 years, water resources have declined by around 15%, droughts have become longer, the Caspian Sea has fallen by more than two metres, and the number of frost days and the area covered by glaciers in the mountains have decreased.

On 26 September, President Ilham Aliyev addressed climate change while discussing food security at the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku. He commented on the issue:

“We have not yet felt the effects of climate change. I go skiing every winter and see that the snow levels in our mountains remain the same. Perhaps the snow is melting somewhere, but not in Azerbaijan.”

Aliyev then reiterated that Azerbaijan “has not yet been affected by climate change”. Yet in the very next sentence of the same speech, the president noted that water shortages required greater attention to food security.

However, the president’s broad assessment contradicts official climate documents prepared by Azerbaijan itself.

What does the government document in force in 2026 say?

One of the most recent sources is NDC 3.0, a document Azerbaijan submitted under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Azerbaijan submitted it in November 2025, and an updated version appeared in August 2026.

The document paints a very different picture from the one Aliyev presented on 26 September:

“Azerbaijan is seriously affected by the climate crisis.”

The document lists rising temperatures, changing weather patterns, land degradation, shrinking water resources and the falling level of the Caspian Sea among the effects of the climate crisis. It notes that these processes threaten biodiversity, water resources, agriculture, economic development and people’s well-being.

This is therefore not merely a matter of future projections. Azerbaijan’s official climate document describes changes that are already taking place.

Azerbaijan has already warmed by 1.1°C

According to NDC 3.0, the average temperature in Azerbaijan has risen by 1.1°C over the past 23 years.

In 2023, the country’s average temperature reached 14.6°C, 1.9°C above the climatic norm. The Baku region has also recorded a significant increase in indicators measuring heatwaves with temperatures above 35°C.

These figures are consistent with data previously published by the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. The ministry reported that temperatures across the country during the first 20 days of June 2024 were 4.8°C above the climatic norm.

These figures do not simply reflect weather conditions in a particular month or year. They show changes against a backdrop of long-term warming.

What about Aliyev’s example of snowfall?

It is unclear which mountain and elevation the president was referring to, or which years he was comparing. It is therefore impossible to independently verify whether the snow levels he observes while skiing have actually changed.

However, heavy snowfall over several winter seasons does not, in itself, reflect a long-term climate trend.

More importantly, data from Azerbaijan’s own government point to changes already taking place in the country’s mountainous regions.

The 2024 National Adaptation Plan states that temperatures have risen across the country in recent decades, while the number of frost days in winter has declined. This trend is particularly pronounced in mountainous areas. The plan also includes a separate section titled “Glacier melting”, which states that observations by the National Hydrometeorological Service indicate that glaciers are melting at an accelerating rate.

The same issue came up in 2020 at a meeting on water management chaired by Aliyev. At the time, Ecology Minister Mukhtar Babayev told the president that rising temperatures in Azerbaijan’s mountainous regions had led to “a decline in the number of frost and snowy days”.

An earlier report that Azerbaijan submitted to the UN states that the total area of glaciers in the Gusarçay river basin shrank from 4.9 sq km to 2.4 sq km over approximately 110 years.

Therefore, the amount of snow at a particular ski resort in a single season cannot serve as an indicator of long-term changes in the country’s mountain ecosystems.

Water resources have already declined

Another detail in Aliyev’s speech effectively points to an existing problem: the president identifies “water shortages” as a risk to food security.

According to Azerbaijan’s NDC 3.0 document, the country’s water resources have declined by approximately 15% over recent decades. Total precipitation over the past decade has fallen by around 3.4% compared with the 1971–2000 climatic norm.

In December 2025, Deputy Ecology Minister Umayra Taghiyeva cited another figure at a UN event: the volume of water flowing into the country had fallen by 30%. This figure reflects a decline in the amount of water entering Azerbaijan, rather than a reduction in the country’s total water resources.

Furthermore, around 67–70% of Azerbaijan’s river flow originates outside the country, making it vulnerable both to climate change and to changes in the use of transboundary water resources.

Droughts are becoming longer

NDC 3.0 states that over the past 30 years, the number of occurrences of hot, dry winds has increased 14-fold, while the duration of droughts has increased by more than 20%. The document also notes that the number of hailstorms has more than tripled over the past decade.

Azerbaijan’s 2024 National Adaptation Plan, which uses calculations covering a slightly different period, states that droughts have become 19% longer.

World Bank modelling suggests that even under a relatively optimistic climate scenario, a significant share of agricultural land in central Azerbaijan will face the risk of water shortages by 2050.

According to the projections, unless adaptation measures are introduced, yields of some rain-fed crops — those grown primarily using rainfall rather than irrigation — could fall by 30% in 2051–2060 compared with

The Caspian Sea has fallen by more than two metres

According to the Azerbaijani government’s NDC 3.0 document, the level of the Caspian Sea has fallen by more than two metres over the past 30 years.

The document attributes this to several factors: reduced river inflows, increased evaporation caused by rising temperatures, and other geological factors. It notes that these processes are already posing risks to coastal infrastructure and ecosystems.

It would therefore be inaccurate to attribute the Caspian Sea’s falling level solely to climate change. However, Azerbaijan’s official document identifies rising temperatures and increased evaporation as factors contributing to the process.

What conclusions can we draw from the official data?

Aliyev’s personal observation about snowfall in the mountains cannot be disproved using the available public data. He did not specify a particular location, measurements or a period for comparison.

However, the broader conclusion he draws from this observation — namely, his claim that “Azerbaijan has not yet been affected by climate change” — contradicts the data in documents that the Azerbaijani government itself has submitted to the UN.

These documents record changes that have already occurred: a 1.1°C rise in temperature, declining water resources, longer droughts, fewer frost days in the mountains, melting glaciers and a falling Caspian Sea level.

Moreover, Azerbaijan’s NDC 3.0 document, which remains in force in 2026, describes a situation very different from the one the president presented in his speech: Azerbaijan “is seriously affected by the climate crisis”.

Climate change in Azerbaijan

World.title: “Saturday march” in Tbilisi: “Abkhazia is Georgia” and solidarity with Ukraine. Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: Baku outraged by Georgian Patriarchate’s “unacceptable” remarks over church in Azerbaijan’s Gakh district
World.content:
Kurmukh Church, Azerbaijan-Georgia

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry has protested against a statement by the Georgian Patriarchate regarding the restoration of a church in Azerbaijan’s Gakh district.

The Patriarchate said the Church of St George, known as the Kurmukh Church, is an important monument of Georgia’s spiritual and cultural heritage. It expressed outrage that restoration work was being carried out without coordination with Tbilisi and without official information from Baku.

The Patriarchate also said the church is located in the “historical [Georgian region of] Hereti”.

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry said the Patriarchate’s statement regarding the church, known in Azerbaijan as Kurmuk, amounted to a territorial claim against Azerbaijan.

What happened

In a statement published on 24 September, the Georgian Patriarchate expressed concern over ongoing work at the Kurmukh Church and the surrounding area, noting that although the church is currently located in Azerbaijan, it is an important monument of Georgia’s historical and spiritual heritage and of the Georgian Orthodox Church.

“Any interventions carried out both in the church itself, in historic Hereti, and in the surrounding area are of particular concern to the Georgian Orthodox Church. Many questions arise due to both the unclear purpose of the work and the restoration of a monument of Georgian cultural heritage without the consent of the Georgian side,” the statement said.

According to the Patriarchate, it has not received any official information from the relevant Azerbaijani state authorities about the ongoing work at the Kurmukh Church.

The church believes that the relevant Georgian state authorities should be involved in the process and determine what work is being carried out at the church, what research it is based on and who is conducting it.

The Patriarchate also called for its representatives and Georgian specialists to be included in the discussions.

“Only timely and coordinated cooperation can ensure the proper protection and preservation of this monument of Georgian spiritual and cultural heritage,” the Georgian Patriarchate said.

What Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry says

Azerbaijan’s Foreign Ministry said that the Georgian Patriarchate’s statement regarding the church, known in Azerbaijan as Kurmuk, amounted to a territorial claim against Azerbaijan.

“Azerbaijan has always respected the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Georgia. At the same time, the Georgian side’s demonstration of the same respect for the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Azerbaijan constitutes an important foundation of the strategic partnership relations established between the two countries. […]

In this regard, repetition of the the known approaches of the Armenian Church or following its path is not recommended. […] All historical, cultural and religious monuments located in the territory of Azerbaijan constitute an integral part of the national heritage of the Azerbaijani people and the Azerbaijani state,” the ministry said.

The statement also said it was “unacceptable to refer to geographical and historical toponyms located in the territory of Azerbaijan by other names.”
