World.title: Russian drone hits Kyiv scientific centre near embassies
World.content:
Russian drones have struck Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences in the historic heart of Kyiv, in the latest deadly daytime attack on the Ukrainian capital.

Kyiv has increasingly faced Russian drones and missiles as Europe's worst conflict since World War II grinds through its fifth year.

Video footage shared online appeared to show a high-speed drone smashing into the National Academy of Sciences at a sharp angle, exploding and sending acrid smoke into the blue sky above.

Ukraine's former national security and defence council secretary Volodymyr Gorbulin told state broadcaster Suspilne that he was at work at the academy at the time and was slightly wounded.

But he said his assistant, who was near the building, was killed.

The National Academy of Sciences is close to the German embassy, a cathedral, the national opera and government buildings.

Russia carried out daytime strikes on Monday as Ukraine braces for a punishing winter. (Reuters: Viacheslav Ratynskyi)

Elsewhere, Russian strikes killed four and wounded at least 19 at a business centre in the central city of Dnipro while authorities reported an unspecified number of fatalities in a strike on a residential area in eastern Kharkiv.

Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said Russian forces damaged an ice cream factory in the Zhytomyr region west of Kyiv, and residential buildings in Sumy, in the north, Rivne, in the northwest, and southern Odesa.

Thirty civilians were wounded, three of them seriously, in strikes on Zaporizhzhia, southeastern Ukraine, the regional military administration said.

During Russia's assault, Poland scrambled jets to defend its air space and warned citizens near the Ukrainian border to stay inside.

The strikes comes as Ukrainians consider their options with winter approaching, after Russian attacks last year on energy infrastructure cut power and heating as temperatures plunged to as low as -20C.

Russia hybrid war 'not working'

Meanwhile, European defence ministers discussed whether the European Union needed its own NATO-style emergency mechanism to bolster coordination against "hybrid attacks" by Russia.

Russia has Germans rethinking Nazi-era protections European intelligence officials say Russia is behind hundreds of hybrid attacks on the continent this year, and that Western allies are too complacent in the face of Moscow's increasing aggression.

European governments say Moscow is stepping up its campaign of sabotage and interference against Ukraine's supporters, as Kremlin troops struggle to make headway on the front lines.

That came as NATO's top military commander said that Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe was failing to put countries off supporting Ukraine.

"State-directed sabotage is growing increasingly brazen," US General Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, told a committee of EU politicians.

General Grynkewich cited recent incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport and a Russian naval ship firing flares at a Danish helicopter.

"These are clear examples of attempts to instil fear and fracture our unified support to Ukraine. It isn't working," he said, pointing at Denmark's fast-tracking of fresh aid for Ukraine after the flare incident.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Seoul says North Korea will be held responsible for landmine explosions
World.content:
North Korean landmines are likely responsible for a blast that injured three South Korean military officers inside the demilitarised zone (DMZ), according to Seoul's military.

Three South Korean ‌soldiers ⁠were hurt in the explosions last week while clearing a patrol route in the western sector of the DMZ, a heavily fortified area bordering North Korea.

Why Seoul has called for peace talks to formally end the Korean War South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has once again called for talks to formally end the Korean War which was only frozen and not ended by an armistice in 1953.

The DMZ is a 248-kilometre long, four-kilometre wide buffer zone that has divided the Korean Peninsula since the 1953 armistice.

But "recently planted mines" by North Korea were believed to have caused last week's explosion, according to preliminary findings from a joint probe between South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff and the United Nations Command.

"We have confirmed that the site was about 10 metres from an area where changes in the terrain were observed and where North Korean forces are believed to have recently planted mines," Kwon Dae-won, vice chairman of South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff, said.

The demilitarised zone is a 248-kilometre long, four-kilometre wide buffer zone dividing the two koreas. (Reuters: Kim Hong-Ji)

"Taking into account the crater and the pattern of the flames from the explosion, the extent of the injuries sustained by the service members… we assess that North Korean landmines are highly suspected to have caused the blast."

Mr Kwon said if the investigation concluded that Pyongyang was responsible, it "would bear full responsibility for the incident".

"Our military will take appropriate and corresponding measures," he said, without giving details.

Mr Kwon said two landmines exploded and a third, unexploded mine was found while soldiers were withdrawing after the blast on September 21.

Edward Howell, an International Relations lecturer at the University of Oxford, said he expected North Korea would continue to provoke South Korea.

"North Korea does not want anything to do with the South; as for any dialogue, Pyongyang has firmly shut the door," he told the ABC.

"North Korea no longer wants to reunify with the South peacefully and, more broadly, North Korea no longer views South Korea as part of the same, albeit divided, Korea.

" We should expect Pyongyang's provocations and brinkmanship towards Seoul to continue. "

Dr Howell said the suspected move came off the back of the United States reducing its military exercises with South Korea which would have "pleased" Pyongyang.

Trump scales back military drills with South Korea US President Donald Trump orders the Pentagon to scale back planned joint military exercises with South Korea, citing his good relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

"Any signals of a weakened US alliance with South Korea and Japan will be framed by North Korea as a victory," he said.

"Pyongyang will take any opportunity to exploit these fissures, real or perceived, in continuing to behave delinquently in order to reap rewards."

With no peace treaty signed, Seoul and Pyongyang technically remain at war.

ABC/AFP

World.title: SpaceX's Starship rocket reaches orbit for first time
World.content:
SpaceX has launched its enormous Starship into orbit for the first time, deploying Starlink satellites before returning to Earth early due to an engine issue.

The spacecraft almost didn't achieve the long-desired goal in its Monday launch, after one of its three engines shut down too soon.

The mission was scheduled to last 10 hours, but was reduced to three hours after the engine problem, and the rocket later re-entered the atmosphere and conducted a controlled and fiery landing in the Pacific Ocean.

The snag with its engine initially led SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot to announce on the company's livestream of the mission that the craft would be unable to reach orbit.

But Mission Control reversed course minutes later after an update from engineers confirmed that the craft could still attempt an engine firing that would boost it into orbit, which Starship successfully did minutes later.

SpaceX recovers rocket off Christmas Island An operation by Elon Musk's SpaceX and the federal government successfully retrieves the rocket after it landed in the Indian Ocean off the coast of Western Australia.

"Starship is orbital," Mission Control announced to cheers.

Founder Elon Musk's showpiece rocket — the biggest and most powerful ever built — carried 26 of the latest and most advanced Starlink satellites to join the 11,000 older models already providing internet service.

It was Starship's 14th full-scale launch from Texas' southern tip in three years.

The earlier test flights ventured no farther than the Indian Ocean halfway around the world, often crashing in flames and briefly skimming space.

This time, SpaceX had hoped the Starship would circle the globe from an altitude of 275 kilometres — not just once but six times over almost 10 hours, ending with a Pacific splashdown near Chile.

The reusable rocket

SpaceX's mega rocket Starship making the test flight from Starbase, Texas, on Monday. (AP: Eric Gay)

The Starship deployed 26 next-generation Starlink satellites while in orbit at an altitude 269 kilometres above the Earth's surface.

The 124-metre rocket was designed from the start to be fully reusable, a key to lowering launch costs, and built to launch SpaceX's Starlink satellites and for future NASA missions to the moon.

If the spacecraft breaks apart over land and rains debris onto people, "our popularity would diminish very rapidly", Mr Musk said at a business summit earlier this month.

Photos show impact of SpaceX rocket that slammed into Moon A NASA spacecraft circling the moon is providing the sharpest views yet of a crater carved by a crashing SpaceX rocket.

"That's why we're being extremely cautious here."

SpaceX is pressing hard to certify Starship for orbital flight, a vital step toward moon and Mars travel.

Mr Musk originally developed Starship for Mars, intending to launch scores of them with the red planet's first settlers.

For now, he plans to focus on the moon and use Starship to haul satellites into orbit by the truckload — phasing out the company's frailer Falcon 9 rocket within several years.

NASA's Artemis IV mission, slated for no sooner than 2028, would have astronauts landing on the moon in either Jeff Bezos' Blue Moon or Mr Musk's Starship, whichever is ready first.

AP

World.title: Men arrested over RAF Fairford probe released on bail
World.content:
Five men arrested near a military base in England early Sunday are all British citizens from London, authorities have confirmed, amid claims Iran's regime was attempting to attack the facility.

Despite counter-terrorism police giving an update into their investigations on Monday, information surrounding the arrests remains confusing.

In a statement, police said the men had been arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, and committing explosives offences.

Authorities later said the five men would be released on bail but remained under investigation.

Laurence Taylor, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said officers were looking into every angle, "including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state".

The complex at the centre of the probe is RAF Fairford, an air force base about 140 kilometres west of London which the US military has used to launch strikes Iran this year.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Monday said he would chair a so-called COBRA emergency meeting, bringing together senior ministers, officials and police officers.

The arrests have sparked concern not just in the local village community — who were evacuated at the weekend — but the United Kingdom more broadly and across the Atlantic, where US politicians have been quick to point the finger at the Islamic Republic.

Florida Congresswoman Kat Cammack asserted, without providing specifics, Iran was "clearly involved" in a plan to attack the base, and US President Donald Trump claimed the arrested men had been under investigation "for a long time".

Explosives experts were called in to examine several vehicles near the base on Sunday. (Reuters: Supplied/BBC News)

However, local residents maintain they were the ones to raise the alarm, after spotting several suspicious vehicles in the area surrounding the base early Sunday.

"I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, who coordinates counter-terrorism policing in the UK, said in a statement on Monday.

She said officers had several new lines of inquiry and needed "space to work carefully and clearly".

"This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation, involving local and national policing, the Ministry of Defence, and local agencies, who are working together to progress the investigation and support for the community," she said.

The five men arrested are all British citizens from London, police confirmed, and aged between 23 and 25. They all remain in custody, although no charges have been laid.

While less common in Australia, UK police routinely announce the nationality and ethnicity of suspects in high-profile investigations to counter disinformation that can spread online, which has previously led to public disorder.

People who live near RAF Fairford have told British media security was ramped up around the base in the days leading up to the arrests.

One resident claimed to the BBC they had been walking near the military facility in the hours before the incident took place and encountered a police officer who instructed them to return home and stay inside.

A local farmer has also claimed they were the ones to alert authorities, after spotting eight to 10 hooded men in the area before 1am on Sunday.

"When they saw me they ran ahead of me. Some into the field and some towards the neighbouring village," she said.

"I then realised that something highly unusual was taking place."

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting on Monday thanked the farmer but said they only had "a partial picture" of the situation.

Police have previously confirmed they are investigating whether Iran could have been involved.

"We know they hate our democracy," Mr Streeting said.

On Monday, Iran's embassy in London released a statement in which it "categorically rejected" allegations the country was involved in the incident.

However, earlier this year, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a paramilitary force which reports directly to Tehran's supreme leader, asserted RAF Fairford would be a legitimate wartime target, given the US had launched strikes from there.

The IRGC has been designated a terrorist organisation in Australia and the UK.

World.title: Trial begins for man accused of hacking friend to death with machete
World.content:
A man accused of hacking his friend to death with a machete in Melbourne's west two years ago hit his victim at least 39 times, the Victorian Supreme Court has heard.

Christopher Reyes Gonzaga, 45, is accused of murdering Gregory Tan, 45, in an empty home in Deer Park in 2024.

Mr Gonzaga's trial began on Monday, when the jury heard CCTV audio of yells and thumping noises ringing out through the quiet suburban neighbourhood in the early hours of April 15 that year.

Mr Tan suffered extensive injuries, including to his jugular, carotid artery and skull, the Crown alleged.

His right hand was also partially severed, which the prosecution told the court was a defensive wound.

"[Mr Tan] tried to defend himself while the accused was striking him in the head with the machete," prosecutor Penelope Thorp told jurors in her opening address.

At the time of his arrest Mr Gonzaga had a gash on his forehead, which the Crown alleged was self-inflicted.

Mr Gonzaga pleaded not guilty to murder, earlier telling police Mr Tan had threatened him with a screwdriver and that he was acting in self-defence.

The pair had been friends for some time and witnesses reported seeing them use drugs together on multiple occasions, the court was told.

Prosecutors allege Mr Gonzaga lit two fires in the home after hacking his friend to death, before leaving and throwing the machete in a drain.

He then called Triple Zero (000) to report the fire and was arrested.

Mr Tan, his brother, their partners and another friend lived next door to the home in which Mr Tan died.

It was empty following the death of the previous resident, jurors were told.

Prior to his arrest, Gonzaga was filmed on CCTV crouching down behind a car parked in a driveway, at which time Ms Thorp alleged jurors would see he did not have any injuries to his face.

While in custody, Mr Gonzaga allegedly admitted to stabbing Mr Tan and accused him and others of having killed the resident of the house they were in, by overdosing her in order to rob her.

"There's a guy there who's also cut," the court heard Mr Gonzaga told police.

" Unfortunately, I made friends with the wrong people. "

Gonzaga's barrister, John Lavery, will make an opening address to the jury on Tuesday morning.

AAP

World.title: Greens leader Larissa Waters steps down due to illness
World.content:
Senator Larissa Waters has announced she is standing down as Greens leader due to illness, after 16 months in the role.

The Greens have revealed she has been managing an existing kidney disease, which has worsened in recent months.

The 49-year-old notified her colleagues of her decision to step away during a virtual meeting earlier this evening.

Senator Waters expressed gratitude for her stint as leader but admitted she needed to go at a "slower pace" as she focused on her recovery.

"It has been a tremendous honour to be leader of the Greens, fighting for people and the planet," she said in a statement on Monday evening.

" I'm really sad that illness means my time as leader has been cut short, but our movement needs a leader in good health to lead us to success at the next election. "

The Queensland senator took on leadership in May 2025, replacing Adam Bandt after he lost his lower house seat in the 2025 election.

She was elected in a race against current deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi and manager of business in Senate Sarah Hanson-Young.

Larissa Waters became leader in May 2025, with Mehreen Faruqi elected as deputy and Senator Sarah Hanson-Young manager of business in the Senate. (AAP Image: Joel Carrett)

Senator Waters will take medical leave, but says she intends to return to work as soon as she can.

A partyroom meeting will be held in coming days to discuss the leadership, with ABC told a decision will be made sooner rather than later.

Environmental wins as leader

Senator Waters hailed last year's deal with Labor to overhaul Australia's environmental laws as a "significant win" during her time as leader.

In November 2025, the Greens secured several amendments to the legislation, including tightening land clearing controls and preventing the fast-tracking of coal and gas projects under a national interest exemption.

The Greens also pushed to split gun safety measures from hate speech laws after the Bondi Beach terrorist attack, helping to pass the firearms changes in January.

More recently, the minor party has used its balance of power in the Senate to stall National Disability Insurance Scheme reforms and successfully secured an extended parliamentary inquiry into the sweeping changes.

Senator Waters was first elected as a senator for Queensland in 2010, making her the second longest-serving member of the Greens partyroom behind senator Sarah Hanson-Young.

World.title: Bangkok locals rally to help each other as flood wreaks havoc
World.content:
In the bustling metropolis of Bangkok, where some neighbourhoods are still paralysed by lingering floodwaters, locals are getting by in true Thai fashion: with a stoic smile.

The disaster has already caused an estimated $466 million worth of damage (฿11 billion), impacted 580,000 homes and killed at least eight people in the country.

Thousands are sheltering in evacuation centres and more than 80,000 people are unable to leave their homes, with the government deploying emergency food deliveries by boat.

But despite the ordeal, Bangkok resident Chris Kenneth has seen many people helping each other and responding to calls for help on social media.

"And it's not only people helping other people," he said.

"There are also cats, birds and other animals struggling in flooded areas, and people have been trying to rescue them.

"From what I've personally seen, there has been a strong sense of people helping one another."

Wading in floodwater to get food

Authorities declared all of Bangkok a disaster zone on Saturday after 300mm of rain fell in approximately 48 hours.

Kenneth noticed roads around his condominium starting to flood and vehicles struggling to get through on Friday.

"The rain just kept going for almost two days continuously," he said.

"The next morning, when I woke up, there was water all around my building."

The disaster has disrupted supply chains, leaving shelves empty and forcing some shops to close.

The water is starting to recede in Bangkok. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Kenneth's local convenience store was "almost empty" when he visited on Saturday, so he walked through floodwater to find food at a large shopping mall.

He is no longer worried about running out of supplies now that the water has started to recede.

But he wished officials had put out emergency warnings much sooner, allowing people to prepare.

"Bangkok is very vulnerable to heavy rainfall and flooding, so I think timely and clear information is extremely important," he said.

Disaster spreads across the region

A woman carrying groceries navigates through a flooded area near a market in Bangkok. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

Heavy rain is common in September during peak monsoon season and the disaster comes less than 12 months after a "one-in-300-year" flood hit southern Thailand, killing at least 145 people and affecting 2.7 million more.

India was also hit with heavy rain over the weekend, with floods and landslides killing at least 56 amid warnings more flash floods could be on the way.

On Sunday, Nepali authorities warned that flash floods could hit 49 of the country's 77 districts, with 14 people already killed.

And Myanmar's southernmost Tanintharyi region has also been hit by heavy rains since Friday night.

Authorities there have not yet released any official toll, but local rescue groups have reported several deaths.

Flooding near a Bangkok mall. (ABC News: Haidarr Jones)

The floodwater is starting to recede in Bangkok, but the city is just one of 41 provinces impacted across Thailand.

Authorities in the east coast province of Rayong ordered an evacuation on Monday after floodwaters pushed two reservoirs above capacity.

Rayong resident Vitavad Kasa said the situation was "still quite serious".

"There is a lot of water in some areas and travelling is difficult. People are worried about their homes and their daily lives," he said.

"It is also difficult for people to get to work and get essential things."

Kasa said Thai people were "sharing food and water, helping people move to safer places".

Lending a hand in times of crisis

Chatchapong Jindapoo is anxiously checking for updates to see if more rain is on the way. (Supplied: Chatchapong Jindapoo)

Kasa's brother, Chatchapong Jindapoo lives in the Phanom Sarakham district, about 100 kilometres east of Bangkok.

He had to evacuate after his home was immersed in "very high" water and is now sheltering at a friend's clothing shop.

The group has set up a kitchen out the front and are cooking free food for those in need.

But Jindapoo remains concerned about the future.

"If the water is still there for a long [time], we will not have food or we will not have electronics or water to use," he said.

Memes and makeshift waterskis

Chatchapong Jindapoo's friends have been using a makeshift raft to try and get around. (Supplied: Chatchapong Jindapoo)

Despite the challenges facing communities, some Thais have found an opportunity to have fun.

Social media is full of light-hearted videos of food delivery drivers sloshing through flooded streets or travelling by boat.

Kasa captured videos of Thais using motorbikes to tow boxes through the flood waters, creating a makeshift waterski.

Loading Instagram content

"I had never seen anything like it before," he said.

"I think people were trying to have some fun in a difficult situation, but they still need to be careful because the flooding can be dangerous."

But some antics have attracted the ire of locals and authorities.

A man who was filmed riding a jetski through the streets of Bangkok, making large waves, has been arrested and charged with causing a public nuisance, according to local media.

World.title: 'No possibility' for Swedish leader to form government after narrow win
World.content:
Swedish Social Democrat leader Magdalena Andersson says she has failed to form a government with the three other parties in the left-wing bloc following the country's September 13 general election.

Sweden's left-wing bloc wins general election Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has led Sweden since 2022 with a three-party centre-right coalition.

The centre-left won a narrow majority of 176 seats to the incumbent right bloc's 173 seats in last month's election. The campaign became less about who could win more votes and more about who could form government.

There are two major political blocs in Sweden: one coalition of parties on the right and another on the left.

The Left Party, one of which form the left-wing bloc, said over the weekend it would back a candidate for parliament speaker from the rival Moderate party, which Ms Andersson says undercut her attempt to build a government.

"Of course, I take the Left Party's message seriously, and based on that and the conversations I have had, I can conclude that there is currently no possibility for me to form a government," she told a press conference on Monday.

Right-wing bloc would also struggle to form government

The speaker of parliament is expected to task another party leader, likely Mr Kristersson, with trying to form a new government.

Ulf Kristersson attended the Moderate Party election watch night. (Reuters: Christine Olsson/TT News Agency)

Mr Kristersson has led since his right-wing bloc won the last election in 2022. He currently leads a caretaker government.

Last month's vote was widely seen as a referendum on Mr Kristersson's promise to form a coalition with the far-right Sweden Democrats.

His coalition relies on outside support from the anti-immigration party, which has far-right roots but has moved toward the political mainstream. The bloc will also struggle to find a majority in parliament.

Mr Kristersson said following the election loss that he was ready to explore options to find a majority among "non-socialist" parties.

The announcement is seen as an attempt to woo the Centre Party, which is now part of the left-wing bloc but used to belong to the right-wing, although it is staunchly opposed to a government which includes the extreme-right Sweden Democrats.

Centre Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist has refused to be a part of or support any government that gives influence to the parties on the far left or far right.

ABC/Wires

World.title: ‘A decade of poor planning’: The new WA schools with the most demountables
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWAEducation ‘A decade of poor planning’: The new WA schools with the most demountables Holly Thompson September 29, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The state government has been accused of failing to properly plan for the sharp growth in demand at schools across the Perth metropolitan area, particularly at newer schools that have opened since Labor took power nearly 10 years ago. Instead, the WA opposition claims the Department of Education has relied on demountable classrooms to accommodate a growing number of enrolments, particularly along the southern growth corridor and in newer suburbs further north. Opposition education spokesman Liam Staltari said Labor came into office decrying the use of transportables in schools but now, after nearly 10 years, the situation had “never been worse”. “More than 4000 transportables are now placed across WA schools, crowding out ovals, green space and other areas in schools that are literally bursting at the seams,” he said.



“And nearly one-in-six WA classrooms is now a transportable, forcing students and teachers into temporary buildings that don’t reflect what they deserve. “At its core, this is the result of a decade of poor planning and underfunding. Even schools established in obvious growth corridors have been underserved and now rely on far too many transportables.” A new document tabled in parliament shows a list of schools opened since 2017, the number of transportables at each, and the percentage of total classrooms that number is. In total, 30 new primary schools and eight secondary schools have opened in that time. More than half of all classrooms at Wellard Primary School, opened in 2018, in addition to Oakwood and Aspiri primary schools, both opened in 2019, are transportable.



At Riva Primary School, currently 38 per cent of classrooms are transportable. Another perspective Education The $611 million bill to upgrade Perth schools – and where it’s being spent However, a new permanent addition, funded in the 2026-27 state budget, will be constructed to accommodate 240 students and reduce the need for transportable classrooms at site. World.title: Fiery splashdown for SpaceX’s Starship as orbital flight cut short
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaSpace Fiery splashdown for SpaceX’s Starship as orbital flight cut short Marcia Dunn Updated September 29, 2026 — 2:47am ,first published 11:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

SpaceX launched its enormous Starship into orbit for the first time on Monday and successfully delivered the most advanced Starlinks yet, but cut the flight short to ensure safety. The spacecraft reentered over the Pacific and splashed down north of Hawaii three hours after blasting off from Texas. The company had been aiming for a 10-hour flight, spanning six full laps around Earth, to prove its readiness for NASA’s Artemis moon program. Starship tipped over and erupted in flames upon splashdown, a dramatic end to the mission. Founder Elon Musk’s Starship almost didn’t make it to orbit when one of its engines shut down too soon. But with everything else working well and the bad engine no longer needed, flight controllers decided after several tense minutes to proceed as planned.



“Starship is orbital,” Mission Control announced to cheers. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX on reaching orbit and “managing every step in a safe, responsible and especially inspirational way”. Musk’s showpiece rocket – the biggest and most powerful ever built – carried 26 of the latest and most advanced Starlink satellites to join the 11,000 older models already providing internet service. They popped out of the spacecraft one by one, drawing more cheers from the SpaceX crowds looking on from the launch site at Starbase, Texas. The decision to end the flight early came soon afterward. No reason was provided. “Starship is orbital,” Mission Control announced. AP Photo/Eric Gay



It was Starship’s 14th full-scale launch from Texas’ southern tip in three years. The earlier test flights ventured no farther than the Indian Ocean halfway around the world, often crashing in flames and briefly skimming space. This time, SpaceX was intent on circling the globe from an altitude of 170 miles (275 kilometres) – not just once but six times over almost 10 hours, ending with a Pacific splashdown near Chile. While Starship achieved the proper orbit zipping along at 17,500 mph (28,000 km/h), flight controllers opted to play it safe and bring it back several hours sooner, after just a couple of laps. The first-stage booster was never meant to return to the Starbase launch site either, instead dropping into the Gulf of Mexico within minutes of the morning liftoff. SpaceX wants to ensure that everything works before flying Starship back to Starbase. If the spacecraft breaks apart over land and rains debris onto people, “our popularity would diminish very rapidly,” Musk said at a business summit earlier this month. “That’s why we’re being extremely cautious here.” SpaceX’s mega rocket Starship makes a test flight from Starbase, Texas. AP Photo/Eric Gay



Depending on the findings from Monday’s orbital debut, the next Starship could return to the launch pad with giant mechanical arms grabbing the hovering spacecraft. If the catch works – Musk gives it even or slightly better odds – then SpaceX will refly the spacecraft by year’s end or early next year. The 407-foot (124-metre) rocket was designed from the start to be fully reusable – a key to lowering launch costs. SpaceX managed to salvage the last Starship from the Indian Ocean in July. Engineers modified the newly launched Starship’s heat shield based on hands-on inspections from the recovered spacecraft, which is being tugged back to Starbase. Related Article Space Need a tow? SpaceX rocket taken to Christmas Island after splashdown SpaceX is pressing hard to certify Starship for orbital flight, a vital step toward moon and Mars travel. NASA’s Artemis III mission is coming up as soon as next summer, a triple-launch docking exercise in orbit around Earth between an Orion capsule full of astronauts and competing lunar landers. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Moon will blast off first, then Orion – which will close in for a linkup – then Musk’s Starship for a docking with Orion once Blue Moon is unleashed.



The next mission – Artemis IV slated for no sooner than 2028 – would have astronauts landing on the moon in either Blue Moon or Starship, whichever is ready first. Subsequent moonshots will alternate between the two billionaires’ landers. Musk originally developed Starship for Mars, intending to launch scores of them with the red planet’s first settlers. For now, he plans to focus on the moon and use Starship to haul satellites into orbit by the truckload, phasing out the company’s frailer Falcon 9 rocket within several years. A second Starship launch site is nearing completion at Florida’s Kennedy Space Centre and a third is planned for Louisiana. World.title: Terror suspects released on bail after UK air base arrests, as Iran denies role
World.content:
Breaking WorldEuropeCrime Terror suspects released on bail after UK air base arrests, as Iran denies role David Crowe September 29, 2026 — 2:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: British police have released five men arrested over a suspected terror plot near a Royal Air Force base, placing restrictions on their movement as investigations continue into their actions and motives. The move ignited debate about the scale of the threat to the base and the surrounding community following fears that the alleged perpetrators could have bombed the airfield, amid suspicions that Iran was behind the plot. Armed police maintain road blocks and security checks around RAF Fairford on Monday. Getty Images The suspects were released on bail about 38 hours after they were detained near the perimeter of the base used by American aircraft to strike Iran. As UK ministers and police officials cautioned against speculating about the source of the threat, the Iranian government declared it had no role in the incident.



Police arrested five men at the Fairford air base before dawn on Sunday after residents saw men in black balaclavas running toward the secure area. Local residents shared this image online of the arrests of the five men. Hours later, US President Donald Trump claimed the suspects had been under surveillance for a “long time” and were attempting to do “big damage” to the base. The president’s statement stirred up doubts in Britain over the true nature of the threat when it emerged that the first person to report the threat was a farmer who came upon the group when she was driving down a local road. The farmer said she saw the men at 1.30am on Sunday (10.30am AEST) and called the police. News of the incident reached the media later on Sunday and police confirmed they had arrested and detained five men. Media coverage showed a bomb disposal robot checking three white vans driven to the scene by the suspects.



Local police said the five were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and that Counter Terrorism Policing had taken over the investigation. On Monday, CTP confirmed the five were arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act contrary to the Terrorism Act. The five were described as British nationals living in London and aged from 23 to 25. Loading Later on Monday, CTP Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the men were released on police bail following “extensive” interviews. “To be very clear, this does not mean that the investigation is over,” he said at about 4pm in London (1am Tuesday AEST).



“They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of enquiry.” Related Article Updated

Middle East at war ‘Masked men’ arrested over suspected bomb plot at UK air base used by US to strike Iran He added that the case might have involved “proxies” such as people who were hired to work on behalf of a foreign state, either knowingly or unknowingly. The Iranian ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, told The Times in March that the American use of the British base was a “very important matter” for Iran to consider when deciding how to strike back and defend itself. On Monday, however, the Iranian embassy denied any role in the incident and denounced claims that its government was involved.



“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK,” it said. “Islamic Republic of Iran reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Parramatta elects Labor mayor after councillor defects from Liberals
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney councils Parramatta elects Labor mayor after councillor defects from Liberals Anthony Segaert September 28, 2026 — 11:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Parramatta councillor who defected from the Liberal Party hours before a vote on the city’s mayoralty used her casting vote to support a Labor lord mayor. Cameron Maclean became lord mayor by a single vote on Monday after a testy and teary meeting that followed a day of drama. Parramatta lord mayor Cameron Maclean. City of Parramatta Councillor Tanya Raffoul, who announced on Monday morning that she had quit the party over concerns about its links to One Nation, only looked up out of a solemn downward stare during the vote to turn her head and make eye contact with her Liberal ex-colleagues as she raised her hand to vote for Maclean. The vote came during a meeting that also featured a former staff member identifying himself as a whistleblower whose reports to the ICAC triggered Operation Navarra, a weeks-long public inquiry into the council’s former chief executive Gail Connolly.



Maclean, 28, defeated Liberal councillor Martin Zaiter who had served in the position for a year. Zaiter described his time leading the council as “an extraordinary term with many ups and many downs”. “Thank you for working together as one along our journey to become Australia’s next global city,” Zaiter told councillors before the vote. Maclean said he accepted the position “with great humility”, telling Raffoul she had “demonstrated immense integrity and courage under fire” for her defection and vote. Councillor Tanya Raffoul quit the Liberals in Parramatta on the day of the council vote for mayor. Instagram Independent Kellie Darley, who has also identified herself as a whistleblower about council staff, was nominated for the position of deputy mayor by Zaiter and Liberal councillor Sreeni Pillamarri. She won against Labor councillor Michael Ng by two votes, with the council’s departing deputy mayor, independent Charles Chen, abstaining from the vote.



The first motion Darley raised as deputy mayor was about strengthening protections for whistleblowers at the council. “My children aren’t here to see me being elected as deputy mayor,” she said through tears. “And that’s because one of the consequences for me, of what happened in the reprisal action [alleged to have occurred as a result of Darley’s whistleblowing], is the impact to my now-former marriage, and that every day I am reminded of that impact.” Related Article ICAC The Pink Ladies tried to take over Parramatta. It all came undone John Crawford, the council’s former IT boss who was called to give evidence at the ICAC inquiry, spoke in support of Darley’s motion. He claimed he had been subjected to retaliation action after his evidence, including the alleged spreading of a “dirt file” against him leading to numerous media articles. “It has created serious risk to my career and reputation, and I have very limited practical means for responding,” he said, receiving a standing ovation from councillors and members of the public gallery.



Liberal councillor Steven Issa told Maclean: “What I hope more than anything is that your resolve is strengthened”, a supposed reference to Maclean’s decision to abstain from a council decision to sack Connolly late last year. By the time Zaiter had walked out of the chamber, his staff had removed the words “Lord Mayor” from his name on Facebook.

World.content:
Step 1 Pour boiling water over the paneer, stand for 10 minutes, then drain. Blend the onion, ginger, garlic and chilli to a smooth purée. Set aside. World.title: She’s got game
World.content:
“The Herald story of economist Cherelle Murphy’s $70 chicken reminds me of my startlement when some Sydney friends told me it cost $75 to buy a fresh rabbit in the city,” says Belinda Scott of Coffs Harbour. “I immediately offered to host any and all gourmet lapine lovers and to dispatch some of the fine, healthy “underground mutton” currently in residence under the jungle at the bottom of my farm garden. I even offered to skin and gut their bunny of choice, ready for transport back to their city kitchens. Sadly, no takers, so the foxes remain the beneficiaries of this free organic protein larder.”

Make of this what you will: “Chris Ritchie, I found the postcard you wrote from Paris in 1986 to your mum in Paddington,” conveys Belinda Keir of Hurlstone Park. “The Bayeux Tapestry sounded wonderful. I hope you had a nice time at the opera!”

Granny has fielded just a couple of missives involving a Chris Ritchie in the relatively recent past. One was a reference to RAN heavyweight Rear-Admiral Chris Ritchie and his dinner-hosting of personnel during the first visit to Australia by China’s navy in 1998. The other is Chris Ritchie of Willoughby, who, in 2004 was puzzled by some Shakespearean graffiti in Artarmon.

Peter Miniutti of Ashbury says that his claim to fame, according to AI (C8), is that he has “‘shared a variety of witty anecdotes’ to C8 which is described as ‘a long-running daily community section dedicated to quirky observations, lighthearted banter, and urban trivia’. Hardly what I would want on my gravestone, but AI may have other ideas.”

“I remember almost nothing of the introductory French and German classes (C8) that I attended during the late ’70s,” laments Sue Casiglia of North Ryde. “Yet I do remember the infectious chorus of the 1974 #1 Billboard Hot 100 song Lady Marmalade by Labelle, which contains the refrain ‘Voulez-vous coucher avec moi, ce soir?‘. Can you imagine preteen and teen girls singing and dancing to the translation ‘would you like to sleep with me tonight?’.” Granny notes that the censors eventually caught up and forced Labelle, and others, to sing it as “Voulez-vous danser avec moi ce soir?”
