World.title: Parramatta elects Labor mayor after councillor defects from Liberals
World.content:
NationalNSWSydney councils Parramatta elects Labor mayor after councillor defects from Liberals Anthony Segaert September 28, 2026 — 11:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Parramatta councillor who defected from the Liberal Party hours before a vote on the city’s mayoralty used her casting vote to support a Labor lord mayor. Cameron Maclean became lord mayor by a single vote on Monday after a testy and teary meeting that followed a day of drama. Parramatta lord mayor Cameron Maclean. City of Parramatta Councillor Tanya Raffoul, who announced on Monday morning that she had quit the party over concerns about its links to One Nation, only looked up out of a solemn downward stare during the vote to turn her head and make eye contact with her Liberal ex-colleagues as she raised her hand to vote for Maclean. The vote came during a meeting that also featured a former staff member identifying himself as a whistleblower whose reports to the ICAC triggered Operation Navarra, a weeks-long public inquiry into the council’s former chief executive Gail Connolly.



Maclean, 28, defeated Liberal councillor Martin Zaiter who had served in the position for a year. Zaiter described his time leading the council as “an extraordinary term with many ups and many downs”. “Thank you for working together as one along our journey to become Australia’s next global city,” Zaiter told councillors before the vote. Maclean said he accepted the position “with great humility”, telling Raffoul she had “demonstrated immense integrity and courage under fire” for her defection and vote. Councillor Tanya Raffoul quit the Liberals in Parramatta on the day of the council vote for mayor. Instagram Independent Kellie Darley, who has also identified herself as a whistleblower about council staff, was nominated for the position of deputy mayor by Zaiter and Liberal councillor Sreeni Pillamarri. She won against Labor councillor Michael Ng by two votes, with the council’s departing deputy mayor, independent Charles Chen, abstaining from the vote.



The first motion Darley raised as deputy mayor was about strengthening protections for whistleblowers at the council. “My children aren’t here to see me being elected as deputy mayor,” she said through tears. “And that’s because one of the consequences for me, of what happened in the reprisal action [alleged to have occurred as a result of Darley’s whistleblowing], is the impact to my now-former marriage, and that every day I am reminded of that impact.” Related Article ICAC The Pink Ladies tried to take over Parramatta. It all came undone John Crawford, the council’s former IT boss who was called to give evidence at the ICAC inquiry, spoke in support of Darley’s motion. He claimed he had been subjected to retaliation action after his evidence, including the alleged spreading of a “dirt file” against him leading to numerous media articles. “It has created serious risk to my career and reputation, and I have very limited practical means for responding,” he said, receiving a standing ovation from councillors and members of the public gallery.



Liberal councillor Steven Issa told Maclean: “What I hope more than anything is that your resolve is strengthened”, a supposed reference to Maclean’s decision to abstain from a council decision to sack Connolly late last year. By the time Zaiter had walked out of the chamber, his staff had removed the words “Lord Mayor” from his name on Facebook.

World.title: Adam Liaw’s Korean spicy rice cakes
World.content:
If using packaged tteok, soak them in cold water for 15 minutes. Boil the eggs for 10 minutes, then shock in iced water and peel. Set aside.

Add 600ml of water or stock with the gochujang, soy sauce, chilli powder, sugar, corn (or maple syrup) and garlic in a wide, low pan and mix.

Step 3

Bring to a simmer and add the tteok, fish cakes and spring onions (reserving a few of the spring onion’s green parts for garnish). Simmer for 5 minutes, then reduce heat to low and cook for a further 5 minutes. Stir the eggs through, then scatter with the sesame seeds to serve.

World.title: Adam Liaw’s palak paneer
World.content:
Step 1 Pour boiling water over the paneer, stand for 10 minutes, then drain. Blend the onion, ginger, garlic and chilli to a smooth purée. Set aside. Bring a large pot of water to a simmer and blanch the spinach for a few seconds. Shock in iced water and drain well. Add the spinach to the blender, with the cashews and blend to a smooth purée.

Step 2 Heat a saucepan over medium heat and add the butter and oil. Add the cardamom, cassia and cloves and fry until fragrant. Add the onion mixture and fry for about 5 minutes until the oil starts to separate. Season with salt, then add the turmeric, about ¼ cup of water and cook for a further 3 minutes.

Step 3 Add the fenugreek leaves and spinach puree and simmer on low heat for 5 minutes. Stir the cream (if using) and garam masala through the spinach gravy, add the paneer, and adjust seasoning. Transfer to a serving plate.

World.title: She’s got game
World.content:
“The Herald story of economist Cherelle Murphy’s $70 chicken reminds me of my startlement when some Sydney friends told me it cost $75 to buy a fresh rabbit in the city,” says Belinda Scott of Coffs Harbour. “I immediately offered to host any and all gourmet lapine lovers and to dispatch some of the fine, healthy “underground mutton” currently in residence under the jungle at the bottom of my farm garden. I even offered to skin and gut their bunny of choice, ready for transport back to their city kitchens. Sadly, no takers, so the foxes remain the beneficiaries of this free organic protein larder.”

Make of this what you will: “Chris Ritchie, I found the postcard you wrote from Paris in 1986 to your mum in Paddington,” conveys Belinda Keir of Hurlstone Park. “The Bayeux Tapestry sounded wonderful. I hope you had a nice time at the opera!”

Granny has fielded just a couple of missives involving a Chris Ritchie in the relatively recent past. One was a reference to RAN heavyweight Rear-Admiral Chris Ritchie and his dinner-hosting of personnel during the first visit to Australia by China’s navy in 1998. The other is Chris Ritchie of Willoughby, who, in 2004 was puzzled by some Shakespearean graffiti in Artarmon.

Peter Miniutti of Ashbury says that his claim to fame, according to AI (C8), is that he has “‘shared a variety of witty anecdotes’ to C8 which is described as ‘a long-running daily community section dedicated to quirky observations, lighthearted banter, and urban trivia’. Hardly what I would want on my gravestone, but AI may have other ideas.”

“I remember almost nothing of the introductory French and German classes (C8) that I attended during the late ’70s,” laments Sue Casiglia of North Ryde. “Yet I do remember the infectious chorus of the 1974 #1 Billboard Hot 100 song Lady Marmalade by Labelle, which contains the refrain ‘Voulez-vous coucher avec moi, ce soir?‘. Can you imagine preteen and teen girls singing and dancing to the translation ‘would you like to sleep with me tonight?’.” Granny notes that the censors eventually caught up and forced Labelle, and others, to sing it as “Voulez-vous danser avec moi ce soir?”

World.title: Court dismisses appeal over police using number plate technology
World.content:
The Court of Appeal has dismissed three cases where it was claimed police have been misusing number plate identification technology for crime fighting.

Police officers are accessing the privately-owned automated systems more and more to see whose vehicle is where and when, with use climbing to 700,000 times last year, up 20 percent.

Lawyers for three defendants argued this was too loose, that police should need a warrant or similar in order to use the evidence in court.

But the court disagreed, ruling the evidence obtained from Auror - one of the two private companies with automated number plate recognition (ANPR) systems that police use - was admissible.

It is expected that might be appealed to the Supreme Court.

The ruling follows a two-day hearing a year ago that followed district court proceedings.

The three appeal court judges imposed strict limits on media reporting as the cases are still live.

The charges against the appellants were disqualified driving, property damage, and burglary.

Auror markets its technology here and in Australia, the UK and US as a retail crime fighting tool. It has partnered with NZ police for over a decade, with usage jumping since 2020, leading to a spike in shoplifting, assault on staff and other retail crimes being accepted by officers for investigation.

The ruling described how Auror can provide a list of detections for a vehicle for up to a 60-day period and links to CCTV footage which police could download. This was more comprehensive and efficient than old ways of investigating, it said.

Rising use

Separately from the court proceedings, police have updated their figures about using the technology.

A police tech report said usage of Auror had "plateaued" at about a quarter of a million requests a year for number plate information on about 80,000 vehicles by about 3000 officers.

But police use of a second system continues to rise rapidly. Their requests to another Auckland company, SaferCities, were up by a third to 450,000 requests last year linked to almost 100,000 vehicles.

This was likely because of "further expansion of this network across the country and broader awareness within police of the utility of SaferCities information ... similar levels of growth were seen in the Auror platform during the first few years of its availability to registered Police users", said the report.

World.title: Coalition parties want to 'bury' Waitangi Tribunal for exposing Treaty breaches - Lady Tureiti Moxon
World.content:
A leading Māori health advocate says efforts to abolish or limit the Waitangi Tribunal are an attempt to "bury" a body that exposes Treaty breaches.

It comes as New Zealand First campaigns on abolishing the tribunal, while ACT wants to end its jurisdiction over contemporary Crown policy and conduct, limiting the tribunal to historical claims and wind it up once that work is completed.

Lady Tureiti Moxon told RNZ the tribunal provided an important avenue for Māori to challenge Crown decisions that breached Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

"It's the only permanent commission that can look into the breaches of Te Tiriti o Waitangi in our country," she said.

"Every decision that the Crown makes against the Treaty of Waitangi has huge impact on our people."

Moxon said the tribunal had an important role in identifying breaches that governments may otherwise fail to acknowledge.

"They won't even acknowledge the breaches that continuously happen," she said.

"What they want to do is to bury the fact that you have a tribunal in this country that raises these issues."

Moxon said the tribunal's findings should also be considered alongside international scrutiny of New Zealand's treatment of Māori.

"You've got the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination at the UN say exactly the same things as the tribunal.

"And yet this government refuses to recognise that they have an important part to play in honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi and making it a real document in this country that has meaning.

"But they give it no meaning. They disregard it whenever they feel like it."

The Waitangi Tribunal is a standing commission of inquiry, set up by law in the Treaty of Waitangi Act 1975. It investigates issues of wrongdoing and makes recommendations to the Government on how to improve the situation. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Her comments follow the tribunal's latest report into the disestablishment of Te Aka Whai Ora (Māori Health Authority), which found the Crown breached multiple principles and had shown a "reckless disregard for the Crown-Māori relationship".

Moxon was a lead claimant, and said the findings were an example of the issues the tribunal continued to bring to light.

"We're still in a predicament and it doesn't matter how many reports that say this, this government has chosen not to adhere to any of it."

She said government policies could have a detrimental impact on Māori, creating "further poverty", "further disenfranchisement", and "further imprisonment".

"The worst of it is when they're finished doing their terms, they walk away and take absolutely no responsibility for the detrimental impact that they have on Māori.

"It wouldn't be so bad if the decisions they make were decisions that were for the well-being and the betterment of the whole country.

"But it's always at the behest of Māori and who we are."

Moxon said the tribunal remained an important part of ensuring Te Tiriti had meaning in Aotearoa.

From left: ACT leader David Seymour, National leader Christopher Luxon, and New Zealand First leader Winston Peters. RNZ

New Zealand First announced its policy on Saturday, saying it would introduce legislation within the first 100 days after the election to abolish the tribunal and replace it with a 'Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission'.

"The Treaty of Waitangi Tribunal has become a make-work organisation - now hearing any and all claims that in a former time would've been dismissed on application as being inappropriate," the party said in its announcement.

"Many claims before the tribunal are directly contesting the right of a mandated parliament to pass laws.That is a direct semi-judicial threat against the very essence of our democracy."

The ACT party outlined its plans for the tribunal in September, saying it would end the tribunal's jurisdiction over contemporary Crown policy and conduct, while completing eligible historical claims before winding up the institution.

"The original need for the Waitangi Tribunal has evaporated as our country has matured into a place with strong property rights, the rule of law, and restraints on the use of military power," ACT leader David Seymour said.

"The historical claims were clearly wrong to anybody, the government of the day illegally used military power to take away people's property. It won't surprise you I'm opposed to that, but it's not dealing with issues like that anymore."

ACT's policy document said every historical claim lodged before 1 September 2008 should be heard and resolved, but any lodged after would not be, including contemporary or kaupapa claims.

National leader Christopher Luxon also said on Newstalk ZB's Mike Hosking Breakfast there was "a very legitimate question" about the tribunal's role once Treaty settlements had been concluded.

"Our election policy is the role of the Waitangi Tribunal will have to change because post-Treaty settlements, the purpose it was originally created for will no longer exist."

World.title: Property market will sort out influx of Airbnbs, Christchurch mayor says
World.content:
Christchurch's mayor is confident the property market will deal with the disproportionate number of inner city homes being rented as short-stay accommodation.

Some councillors and inner-city residents have raised concerns about the concentration of Airbnbs and similar short term rentals, as tourist hotspots around the country struggle to balance housing and tourist accommodation.

But Phil Mauger said he believed the "market would sort itself out".

Once developments such as the new Sheraton Hotel opened the gloss would come off for Airbnb investors, Mauger said.

"I think the days of Airbnbs are going to change as more and more hotels get built in Christchurch because it's like an Uber going to the airport. If the Ubers are busy, the price goes up, so I'm sure something's going to change.

"Then people will say, oh, this isn't as lucrative as it used to be. Let's sell it and people will buy it and live in them, so I think there will be a change coming."

Mauger said he did not have estimates on how many owners were not complying with the rules, including notifying council, requiring resource consents in some cases, paying the relevant rates or enforcing maximum length of stays.

"It's a stab in the dark."

Christchurch mayor Phil Mauger. RNZ/ Anna Sargant

But he was not convinced spending more on compliance was a good investment.

"We've got to watch also that the ship hasn't left the wharf and we spend a lot of time chasing something that there's not that much ... that might not be as bad as what we think."

"Do you spend a dollar to save fifty cents? That's the thing I'm looking at, and I think staff are looking at it, but I'm not quite sure where they're at with it."

Mauger said he understood the attraction for property owners.

"I've got a couple of nephews who have got some Airbnbs and it's what young people do, you know, everyone's looking for an angle. They say oh, it's pretty good, we get good money on game nights and stuff like that ... real good money."

But he said some inner city residents had told the council it was coming at the expense of a sense of community.

The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment recently backed a Christchurch City Council decision that a residential unit rented as short term accommodation breached the Building Act.

Mauger said he understood the owners were appealing the MBIE determination, but he was not concerned.

"I'm sure the market will sort itself out. All good that they're going to appeal ... because they can.

"But I think in the long run, it'll sort itself out."

World.title: Visitors avoiding Mackenzie District paid toilets, leaving mess for council
World.content:
Some people are pooing behind Mackenzie District public toilets and tourists are swarming into cafes to avoid spending money on user-pay loos but the mayor says more pay-to-go toilets are needed to help reduce the burden on ratepayers.

Three of the Mackenzie District Council's 25 public toilets are user-pays but overwhelming pressure from a large number of tourists has resulted in a staff recommendation to make people pay to use more and request electronic donations at others.

A report being considered by the council on Tuesday recommends introducing payments for toilets in Fairlie, Burkes Pass, three sites in Tekapo and the main block in Twizel.

Staff also recommended setting up a system to enable electronic donations in Ruataniwha, Edwards Stream, Punatahu/Pines and Lake Wardell.

Mackenzie District mayor Scott Aronsen said the user-pays toilets had been introduced because of the growing cost of maintaining and cleaning them.

He said the council budgeted $800,000 for toilet maintenance, which was around four percent of the total rates take, in the last year.

Mackenzie mayor Scott Aronsen. Supplied / Mackenzie District Council

"The burden on our ratepayer was just becoming larger and larger. High tourist traffic flow coming through and the toilets were just getting hammered," he said.

"Our cleaners would come through three times a day, that is between Fairlie, Twizel and Tekapo, and within half-an-hour they'd need to be cleaned again. It just becomes unsustainable from a financial perspective.

"With the influx of tourists that we are expecting this year it just keeps adding and adding waves of costs on our ratepayers and not every ratepayer benefits from tourism, that's the important thing to remember here.

"We have pensioners and people who don't work in tourism or benefit directly from tourism. We've got to be able to spread that cost a bit more."

The first three user-pays toilets were introduced in mid 2025 and charge $1.50 a visit, but Aronsen said they brought unintended consequences including people avoiding the use-pays toilets to use other free public toilets, tourists charging into cafes and people pooing behind the toilets.

"People pull up and then just go around the back. Our contractors are having to clean up human excrement from around the back of the toilet block when they shouldn't have to. I hear about that on a regular basis," he said.

The Lake Pukaki carpark is reasonably busy with international tourists despite the shoulder season. Supplied / Scott Aronsen

Aronsen said cafe owners near Lake Pukaki had reported bus loads of tourists turning up to use the toilet and leaving without buying anything.

The council had also seen a flow-on impact on its other free public toilets, with the formerly little-used Burkes Pass toilet now in hot demand.

Aronsen said the council had $2.5 million in funding from the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment to cover the cost of the new user-pays toilets, devices to enable donations at four toilets and for a toilet upgrade at one site.

"I think the central powers are interested to see how we deal with it this coming season and whether or not it is something that should be implemented elsewhere. If it works well for us then I'm sure we will see some other regions follow suit in other some shape or form," he said.

World.title: 'We're coming to get you': A rural town tackling its meth problem
World.content:
A rural town in Central Hawke's Bay has one of the highest levels of meth in the country, and its community is trying to tackle the issue together.

With a population of just 5000, Waipukurau is a friendly and quiet town, but its reputation as a close knit, hard working community is tainted by meth.

In 2024, wastewater testing in the town found meth consumption had soared 333 percent in 12 months, to more than 4.8 grams per day, per thousand people.

Results have remained consistently high ever since, despite a covert police operation that ended in three people being arrested in December 2025 for supplying methamphetamine.

Waipukurau's wastewater ponds, where testing has revealed some of NZ's highest levels of methamphetamine. RNZ / Alexa Cook

A Waipukurau social support worker, who wants to be known only as Bob, told RNZ that meth is everywhere in the town.

"I'm tired of working with this s***, it is draining and it will suck the life out of you.

"Who isn't on it?" he said.

Bob is a former addict, and through his work helping others with their addictions, he feels meth is becoming normalised - like alcohol.

"There are so many people accepting it as is, it's just their day-to-day norm... their routine along with having a cup of tea in the morning.

"This isn't to say it's accepted - but in pockets, and there are a variety of pockets, it is not limited to one pocket of society - this is just normal," Bob said.

Hawke's Bay police area prevention manager, Inspector Caroline Martin and Central Hawke's Bay officer in charge Sergeant Neil Baker. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The local police officer, sergeant Neil Baker, is trying to understand why Waipukurau's meth rates are so high.

"It definitely appears to be more acceptable in people's lives now and the number of people that you come across who... would have cannabis in their pocket, now they have a meth pipe and utensils or something along those lines.

"So yes, I think it is becoming more and more common, which is very sad," Baker said.

He told RNZ the issue is hard to get his head around, but he does have a theory.

"I believe that we potentially have a number of functioning users who are able to use methamphetamine on a daily basis, go about their business, go about their employment, and still function as every day members of the community, but have a habit. We're certainly hearing more and more stories like that.

"We're seeing more people being affected by methamphetamine. And the number of those contacts is certainly increasing, those who are regular users of methamphetamine," Baker said.

He said while there is a definite gang link to the distribution and sale of meth in Central Hawke's Bay, it's a much broader demographic who are actually using it.

"The more I learn into the distribution of it, it's certainly a lot wider. And I think that what we see on the ground is just one portion of a very big problem for the country."

Baker's vowing to keep fighting back against the rise of meth in his community.

"I certainly hope that we haven't lost the battle just yet. We're going to continue the good fight and keep coming to work every day to try and catch as many as we can."

His message to those supplying methamphetamine is clear: "Get ready, we're coming to get you."

With a population of just 5000, Waipukurau is a friendly and quiet town, but its reputation as a close knit, hard working community is tainted by meth. RNZ / Alexa Cook

Wastewater testing can't tell police who is consuming meth or how much they are taking, that's why they rely on information from the public.

Hawke's Bay police area prevention manager Inspector Caroline Martin said last year's arrests were thanks to people helping police, and they're urging others with any information to do the same.

"Seeing any consumption levels high in a community is concerning. To try and understand that, we need the community support. We do know that there are users in the community.

"We rely on information from the public to help us with this issue. We need people to come forward. We need people to tell us what's happening in our local community here in Central Hawke's Bay," she said.

In response to the spike of meth in the wastewater, the Central Hawke's Bay Methamphetamine Harm Reduction Group was formed in 2024, which includes local leaders, organisations, health services and police.

It's funded by the Resilience to Organised Crime in Communities (ROCC) programme. The programme's manager Hannah O'Leary said that support has led to the community group developing a localised strategy.

"Subsequent to that, there has been a road map that has been developed on actually how to implement that strategy. It's very much community based ... I think there were about 30 different people in the room discussing what works for their community.

"Making sure we've got the right people sitting around that table from all the different walks of life is really important," she said.

The ROCC programme is now in 13 communities across New Zealand.

"What we do know is that organised groups exploit vulnerability such as disconnection, trauma, economic hardship, addiction, where there's limited access to opportunities and weakened protective factors," O'Leary said.

Central Hawke's Bay mayor Will Foley. RNZ / Alexa Cook

The Central Hawke's Bay Methamphetamine Harm Reduction Group has created a strategy to try and drive down Waipukurau's high meth consumption. Mayor Will Foley said that includes education and awareness around the impacts of meth, and where to go for help.

"The good thing about a plan is then it shows what we do need when we ask for further support.

"Being a small community, we don't necessarily have good facilities and services for things like that, as opposed to some of the bigger cities. So seeing what we could do to set up and just have people and services available for those people that need help."

The mayor said it's a community-wide effort to tackle the town's meth problem, but he's also being realistic.

"We hope to reverse that trend, but we know it's going to be an ongoing issue," Foley said.

Bob said he was sceptical about the group's strategy.

"So far nothing has worked. America's 'war on drugs', it's not unique to them... the only winner is drugs," he said.

When asked if there is anything that could help reduce meth use in Central Hawke's Bay, Bob said there needs to be more facilities for addicts to "dry out".

"There's a real lack of detox centres. I've always bitched and moaned about that - only one detox bed for the whole of Hawke's Bay," he said.

Mental Health Minister Matt Doocey told RNZ the government is investing more in Hawke's Bay to help people access faster drug addiction support.

"Through the Government's Reducing Demand for Methamphetamine plan, we have committed $2.32 million over four years to Hawke's Bay, including Central Hawke's Bay and Wairoa.

"This investment will provide community-based, peer-led support as well as additional specialist addiction practitioners and registered nurses, with a specific focus on reducing meth harm and supporting people through withdrawal," Doocey said.

World.title: Why Mt Albert could be pivotal for National as it plots its way back to power
World.content:
The Auckland electorate seat of Mount Albert could prove to be pivotal for National as it plots it way back to power.

Labour has held the seat for decades but nearly lost it in 2023, only holding on by the slimmest of margins.

But, there is a new contender whose party could tip the balance of power come 7 November.

Incumbent Labour MP Helen White told RNZ that the cost-of-living (which all candidates RNZ spoke to said) was the biggest issue it wanted sorted.

Specifically, White said, housing and infrastructure were issues her constituents told her about constantly.

"Things like secure rentals [because] it's really expensive if you have to move house... because kids have to move from their school often if they have to move from their house.

"We get lots around here about flooding because the soil around here and the rock underneath it means that you get particular areas where you get a lot of flooding and they're not necessarily where you expect them to be - we need a stormwater system."

Labour's Helen White. RNZ / Tom Taylor

The seat is a Labour strong hold; three Labour leaders, two of whom became prime minister, have held it, and the party's dominance over it stretches back to the end of the Second World War.

But it was close to flipping blue last election. White only beat National's long-time candidate Melissa Lee by 18 votes.

She reckoned people had got to know her better since then.

"I was at the supermarket the other day and people kept on smiling at me and I was like, what?"

"But it's because they know who I am and they know I'm in for a fight here - so it's a pretty cool experience when that happens," she said.

Labour's track record wasn't lost on Lee, who told RNZ the electorate was the first place whānau called home when moving to New Zealand.

National's candidate Melissa Lee. RNZ / Nick Monro

Although she didn't live there now, she said people in the electorate still knew her well.

"The people have known me for 18 years. I've been in the Mount Albert electorate for 18 years, longer than the current sitting electorate MP.

"Even Labour people actually know me [because] when I do knock on the door, I say, 'it's about time you actually voted for me now' - we joke about that."

Like White, Lee heard a lot about flooding infrastructure. She said housing intensification had changed the electorate a lot since she first moved there.

"I've encouraged everyone who's actually talked to me when I was actually at their door, concerned about it to actually make a submission as to why they don't think that they should have six storey houses on the street, because the council has technically zoned it for that."

The Green Party's Ricardo Menendez March wasn't too far behind, racking up over 9000 votes in 2023 - around 4000 less than the top two.

The Green Party's Ricardo Menendez March. VNP/Louis Collins

This time, he's in it to win it.

"The key message here is that no politician should take any seat for granted.

"As an MP, I have managed to successfully shepherd member's bills. I have successfully advocated for migrant families and have fought to end things like benefit sanctions on solo mums.

"Westley, Waterview and other parts of the electorate saw what happens when you build housing in areas that are flood-prone. This is why I think we need to bring the community with us when we're building housing, to not repeat the damage that was done" he said.

Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong. RNZ/Calvin Samuel

And there's a new contender, Qiulae Wong, offering voters the opportunity to go in a different direction.

Wong told RNZ the contest would likely be a four-horse race, bolstered, perhaps, by polling showing Opportunity being a power broker come election day.

"We've had another three years of the status quo, and I think there's still a bit of a scepticism as to whether Labour is the right party for the area - there's a lot of young people looking for something different.

"A lot of the people that live in Mount Albert are part of industries that are quite future focused as well and so they want to see that economic engine starting to hum a bit more in New Zealand, but locally as well," she said.

Two more candidates are standing for the seat, although they're campiagning for the party vote.

Sheldon Eden-Whaitiri. Supplied / NZ First

For New Zealand First, Sheldon Eden-Whaitiri, a veteran rugby referee who worked in sales at Mediaworks and NZME. He resigned due to potential conflicts of interest.

Eden-Whaitiri told RNZ he is the nephew of former Labour MP Meka Whaitiri, and like his aunty, he didn't want anything to do with them.

"It is, I believe, a blue-collar electorate ... but I don't feel Labour necessarily represents those working-class families and people anymore.

"The Labour Party have become the party of the common room, they used to be, the party of the smoko room, and I'm really going to gun for those old Labour supporters that feel miffed by that party, that have left them behind," he said.

ACT's Mt Albert candidate Alex Price. Supplied / ACT

And for ACT, Alex Price the chief executive of Fertility Associates - a company which boasted about the births of more than 30,000 babies.

It's fitting then that Price told RNZ it was his own children leaving home that encouraged him to get into politics.

"Both my children have now left home so it's a good time to look at politics from a logistics family perspective but they've both also chosen to study in Australia.

"I do want to help contribute to a New Zealand where my children, grandchildren want to come home to," he said.

Each candidate identified the cost-of-living as the big issue Mt Albert residents want sorted, no surprises there.

World.title: 'There's a long way to go' - ACT, Greens on gains in polling, and working with Opportunity
World.content:
The Greens and ACT are both playing coy about their respective gains in the latest polling - and on working with the Opportunity Party.

The 1News-Verian poll out Monday showed Opportunity down two points to 6 percent - dangerously close to the threshold that would see them out of Parliament without an electorate win.

But both the left and right bloc would need Opportunity's seven seats to form a government.

The Greens made the biggest gains of 4 percentage points, netting them a record 19 seats, and co-leader Chloe Swarbrick gained 2 points to put her third on the preferred prime minister rankings, just six points behind Labour's Chris Hipkins.

She told RNZ the party was not taking anything for granted and would work hard to share its vision with New Zealanders, but the country was in "pretty unprecedented political times".

The Greens would work with "whomever we have values alignment" and that was true of Opportunity - in some areas.

"But I think that there is maybe a little bit of divergence when it comes to the willingness to allow corporations to kind of write the rules when it comes to environmental and climate policy.

"We don't begrudge anyone who's bringing evidence-based policies to the table, but ... there are only two political parties asking for your party vote who are committed to changing the government, and that's the Green Party and the Labour Party."

Greens co-leader Chloe Swarbrick. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Swarbrick laughed off questions about the preferred prime minister stakes, saying "you don't join the Green Party because you have grand designs on climbing up the greasy pole".

David Seymour and his ACT Party were both up 2 points and - like Swarbrick - not counting chickens.

"We're very grateful for the people saying they will support ACT, but we know there's a long way to go and we're going to have to keep working hard to truly earn their vote."

National has ruled out working with Opportunity, and Seymour was initially vague about whether that should change.

"The ACT party is here to lock Labour out of government and lock Labour's policies out of the National Party - which has been necessary lately ... we don't mind who we need to work with, notwithstanding there's a few that are non-starters."

Asked if that included Opportunity, he said it was "very hard to know what you're getting with them".

"They seem to have launched with some bold policies that they now say are just ideas; they say they're here to clean up politics and stop big money, but they were founded with a $3 million donation, which is still the largest in New Zealand history. So, look, I can't make head nor tail of them.

"What we hear from Opportunity is 'everyone's a bit silly and they're here to fix it for us', I have another theory: politics might be a little bit harder than the Opportunity Party think, and they're a bit naive."

ACT leader David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

RNZ has sought comment from the Opportunity Party.

With some advocating for National Party supporters to use their party votes to support the smaller parties in the coalition, Seymour stands to gain.

He and NZ First's Winston Peters criticised National's leader Christopher Luxon for calling it an "insanely stupid idea", saying voters were "often busy, but they're not stupid, and it's never wise to talk down to them".

Te Pāti Māori has made the tactic a core strategy, but Swarbrick aligned closer to National.

"A strategic vote only actually makes sense if everybody, a critical mass of people are on board ... if everybody is running their own strategy, it's not particularly strategic."

She said New Zealanders should be voting for their values and the candidates and policies they believed in.

World.title: Is now the time to move tax brackets?
World.content:
Audio player for " Why do I pay tax on my KiwiSaver? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/business/1637709%2Fis-now-the-time-to-move-tax-brackets

New Zealanders are paying more tax due to bracket creep, but is now the time to tackle it?

Treasury will on Tuesday give its Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (PREFU), revealing the state of the government's books heading into the election.

Finance Minister Nicola Willis, speaking as National's finance spokesperson, earlier expressed a desire to adjust tax brackets once the government's books were in better shape.

She said she would have more to say about National's tax plans after PREFU.

What's the issue?

Fiscal drag, or bracket creep, refers to the way that, if tax brackets don't move, rising incomes can push people into higher tax rates, even if the increases are only keeping pace with inflation.

Advice given to Willis by Inland Revenue said that in March 2010, the average amount of income tax paid on every dollar was 31.4c. That fell to 18.9c in the 2011/12 year, when tax brackets were adjusted, then crept up to 22.6c in 2023/24 before dropping to 22.3 in 2024/25.

An analytical note for Treasury in October last year by Shane Domican and Sijin Zhang said that fiscal drag on New Zealanders had been "significant".

"From 2011 to 2023, fiscal drag led to personal tax revenues rising by 1.6 percent of GDP. The distributional impact of fiscal drag is uneven and the full impact on New Zealanders depends on how the revenue is used. However, in the future, if fiscal drag continues, it's likely to increasingly impact lower income individuals."

They said that if inflation was running at 2 percent and real wage growth at 1 percent, personal tax revenue could rise by 2.1 percent of GDP between 2025 and 2038. If tax bands were indexed to inflation, that would fall to 0.9 percent.

They said fiscal drag had had the biggest impact on people earning around $70,000 in 2025.

"The total distributional impact on New Zealanders will also depend on how the revenue is used. For example, if used to fund broadly provided public services, the distributional impact is likely to be overall redistributive, with lower income earners benefiting and higher income earners having a net cost."

Tax expert Terry Baucher said he thought there should be regular threshold adjustments.

Terry Baucher. Supplied

"There are a lot of unintended consequences and then you get to a point where you simply can't catch up and you've basically baked in tax increases permanently which is what happened between 2010 and 2024.

"It's not transparent. In America, the tax thresholds there are adjusted for inflation very year and in Britain, for the personal tax allowance, which is tax-free, they are required to pass an amendment if they are not increasing it by the rate of inflation."

Kelly Eckhold, chief economist at Westpac, agreed it would be desirable to tackle fiscal drag.

Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

"The adjustment in tax brackets that was done a couple of years ago was estimated to have reduced maybe a third of the accumulated bracket creep that occurred up to that point. There's obviously some more that could be done."

Fiscal drag was pro-cyclical, he said, and the government brought in more tax during times when the economy was improving.

Deloitte tax partner Robyn Walker pointed out the Greens, Te Pāti Māori, and New Zealand First were already proposing personal tax rate and threshold changes. Opportunity also proposed to change personal taxes as part of its tax reset.

Robyn Walker. Supplied / Deloitte

"From a tax perspective, it is compelling to consider whether bracket creep should be addressed as part of an election policy, but it's also worth considering what the most fiscally responsible thing to do [is]. Some will hold the sentiment that the better answer is to take the benefit of fiscal drag and to apply this to the repayment of debt. This has the benefit of reducing future interest costs therefore providing the option of tax rate or threshold reductions in the future.

"A compromise could be a commitment to tax reductions if core Crown debt falls below a specified level of GDP - currently 41.3 percent. The right answer is all about trade-offs and priorities.

"It may be difficult for any modest threshold adjustments to compete with the larger reductions which are being proposed for low- and middle-income earners by other political parties."

But the problem is the cost of moving tax brackets.

Brad Olsen, principal economist at Infometrics, said while the Government was borrowing to pay for spending, it was not appropriate to move the tax brackets.

Brad Olsen. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"The concept of trying to reduce fiscal drag - absolutely, huge fan. Definitely keen. Practically, the challenge, we saw this when the Government introduced the last set of tax cuts and changes to adjust for some level of fiscal drag was that it was a fairly limited amount per person but because it's across everyone it starts to add up quite a lot in terms of the fiscal position."

He said until the government could get out of deficit, it would be irresponsible to offer tax cuts.

"A treat for the current set of taxpayers who have to pay a little bit less but it also means that future generations would have to pay more and more debt, that is simply not a reasonable position for any Government to think about."

Eckhold said while Willis indicated there could be good news in PREFU, the forecasts were finalised at the end of August, before long-term interest rates lifted and fuel prices increased again. He agreed the cost of any adjustment could be prohibitive.

World.title: Bombers poach former Swans premiership coach John Longmire
World.content:
Essendon have poached former Sydney premiership coach John Longmire as their new general manager of performance in a huge recruiting coup.

Longmire departs Sydney after 25 years in various roles to reunite with his former assistant, new Bombers coach Mark McVeigh, in a new role.

"I'm really excited to be joining the Essendon Football Club," Longmire said in a statement.

"I've known Mark for a long time and have worked with him as well. He is passionate about the Bombers and has a clear vision for the team.

"I look forward to supporting both him and the staff as the club looks to take the necessary steps back towards being a consistent team who challenge the opposition every week."

The Bombers have effectively split the football boss role in two, with Longmire to oversee game strategy, player development, leadership, the coaching group, performance analytics and strength and conditioning.

The 55-year-old, most recently Sydney's executive director of club performance, will start this week ahead of the trade period.

John Longmire won the 2012 AFL premiership with the Swans in a 14-season spell as head coach. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Landing Longmire, who did not pursue any vacant head coach roles, is a huge result for the battling Bombers, who finished last on the ladder and needed to put support around first-year coach McVeigh.

"John's football experience and leadership are exactly what we have been looking for in this role," Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said in a statement.

"We have made no secret of our ambition to build a football program capable of delivering sustained success, and bringing in someone of John's calibre is a significant investment in that goal.

"Over 14 seasons as senior coach of the Sydney Swans, John built a program that consistently competed at the pointy end, including the 2012 premiership and four further grand final appearances.

"He knows what a winning program looks like from the inside and how to sustain it year after year.

"Just as importantly, John will be an enormous asset to Mark McVeigh.

"Very few people understand the demands of the senior coach role like John does and having someone of his experience alongside Mark to provide support, guidance and a sounding board will allow Mark to focus on coaching and developing our players."

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham hailed Longmire as a "much-loved and respected figure" and "legend".

Longmire joined Sydney as an assistant coach in 2002 and was involved in the drought-breaking 2005 premiership, later succeeding Paul Roos.

Across 333 games, Longmire, the Swans' longest-serving coach had a 63 per cent winning record, won the 2012 premiership and led Sydney to five grand finals and 12 finals campaigns.

He stepped down after the 2024 grand final loss to Brisbane.

"Having arrived at the Swans 25 years ago this club has meant so much to me and my family," Longmire said in a Swans statement.

"I will look back with extreme fondness of my time in Sydney and always be proud of what we achieved as a football club."

AAP

World.title: 'I'll be back': Cleary vows to return after surgery
World.content:
Penrith Panthers star Nathan Cleary has vowed to return after his 2026 season was brutally cut short on Sunday, thanking fans for their support from his hospital bed.

The 28-year-old suffered a horrific compound fracture of his left ankle in the Panthers' NRL preliminary final defeat against Newcastle, ruling him out of the Kangaroos' World Cup campaign.

The Panthers, who led 14-6 at half-time, ultimately fell apart to lose to the 12-man Knights, 22-14.

On Monday, the star halfback posted a photo from hospital, with his left leg bandaged following surgery.

"Surgery done," he wrote on Instagram, with a photo of him smiling and giving thumbs up to the camera.

"Thank you so much to everyone that has reached out, the support has been unbelievable.

"Yesterday sucked but it's all part of the journey and it's made me even more grateful for the people I have around me.

"I'll be back."

Nathan Cleary was taken from the field in agony. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The gruesome injury cast a pall over the Sydney Olympic Stadium, with Panthers players visibly distressed on field while their star was being treated by medical staff.

"He's one of my best mates," Panthers captain Isaah Yeo said post-match.

"He's your brother out there. You don't like seeing anyone like that. You just want to be there for him.

"It's a lonely little place out there when you've got something like that going on."

Cleary's father, coach Ivan Cleary, also revealed that seeing his son in such a state at half-time was "emotional".

It was later revealed that Cleary, who started the game from the bench, was already playing with a broken bone in his right foot as the Panthers hoped to manage his involvement in the prelim with half an eye looking forward to next weekend's grand final against the Sydney Roosters.

Cleary came onto the field 25 minutes into the first half, but only lasted 10 minutes before Newcastle hooker Phoenix Crossland fell onto his ankle in a tackle.

Crossland was sent off for a hip drop and was sent straight to the NRL judiciary by the match review committee, where a lengthy suspension could not only rule him out of Newcastle's first NRL grand final in 25 years, but also impact the Kiwi's World Cup campaign.

Slater calls for change

Phoenix Crossland is unlikely to play in the grand final. (Getty Images)

Crossland is likely to face a lengthy ban, but has been given support from former Maroons coach Billy Slater.

Speaking on The Billy Slater Podcast, Slater said the current rules were leaving players unsure as to how to tackle players effectively without giving away a penalty.

"It has to come down to the responsibility of the tackler," Slater said.

"[But] I honestly feel the game has a little bit of a responsibility in this as well. When you change interpretations and change rules, you always have a flow-on effect.

"If you think about the protection of kickers and ball players and not being able to tackle them even fractionally after they pass the ball … 10 years ago this wouldn't have happened. Fifteen years ago that tackle would not have happened because Phoenix Crossland would've had more speed and force going into that tackle.

"But because he was worried about tackling Nathan after he passed the ball he was actually in a passive position.

"He was on his inside, which is normally when you put pressure on the ball player and you go out and you make tackles on that ball player, even after they pass the ball slightly.

"Phoenix wasn't in that mindset. He was in a passive mindset thinking Nathan was going to pass, then all of a sudden Nathan threw a dummy and he had to make a tackle and he didn't have that force behind him.

"I've got no doubt that has contributed to why Phoenix Crossland is in this grabbing and sitting down position, because he doesn't have that momentum and force and mindset of making a tackle."

The NRL judiciary will sit on Tuesday, with Crossland needing to argue his case to have any chance of playing in the 2026 grand final.

World.title: Socceroos expect Brazil backlash in Brisbane
World.content:
Ageless Socceroo Aziz Behich has no plans to pull the pin with the side on the rise, buoyed by a performance against Brazil they are keen to do better than in Brisbane.

Australia conceded a goal with the final play of their Townsville clash on Friday to walk away with a 1-1 draw that, tellingly, left them disappointed.

A Brazilian backlash is expected at Lang Park on Tuesday night, and the A-League's only player in the 26-man squad is primed to counter it.

"We've set the bar high for ourselves … it was good, but we need to be better," the 35-year-old said.

"How brave we were on the ball … we trusted each other and took the game on.

"When you do that against an opponent like that, you earn their respect and we need to do that again, that's for sure."

Incredibly Behich's 88th national appearance was his first game since the World Cup, but the veteran was able to display his trademark pace and work rate despite being in preseason mode with Melbourne City.

There is optimism the next generation of talent will take the Socceroos to new heights and, with the Asian Cup on the horizon in January, Behich plans to do more than stick around.

"I wouldn't call it hanging on … I'm still playing at a high level … it's exciting times," he said.

"I feel great. I'm a player that's always honest with myself. I know when I'm not at a level I should be. But I have a lot in the tank to give."

The Socceroos took the lead against Brazil, and deserved it as well. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Coach Tony Popovic echoed Behich's sentiment ahead of the Brisbane rematch.

"Being confident, being brave … we've clearly seen a difference in the players' demeanour since the World Cup," he said.

He said the challenge would be to back-up that performance on a short-turnaround.

"We don't have players playing regular Champions League, or in the top leagues, 60 games a year," he said.

"It's a great test."

The Brisbane fixture serves as a homecoming for rising defender Lucas Herrington.

The 19-year-old played his last game for the Roar in January this year, before using the World Cup to springboard from Colorado in the MLS to Hull in the Premier League.

"We've seen against Brazil a confident young man, defending against the very best," Popovic said.

"Now he's got the challenge of doing something he maybe hasn't done in a while, against that calibre, backing up three, four days later.

"Can the body do it and are you ready to play at that level once more?"

AAP

World.title: Matthews claims world championship silver after life-threatening crash
World.content:
Michael Matthews felt that his career was probably over at the start of the season.

Having missed a large portion of the 2025 season after a pulmonary embolism was discovered in his lung, a horrific collision with a fire truck while training in March could have cost him an awful lot more than just his career.

But less than eight months later the 36-year-old was standing on the world championship podium for the fourth time in his career, claiming second place in what was the greatest possible silver lining after two years of desperately bad luck.

"I'm pretty speechless I'm sitting here with a silver medal around my neck," Matthews said.

"Honestly, I wasn't sure exactly how today was going to go.

"The field was so strong. Leading into the race, I was quietly confident, but the world championships is always a bit of a lottery."

Michael Matthews felt he might not have been able to ride during the world championships after a horrific two seasons. (Supplied: AusCycling/Craig Render)

Matthews led the chasing pack home 13 seconds behind surprise American winner Brandon McNulty after a brutal 273.4-kilometre course in and around Montréal in Canada.

The Australian edged out former champion Mathieu van der Poel and Quinn Simmonds, who were both classified with the same time.

His silver medal will sit alongside the road race silver he won 11 years ago in Richmond, Virginia, as well ass road race bronze medals in 2017 (Bergen) and 2022 (Wollongong).

Matthews also has two gold medals and a bronze in the mixed team relay at world championships, and was the winner of the under 23 title in Geelong in 2010.

"I think this was probably my last opportunity to be a world champion. So, obviously, mixed feelings, but at the same time, I have to be proud of what the way I've bounced back," Matthews said.

"To be second around here on a circuit that many said was out of my reach, to show everyone that I'm still up there with the best in the world even after what I've been through, at the moment feels like a win."

Just getting to the start line would have been a victory of sorts for Matthews.

On March 5, the veteran Australian rider crashed head-on with a fire truck at a combined speed of 100km/h.

Michael Matthews was lucky to be able to continue after his horrific crash in March. (Supplied: Instagram/@Bling90)

Matthews suffered an open arm fracture, severed thumb tendons, broke both wrists and sustained a sinus fracture that required stitches to his face.

"I hit a fire truck at pretty much 100km/h, I was doing 50 and the truck was doing 50," Matthews told the Detour podcast prior to this year's Tour de France.

"With a crash like that, it could have ended my career, or even worse.

"I might not be here right now. I'm extremely blessed to be able to tell the story and how lucky I was."

Matthews said there were a couple of times over the past two years when he felt he would never be back at the pointy end of the professional peloton, crediting his family for always believing in him.

"What I've been through the last two years, with embolia in my lungs, thinking my career was done, to breaking both my arms at the start of this year, thinking my career was done. Now, bouncing back to being second in the Worlds road race — just speechless, honestly," he said.

"I said to my wife at the start of today, 'Let's just leave it all out there and be proud of the ride at the end of the day, make sure you finish with nothing.'

"It's exactly what happened today when I crossed the finish line. I put my head in my hands almost in disbelief.

"Honestly, it's just credit to my family, to the team, to all the support crew around me that didn't stop believing this could happen right now. So, I owe everything to them."

Michael Matthews was almost in disbelief at winning silver. (Getty Images: Dario Belingheri)

The race itself was an absolute barnstormer of a contest from the very off.

Two-time defending champion Tadej Pogačar was absent from the race, recovering from a fractured neck and collarbone that he suffered in a crash that took him out of the Vuelta a España last month.

That left the race wide open, with a number of riders all believing they had a chance to claim the rainbow bands on a course that was hard enough to interest the climbers as much as the one-day specialist rouleurs.

The race exploded with 90km to go as Oscar Onley, van der Poel, Wout van Aert, Simmons and Primož Roglič built a lead, which was whittled down by the French team, led by Paul Seixas, and Isaac del Toro.

A flurry of frantic accelerations and regroupings at the front made for a frenetic, thrilling race, with the USA well placed with three of the leading 13 riders.

McNulty fired off the front with just over 30km to go and, despite brilliant surges from Ireland's Ben Healy and Britain's Tom Pidcock, the American soloed to victory.

Brandon McNulty is America's third male world road race champion after Lance Armstrong and Greg Lemond. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

The 28-year-old American, who rides with Pogačar at UAE Team Emirates-XRG, is just the third American to win the men's world road race title and the first since Lance Armstrong in Oslo in 1993.

"I'm really at a loss," McNulty said.

"Until the last hundred metres, I didn't believe it, I was so tired. I was just dying, but I kept pushing. We have said for weeks now that we had a super strong team. We talked about it, but I knew it would take a miracle. I guess miracles happen."

World.title: Hauser wins thrilling World Triathlon sprint, Parker breaks record
World.content:
Australian triathlete Matt Hauser showed he was up for the fight at the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Pontevedra, Spain overnight, beating Vasco Vilaça to the line in a thrilling sprint finish.

Defending series champion Hauser came into the series finale knowing he would be up against it to retain his title.

A number of crashes throughout the year meant Hauser needed to win and beat Vilaça by five places.

The Portuguese triathlete was in no mood to let the Australian get any sort of gap though, sticking with him through the swim and shadowing on the bike before the tremendous run stage.

"That's just ridiculous. I was just telling myself I can't lose this one, I can't lose this one," Hauser said.

"I've been so up and down this year and so inconsistent. I just really wanted it out there today.

"There is a lot to be thankful for and pleased for. I was really happy to get the win out there today and to execute when it really mattered.

"I'm not back-to-back world champion, but I can hang my head high. I achieved what I set out to achieve today and now looking onwards and upwards for next year."

Matt Hauser pushed the pace on the front during the run. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Hauser and Vilaça ran away from Olympic champion Alex Yee, whose stunning run leg bought him into contention in the closing stages.

The Briton could not stay with the leading pair though as they engaged in what turned into a furious battle for the line.

Hauser's 'world champion persona' Despite being Australia's first male triathlon world champion in 20 years, Matt Hauser is still building the blocks towards his aim of Olympic success in 2028.

Both men were credited with a time of 1:39:31, but the Australian's dip on the line ensured he would claim victory by 0.08 seconds.

"Credit to Vasco, what a champion," Hauser said.

"I mean we got a bit pushy, shovy in the end. Apologies to him. I gave him a bit of a bump on my way through to get to the line first.

"[But] you have to do these things to get the victory sometimes, to have that dog in you.

"I didn't want to lose the sprint finish to Vacsco. I haven't lost all year to him.

"I have this notch in my belt this year and will take the momentum into next year and to LA2028."

Lauren Parker breaks record

Lauren Parker now has a record six world para triathlon titles. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

Lauren Parker also claimed victory in the PTWC race in Pontevedra, cementing her status as one of Australia's greatest-ever para triathletes.

PTWC events are for athletes who use a wheelchair in their daily life.

Racers in the PTWC category compete in a standard 750-metre open-water swim, but can use swim-exit handlers to help them out of the water. They then race a recumbent handcycle for the 20km cycling leg, before using a racing wheelchair for the 5km run leg.

The reigning Paralympic champion was never troubled in the race, leading from early on in the swim and thereafter, cruising to victory.

"I felt awesome out there in swim, bike and run," Parker said.

"I got a decent lead in the swim … I got on the bike and I felt so strong out there and I was pulling time into the girls, and extended my lead."

"And in the run, I was just holding them off."

The win secured the 37-year-old multi-sport star a sixth PTWC World Championship title.

It made Parker Australia's most successful ever Para triathlete, beating the legendary Bill Chaffey's previous benchmark of five world championship titles.

"It's just as special as my first title," Parker said.

"My first title was obviously [special because] it was my first. Number six means I've overtaken Bill Chaffey. It's awesome."

Parker won the PTWC class para-triathlon race at the Paris Olympics, having won silver in the same event in Tokyo in 2021.

She then backed up that performance to win para-cycling gold in the H1–4 road race and silver in the H1-3 time trial as well.

Not only that, but Parker can add four rainbow jerseys as a cycling world champion to her triathlon titles.

The Newcastle athlete also took to the snow in the past year, competing in both the biathlon and cross-country skiing at the Milano-Cortina Paralympic Winter Games in 2026.

Elsewhere, Anu Francis secured silver in the Women's PTS2 World Championship race.

The PTS2 classification is for non-wheelchair users for athletes who live with muscle power disorders or limb deficiencies.

World.title: Sandon Smith leads Newcastle out of an Immortal shadow
World.content:
It's rare that anybody in Newcastle shares an accolade with Andrew Johns, but Sandon Smith has managed it.

Fresh off his electric double in the Knights' 22-14 win over Penrith on Sunday, Smith will join Johns as the only men to play halfback for Newcastle in a grand final.

"It's pretty cool to hear. I don't think I'm anywhere near that [Johns]," Smith said.

"But it's an honour."

Talking about Johns is part of the deal when you play halfback for Newcastle but it's wrong to compare the two because it's wrong to compare anyone to Johns, who stands alone as the club and the city's ultimate legend and hero.

Johns was more than just a player to the Knights, even if he's the best player they have ever had or will ever know.

The 1997 and 2001 premierships made Johns a Newcastle folk hero and the personification of the Novocastrian dream, larger than life through his greatness and profoundly human at the same time, like if they found a demigod in the front bar of a Cessnock pub.

Every Newcastle halfback since his retirement in 2007 exists, to one extent or another, in his enormous shadow which has a gravitational pull from which some players never escaped.

Andrew Johns remains Newcastle's greatest ever player. (Getty Images via All Sports: Chris McGrath)

You'd have an easier time replacing Christ in Christianity, because at least then there's supposed to be a second coming.

The only way to do it is to opt out of that framing altogether, because it's a game that cannot be won and therefore shouldn't be played.

Smith doesn't need to be Andrew Johns for Newcastle to make a grand final, the prelim is proof that being himself is enough.

His first try was a clever effort backed by his speed but his second, a length of the field intercept in the dying seconds that sealed the club's first grand final berth in a quarter century, was something else entirely.

It brought Johns himself to tears and for the post-Johns generation, many of whom are seeing the Knights in a grand final for the first time, it was the greatest moment of their supporting lives.

"The first one I was just trying to stay in the game and I saw an opportunity. Those don't always come off, but it worked well," Smith said.

"The second one, I didn't know if I could make it. My little legs were hanging on for dear life. But I was happy to make it, I'm ecstatic.

"It's hard to put into words. There's so much emotion going on.

"I think there was a few tears coming out. I was happy, I was tired, I can't really explain it.

"When I came to the club, I heard a lot about the town and how our football affects the town.

"It's hard to put into words when you're a part of it, but it's so true and it's so special, to be a part of something like this that is bigger than ourselves."

One of those supporters was Johns himself, who wept openly and spoke with a voice clouded with emotion on Channel Nine commentary in the aftermath of Smith's last score.

It was a gift of a moment, a slice of heaven wrapped in red and blue, the kind that Johns gave his team and his town back in those olden days, but until Smith went all the way the Immortal had never received it himself.

That alone would be a high honour, but Smith stood up multiple times on his team's biggest game since the Johns age, creating the break that led to Dominic Young's try early in the second half and forcing a key error from Lindsay Smith late on.

It sets up a grand final berth against the Roosters, where Smith played from 2023 to 2025 before he travelled to Newcastle in an effort for more NRL starts after the Bondi club signed Daly Cherry-Evans.

He insists there's no bad blood with the Tricolours as he tries to pilot the Knights to a premiership at their expense.

"It won't change anything for me. I'll enjoy it, I'll embrace this whole week. I'll stay in the moment. It's just another team and it doesn't change anything for myself or the team," Smith said.

"If we win a grand final, I don't think it matters who it'd be against.

"They were transparent with me [around Cherry-Evans]. I've got no remorse, I loved the club and loved my time there, but I'm a Knight now."

Like many of his teammates, Smith's been trusted to do more than one job this season.

He's at halfback now, in relief of the injured Dylan Brown, but has also spent time at five-eighth and as the bench utility.

Sandon Smith joined Newcastle this year from the Roosters. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

But he's played them all well and it's added up to the best season of his young career with Smith thriving under the coaching of Justin Holbrook, who he'd worked with as an assistant at the Roosters.

"Justo's been such a rock for me over the past few years, [especially] coming to the club with him when I was unsure about what this year would look like for me," Smith said.

"He constantly reassured me to keep my head down, keep enjoying myself and keep getting better.

"The NRL season is a long season and your moment will come. He kept saying you need to be ready when that moment comes."

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

All halfbacks wear pressure on their shoulders in grand finals and Smith does so with the added spectre of Johns's legacy.

But having already earned one opportunity that has eluded all other Knights halfbacks since Johns, Smith has a chance to win an even greater prize.

Newcastle's most glorious times are inextricably tied with Johns but now Smith and his teammates can write a new legend with victory on Sunday.

It is one which, for the first time in Knights history, can exist beyond Johns and his titanic legacy.

His shadow will always be longest, but now Smith and these Knights have stepped outside it they have the chance to cast one of their own.

World.title: Baird quits as CA chair as Big Bash sell-off fallout continues
World.content:
Mike Baird has sensationally quit as Cricket Australia chair, after his own state association refused to back its representative in the fallout over the privatisation of Big Bash League clubs.

The former NSW premier informed fellow board members on Monday he would not seek re-election at next month's annual general meeting, with David Boon to take over as interim chair.

The decision comes after Baird lost the support of Cricket NSW, with the country's most powerful state unhappy with the decision to allow private investment.

Baird had served as NSW's representative on the board, and approached it recently to confirm it would not support him in the current circumstances.

David Boon will step in as the interim chair. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

He did have the option of moving into an independent role, but AAP was told he did not wish to continue without the support of all states.

Cricket Australia (CA) officials maintain they continue to back the call for the privatisation of clubs, which was confirmed earlier this month.

"After much consideration I have decided to stand down as CA chair and director," Baird said in a statement.

"I am delighted that David Boon has agreed to undertake the interim chair role while we complete the formal chair process, and I will undertake a transition process with David over coming weeks."

Baird had been on the CA board for six years and had served as chair since February 2023.

Alongside Todd Greenberg, he formed one of the most powerful duos in Australian sport.

In a statement on Monday, he again referenced the privatisation of the BBL as a positive move for the sport.

"This year CA will report record revenue, profit, attendance and viewership, and most importantly a 40 per cent increase in participation over the past four years," Baird said.

"With recent decisions on the Big Bash I also believe the long-term sustainability is assured.

"I believe Australian cricket continues to be well lead by the CA board."

Baird's exit comes after Cricket NSW slammed the decision to allow privatisation earlier this month.

"This decision risks leaving cricket in NSW and Australia strategically and financially worse off, with direct consequences for our ability to invest in grassroots cricket," a Cricket NSW statement said.

World.title: Knights star sent to NRL judiciary for tackle that broke Cleary's leg
World.content:
Phoenix Crossland will have to argue his case at the NRL judiciary if he is to have any chance of playing in the grand final after he was cited for the hip drop that broke Nathan Cleary's leg.

The Newcastle hooker was sent off during the Knights' thrilling preliminary final win over the Penrith Panthers on Sunday and the match review committee referred him straight to the judiciary.

Crossland landed on Cleary's lower left leg as the Panthers superstar took on the line in the 36th minute at Stadium Australia and was wrapped up high by Knights back rower Francis Manuleleua.

The injury was immediately visible, and Manuleleua quickly signalled for medical attention.

NRL final swings on Cleary's horror injury Penrith and Newcastle were going hammer and tongs when Nathan Cleary's horror ankle injury turned the NRL preliminary final on its head.

As Cleary was receiving medical attention, including painkillers via the famed green whistle, replays on the big screen prompted Penrith fans and players to urge referee Gerard Sutton to send Crossland off.

Sutton called out Crossland and explained the incident in detail to him and captain Kalyn Ponga.

"Initially he's up high, he makes a definite action to twist," Sutton said.

"[He] comes down on the leg with weight, there's extreme risk of serious injury. You're off."

Crossland will need a miracle to play in the grand final.

Crossland was dejected in the sheds before his team pulled off a stunning 22–14 comeback win to reach its first men's NRL grand final in 25 years, but was greeted on the field after the game, embraced by a number of his teammates.

He seems at long odds to take the field in the grand final against the Roosters on Sunday.

Dragons forward Ryan Couchman was referred straight to the judiciary in round three for a hip drop that ended the season of Parramatta's J'Maine Hopgood.

Couchman was suspended for four games for the tackle that left Hopgood with a torn ACL after a 90-minute hearing.

"Whilst the panel accepted that this did not incorporate any element of intention or recklessness, it took the view that the player's level of culpability was significant, a factor reflected in the serious injury sustained by the ball carrier," judiciary chair Geoff Bellew said.

But earlier this season, Broncos hooker Cory Paix was not penalised or charged for a tackle that left Manly prop Siosiua Taukeiaho with a visible leg injury similar to Cleary's, breaking both the fibular and tibia.

"It's a horrible injury and I'm sure I speak for all Manly fans in wishing Siua a speedy recovery," Manly chief executive Jason King said at the time.

The Sea Eagles reportedly queried the decision not to cite Paix with the NRL.

Tech.title: Volkswagen replaces ID.4 with all-electric Tiguan
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

In a widely expected move, Volkswagen announced Monday that it will replace the recently retired ID.4 crossover with the upcoming ID.Tiguan. The decision is an acknowledgment by the German automaker that its more recognizable nameplates like Tiguan are likely an easier sell with consumers, especially when it comes to EVs.

When it lands in Europe in early 2027, the ID. Tiguan will join the ID.Polo and ID.Cross to round out Volkswagen’s new-and-improved electric lineup. VW also confirmed that the ID.Tiguan will come to the US, where the ID.4 was previously manufactured, “at a later date.” Design details remain under wraps, as the ID.Tiguan is being kept under camouflage for now.

Previous Next











1 / 7

First introduced in 2020, the ID.4 was intended to be VW’s push into mass-market EVs. But rather than go up against big sellers like Tesla’s Model Y, the automaker wanted to compete with high volume gas vehicles like the Toyota RAV4 and Honda CR-V. While it never fully dethroned those rivals, the ID.4 did have some success, selling 950,000 units since 2021. VW says it ranks “among the most successful battery-electric vehicle model series of Volkswagen AG.” VW ended production of the ID.4 at its Chattanooga factory in April 2026.

The electric Tiguan will retain much of what worked about the ID.4, while correcting some of its shortcomings, such as its frustrating lack of physical controls. VW plans on giving the ID.Tiguan the same interior look as its ID.3 NEO and ID.Polo, the latter of which is a surprise sales hit in the EU. That means we can expect buttons for all four windows, rather than just two, as well as physical controls for both the volume and climate settings. VW’s Android Automotive-based operating system will also be featured — which means we’ll probably see a Gemini-powered voice assistant.

Volkswagen didn’t say whether the ID.Tiguan will get the new Rivian-developed software and zonal architecture that is expected to make its debut on the low-cost ID.Every1 hatchback.
